47	/** Each pending protocol request owns and removes its cancellation listener. */
48	export function callSsh<T>(
49		signal: AbortSignal,
50		start: (done: (error: Error | undefined, value: T) => void) => void,
51	): Promise<T> {
52		return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
53			if (signal.aborted) {
54				reject(signal.reason);
55				return;
56			}
57			const abort = () => reject(signal.reason);
58			signal.addEventListener("abort", abort, { once: true });
59			try {
60				start((error, value) => {
61					signal.removeEventListener("abort", abort);
62					if (signal.aborted) {
63						reject(signal.reason);
64						return;
65					}
66					if (error) {
67						reject(
68							error instanceof SshError ? error : new SshError("remote_error"),
69						);
70					}
71					else { resolve(value); }
72				});
73			} catch (error) {
74				signal.removeEventListener("abort", abort);
75				reject(error instanceof SshError ? error : new SshError("remote_error"));
76			}
77		});
78	}
79	
80	/** Own one connection and its deadline. Operations must await all protocol work. */
81	export async function withSshConnection<T>(
82		options: SshConnectionOptions,
83		operation: (scope: {
84			client: Client;
85			signal: AbortSignal;
86			fail: (error: SshError) => void;
87		}) => Promise<T>,
88	): Promise<T> {
89		const input = { ...options, hostKey: Uint8Array.from(options.hostKey) };
90		if (
91			!isIP(input.address) ||
92			!Number.isInteger(input.port) ||
93			input.port < 1 ||
94			input.port > 65_535 ||
95			!input.username ||
96			input.username.includes("\0") ||
97			Buffer.from(input.username, "utf8").toString("utf8") !== input.username ||
98			!input.privateKey ||
99			!input.hostKey.length ||
100			!Number.isSafeInteger(input.timeoutMs) ||
101			input.timeoutMs < 1 ||
102			input.timeoutMs > 60_000
103		) {
104			throw new SshError("invalid_request");
105		}
106		const pin = Buffer.from(input.hostKey);
107		const client = new Client();
108		const lifetime = new AbortController();
109		const signal = lifetime.signal;
110		const cancel = () => lifetime.abort(new SshError("aborted"));
111		input.signal?.addEventListener("abort", cancel, { once: true });
112		if (input.signal?.aborted) { cancel(); }
113		const timer = setTimeout(
114			() => lifetime.abort(new SshError("deadline_exceeded")),
115			input.timeoutMs,
116		);
117		let hostMismatch = false;
118		client.on("error", (error: Error & { level?: string }) => {
119			lifetime.abort(
120				new SshError(
121					hostMismatch
122						? "host_key_mismatch"
123						: error.level === "client-authentication"
124							? "authentication_failed"
125							: "connection_failed",
126				),
127			);
128		});
129		client.on("close", () => lifetime.abort(new SshError("connection_closed")));
130		try {
131			await callSsh<void>(signal, (done) => {
132				client.once("ready", () => done(undefined, undefined));
133				client.connect({
134					host: input.address,
135					port: input.port,
136					username: input.username,
137					privateKey: input.privateKey,
138					readyTimeout: input.timeoutMs,
139					authHandler: ["publickey"],
140					hostVerifier: (key: Buffer) => {
141						const accepted = pin.equals(key);
142						hostMismatch ||= !accepted;
143						return accepted;
144					},
145				});
146			});
147			return await operation({
148				client,
149				signal,
150				fail: (error) => lifetime.abort(error),
151			});
152		} finally {
153			clearTimeout(timer);
154			input.signal?.removeEventListener("abort", cancel);
155			// Destroy also releases remote handles after errors, cancellation, or stalls.
156			client.destroy();
157		}
158	}

/// <reference types="bun" />
import { describe, expect, test } from "bun:test";
import { AuthorizedKeysFile } from "./authorized_keys";

const encode = (text: string) => new TextEncoder().encode(text);
const key = { type: "ssh-ed25519", base64: "AAAA" };
const line = `${key.type} ${key.base64}`;

test("an unchanged plan preserves arbitrary bytes, including malformed lines", () => {
	const bytes = new Uint8Array([
		...encode(`# comment\r\n${line}\n`),
		255,
		0,
		13,
	]);
	const file = new AuthorizedKeysFile(bytes);
	expect(file.plan(bytes, [])).toEqual({ ok: true, candidate: bytes });
});

test("an update selects a duplicate occurrence without changing its neighbors", () => {
	test("stale contents reject even a request that would otherwise succeed", () => {
		const file = new AuthorizedKeysFile(encode(`${line}\n`));
		expect(
			file.plan(encode(`# changed\n${line}\n`), [{ kind: "remove", line: 1 }]),
		).toEqual({ ok: false, reason: "changed" });
	});
	test.each([0, -1, 1.5, Number.NaN, Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY, 4])(
		"invalid line %s",
		(target) => {
			const file = new AuthorizedKeysFile(encode(`${line}\n`));
			expect(
				file.plan(file.bytes(), [{ kind: "remove", line: target }]),
			).toEqual({ ok: false, reason: "invalid_target" });
		},
	);

	).toEqual({ ok: false, reason: "invalid_edit" });
});

test("arbitrary byte sequences round-trip through the public boundary", () => {
	let seed = 20_260_914;
	for (let sample = 0; sample < 256; sample++) {

35	function decodeTurboStream(flat: unknown[]): unknown {
36		const decoded = new Map<number, unknown>();
37		const hydrate = (index: number): unknown => {
38			if (index < 0) { return SpecialValues.get(index); }
39			if (decoded.has(index)) { return decoded.get(index); }
40			const raw = flat[index];
41			if (Array.isArray(raw) && typeof raw[0] !== "string") {
42				const array: unknown[] = [];
43				decoded.set(index, array);
44				for (const item of raw) { array.push(hydrate(item as number)); }
45				return array;
46			}
47			if (raw !== null && typeof raw === "object" && !Array.isArray(raw)) {
48				const object: Record<string, unknown> = {};
49				decoded.set(index, object);
50				for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(raw)) {
51					object[String(flat[Number(key.slice(1))])] = hydrate(value as number);
52				}
53				return object;
54			}
55			return raw;
56		};
57		return hydrate(0);
58	}
59	
60	function findSharedConversation(
61		value: unknown,
62		seen = new Set<unknown>(),
63	): SharedConversation | undefined {
64		if (value === null || typeof value !== "object" || seen.has(value)) {
65			return undefined;
66		}
67		seen.add(value);
68		if (!Array.isArray(value) && "linear_conversation" in value) {
69			return value as SharedConversation;
70		}

111			(match) => JSON.parse(match[1] as string) as string,
112		);
113		const firstLine = chunks.join("").split("\n")[0];
114		if (!firstLine) { throw new Error(`${url} contains no conversation data.`); }
115		const shared = findSharedConversation(
116			decodeTurboStream(JSON.parse(firstLine) as unknown[]),
117		);
118		if (
119			!shared ||
120			typeof shared.title !== "string" ||
121			typeof shared.create_time !== "number" ||
122			!Array.isArray(shared.linear_conversation)
123		) {
124			throw new Error(`${url} has an unexpected conversation format.`);
125		}
126	
127		const turns: Conversation["turns"] = [];
128		for (const node of shared.linear_conversation as { message?: Message }[]) {
129			const role = node.message?.author?.role;
130			if (!node.message || (role !== "user" && role !== "assistant")) { continue; }
131			const text = visibleText(node.message);
132			if (text !== undefined) { turns.push({ role, text }); }
133		}
134	
135		return {
136			title: shared.title,
137			createdAt: new Date(shared.create_time * 1000),

19	function kebabCase(text: string): string {

22			.normalize("NFKD")
23			.replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-")
24			.replace(/^-|-$/g, "");

27	async function importConversation(url: string): Promise<string> {

29		if (!reader) { throw new Error(`No reader supports ${url}.`); }
30		const conversation = await reader.read(url);
31	
32		const date = conversation.createdAt.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
33		const file = join(
34			ResearchDirectory,
35			`${date}-${kebabCase(conversation.title)}.md`,
36		);
37		const header = `# ${conversation.title}\n\nSource: ${url}\n`;
38		const existing = Bun.file(file);
39		if (
40			(await existing.exists()) &&
41			!(await existing.text()).startsWith(header)
42		) {
43			throw new Error(`${file} already exists for another conversation.`);
44		}
45	
46		const turns = conversation.turns.map(({ role, text }) => {
47			const label = role === "user" ? "User" : conversation.assistant;
48			return `---\n\n**${label}**\n\n${text}`;
49		});
50		await Bun.write(file, `${header}\n${turns.join("\n\n")}\n`);
51		return file;
52	}
53

1	# Decisions
2	
3	Only choices that the code does not explain. Rewrite an entry when it changes; git keeps the history.
4	
5	Node runs Next.js; Bun only installs, runs scripts, and tests. Next.js on Bun has open runtime issues.
6	
7	The Content Security Policy is static in next.config.ts. Clerk's generated policy allows scripts from any host unless nonces make every page dynamic.
8	
9	The header and the page fill the large viewport, so the footer is below the fold and every page scrolls. The scrollbar is then always present, and no `scrollbar-gutter` is reserved. A reserved gutter doubles the scrollbar padding that Clerk's modal adds when it locks scrolling, which moves the page sideways.
10	
11	`/` is one page for everyone. Signed-in parts render in the browser inside fixed-size regions, so the page stays static. Each server gets its own protected page.
12	
13	Clerk's prebuilt components do sign-in, sign-up, and the profile inside the app: `<SignIn />` on `/sign-in`, and `<UserButton />`, which opens `<UserProfile />`. They include CAPTCHA, legal consent, the username step after Google sign-up, and reverification, which custom flows must build and maintain. There is no sign-up URL, so `<SignIn />` signs up new users in the same flow and shows no sign-up link. Sign-in is email code or Google, sign-up is public, and usernames are required. Passkeys and MFA need a paid plan.
14	
15	Clerk's components keep its default theme. `--clerk-*` CSS variables refer to the semantic tokens, and Clerk hard-codes round avatars, so element classes make them square. Clerk's primary color is the neutral primary, not the brand color, because Clerk also uses it for text links and selected items.
16	
17	Clerk's component code loads from Clerk's CDN, not from the `@clerk/ui` package. The package pins that code but adds hundreds of dependencies, and clerk-js loads from the CDN anyway.
18	
19	A username is the user's only handle and display name. Clerk stores usernames in lowercase and rejects duplicates that differ only in case.
20	
21	Convex keeps a users table synced from Clerk, because users will see other users when servers are shared, and billing needs a local user. It is keyed by the Clerk user ID, not tokenIdentifier: the deployment trusts one issuer, and Clerk's webhooks and API know only that ID.
22	
23	One function syncs a user from Clerk's current state. The Clerk webhook, the client, and hourly reconciliation call it because webhook delivery is not guaranteed. Incomplete profiles disable app access while retaining existing ownership. Confirmed account deletion removes the user and requests durable cleanup of owned infrastructure.
24	
25	Server ownership is stored on the server, separate from membership permissions. Membership grants reads. Rename, power, member management, SSH management, and deletion have independent permissions; new memberships default to every permission the caller can grant. Delegates can grant only permissions they hold and cannot change or remove a member with broader permissions. Only the owner can transfer ownership, to an existing active member; the previous owner stays with every membership permission. The owner cannot leave; deleting the owner's account requests durable server deletion.
26	
27	Platform permissions do not restrict direct SSH or filesystem access. Membership removal does not remove native SSH authorizations. SSH entries have no required platform-member association. Ownership transfer does not move the operator grant that funded an allocation; capacity stays reserved until that allocation's infrastructure is confirmed absent. Billing transfer is not implemented.
28	
29	SSH files remain authoritative on the server. Explicit file updates compare observed bytes and metadata, coordinate cooperating writes, replace the file, and verify the result. This is not compare-and-swap against independent editors. An uncertain outcome must not trigger a blind retry or rollback. OpenSSH authentication and sessions retain their native behavior.
30	
31	Each allocation has a separate backend management key. Its private key is encrypted with an allocation-bound AES-GCM envelope. Cloud-init receives only its public key and a short-lived host-registration token. The server generates its host key locally; authenticated registration pins the public key without trusting the first SSH response. Duplicate registration can confirm the same key but cannot replace it. Deletion removes stored credentials after infrastructure cleanup. Host-key registration and provider running state do not establish SSH reachability.
32	
33	Server names are permanently claimed by one server identity. A server can rename back to its own historical name; other servers cannot claim it, even after deletion. Every claim stays in serverNames, and an old name resolves to the current one. The name follows DNS label rules because it may become a subdomain. The reserved list in convex/names.ts is deliberately large, and a reserved name is reported as taken.
34	
35	The code and product copy use the same term, name. There is no separate display name.
36	
37	Rate limits exist to protect the system, not to slow people down: an account may have one server or hundreds. Limits are per user; a global limit would let one attacker block everyone. Expected failures such as a taken name are returned instead of thrown, because a thrown error rolls back the rate limit attempt it counted.
38	
39	Provider API pacing is separate from user admission. Cleanup has reserved worker capacity and API allowance. Operator grants authorize billable allocations before billing exists. Capacity is released only after owned provider resources are confirmed absent.
40	
41	The server identity is independent of its allocation backend and provider name. Hetzner resources use an opaque controller identifier, allocation identifier, and resource kind for ownership checks. Human-readable infrastructure names contain no project or deployment name. New allocations resolve the current configuration; existing allocations retain theirs.
42	
43	Convex function module paths do not accept hyphens, so Convex modules use snake_case with a directory-specific filename lint rule.
44	
45	Server pages call `auth.protect()` themselves instead of matching routes in the proxy. Clerk deprecates `createRouteMatcher` in favor of checks at the resource.
46	
47	All corners are sharp. The icon is a sharp square, so the site uses the same shape at every size. The Tailwind theme has no radius tokens.
48	
49	Two typefaces give two voices. Chakra Petch (`font-display`) is for the logo, buttons, labels, and facts such as resource sizes: the places where the product acts or makes a promise. Onest (`font-sans`) is for everything people read, including headings. Chakra Petch alone feels distant to people who have never used a server, and Onest alone does not signal infrastructure. Chakra Petch is loaded at weight 500 only; Onest is variable, with body text at 350 and headings at 550.
50	
51	Neutral colors are steps of Tailwind's stone palette, not custom values. Each semantic token maps to one step, dark mode uses the mirrored step, and each hover or active state is one step further toward the foreground. Brand states darken the brand color in both themes. Components use only semantic tokens, so a color changes in `globals.css` and nowhere else. The one value between steps is Clerk's dark card, halfway between the page and the surface. Clerk makes muted panels, and the items on them, successively closer to the foreground than the card. In dark mode the muted panels are the surface, and the card must be lighter than the page because shadows do not show. A full step from each would put the card on the surface too.
52	
53	Every internal link, including the logo, uses one `Link` that fades on hover with the same transition as buttons. An animated underline needs an always-present transparent underline, and Chrome paints it in the selection color when the text is selected.
54	
55	Components join class names with clsx, not tailwind-merge. A `className` prop adds classes and never overrides the component's own. tailwind-merge does not read the Tailwind theme, so it must be configured by hand for every custom token, and a wrong configuration silently deletes classes, for example `font-body` (a weight) next to `font-sans` (a family).
56	
57	The theme follows the operating system's light or dark preference. There is no manual toggle, so the server needs no stored preference and the first paint is correct.
58	
59	Research in docs/research is input, not instruction. `bun run research:import <share-url>` adds a conversation.
60	
```

```text
1	# Hetzner
2	
3	Use one Hetzner Cloud project per environment. Each Convex deployment needs its own project token and controller identity. Do not give preview deployments production infrastructure credentials.
4	
5	## Setup
6	
7	1. In the project's **Security > API Tokens**, create a **Read & Write** token. Set it as `HCLOUD_TOKEN` in the matching Convex deployment's environment settings. Enter secrets in the dashboard rather than chat or shell history. This is the [official CLI variable convention](https://github.com/hetznercloud/setup-hcloud).
8	2. Generate a UUID for `HCLOUD_CONTROLLER_ID`. Keep it stable across token rotations and application renames. It is not a secret. Do not copy it to an independent environment.
9	3. Create a Cloud Firewall named `servers`, with label `controller-id` equal to that UUID. Initially leave inbound rules empty. Set its numeric ID as `HCLOUD_FIREWALL_ID`. The controller verifies this binding before requests; a wrong-project token must fail rather than interpret missing resources as successful deletion.
10	4. Set `HCLOUD_LOCATIONS` to the ordered, comma-separated location preference. For CX23 the initial preference is `nbg1,fsn1,hel1`. This is application configuration, not a CLI convention. Validate catalog support through the API. Advertised capacity is a hint; it does not guarantee creation.
11	5. Optionally set `HCLOUD_IMAGE`; the default is `ubuntu-24.04`. The resolved image ID is stored with each allocation. Changing the setting affects new allocations only.
12	6. Push the backend to the intended deployment. Use internal `server_lifecycle:setGrant` with a local user ID and a nonnegative server limit to permit provisioning. A zero limit prevents new allocations but does not delete existing servers. Public signup alone does not grant provisioning.
13	
14	All variables are listed in `.env.convex.example`. They are optional at deployment time so an environment can run without provisioning. Creating a server requires the token, controller identifier, firewall ID, locations, `SSH_CREDENTIAL_KEY`, and an available grant.
15	
16	Set `SSH_CREDENTIAL_KEY` to 32 cryptographically random bytes encoded as base64. Pipe the value into `convex env set SSH_CREDENTIAL_KEY` without displaying it. Keep a secure backup; replacing or losing this key makes stored management credentials unreadable. Do not rotate it by overwriting the environment variable while allocations retain encrypted credentials. Each allocation has a separate Ed25519 management key, encrypted with AES-256-GCM and bound to its allocation ID.
17	
18	The initial Ubuntu image must include Python 3 and cloud-init. Allow outbound HTTPS to the deployment's `CONVEX_SITE_URL`. Cloud-init installs the public management key for root, generates the native host keys, and reports the public Ed25519 host key to `/bootstrap/ssh`. A provisioning-delivered token authenticates the report, expires after one hour, and cannot replace an already registered host key. The report retries for a bounded period. Provider running state does not establish that registration or SSH login succeeded. Callback failure must not fall back to trusting a network-observed key. Cloud-init and provider metadata can retain the expired bootstrap token; they never receive the management private key.
19	
20	Do not delete or change the controller label on the shared firewall while it manages allocations. If it must be replaced, reconcile existing allocations with the replacement deliberately; changing the environment variable alone does not rewrite stored allocation bindings. Rotate tokens within the same project. Moving to another project is not token rotation.
21	
22	## Local verification
23	
24	An authenticated Convex CLI can retrieve `HCLOUD_TOKEN` into a private subprocess or shell variable for local API checks. Capture stdout without displaying it, use it only in authorization headers, and discard it. Never print environment values, raw create responses, root passwords, or authorization headers. A second persistent token copy in `.env.local` is unnecessary.
25	
26	Use one disposable CX23 at a time and the agreed approximately EUR 1 total ceiling. Verify the provider VM and both Primary IP IDs are absent after deletion, including after interrupted tests. Stopping a VM does not end its allocation charges. Leave the shared `servers` firewall in place.
27	
28	Guest login is a separate check from provider running state. Backend SSH needs an inbound firewall rule that admits the backend's egress addresses. A host-key callback proves neither inbound reachability nor login. Do not broadly open inbound access just to make a check pass.
29	
30	## Recovery
31	
32	Inspect the allocation's error, operation, resources, and due time. `serverInventory` contains scan progress/errors. Unresolved `serverFindings` require operator review; the controller never destroys unknown resources on that basis.
33	
34	For a corrected configuration or definitive provider rejection, call internal `server_lifecycle:retry` with the allocation ID. For an uncertain create, first search provider inventory and verify that no outstanding request can still create the resource. Only then may an operator supply `confirmedAbsent` (`ipv4`, `ipv6`, or `server`). An empty lookup alone is not sufficient proof. The normal worker automatically adopts matching resources that appear later.
35	
36	Customer app domains, billing credentials, and customer SSH credentials are not required for this lifecycle.
37	
```

Inventory scans inspect one bounded provider page at a time. They wake allocations with uncertain resources and record unrecognized resources in `serverFindings` for operator review. They do not delete unknown resources. Findings are evidence requiring review, not automatic destructive instructions. Missing or changed ownership labels cannot reliably be attributed to this controller.

## API

- `servers.create({ name, requestId })`: requires a provisioning grant; retries reuse the exact request ID and name.
- `servers.rename({ serverId, name })`: permits names previously claimed by the same server.
- `server_lifecycle.status({ serverId })`: member-authorized status, addresses, observation time, and current operation.
- `server_lifecycle.power({ serverId, requestId, command })`: `start`, `stop`, or `forceStop`.
- `servers.remove({ serverId })`: owner-authorized durable deletion.
- Internal `server_lifecycle.setGrant({ userId, limit })`: operator admission control.
- Internal `server_lifecycle.retry({ allocationId, confirmedAbsent? })`: operator recovery. Only confirm absence for an uncertain resource after provider verification.

No frontend changes or committed test framework are included. Disposable checks belong in `tmp/`. Setup is in [Hetzner](setups/hetzner.md).

## Research disposition

  "content": "# Vocabulary\n\nThe words that code, copy, and docs use for one meaning each. AGENTS.md holds the rules; this file holds the words those rules choose. Change it in the same commit as the code, and add a concept before using it. [The session that set this vocabulary](sessions/2026-09-14-claude-vocabulary.md) records the reasoning behind these choices.\n\n## Domain nouns\n\n| Word | Meaning | Not |\n|---|---|---|\n| `user` | A person with a Clerk account, synced to `users` | account (except in copy for the person's own settings) |\n| `server` | What a user owns and shares. Never a thing at a provider | machine, vm, instance |\n| `name` | A server's DNS-safe label. There is no separate display name | slug, display name |\n| `claim` | A permanent association of a name with one server | reservation |\n| `membership` | A user's access to one server, with its permissions | member (for the row) |\n| `member` | The user in a membership | |\n| `owner` | The one user who can transfer or delete ownership | |\n| `permission` | One platform authority on a server, such as `rename` or `power` | role, right |\n| `grant` | Operator-controlled capacity for a user's servers | quota |\n| `allocation` | One real instance of a server: what currently runs it, for its lifetime | provisioning, incarnation |\n| `operation` | A recorded command on a server: `create`, `start`, `stop`, `forceStop`, `delete` | command, job |\n| `backend` | The mechanism that makes an allocation real, such as `hetznerCloud` | version, v1, v2 |\n| `provider` | The company and API that a backend calls, such as Hetzner | vendor |\n| `resource` | One thing that a backend owns at its provider | |\n| `finding` | Evidence about an unknown resource, for operator review | alert |\n| `SSH access` | The backend's management key and the server's pinned host key for one allocation | credential (for the whole row) |\n\n## Verbs\n\n| Words | Meaning |\n|---|---|\n| `create` / `delete` | A record or resource starts or stops existing |\n| `add` / `remove` | An item enters or leaves a collection that continues to exist, such as a member or a key line |\n| `reserve` / `release` | Capacity is held or given back |\n| `start` / `stop` | Power |\n| `request` | Record intent that a worker completes later: `requestPower`, `requestDelete` |\n| `store` | Create or replace a record from another system's current state |\n| `sync` / `reconcile` | Copy one record from another system / compare all records and repair differences |\n| `sweep` | Queue the work that is due |\n| `claim` | Take a lease on work, or permanently associate a name. The file says which |\n| `encrypt` / `decrypt` | Protect or read a stored secret |\n| `register` | Record a fact that another system reports, such as a host key |\n\nJavaScript reserves `delete`, so a registered Convex function that deletes is named `remove`.\n\n## Name prefixes\n\n| Prefix | Returns |\n|---|---|\n| `is`, `has`, `can` | A boolean |\n| `get` | One item, or `null` |\n| `list` | Many items |\n| `find` | An item that a search can miss, or `null` |\n| `require` | A value, or throws |\n| `check` | A failure, or `null` |\n| `set` | Nothing; replaces a value |\n| `to` | A converted value |\n| `render` | Text in an external format |\n| `call` | The response of an external call |\n\n## Status words\n\nA command is a verb (`create`), its progress adds `-ing` (`creating`), and its outcome describes the result (`running`, `stopped`, `deleted`). Operation outcomes are `pending`, `succeeded`, `blocked`, and `superseded`. Whether a resource exists is `pending`, `uncertain`, `present`, or `absent`. All of these are `status`, never `state` or `phase`.\n\n## External words\n\nA provider's words stay in the files named for that provider. Hetzner's `server`, `primary_ip`, and `off` appear only in `convex/allocations/hetzner_cloud/`; everywhere else the words are `allocation`, `ipv4`, `ipv6`, and `stopped`.\n"
}

## Assistant · 2026-09-14T17:06:20.185Z

The whole refactor is in one commit, `d418aa7` ("restructure backend by domain and enforce naming policy"). Everything passes: all checks (Biome, characters, three type-checks), the 58 SSH tests, the production build, and a push to your dev deployment. I left the co-author line off, like the earlier commits.

## What changed

- **Rules and vocabulary:**
  - AGENTS.md has the casing, word, external-system, naming, structure, kind-handling and character rules, plus the extended suppression bullet.
  - `docs/vocabulary.md` has the domain nouns, verb pairs, name prefixes and status words, and links to your session export for the reasoning.
- **Backend layout:**
  - `convex/servers/`, `convex/allocations/` (with `hetzner_cloud/` inside) and `convex/ssh/` each own their tables in their own `schema.ts`.
  - Hetzner's frequently changing worker state lives in its own `hetznerCloudAllocations` table.

You’re right—I answered a naming question when you were asking about **different ways to represent authority**.

There are several fundamentally different models:

| Model | How it works | Main tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| **Roles on a relationship** | Each person has one server role, such as owner or collaborator. The role determines their permissions. | Simple, but exceptions require more roles or overrides. |
| **Direct permission grants** | A person receives specific permissions: connect, manage access, delete, manage billing. No role is required. | Flexible, but inviting someone can become a checklist. |
| **Roles as permission bundles** | Permissions are the foundation; roles are named bundles. Assigning a role grants its permissions. | Simple presets with room for customization, but more machinery. |
| **Ownership separate from access** | The server has an owner. Separately, people receive access to use it. Ownership is not an access role. | Clearly separates responsibility from usage; transferring ownership needs an explicit access decision. |
| **Resource-specific grants** | Access is granted separately to the server, individual apps, billing account, and other resources. | Handles different audiences well, but needs a clear resource hierarchy. |
| **Credential-based authority** | Whoever holds a credential can perform its permitted actions; a product membership is unnecessary. | Good for automation and temporary sharing, but weaker person-based management. |

These models can also combine. In particular, **ownership separate from access** can use either simple access grants or detailed permissions.

For your product, I now think **ownership separate from access is worth preferring over “owner is a special membership.”**

The shape would be:

```text
Server
  owner → Alice

Server access
  Bob
  Charlie

SSH credentials
  Alice → Laptop
  Bob   → Desktop, Automation
```

Alice gets access through ownership. Bob and Charlie get full server access through their grants. Each person can have multiple credentials. Ownership controls transfer, deletion, and managing access; an access grant permits working on the machine.

That produces concrete behavior:

- **Invite Bob:** create an access grant.
- **Remove Bob:** remove his grant and revoke his associated credentials.
- **Transfer to Bob:** change ownership and explicitly decide whether Alice retains access.
- **Share an app with Dana:** create an app grant; Dana does not receive server access.
- **Add delegated billing later:** grant access to the billing resource, rather than inventing a server role that includes billing.

Credentials can still reference the person and server. They remain authorized only while that person owns the server or has an active access grant. We do not need a membership row for the owner.

By comparison, the **permission-bundle model** would look like:

```text
Person → Server role → Permissions
```

That becomes attractive if you expect combinations such as “can invite people but cannot delete” or “can restart but cannot connect.” Users could pick presets while advanced users edit permissions. It is a valid direction, but those combinations are not currently central to your full-access sharing model.

**The important distinction is whether ownership is a responsibility attached to the server, or just the highest role someone can hold.** Neither is universally correct. Your emphasis on a personally owned VPS that can be shared and transferred makes the first interpretation feel more natural.

**Would you prefer explicit server ownership plus separate full-access grants, with no server role system initially?** I recommend **yes** because it captures the two concepts you actually need without anticipating a permissions editor. **y / n**.

**The unresolved issue we were heading toward is how a copied prompt becomes durable, revocable SSH access.** The enrollment flow is clear: short-lived, single-use secret; local key generation; no additional browser approval. What remains is the mechanism behind it.

There are two serious candidates:

| | Installed SSH keys | Short-lived SSH certificates |
|---|---|---|
| After enrollment | The public key is installed on the server | The client receives a signed authorization for its key |
| Everyday use | Ordinary SSH, with no renewal helper | A helper renews authorization automatically |
| Revocation | Requires successfully updating the guest | Stops renewal; existing certificates expire |
| Our service is unavailable | Installed keys continue working | New authentication works until the certificate expires |
| Main complexity | Reliable guest updates and detecting failed updates | Signing infrastructure and seamless client renewal |

**That is the meaningful tradeoff: independence from our service versus revocation without updating every guest.** Neither automatically ends existing SSH sessions.

My current preference is to **prove certificate renewal works transparently with ordinary SSH before selecting certificates**. The research favors them, but it has not demonstrated that their client-side machinery fits your frictionless experience. If renewal introduces fragile wrappers or frequent intervention, installed keys may fit the product better.

Two other unresolved details deserve engineering investigation, rather than more abstract questions:

- **The default login environment.** Separate credentials can use one account, but then agent settings, home directories, and provider logins may collide. Separate accounts reduce those collisions but require more guest setup. We should test actual workflows before choosing.
- **Recovery and server identity.** Enrollment must verify that it reached the correct machine. If the user replaces SSH configuration or reinstalls the OS, there must be a deliberate recovery path that works without functioning SSH.

I would leave raw SSH settings, granular credential restrictions, and desktop-specific convenience buttons out of this decision round. They do not need to block the foundation.

**The one product preference worth settling now: should an outage of our service still allow previously enrolled users to start new SSH sessions indefinitely?** I recommend **no guarantee of indefinite offline access**: accept a bounded validity window if renewal proves seamless, which lets revocation take effect without needing to reach the guest. **y / n** to that recommendation.

So **automatic key removal on membership removal is not an established requirement**. I should not have recommended it as the necessary continuation of the earlier work.

I understand “branches on” to mean: *which inputs actually determine what someone using a key can do?* There is a bounded answer for an authorized-key entry, and a larger answer for their total authority.

**There are three independent relationships:**

```text
Platform member
  └── platform permissions
        └── which API operations they may request

SSH private-key holder
  └── accepted authorization
        ├── target Linux account
        └── SSH authorization options

Linux account
  └── operating-system privileges and accessible resources
```

There is no inherent one-to-one mapping between those relationships. We would introduce such a mapping only for a specific product behavior.

**Within the authorized-key domain, these are the native option families.** This covers the options in the current OpenSSH manual; implementation support must follow the server version.

| What varies | Native options |
|---|---|
| Accepted source | `from` |
| Authorization expiration | `expiry-time` |
| Forced command | `command` |
| TCP forwarding | `restrict`, `port-forwarding`, `no-port-forwarding`, `permitopen`, `permitlisten` |
| Agent forwarding | `agent-forwarding`, `no-agent-forwarding` |
| X11 forwarding | `X11-forwarding`, `no-X11-forwarding` |
| Terminal allocation | `pty`, `no-pty` |
| Login initialization | `environment`, `user-rc`, `no-user-rc` |
| Tunnel device | `tunnel` |
| Hardware-key authentication requirements | `no-touch-required`, `verify-required` |
| Certificate authority and accepted principals | `cert-authority`, `principals` |

`restrict` disables several session facilities; **it does not prohibit command execution**. `command` selects a program, whose behavior still matters. Certificate-authority entries authorize certificates rather than one ordinary key holder. Comments do not grant permissions. [OpenSSH authorized-key format](https://man.openbsd.org/sshd.8#AUTHORIZED_KEYS_FILE_FORMAT)

The **target account** is another input, established by where the authorization is used. Key material identifies which private key can authenticate; selecting another key algorithm does not select another Linux privilege level.

**Those entry-level controls are not the complete definition of effective access.** Two further layers matter:

- **SSH server policy:** authentication requirements, root-login policy, `Match` rules, forced commands, forwarding limits, chroot configuration, and other authorization sources can affect whether authentication succeeds and what session is available. [OpenSSH server configuration](https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config)
- **Operating-system authority:** user and group identities, filesystem permissions, capabilities, and available privilege-elevation mechanisms determine what the resulting processes can access or change. Different account names alone do not establish isolation. [Linux process credentials](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/credentials.7.html), [Linux capabilities](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html)

That gives us the important distinction: **we can completely manage a defined authorization entry without claiming to calculate everything its holder could ultimately do on an arbitrary server.**

For your product choices, the consequences are:

| Choice | What it actually changes |
|---|---|
| Multiple keys for the same account with the same options | Separate authentication material and replacement/removal; generally the same account authority. |
| Different options for different keys | Different SSH entry conditions or session behavior. |
| Different Linux accounts | Different process identities, environments, and potentially permissions. |
| One key authorized for several accounts | The holder may authenticate to each permitted account; a key is not inherently tied to one username. |
| Associating an entry with a platform member | Product metadata and any explicitly chosen lifecycle behavior; no additional Linux restriction by itself. |
| Allowing a member to edit all authorized-key entries | Authority to change other people’s authorizations and potentially grant themselves administrative login. |

**Yes, granular access is possible. But the granularity must survive all the authority the person has.**

For example, an owner can authorize a key for a narrowly configured account and operation. The recipient need not have any Composery membership. That can be useful restricted access.

But if the same recipient also has permission through our API to authorize their own unrestricted key for `root`, the narrower authorization does not restrict their overall access. Similarly, allowing them to remove their own forced-command restriction defeats that restriction.

Conversely, **viewing public-key entries does not provide SSH access**. Reading authorizations, editing authorizations, and possessing a usable private key are distinct abilities. The earlier discussion sometimes blurred them.

Here is the implementation agenda, including the original server scope:

| Work | What must be delivered | Current position |
|---|---|---|
| Server lifecycle | Provision, observe, operate power, delete, and recover failed operations; preserve provider-independent server identity | Existing implementation; SSH must integrate with it |
| Memberships | Separate ownership, permission checklists, delegation rules, ownership transfer, blanket SSH administration permission | Agreed direction; existing role model still needs migration |
| Management access | Trusted bootstrap, backend-to-server connectivity, management credential handling, firewall configuration, recovery after access breaks | Needs an end-to-end proof |
| Authorized keys | Discover supported files/accounts; read entries; add, edit, remove; preserve options and unrelated content; handle conflicts and uncertain outcomes | Local mechanism demonstrated; production module remains |
| Ordinary connection setup | Correct address, username, port, host verification, and local identity configuration | Needs implementation |
| Delighter handoff | Let an authorized person enable a local agent to register its public key without disclosing secrets accidentally | One substantive product tradeoff remains |
| Client integrations | Prompts and editor actions that consume the same authorization and connection operations | Build after the ordinary path works |
| Acceptance checks | First connection, existing key, second device, external edits, interrupted requests, lost key, platform outage, server replacement, unsupported configuration | Define alongside each implemented path |

Billing, snapshots, and authenticated app exposure remain later features from your original scope. They should not force a general server-management framework into this implementation.

Server → Connect
           ├── Use existing local SSH access
           └── Set up access
                 ├── Supply a public key manually
                 └── Use an agent-assisted setup

Authorized-key entry → Connection instructions
                         prefilled with relevant account/key details
```

A public-key entry alone is insufficient to connect: the client needs the corresponding private key or signing agent. The website also cannot infer where that private key lives on each computer. OpenSSH’s local configuration handles that identity selection. [SSH client configuration](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh_config)

It can be available from the server’s Connect flow and from suitable entry details. VS Code Remote-SSH uses ordinary SSH, but also installs and runs its remote server; an authorization restricted to a backup command will not necessarily support it. | 07 | [Application API](research/2026-09-14-design-ssh-api-boundary.md) | Shared operations are useful. Dedicated files, persisted snapshots, timeouts, and grant mechanisms are optional design proposals. |
| 08 | [Agent handoff](research/2026-09-14-ssh-handoff-comparison.md) | Browser approval of an immutable public-key proposal is a candidate. It still needs a product choice and an end-to-end proof. |
| 10 | [Libraries](research/2026-09-14-evaluate-ssh-tools.md) | Transport candidates are useful. Its claim about Ansible losing repeated options is incorrect. |

These answers are not independent votes: they share a supplied product framing. Agreement is not a substitute for source evidence or executable checks.

## Findings that affect implementation

### An entry is an occurrence, not a fingerprint

The same public key can occur more than once with different restrictions. A local authentication experiment succeeded through a later duplicate when an earlier entry's source restriction failed. An edit must identify the intended occurrence within an observed file revision. A fingerprint identifies key material; it cannot identify which occurrence to remove.

Option order also matters: the local server permitted a terminal for `restrict,pty` and denied it for `pty,restrict`. Two `command` clauses rejected authentication. Preserve ordered options and untouched bytes; do not reduce the file to a set of keys or an unordered options object. The parsing order is visible in [OpenSSH 9.6p1 auth-options.c](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_9_6_P1/auth-options.c).

### Configuration inspection has a narrower meaning than live daemon inspection

The experiment changed the configuration file to `AuthorizedKeysFile none`. A new `sshd -T` process reported that value while the already running daemon continued to accept the key under its original configuration. Therefore, output from that command is evidence about the supplied on-disk configuration and context, not proof of every running daemon's loaded settings.

The experiment also showed that `sshd -t` accepted a server configuration whose authorized-key file contained an invalid option. Actual authentication rejected that entry. Configuration validation, entry validation, successful authentication, and permitted session behavior need separate checks.

### Atomic replacement is not conditional replacement

A content hash can detect a changed snapshot. An advisory lock can coordinate Composery operations. Atomic rename prevents readers from seeing a partially replaced file. None of these stops an independent writer from changing the target between a final check and replacement. Linux [rename semantics](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html) do not offer replacement conditional on an expected content hash.

The file-edit report recognizes this limit. Other reports use "CAS" too loosely. We must not promise that arbitrary simultaneous external edits can never be overwritten. Moving to a dedicated file reduces normal contention but changes the product boundary and does not prevent root from writing it.

A separate retry problem remains: bytes can change from A to B and back to A. The original hash then matches again. Our local check reproduced this. A file revision cannot prove that an earlier operation never ran. Mutation identity, uncertain outcomes, and retry policy need their own contract.

### There are real errors in the reports

The library report says Ansible collapses repeated options because it uses a dictionary. In the reviewed version, `keydict` explicitly preserves insertion order and multiple values. However, `parsekeys` indexes entries by the key blob, so duplicate key occurrences are collapsed there. The latter is relevant to a lossless occurrence editor; the former criticism is false. See [ansible.posix 2.2.2 source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ansible-collections/ansible.posix/2.2.2/plugins/modules/authorized_key.py).

The transport report discusses `composery-web`, an existing `ssh2.Client`, and `SSH_PRIVATE_KEY`. Searches of this workspace's backend and package manifest found none of those SSH integration symbols. Its alleged current host-verification bug must not be recorded as a finding about this implementation. Host verification remains a requirement for any transport we add.

The membership report reopens the former owner's permissions and proposes a different owner-deletion policy. Those are product recommendations, not SSH requirements. They do not supersede the prior ownership discussion or the existing account-deletion decision.

## Product boundary carried forward

The working direction is structured management of native authorized-key entries for supported accounts and files, with the server as the source of truth. It does not require a raw text editor, a persistent key inventory, automatic restoration, or key ownership tied to membership.

One blanket SSH administration permission can govern these application operations. It is separate from the user's Linux authority and from other platform permissions. Removing membership does not automatically remove SSH entries. Editing authorizations for a privileged account can confer that account's authority; native key restrictions do not constrain an administrator who can remove those restrictions.

The UI, a future public API, and Delighter must share application operations and authorization checks. Authentication adapters can differ. Reports proposing bearer grants or an extra browser approval do not settle the handoff UX.

The current code and `docs/decisions.md` still describe the older owner/write/read role model. The membership redesign remains implementation work. This audit does not silently migrate that model or replace its decision record.

## Local evidence

The disposable probe in `tmp/ssh-boundary-probe/` passed all 18 checks against extracted Ubuntu package `openssh-server` `1:9.6p1-3ubuntu13.19` in WSL. It used generated fixture keys, explicit host trust, and a loopback daemon. It did not install a system SSH service or modify a customer server.

The checks cover authentication through two configured files, immediate remote write/readback, subsequent-login effects, removal with an existing session, invalid options, option order, duplicate entries, loaded-versus-disk configuration, content revisions, and advisory locking. The script and results remain disposable evidence; production tests must reproduce relevant behavior in their own fixtures.

This is not proof of hosted Convex connectivity, automatic bootstrap trust, crash-safe production writes, complete option support, arbitrary configuration discovery, or the Delighter journey.

## Implementation sequence and gates

| Slice | What can start | Required result before advancing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Native file model | Lossless parsing and pure edit planning for a concrete file observation; finish the missing option matrix alongside it. | Unchanged bytes round-trip exactly; duplicates remain distinct; ordered options retain meaning; malformed or unsupported content is preserved; ambiguous edits fail explicitly. |
| Trusted read | A hosted transport experiment against a disposable server with independently established host trust. | The actual Convex deployment reads the intended file; a wrong host key fails; unavailable access is reported accurately; output and time are bounded. |
| Production mutation | After filesystem and operation contracts are explicit. | Target-path and metadata handling, conflict behavior, cooperating-writer serialization, durable outcomes, lost replies, retries, and readback have executable acceptance checks. The external-writer limitation is explicit. |
| Memberships and adapters | Implement the agreed policy through shared application operations. | Delegation and ownership rules hold; queued work rechecks authority at a defined dispatch boundary; removal is not presented as undoing an already dispatched remote effect. |
| Manual connection | After trusted management and mutation work end to end. | A client-held key can connect using the correct account, endpoint, and host trust; ordinary SSH continues without the platform. |
| Delighter | After the handoff authority channel is chosen. | An unauthenticated agent cannot gain write authority from public prompt text alone; approved setup invokes the same operations as manual setup. |

The first slice is ready to begin. Its interface can use file bytes and explicit edit requests without committing to a transport, database inventory, or general server-state framework. Full structured option support is not ready to be declared complete until the missing inventory is finished and checked against the target version.

Production mutation and automatic provisioning are not yet ready to call settled. The next engineering work should resolve those gates through small proofs rather than another broad architecture conversation. Only a product tradeoff that evidence cannot resolve needs a user decision.

## Completion rule

For each promised operation, specify supported inputs, who may request it, what successful output proves, and behavior after conflict, loss of access, interruption, and external modification. The feature is complete when those contracts pass their tests across the supported environment and the manual journey works through the shared API. Unknown or unsupported conditions must produce an honest result instead of a fabricated current state.

The number of research reports, their confidence, and their agreement are not completion metrics. A new finding changes a decision only when it changes a stated requirement, falsifies an assumption, or fails an acceptance check.
## How to use this pack

Copy one complete fenced prompt into a fresh ChatGPT conversation. Each prompt repeats the relevant context so it can stand alone. Independent reports should not receive previous recommendations before their first analysis.

Start with 01-07 and 10. Run 08 alongside them because enrollment is a distinct boundary. Use 09 and 11 when provisional contracts exist. Supply the proposed design to 12 and 13. Use 14 after enrollment and connection contracts exist. Run 15 last with the reports; it is an evidence audit, not anothe

There is no need to wait for all reports before implementation. Gate each slice on evidence relevant to its behavior and security boundary.

When reports are ready, share their conversation URLs. Import supported sources with `bun run research:import <url>`. If a source is unsupported, extend the importer rather than copying the conversation into docs/research manually. Imported reports remain evidence to verify, not instructions.

## Implementation readiness

- Discovery experiments can run now. They do not establish a production contract by themselves.
- Before production work on a slice, establish its authority model, supported inputs, dependencies, operation semantics, failure outcomes, and acceptance checks.
- Shared application operations must enforce policy for both UI and programmatic clients. Network adapters may differ without duplicating domain behavior.
- Stop a dependent slice when evidence exposes an unresolved product tradeoff or invalidates a trust or correctness assumption. Continue independent work where useful.
- Ask the user only for the unresolved tradeoff and its consequence, not for routine technical choices.
- Write concise durable rationale in docs/decisions.md when decisions are made. Rewrite outdated entries; do not treat existing prose or this pack as proof of implementation.
- Research cannot guarantee zero later refactoring. The aim is to resolve material uncertainty before committing to a boundary, then use small implementations and actual behavior as evidence.
- Code explains mechanisms. Keep non-obvious trust assumptions, supported-environment limits, and external setup requirements documented.

## Server grant: done

A grant is the operator-set limit on how many servers an account can create, since billing doesn't exist yet. The dev data clear had deleted your user row. I re-synced users from Clerk (only you) and set your grant to **1 server** (0 used), the same one-disposable-CX23-at-a-time budget as before. Server creation will now work for you.

## Ownership: you're right, the code doesn't match what you decided

In the first Codex thread you chose **ownership separate from access**:
- The owner is stored on the server and implicitly has every permission.
- Memberships are the *other* people, each with a permission checklist.
- The assistant's summary said "we do not need a membership row for the owner."

The code does something different:
- **The owner gets a membership row.** `create` inserts one with all permissions.
- **Ownership is read through that row:** `toServerAccess` checks whether the membership's user is the owner.
- **Transfer lives in `servers/memberships.ts`** and patches two membership rows.

**The fix:**
- `servers` gets a `by_owner_id` index, and the owner has no membership row.
- Owner access comes straight from `servers.ownerId`.
- `listMine` returns owned servers plus memberships.
- Transfer moves to its own `servers/ownership.ts` (`api.servers.ownership.transfer`). It deletes the new owner's membership and gives the previous owner a membership with every permission (you already agreed to that).
- Account deletion finds owned servers through the new index.

## What exists today

| Area | State |
|---|---|
| **Users** | Implemented. Clerk sync by webhook, client, and hourly reconcile. Incomplete profiles are disabled; deletion cascades to owned servers. |
| **Server lifecycle** (create, rename, status, start/stop/force stop, delete, operator retry, inventory findings) | Implemented. Codex tested it on a real VPS before my refactor. **After the refactor, only the inventory scan was re-checked live.** Create, power and delete need a disposable-VPS run again. |
| **Admission and capacity** | Implemented: grants, name claims, per-user rate limits, Hetzner request pacing, a separate cleanup queue. |
| **Memberships** | Implemented: permission checklist, delegation limited to the delegator's own permissions, owner-only transfer. Ownership is modeled wrong (above). |

## What's missing to reach the state you described

**1. Make V1 servers actually usable**
- **Firewall policy you agreed:** inbound TCP 22, 80, 443, UDP 443 and ICMP; everything else blocked, with exceptions only through support; outbound allowed.
- **End-to-end check on a disposable CX23:** create, host key registration, backend SSH login, power, delete, and cleanup confirmed. This also re-verifies the lifecycle after the refactor.
- **The ownership fix** above.
- **Server UI:** list, create, server page, status, power, rename, delete, members and permissions, ownership transfer.

**2. The SSH feature** (the agreed scope: manage native `authorized_keys` entries, with the server as the source of truth)
- **Public operations behind `manageSsh`:** list entries, add, update, remove. They use the existing read/plan/write path and return explicit results for conflicts and uncertain outcomes.
- **Native validation for new entries.** Key inspection exists; validating authorization options is still open.
- **Which accounts and files are supported.** Today only root is implied.
- **Connection information:** address, user, port, and a `known_hosts` line built from the pinned host key.
- **Recovery when management access breaks.** If a user removes our key, breaks `sshd`, or reinstalls, nothing recovers today, and a pinned host key can never be replaced. Your policy was "the user may break things, but we detect it and tell them," and none of that exists yet.

**3. Your agent setup flow** (copy a prompt, an agent sets up SSH access)
- **Blocked on one product decision:** how authority crosses from your signed-in browser to an agent that isn't signed in.
  - You leaned toward a short-lived link with no approval step.
  - The research proposed approving the agent's exact public key in the browser.
- Both then call the same add-entry operation as the manual flow.

**4. The shared API**
- You asked that UI and programmatic use go through the same operations. Convex functions do that for the UI.
- A public API (tokens, HTTP surface) is not designed yet.

**5. Later features you named, not started**
- **Snapshots:** the design is open, including whether V1 uses Hetzner snapshots.
- **App exposure** behind authentication: research exists.
- **Billing:** grants stand in for it today.
- **Admin and abuse tools:** alerts, suspension, observability.
- **V2 backend:** the layout is ready for it.

**6. Production operations**
- **Separate prod environments:** Clerk instance, Convex deployment, Hetzner project.
- **An `SSH_CREDENTIAL_KEY` rotation path:** overwriting it today makes every stored credential unreadable.
- **A backup plan for Convex data.**
- **Automated tests for lifecycle, membership and SSH writes.** Only the parser has tests; the Codex fault experiments were throwaway scripts.

## How production-ready is the backend?

**The foundations are solid; the product is not production-ready.**

**Solid parts:**
- The lifecycle handles lost responses, uncertain creates, leases, backoff, blocked operations, cleanup priority, and inventory findings.
- Admission, rate limiting and account-deletion cleanup are careful.
- The SSH write path is conservative, with explicit limits.

**What blocks production:**
- Users can't reach their servers: the firewall blocks everything and there's no UI.
- The SSH feature isn't exposed.
- A server with broken management access can't be recovered.
- There are no abuse controls. Codex noted you need these before opening provisioning to untrusted users; grants gate it for now.
- There's no production environment.
- The post-refactor lifecycle hasn't been re-run on a real server.

## Decisions only you can make

1. **Hostname.** New servers probably get Hetzner's internal resource name (`c-<id>-server`) as their hostname, which is what SSH prompts show. Should creation set the hostname from the server name? And should rename change it, or leave it alone as you leaned before?
2. **How the agent setup flow gets authority:** a short-lived link, or approving the agent's exact public key in the browser.
3. **Snapshots,** when that feature comes up. Not needed now.

**Yes—there is a simpler, recognizable feature here: an editor for OpenSSH authorized-key files.** We were adding complexity by treating those files as a projection of a separate credential system in our database.

Your latest explanation supplies a reason to reconsider that model: **the server is authoritative, and Composery is an interface for inspecting and changing it.** Under that model, an entry’s origin need not determine whether it appears.

That is a specific change in premise, rather than another arbitrary reversal.

**The feature’s edge would be “authorized keys,” rather than “all SSH access.”** For a supported account and server configuration, we inspect its configured authorized-key files and show their entries, including entries added through a terminal. Creating, editing, and removing entries changes those files. We preserve native authorization options and unrelated content.

OpenSSH also supports authorization sources outside those files, such as `AuthorizedKeysCommand`. We should identify those sources when detected and explain the boundary, rather than represent them as an empty key list or claim we manage them. Account privileges and global SSH configuration remain separate. [OpenSSH configuration](https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config#AuthorizedKeysFile)

This removes several unnecessary concepts:

- No marker that someone must copy to make a key appear.
- No database record that claims an externally deleted key still exists.
- No automatic restoration of keys merely because we previously created them.
- No requirement to associate every entry with a platform member. We can record who requested an operation without pretending that identifies whoever possesses the private key.

**I ran the experiment in WSL using an isolated OpenSSH 9.6 server.** It used temporary keys and a loopback listener, which I stopped afterward. Twelve checks passed, including:

| Experiment | Result |
|---|---|
| Add an entry to a second configured authorization file | SSH accepted it without any product-specific marker. |
| Apply an edit through SSH and read back the result | The same operation returned the resulting file revision. |
| Change authorization options | The next connection used them without restarting SSH. |
| Remove an authorization externally | New authentication failed; an existing session continued. |
| Validate an invalid authorization option with `sshd -t` | Configuration validation passed, but actual authentication failed. |
| Hold a file lock while another process writes without taking it | The other process could still change the file. |

The last two findings matter: OpenSSH’s configuration check is not a complete authorized-entry validator, and locks cannot exclude arbitrary external editors.

[Experiment and limitations](C:/Users/sloik/Documents/Projects/composery/tmp/ssh-boundary-probe/README.md)

**For the shared mechanism, I recommend immediate operations plus background observation.** They should use the same resource-specific reading code:

```text
Explicit edit
  → authorize and record the request
  → read current server state
  → check the edit's preconditions
  → apply the change
  → read back the result
  → record the observation and operation outcome

Refresh / periodic check
  → read current server state
  → record the observation
```

There is no reason to wait for the next cron after an edit. The remote operation can return its own verification. If the connection fails after writing but before returning, we record an uncertain outcome and investigate it; we do not invent success.

Likewise, **a successful edit remains a successful historical operation even if someone changes the file afterward.** Its completion record and the latest observation answer different questions.

A periodic check covers changes made outside our API and missed work. An explicit refresh provides an on-demand check. Requests trigger immediate work. These are different triggers, not three implementations. We can select the background interval from the acceptable detection delay and measured cost; it should not determine how quickly our own edits appear.

**Observation and enforcement should share plumbing, but enforcement must be a deliberate feature policy.**

| Resource | Authority and behavior |
|---|---|
| Authorized-key files under this proposal | Server contents are authoritative. Observe them and apply explicit edits. |
| A future integration file explicitly maintained by Composery | Product configuration defines its intended contents while that integration is enabled. Check and repair according to that feature’s contract. |
| Initial machine setup | Establish the starting configuration. Do not silently make every initial value a permanent requirement. |

This distinction lets us support future maintained files without turning today’s SSH feature into an enforcement system. “It differs” must not automatically mean “overwrite it.”

**I would keep this inside the backend initially, with a small server-system module—not a separate package or general configuration language.** The useful shared responsibilities are authenticated remote execution, bounded execution time, operation tracking, and observation results. Authorized-key discovery, parsing, editing, and validation belong together in their own module. Future features can reuse the remote machinery without inheriting SSH’s ownership policy.

One limitation remains material: comparing file revisions detects changes before an edit, but comparison and replacement do not create a transaction with arbitrary terminal editors. We must handle detected conflicts and serialize our own writes without claiming stronger guarantees. Linux file locks are advisory. [Linux `flock` documentation](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/flock.2.html)

If the read fails, return “Could not read authorized keys,” with the reason. No database mirror is required. A previously displayed result can remain visibly stale while refreshing, but it must not masquerade as a successful new observation.

The backend would still store things it independently owns:

- Whatever is necessary to authenticate our management connection.
- Operation records where needed to handle retries, interrupted requests, or audit history.

That last item is **a record of a requested action**, not a second source of truth for the file. We should retain only what the operation’s guarantees require.

Similarly, periodic checks are unnecessary merely to support an editor. They become useful if we deliberately offer background monitoring, change notifications, or enforcement. Future features needing those behaviors do not justify making every server feature use them today.
