````text
## Recommendation

Use a **device-flow-inspired pending operation with authenticated browser approval, but do not issue an enrollment bearer token to the agent at all**.

The agent should submit the exact proposed ordinary SSH-authorization operation—server ID, Linux account, structured OpenSSH options, and public key—to Composery. Composery stores that proposal immutably and returns only a **request identifier** plus an approval URL/display code. The authenticated browser reviews and approves that immutable request, and the approval handler invokes the **same ordinary SSH authorization application operation** that the normal UI and authenticated programmatic clients use. The unauthenticated agent only observes status and then tests SSH with its locally held private key.

That gives you the broad compatibility of OAuth device flow without turning the handoff into a second credential system. It works when the browser and agent cannot communicate directly, requires no existing CLI token or helper, and never requires private-key material or enrollment authority to appear in a model-visible prompt.

There is one unavoidable UX/security tradeoff: **a single-click approval link is remotely phishable**. RFC 8628 specifically identifies this problem and recommends showing device/request context and, for complete verification links, having the user verify a code displayed by both sides. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628.html)) For an SSH-administration operation I would keep the additional visual code comparison rather than silently sacrifice that protection.

### Evidence boundary

The deployment-relevant SSH implementation is not OpenBSD-current or OpenSSH Portable master. As of September 14, 2026, Ubuntu 24.04 Noble Updates publishes `openssh-server 1:9.6p1-3ubuntu13.19`; Ubuntu's package is a patched build and should be the final compatibility target. ([Ubuntu Packages](https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble-updates/openssh-server))

| Source | Exact version/date consulted | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Noble | `openssh-server 1:9.6p1-3ubuntu13.19`, package page checked Sept. 14, 2026 | **Deployment authority** for your initial image. ([Ubuntu Packages](https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble-updates/openssh-server)) |
| OpenSSH Portable | tag `V_9_6_P1`, annotated Dec. 18, 2023; commit `8241b9c0529228b4b86d88b1a6076fb9f97e4a99`  | Ubuntu upstream base, before Ubuntu patches. [tag](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/tree/V_9_6_P1?utm_source=chatgpt.com) |
| OpenSSH Portable master | `7fe3b24c922b7af2d743737f7cf37df61ea06426`, Sept. 3, 2026  | Current upstream contrast only; **not** evidence of Noble behavior. |
| OpenBSD-current | `sshd.8,v 1.332`, Sept. 2, 2026  | Upstream OpenBSD-current semantics/documentation; **not** the Ubuntu package. |
| SSH protocol | RFC 4252 / RFC 4253, January 2006 | Protocol-level public-key authentication. RFC 4252 signs the session identifier, username, service, algorithm and public key, so ordinary SSH later proves possession of the private key independently of Composery. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4252/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |

The Portable 9.6 source documents `authorized_keys` entries as optional options followed by key type, encoded public key and comment.  That is consistent with your structured-controls direction, but I would validate all rendering/parsing rules against the exact Noble binary rather than treating Portable master or OpenBSD-current as normative.

## Handoffs on equal terms

| Flow | Minimum user interaction | Prerequisites | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pending request → browser approval → server executes ordinary operation** | Open approval page; compare request/code; click Approve. Authentication only if Clerk session has expired. | Agent needs outbound HTTPS and the public key. Browser can even be on another device. | **Recommended baseline.** No enrollment bearer has to reach the agent. |
| **Already-authenticated Composery client** | Normally none beyond invoking setup. | Agent/client already holds usable Composery authentication with the ordinary `SSH administration` permission. | Best fast path when available; cannot be assumed. |
| **Browser → loopback callback with PKCE** | Agent opens browser; user clicks Approve. | Same machine, ability to bind `127.0.0.1`/`::1`, open external browser and run a native/helper component. | Sound, but more platform machinery than necessary for your baseline. RFC 8252 explicitly supports desktop loopback redirects and requires PKCE for public native clients. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252.html)) |
| **Browser issues a one-time operation bearer; authority delivered separately to agent** | Approve plus delivery/import of the capability. | A secret delivery channel not exposed in the model transcript: helper, credential broker, downloaded protected file, etc. | Feasible but strictly worse here unless another product need requires it. |
| **Manual public-key transfer into existing UI** | User copies/uploads public key, selects/reviews server/account/options and submits. | Only the normal browser UI. | **Strongest simpler alternative.** Lowest protocol complexity, more user work. |

RFC 8628 is especially close to your topology: an unauthenticated/device-side client gets a device code plus a user-facing identifier, the user authenticates separately, and the client polls. It also defines expiration, denial, pending status, polling limits and retry/backoff behavior. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8628/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) I would borrow those state-machine ideas, not copy its token issuance: after browser approval, Composery can simply execute your existing SSH-authorization operation.

### Identifier versus bearer capability

This distinction should be explicit in the protocol.

A `request_id` is an **identifier** if knowing it lets a caller do no more than locate a pending operation or observe non-sensitive state. It must not be accepted as proof that the caller may install a key. An approval URL containing only this identifier remains an identifier: opening it must require an authenticated Clerk session, current platform authorization, and an explicit state-changing approval action.

A token that lets its holder approve, redeem, install, or otherwise exercise the SSH authorization is a **bearer capability**. Whether its value is hidden by the frontend or omitted from console output changes nothing. RFC 6750 defines a bearer by possession and specifically warns against putting bearer tokens into page URLs because URLs leak through history, logs and other infrastructure. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6750/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So a public-looking `https://…/ssh-setup/<request-id>` URL is fine **only because it carries no authority**. “Nobody prints the response” is not an authorization mechanism.

## Recommended baseline semantics

The agent should create or select the SSH key locally and transmit only the public material. The backend creates an immutable proposal whose security-relevant payload is something equivalent to:

`AddSshAuthorization(serverId, linuxAccount, structuredOptions, publicKeyAlgorithm, publicKeyBlob)`

Bind to the immutable platform server ID, not just an IP or hostname. Bind the exact Linux account and the complete structured options set. Bind the exact public-key blob, not merely a human-readable fingerprint; the fingerprint is for review. Canonicalize the structured options before calculating any operation digest.

The browser loads that stored proposal from Composery rather than trusting server/account/key/options copied from query parameters. It checks the signed-in user's current platform permission and visibly presents server, Linux account, key type/fingerprint and effective options. Approval invokes the same ordinary authorization operation used elsewhere.

The request state can stay small: `pending → approved/applying → installed`, with terminal `denied`, `cancelled`, `expired`, or `failed`. Approval and installation should be separately recorded so “approved but remote edit failed” is observable.

This addresses the requested failure cases as follows:

| Issue | Baseline behavior |
|---|---|
| **Request substitution** | Proposal is immutable after creation. Browser fetches it server-side. Changing URL parameters cannot change the operation. A different tuple requires a new request/approval. |
| **Exact binding** | Approval is bound to the canonical server ID + Linux account + option structure + full public-key blob + operation type. |
| **Replay** | Approval is idempotent and request-scoped. A completed/expired/cancelled request cannot create another operation. |
| **Phishing** | Browser shows exact operation and a short code also visible to the initiating agent. RFC 8628 identifies unsolicited device-flow approvals as a remote-phishing risk. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628.html)) |
| **Expiration** | Pending requests expire quickly. An approved-but-not-applied request also gets a bounded execution deadline; after it, fresh approval is required. |
| **Cancellation** | Authenticated browser can cancel before successful application. Stopping the agent merely stops polling; it does not silently revoke an already-installed key. Removing an installed key remains the ordinary remove-authorization operation. |
| **Retries** | Retry only the same durable operation ID and immutable tuple. Network retry must never reopen the authorization decision. |
| **Duplicate execution** | Ordinary authorization operation needs idempotency. If the remote write may have happened before the response was lost, perform a live read and recognize that the exact authorization is already present instead of appending a duplicate. |
| **Failure after approval, before installation** | Preserve `approved/failed` state and allow bounded retry of exactly that operation while approval remains valid. Recheck platform authorization before applying. |
| **Cleanup** | Expire the handoff record and transient codes. Do not turn it into the persistent per-member key inventory your working direction explicitly does not require. |

That last permission recheck matters: if platform membership or SSH-administration permission disappears after browser approval but before installation, installation should fail. That does **not** imply automatic removal of an already-existing native SSH authorization; it only prevents a still-pending platform operation from executing.

### Phishing and the minimum-interaction conflict

You cannot simultaneously get the strongest possession confirmation and a pure “click one link, approve once” experience.

RFC 8628 permits a complete verification URI for convenience, but still says the authorization server should display the user code and ask the user to verify that it matches the code shown on the initiating device; it explicitly gives remote phishing as the reason. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628.html))

For Composery I would make the minimum normal path: **agent opens/copies approval URL → browser shows matching short code and exact SSH authorization → user clicks Approve**. No code typing is necessary when the link identified the request; visual comparison is enough. If you omit the comparison, document remote approval-link phishing as an accepted residual risk.

A loopback+PKCE variant does not eliminate this phishing class. PKCE protects an intercepted authorization code from being redeemed by a different client; it does not stop a user from deliberately approving an attacker's request. RFC 8252 is explicit that PKCE addresses code interception. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252.html))

## Why I would not deliver enrollment authority to the agent

A one-time, narrowly scoped capability can be made technically respectable: bind it to the exact operation digest and audience, give it a very short lifetime, make it one-use, consume it atomically only after creating a durable operation record, and never put it in a URL. Those measures follow standard bearer-token threat mitigations around scoping, expiry and replay. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6750/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

But it buys nothing necessary in the baseline. The browser can exercise its authenticated authority directly. Delivering a bearer to the agent creates another theft/replay/cleanup problem purely to hand authority back across the boundary you already crossed.

There is also an important distinction in your secret requirement: **preventing accidental model disclosure is achievable; isolating a secret from an agent with arbitrary filesystem/process access is not.** A secret stored in a `0600` file, environment variable, keychain export or hidden pipe can avoid appearing in prompts, shell history and tool output. But if the agent itself may arbitrarily read the same filesystem/process context, that is not a security boundary against that agent. Actual isolation requires another principal or mechanism—a credential broker/helper, OS-protected service, hardware key, sandbox boundary, etc. The recommended baseline avoids needing such a boundary because

======
## Recommendation

Use a **downloaded, inert enrollment file whose contents are exactly one HTTP authorization header**, and have the local agent invoke the platform's existing `ssh-keygen` plus `curl`, passing only filenames on the command line.

The file should contain:

```text
Authorization: Bearer <opaque-short-lived-token>
```

Not JSON, not a shell script, not a helper executable, and preferably not a full curl config file.

This is the smallest design I would ship. It requires no installed app, extension, protocol handler, localhost daemon, fixed download directory, clipboard integration, or second browser authorization. It also gives you a straightforward way to keep the bearer value out of prompts, argv/process listings, normal command output, and normal shell tracing: curl itself reads the header file. curl explicitly supports `-H @filename`, and its documentation recommends retrieving sensitive values from files rather than putting them on the command line. ([cURL](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html))

## Unavoidable user interactions

In the normal successful case I think there are only **two** fundamental interactions: the user clicks **Download enrollment file**, and the user tells the local agent where that file was saved. A browser configured to ask for every download adds its own save-location selection; that is browser policy, not part of your authorization protocol. Chrome explicitly documents both automatic default-location saving and the ask-each-time mode. ([Google Help](https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/9575

There is no security requirement for a second “Approve this agent” browser step here. The authenticated download action can itself authorize creation of the narrowly scoped bearer token. Avoiding model visibility does not imply a device-code ceremony.

## Experiments I would run before freezing the design

1. **Browser handoff matrix.** Put a sentinel—not a real credential—in a staging attachment returned by the exact authenticated `POST`. Test current Chrome/Edge, Firefox, and Safari with both normal download settings and “ask where to save.” Record whether the page remains usable, whether a save dialog appears, how duplicate filenames are handled, and whether your custom `.enroll`/octet-stream file is ever automatically opened. The expected invariant is only “a local file exists and it

2. **Agent secret-visibility test.** Put `Authorization: Bearer SENTINEL_UNIQUE_123...` in a file, then have every supported coding-agent runtime execute the real curl shape against a staging endpoint. While curl is blocked for several seconds, inspect its process command line (`ps` on macOS/Linux; `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` on Windows), then search the agent transcript/tool logs and your normal shell logs for the sentinel. It should exist only in the source file and the staging server's de

3. **Tool availability and quoting.** On the Windows images, macOS versions, and representative Linux distros you actually support, probe `ssh-keygen` and `curl`; record curl versions and verify `-H @file`. Test the exact no-passphrase `ssh-keygen` invocation under Windows PowerShell, PowerShell 7, and whatever shell abstraction the agent uses. Treat this test matrix—not an OS-family assumption—as the compatibility contract.

4. **Lost-response/idempotency test.** Instrument staging so the server commits the public key and deliberately closes the connection before returning its response. Rerun the exact same request: it must report the existing success without adding another key. Fire two copies concurrently: one state transition only. Then reuse the same token with a different public key: it must fail. Finally, verify that success deletes only the enrollment file, while an ambiguous network failure preserves the fil

### Bottom line

The downloaded file survives the challenge against the “simpler” alternatives because it exploits something all three desktop OSes and all browsers already know how to do: **save opaque bytes to a user-selected filesystem location**. The local side then exploits a narrowly constrained curl feature specifically intended to read headers from a file.

# Hetzner Cloud Rescue System Summary

**What It Is:**
The Hetzner rescue system allows administrators to boot a server over the network using a temporary OS, enabling troubleshooting and recovery tasks when the primary system is inaccessible.

**Access Credentials:**
Users receive authentication through one of two methods: "Once you select _Enable rescue_, you will be given a root password directly on your Hetzner Console" if no SSH key is configured, or they can "select an SSH key that will be used to connect to the server" beforehand.

**Capabilities:**
While the documentation doesn't explicitly detail all recovery functions, it confirms that "Once the server booted over the network of the rescue system, rescue will remain active until you restart the server again," implying users can perform administrative tasks during this window.

**Activation:**
The documentation describes enabling rescue via the Hetzner Console with two methods: "Enable rescue" (manual restart required) or "Enable rescue & power cycle" (automatic restart). The document does not mention API-based activation.

**Duration & Deactivation:**
"Rescue remains activated for 60 minutes" after enabling, automatically deactivating upon restart beyond that window. Users can manually deactivate it through the console within the 60-minute window.

**Lost SSH Access:**
The documentation does not address recovery procedures for lost SSH key access or password recovery mechanisms.

# Hetzner Cloud FAQ: SSH Keys, Access, and OS Restrictions

## SSH Keys and Server Creation

SSH keys can only be added during server creation: "When creating a new server, you can select an SSH key that will automatically be added to the server."

Hetzner cannot retroactively add SSH keys to existing servers: "Unfortunately, we cannot add SSH keys to existing servers. On those, you will have to add your SSH key manually."

## Lost Access and Password Reset

For root password recovery, users can utilize the rescue system: "In the upper navigation bar click on `Rescue`. At the bottom of the page you will find a button called 'Reset Root Password'."

The web console provides emergency access: "The VNC console is provided as a tool for emergency situations, such as installing an operating system or resetting a password."

## Web Console (VNC)

The console functions as a virtual interface: "VNC consoles allow you to connect to a server as if you were sitting directly in front of the device with keyboard and mouse."

## Rebuild and Rescue

Rebuilding resets the server to factory state: "In order to reset the server to its delivery state, please select the server and then `Rebuild`. Next, select and restore the desired OS."

The rescue system allows repairs without affecting data: "The environment starts using network boot (PXE) and runs in the memory of the server, without touching the drives or your data on them."

## OS Restrictions

Hetzner explicitly restricts Windows 10/11: "We do not and cannot provide Windows 10/11 ISO files for you."

They also prohibit end-of-life operating systems: "we don't provide operating systems that have reached their end of life."

The character check now keeps the literal characters in its table and replaces dashes too. Both are committed as `2ab34be`. The rest of this answer draws on both Codex threads, the research they cited, and Hetzner's own docs.

## Done in this turn

- **Firewall policy applied** to the shared Hetzner firewall: inbound TCP 22, 80 and 443, UDP 443, and ICMP from anywhere. There are no outbound rules, so outbound stays open. `docs/setups/hetzner-cloud.md` now lists the rules.
- **Full test on one disposable CX23**, on the refactored code:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Create | IPv4, IPv6 and the machine all present; host key registered; grant used 1/1 |
| Backend SSH login | Logged in as root through the pinned host key |
| Graceful stop | `stopped` after 47 s (Hetzner's `off`, translated) |
| Start | `running` after 31 s |
| Delete | Resources absent; server, memberships and SSH access rows deleted; grant back to 0; Hetzner lists 0 servers and 0 IPs |

- **Is anything else blocking backend SSH login?** No. The empty firewall was the only blocker, and login works now.
- **Hostname:** the test showed the machine's hostname is `c-<allocationId>-server`, Hetzner's internal resource name.
- **Character script:** the table is now the literal characters, inside one `characters-ignore` range, so the list is easy to edit.
  - Dashes are now simply replaced with `-`, so there's one kind of finding and no "reword this" case. The AGENTS.md rule says the same.

## Your questions

**"Incomplete profiles are disabled."** This is not backfilling.
- Our `users` table requires an email and a username, because the username is how people get added to a server.
- Clerk normally enforces both at sign-up, but a Clerk user can still lack them. That happens when a user is created from the Clerk dashboard or Backend API, or when a field becomes required after users already exist.
- The original sync deleted such a user's row. Deleting a row also deletes the servers they own.
- The first Codex thread changed that: a Clerk settings mistake must not delete infrastructure, so the account is blocked from the app until the fields exist.
- It's a small guard, and I'd keep it.

**Grants.**
- **Where it came from:** in the first thread, the agent added "an operator-only provisioning grant, so signing up alone cannot create billable VMs." A research prompt then framed it as "operator-controlled provisioning grants," and the research recommended a grant (capacity a user is allowed) plus claiming a slot from it atomically. Billing later becomes another source of that same allowance.
- **What it is:** one row per user with `limit` and `used`. A slot stays used until Hetzner confirms the machine and IPs are gone.
- **Why it matters now:** sign-up is public, so without it anyone could create servers on your Hetzner bill. The limit of 1 is simply a dev budget guard.
- **After billing:** subscriptions set the capacity. A per-account cap is still useful, because Hetzner itself limits servers per project.
- **The name** is research jargon; see decision 3.

**"Operator."** Yes, the code, docs and comments say "operator." It means a person on your team with Convex CLI or dashboard access. That surface is exactly two internal functions: `allocations/grants:set` and `allocations/hetzner_cloud/worker_state:retry`. It will clash with "operator" in V2 (for example, a Kubernetes operator), so I'd rename it to **admin**.

**Name claims** apply to server names only. Usernames are Clerk's; we only copy them.

**Programmatic abuse controls today:**

| Control | Scope |
|---|---|
| Grant (server count) | Per user |
| Server name checks: 200 at once, 1000/hour; new claims: 200 at once, 1000/day | Per user |
| Username lookups when adding members: 50 at once, 200/hour | Per user |
| Server changes (power, delete, permissions, removals, transfer): 200 at once, 1000/hour | Per user |
| Account sync from the client: 3 at once, 10/hour | Per user |
| Hetzner API pacing, with a separate cleanup allowance | Deployment-wide |
| One pending operation per server, request IDs for retries, name format and reserved names | Per request |

The limits are about right, with three gaps:
- **`/bootstrap/ssh` has no rate limit.** Guessing the token is impossible, but a flood still starts Node actions, which cost money.
- **List page sizes come from the client** and aren't clamped.
- **No per-server member cap** (only the lookup limit).

**Public API vs Convex functions.**
- **Convex functions already are an API.** Every public query and mutation can be called over HTTP or WebSocket, with a token from the auth provider (Clerk today). The pieces that make an action work are already in place.
- **`http.ts` only holds the Clerk webhook and `/bootstrap/ssh`.** There's no separate HTTP service.
- **A public API later needs:**
  - API tokens that `requireUser` accepts (Convex supports custom JWT providers)
  - either treating the function paths as a stable, versioned contract, or a versioned HTTP layer over the same helpers
  - per-token rate limits
  - docs
  - machine-readable error codes: failures carry only a human `message` today
- **The error codes should be added now.** The UI needs them too, and they're the only item that would otherwise force a breaking change later.

## SSH: what was actually settled

Your question was whether this is "only our credentials," "a full key manager," or "a full manager for our keys only." It moved over time:
1. **First thread:** it started as our own credentials, with prompt setup and revocation. You then pushed toward "align to SSH, don't promise revocation, expose standard SSH actions."
2. **Second thread, 03:36:** the premise changed to "the server is the source of truth." It became **structured management of the native `authorized_keys` entries**: all entries, including ones added from a terminal, with no markers and no database copy (03:39).
3. **Second thread, 03:54, settled:**
   - keys don't belong to members, and removing a member doesn't remove keys
   - one blanket SSH permission
   - every native option is available, because you wanted "the entire surface of what you can do for a credential"
   - live reads and verified writes

So **the model is a live manager for all native SSH keys, not just ours.** "Only our credentials" was rejected: it needs records to keep in sync and pushes users into hacks to make their own keys show up. "Only our keys" was never chosen, and it would combine the worst of both. The model you chose is also the easiest to recover, because there's nothing to reconcile.

**Built, but not exposed to users:**
- the lossless parser and editor, covering every option family
- the bounded file read and conflict-aware write
- removal of selected entries
- `ssh-keygen` key inspection
- management access and host key pinning
- and now proven login

Nothing calls these, and the `manageSsh` permission is never checked.

**SSH decisions still open:**

| # | Decision | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Which accounts and files | Root only, or every login account. Files can come from `sshd -T -C user=<account>` instead of hardcoded paths, matching your "use defaults, stay dynamic" preference. |
| S2 | Option validation | OpenSSH has no validator for entry options: `sshd -t` passes entries that authentication then rejects. We'd validate per the OpenSSH 9.6 source rules, and show unknown content as-is. |
| S3 | Presentation | Simple default (paste a public key, pick the account), with every native option under "Advanced". |
| S4 | Our management key | It appears in root's list. Show it labeled and warn before removal, or refuse removal from our UI. |
| S5 | Host key changes | See recovery below. |
| S6 | Connection details | Host, user, port, and a `known_hosts` line from the pinned key. Engineering only. |

## Agent setup flow

**Server-level, not per key.** In the model you chose there's no "our credential" object. "Set up access for an agent" creates a new entry, labeled by its comment. "Open in VS Code" uses a key the computer already has. So this comes after the add-entry operation exists, and it calls that same operation.

**The real options.** If the user does nothing after the agent starts, whatever authorizes the agent must travel inside the prompt, so it is a bearer secret. Any zero-click design reduces to that.

| Option | Extra clicks | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Short-lived, single-use token in the prompt**, sent in the request body, not the URL | 0 | Anyone who reads the prompt before the agent uses it can add their own key first, and that key is root. The copies aren't under your control: the AI provider's logs, synced chat history, shared conversations, clipboard managers, screen sharing. Network sniffing isn't the concern; HTTPS covers that. |
| **B. Approve in the browser** (like `gh auth login`): the agent submits its public key and gets a code, and you click Approve on a page showing the fingerprint and code | 1 | Nothing secret is in the prompt. Remaining risk: someone phishes you into approving their request. The research recommended this. |
| C. Paste the agent's public key into the UI | Several | Simplest mechanism, most friction. |

About your intuition: copying while signed in does prove who you are. The second step isn't a second identity check. It keeps root authority in your browser instead of sending it through systems you don't control, and that holds even over a short window. **I'd recommend B.** A is defensible if you accept that residual risk.

## Permissions, from first principles

A permission should exist only for an action our backend performs. What happens inside the machine is governed by Linux and SSH, not by us.

| Group | Permission | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| Server | Rename | Name (and hostname, see below) |
| | Power | Start, stop, force stop |
| | Delete server | |
| People | Add members | Only with permissions you hold |
| | Remove members | Only members whose permissions you hold |
| | Change permissions | Same ceiling |
| Access | SSH keys | List, add, edit, remove; the agent setup flow requires it |
| Later | Snapshots: create, restore, delete; Rebuild; Apps | Added with each feature |
| Owner only | Transfer ownership | |
| Every member | See status, addresses, members, connection details | Implicit |

**Why SSH keys is one permission:** adding a key for root already means root. Root can then edit every other key and remove our management key, so splitting "add" from "remove" would promise a restriction that doesn't exist.

**Edge cases and how they resolve:**
- **Escalation:** you can't grant, edit or remove authority beyond your own (built).
- **Leaving:** always allowed. The owner must transfer or delete first.
- **Owner:** is not a membership (fix pending).
- **Revoked mid-operation:** a queued power operation authorized at request time still completes. Decide whether that's acceptable, or whether authority is rechecked when the worker picks it up.
- **SSH keys equals root:** whoever holds it can lock others out or break our management access. We document it; the platform can't prevent it.
- **Delete is grantable,** so a member can delete the owner's server (you chose this).
- **Owner account deleted:** their servers are deleted even when other members remain (decided).
- **Removing a member** doesn't remove their SSH keys (decided). The UI should say so.

## Broken management access and recovery

Management access means three things: our key in root's `authorized_keys`, a pinned host key, and SSH reachable. Only SSH-key features and hostname changes use it. Power, delete and snapshots go through Hetzner's API and are unaffected.

**Hetzner's own model:** SSH keys are added only at creation, and after that the user is responsible. Recovery tools are the rescue system (boots a temporary Linux in memory without touching the disks), a VNC console, root password reset, rebuild (wipes the server), and backups or snapshots.

| Scenario | Minimal response |
|---|---|
| User removed our key, disabled root key login, changed the port, or stopped `sshd` | SSH features show "Composery can't sign in" plus the exact line to add back. The public key isn't secret. No extra machinery. |
| Host key changed (regenerated, or OS reinstalled from inside) | We must not trust it silently. Options: re-trust only through our Rebuild action (fresh bootstrap), or a registration command the user runs on the server. Decision. |
| User fully locked out | Offer Hetzner-level actions: **restore snapshot** and **rebuild**; both also re-establish management access. Optionally rescue mode for advanced users. The console is heavy. |
| OS replaced (no OpenSSH, Python or Linux) | SSH features report "unavailable". Power, delete and snapshots still work. No OS enforcement. |

**Snapshots:** your "headless snapshots" is exactly what Hetzner snapshots are: disk images the provider takes from outside the machine. They live at project level, survive the server's deletion, and can create new servers. V2 can do the same at the hypervisor. That fits your thinking; the details can wait.

## Hostname options

| Option | Behavior |
|---|---|
| a | Set from the server name at creation only |
| **b** | Set at creation. On rename, update it only if it still equals the old name; otherwise leave it and say so |
| c | Rename offers an "also change hostname" checkbox |

For b and c: the hostname change needs management access, so the rename itself always succeeds and the hostname part can report that it was skipped. I'd recommend **b**. Simple users never see it, and a hostname they changed is never overwritten.

## Production readiness, by your definition

Your bar is that the existing surface holds up in production, not that future features exist. That bar isn't met yet. These are the gaps in what already exists:
1. **Ownership is modeled as a membership.**
2. **Failures have no machine-readable codes.**
3. **`/bootstrap/ssh` has no rate limit, and list page sizes aren't clamped.**
4. **`SSH_CREDENTIAL_KEY` can't be rotated.** Overwriting it makes every stored management key unreadable.
5. **Management-access and host-key failures aren't surfaced as a server state.**
6. **Revoked-while-queued semantics aren't settled.**
7. **"Operator" and "grant" wording.**

## Decisions for you

1. **Permission checklist:** the table above. In particular, split member management into three permissions, and rename `manageSsh` to "SSH keys".
2. **A queued operation after its requester's permission is revoked:** complete it, or recheck authority when the worker picks it up.
3. **Grants:** keep the concept with a plainer name (for example, `serverLimits`), or keep "grant" as the future billing allowance.
4. **Incomplete Clerk profiles:** keep blocking such accounts (recommended).
5. **SSH:** S1 accounts and files, S4 handling of our management key, S5 host key changes.
6. **Agent setup:** A (token in the prompt) or B (one-click approval).
7. **Recovery actions:** rebuild and snapshot restore, with or without rescue mode.
8. **Hostname:** a, b or c.

**Needs no decision; I can do it next:**
- the ownership fix
- machine-readable failure codes
- the `/bootstrap/ssh` rate limit and page-size clamps
- renaming "operator" to "admin"
- updating the docs to match

Should we make 'best-effort' like an explicit principle/instruction/guidance/documentation when dealing with on-VPS content like this, where user really has almost full freedom to do whatever, but we may force certain things, or dynamically attempt to detect certain things? And should we even 'force' anything, or simply do it in a best-effort manner and give up if system state doesn't allow us to, then visibly degrade? Surely there has to be a way to not require an ssh credential on the system and for the user to not nuke it, for us to be able to do things with the system, right? I mean we somehow put the credential on there in the first place. Is there something other than ssh, or something provided by hetzner? Would we want to use this, or not really, considering that V2 will have a different architecture? Or is the case here the same as for snapshots, where we need this external authority that we otherwise just can't get, and that's going to be present both now, in V1, at the hetzner cloud -> each vps, but also later, in V2, at the dedicated/bare metal server -> multiple vpss? Any grounding needed here, or decisions/forks to inspect?

As for the agent setup flow, I feel like designing it now along with everything else may be premature and might result in hasty decisions or slop-code. Maybe let's revisit. Again, like I already said, documentation would have to be properly annealed right about now, regardless. But also just a quick word on this:

"Set up access for an agent"

I feel liike it shouldn't always create a new entry though. But maybe, maybe. Depending on how we do it. I could picture us implementing it in such a way where it would be able to be used for existing keys as well. And after all, if we are to make further clarifications, since they're easy with the way you pose questions, as for what you said in terms of the options, I think the credential being in the AI provider's logs should not be an issue, if we just design it in a way where the agent will know where the actual sensitive bit is, and is able to have a choice on what to ingest, instead of just printing out the credential raw, if that makes sense. Pretty much every agent is smart enough to know how to deal with credentials, and tries to avoid ingesting them already. If we add some instructions and design it in a proper way, a good-faith agent will not ingest it. 'Anyone who reads the prompt before the agent uses it can add their own key first, and that key is root.' isn't a failure mode - it's the entire point of the feature. Just because it's technically a 'prompt' doesn't mean it's not sensitive. It also doesn't mean that it has no potential for depth, when constructed in a way to be used with agents as of september 2026, where it doesn't have to be sensitive-by-default, which is what I'm going for, basically, progressive disclosure. We could still explore a download file shape, but I'm not sure how good that would really be. Agents pretty much all have python, or terminal, to execute different things, as you know, since you're one such agent that is one of the most used ones, so you can design in a way in which you would genuienly personally believe that it's the easiest, fastest, and most frictionless for you to work with. The only thing is that perhaps when a prompt or this sort of enrollment potential entity is already created, the credential may be degraded or polluted or non-fresh or whatever, or at the very least the user would know which credential the thing they copied is tied to, so that they can properly revoke it before someone gets root.   Why SSH keys is one permission: adding a key for root already means root. Root can then edit every other key and remove

See docs/api.md.\n */\nexport const errorCodes = [\n\t\"already_member\",\n\t\"configuration_invalid\",\n\t\"creation_disabled\",\n\t\"membership_limit_reached\",\n\t\"membership_not_found\",\n\t\"name_invalid\",\n\t\"name_taken\",\n\t\"operation_pending\",\n\t\"owner_required\",\n\t\"ownership_target_invalid\",\n\t\"permission_ceiling\",\n\t\"permission_denied\",\n\t\"power_unavailable\",\n\t\"rate_limited\",\n\t\"request_id_conflict\",\n\t\"request_id_invalid\",\n\t\"server_busy\",\n\t\"server_deleted\",\n\t\"server_deleting\",\n\t\"server_limit_reached\",\n\t\"server_not_found\",\n\t\"unauthenticated\",\n\t\"user_disabled\",\n\t\"user_not_found\",\n] as const;\n\nexport type ErrorCode = (typeof errorCodes)[number];\n\nconst errorCode = v.union(...errorCodes.map((code) => v.literal(code)));\n\n/**\n * An expected failure that a function returns. A function returns a failure\n * instead of throwing when it has already counted a rate limit attempt, because\n * a thrown error rolls the attempt back.\n */\nexport const failure = v.object({\n\tok: v.literal(false),\n\tcode: errorCode,\n\tfield: v.union(v.string(), v.null()),\n\tmessage: v.string(),\n});\n\nexport type Failure = Infer<typeof failure>;\n\nexport function fail(\n\tcode: ErrorCode,\n\tmessage: string,\n\tfield: string | null = null,\n): Failure {\n\treturn { ok: false, code, field, message };\n}\n\n/** A thrown error has the same code and message as a returned failure. */\nexport function toConvexError(code: ErrorCode, message: string) {\n\treturn new ConvexError({ code, message });\n}\n"

```text
} as const satisfies Record<string, RateLimitConfig>;

export const rateLimiter = new RateLimiter(components.rateLimiter, rateLimits);

type RateLimitName = keyof typeof rateLimits;

function toTooManyAttemptsMessage(retryAfterMs: number) {
	const minutes = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(retryAfterMs / MINUTE));
	return `Too many attempts. Try again in ${minutes} ${minutes === 1 ? "minute" : "minutes"}.`;
}

/** Counts one attempt. Return the failure, so that the counted attempt stays counted. */
export async function checkRateLimit(
	ctx: RunMutationCtx,
	name: RateLimitName,
	key: string,
): Promise<Failure | null> {
	const rateLimit = await rateLimiter.limit(ctx, name, { key });
	return rateLimit.ok
		? null
		: fail(null, toTooManyAttemptsMessage(rateLimit.retryAfter));
}

/** Counts one attempt and throws when the limit is reached. A refused attempt is not counted. */
export async function requireRateLimit(
	ctx: RunMutationCtx,
	name: RateLimitName,
	key: string,
) {
	const rateLimitFailure = await checkRateLimit(ctx, name, key);
	if (rateLimitFailure !== null) {
		throw new ConvexError({ message: rateLimitFailure.message });
	}
}
```

export const registerHostKey = internalAction({
	args: {
		allocationId: v.id("serverAllocations"),
		token: v.string(),
		hostKey: v.string(),
	},
	returns: v.boolean(),
	handler: async (ctx, { allocationId, token, hostKey }): Promise<boolean> => {
		if (
			!bootstrapTokenPattern.test(token) ||
			hostKey.length > maxHostKeyLength
		) {
			return false;
		}
		const parsed = utils.parseKey(hostKey);
		if (
			parsed instanceof Error ||
			Array.isArray(parsed) ||
			parsed.type !== hostKeyType ||
			parsed.isPrivateKey()
		) {
			return false;
		}
		const canonical = `${hostKeyType} ${parsed.getPublicSSH().toString("base64")}`;
		if (canonical !== hostKey) {
			return false;
		}
		return await ctx.runMutation(internal.ssh.bootstrap_state.registerHostKey, {
			allocationId,
			bootstrapTokenDigest: toTokenDigest(token),
			hostKey: canonical,
		});
	},
});

27:Platform permissions do not restrict direct SSH or filesystem access. Membership removal does not remove native SSH authorizations. SSH entries have no required platform-member association. Ownership transfer does not move the operator grant that funded an allocation; capacity stays reserved until that allocation's infrastructure is confirmed absent. Billing transfer is not implemented.
28:
29:SSH files remain authoritative on the server. Explicit file updates compare observed bytes and metadata, coordinate cooperating writes, replace the file, and verify the result. This is not compare-and-swap against independent editors. An uncertain outcome must not trigger a blind retry or rollback. OpenSSH authentication and sessions retain their native behavior.
30:
31:Each allocation has a separate backend management key. Its private key is encrypted with an allocation-bound AES-GCM envelope. 32:
33:Server names are permanently claimed by one server identity. A server can rename back to its own historical name; other servers cannot claim it, even after deletion. Every claim stays in serverNames, and an old name resolves to the current one. The name follows DNS label rules because it may become a subdomain. The reserved list in convex/servers/reserved_names.ts is deliberately large, and a r
34:
35:Rate limits exist to protect the system, not to slow people down: an account may have one server or hundreds. Limits are per user; a global limit would let one attacker block everyone. Expected failures such as a taken name are returned instead of thrown, because a thrown error rolls back the rate limit attempt it counted.
36:
37:Provider API pacing is separate from user admission. Cleanup has reserved worker capacity and API allowance. Operator grants authorize billable allocations before billing exists. Capacity is released only after owned provider resources are confirmed absent.

Hetzner resources use an opaque controller identifier, allocation identifier, and resource kind for ownership checks. Human-readable infrastructure names contain no project or deployment name. New allocations resolve the current configuration; existing allocations retain theirs.
40:
41:Each backend keeps its own state in its own table, with one row for each allocation, instead of fields or a nested object in `serverAllocations`. The worker changes its lease fields every few seconds, and a change to `serverAllocations` reruns every status query that reads it. A second backend adds its own table and one `backend` value, and changes no existing table.

Server ownership is stored on the server, separate from membership permissions. Membership grants reads. Rename, power, member management, SSH management, and deletion have independent permissions; new memberships default to every permission the caller can grant. Delegates can grant only permissions they hold and cannot change or remove a member with broader permissions. Only the owner can transfer ownership, to an existing active member; the previous owner stays with every membership permission. The owner cannot leave; deleting the owner's account requests durable server deletion.

## Verification and next boundary

Run `bun test convex/ssh/authorized_keys.test.ts` for the pure module's behavior. Tests exercise duplicate occurrences, exact preservation, quoting, unknown content, stale observations, conflicting targets, field injection, immutable snapshots, batch edits, and appends. A deterministic byte corpus checks round-trip preservation. Some fixtures deliberately use incomplete key blobs to prove that structural recognition does not masquerade as native validation.

The module adds no API admission policy. Future operations must bound remote reads, response sizes, and edit batches before calling it; those limits belong to the actual transport and application contract.

The first implementation slice ends at candidate bytes. Native semantic validation and the trusted remote read/write lifecycle remain explicit gates. The full option support matrix is not implemented by this lexer. No membership policy, persistent key inventory, polling, or enforcement was added.
```

  "content": "# API\n\nEvery public Convex function (`query`, `mutation`, `action`) is the application API. The web app is its first client. A future public API documents and exposes these same functions to other clients; it adds authentication for those clients, not a second set of operations. Internal functions (`internalQuery`, `internalMutation`, `internalAction`) are not part of it.\n\n## Rules for public functions\n\n- **Authorize inside the function.** Use `requireUser`, `requireServerAccess`, and `requireServerOwner`. Never trust an ID, username, or permission that the client sends.\n- **Validate the contract.** Every function has argument and return validators. The return validator is the documented response.\n- **Report failures with a code.** A code from `convex/errors.ts` identifies the failure; the message is for people and can change. A function returns `failure` (`{ ok: false, code, field, message }`) when it has already counted a rate limit attempt, because a thrown error would roll that attempt back. Otherwise it throws `toConvexError(code, message)`, whose data is `{ code, message }`. A client handles both by `code`.\n- **Make repeatable requests safe.** A request that starts work outside Convex takes a client-generated `requestId`. Repeating the same request returns the same operation instead of starting new work.\n- **Bound lists.** Lists paginate with `paginationOpts`, and `toBoundedPagination` limits a page to `maxPageSize` items.\n- **Name by resource.** The module path names the resource and the function names the action: `api.servers.lifecycle.create`, `api.servers.memberships.add`.\n\n## Changes\n\nThese changes keep existing clients working: a new function, a new optional argument, a new return field, and a new code.\n\nThese changes break clients: moving or renaming a function, removing or renaming an argument, a return field, or a code, and changing what a value means. Until the public API is released, make them and update the web app in the same change. After release, add a new function next to the old one, and remove the old one only when no client uses it.\n\n## HTTP routes\n\n`convex/http.ts` holds routes for callers that cannot use a Convex client. `/webhooks/<system>` receives events from another system. Other paths name the resource they act on, such as `/ssh/host-keys`. A route authenticates its caller itself and does no work before it has checked the request.\n\n## Not built yet\n\n- Credentials for clients other than the web app, such as API tokens that `requireUser` accepts.\n- Rate limits for each such credential.\n- The choice between calling Convex functions directly and a versioned HTTP layer over the same helpers.\n- Public documentation of each function.\n"
}

The company wants to let customers manage SSH access to their instances from the panel after creation, while the instance stays the source of truth.\n\nQuestion: How do existing cloud providers and server-management products manage SSH keys and access on machines that are already running, and what do they deliberately not support?\n\nCover at least: AWS (EC2 Instance Connect, Systems Manager), Google Cloud (metadata keys through the guest agent, OS Login), Azure (VMAccess extension), DigitalOcean, Hetzner Cloud, Linode or Akamai, Vultr, OVHcloud, Fly.io, GitHub Codespaces, and server-management products such as Laravel Forge, Ploi, RunCloud, and Coolify. For each: the mechanism (direct authorized_keys edits, an agent, certificates, an AuthorizedKeysCommand, other), whether keys exist only at creation or can change later, which authorized_keys options the product exposes, what happens when the customer edits the files directly, how conflicts and failures are shown, how a customer who loses access recovers, and any documented limitations.\n\nEvidence rules: Cite official documentation and, where available, the source of agents or tools. Give dates for documentation you read. Distinguish current behavior from deprecated products. Say where documentation is silent instead of guessing.\n```\n\n## 05: A conformance harness for sshd behavior\n\n```text\nContext: A web control panel edits OpenSSH authorized_keys files on customer Linux machines and claims to support every native option. To keep that claim true as OpenSSH changes, the team wants automated checks that show how real sshd builds treat each entry form.\n\nQuestion: How should a small, maintainable test harness verify authorized_keys parsing and option behavior against real sshd builds?\n\nCover: which sshd builds to test (versions and distribution packages) and how to run them reproducibly; how to assert authentication success or failure, and session behavior for each option family (forced commands, forwarding, pty, environment, source address, expiry time, certificate authorities and principals, security-key requirements); how to generate keys and certificates for fixtures; how to structure a corpus so that one fixture answers one question; how long a run takes and what it costs in CI; how to detect a semantic change when a new OpenSSH release appears; and which behaviors cannot be tested automatically.\n\nEvidence rules: Base the design on documented sshd and ssh flags at exact versions. Describe experiments that show each assertion is observable. Compare at least two harness designs and state the tradeoffs. Keep the design as small as the goal allows, and say what a smaller design would miss.\n```\n\n## 06: Finding the accounts and files that apply\n\n```text\nContext: A web control panel connects over SSH to customer Linux machines where the customer has root and can change the SSH server configuration, the accounts, and even the operating system. The panel wants to show which accounts can sign in with keys and which authorized_keys files apply to each account, discovering this from the live system instead of assuming default paths.\n\nQuestion: How can a program reliably determine, on a live Linux machine, which accounts can sign in with public keys and which authorized key sources apply to each?\n\nCover: AuthorizedKeysFile and its tokens, multiple files, Match blocks, Include files, AuthorizedKeysCommand, AuthorizedPrincipalsFile and certificate authorities, StrictModes and file permission requirements, PermitRootLogin, PubkeyAuthentication, AllowUsers and DenyUsers, account shells that forbid login, and PAM effects. Evaluate `sshd -T` with `-C user=,host=,addr=` and its limits, including the difference between the configuration on disk and the settings of the running daemon. Cover machines that run another SSH server (for example Dropbear) or no SSH server. Give the smallest set of commands that answers the question, how to report partial answers, and how each approach fails.\n\nEvidence rules: Cite OpenSSH source and man pages at exact versions. Describe reproducible experiments for runtime claims. Include counterexamples where discovery gives a wrong or incomplete answer.\n```\n\n## 07: Presenting authorized_keys options\n\n```text\nContext: A web control panel lets customers manage entries in OpenSSH authorized_keys files on their Linux VPS. Most customers are new to Linux and SSH; some are experts. The panel wants a simple default form and a complete advanced form, both mapping exactly to native OpenSSH options, without inventing semantics or hiding what an entry allows.\n\nQuestion: How should authorized_keys options be presented so that beginners can add a key safely and experts can use every native option?\n\nCover: which fields belong in a simple default (for example key, account, and comment) and why; how to group advanced options; conflicts and dependencies between options (for example `restrict` with explicit permits, or `command` with pty options); how to show entries that contain options the form does not understand, or malformed content; how to enter and display time values such as `expiry-time`; how to explain what an entry permits without overstating the protection it gives; and examples from existing products.\n\nEvidence rules: Cite product documentation or screenshots with dates, and OpenSSH man pages for option semantics. Separate evidence from opinion. Name the usability risks of each design you describe.\n```\n\n## 08: Reaching a machine without SSH\n\n```text\nContext: A company runs customer VPS instances on Hetzner Cloud today and plans to run its own virtualization hosts later. Its control panel connects to each instance over SSH with a management key that cloud-init installs at creation. Customers have root, so they can remove that key, change the SSH configuration, or replace the operating system. The company wants to understand every way it can act on an instance, or restore its own access, without depending on SSH inside the instance.\n\nQuestion: Which out-of-band channels exist for running commands, changing files, or restoring access on a virtual machine, and what are their tradeoffs?\n\nCover: Hetzner Cloud features (rescue system, rebuild with user data, root password reset, console, images, backups) and exactly what each allows; QEMU guest agent commands such as guest-exec and file writes; cloud-init behavior on later boots; virtio-serial and vsock agents; libvirt, Proxmox, Firecracker, and Cloud Hypervisor facilities; and what major cloud providers use. For each channel: whether the customer can disable it, what it needs inside the guest, security implications for the customer and for the company, whether it works on non-Linux guests, and whether the same design works on Hetzner Cloud and on the company's own hosts.\n\nEvidence rules: Cite official documentation and source at exact versions. Distinguish provider-level actions from agents inside the guest. State the conditions under which each channel fails. Do not assume that a feature available on one platform exists on another.\n```\n\n## 09: Trusting a server's host key over time\n\n```text\nContext: A control panel connects over SSH to customer VPS instances. At creation, the instance generates its host key and reports it over an authenticated channel, and the panel pins that key. Customers have root and can regenerate host keys or reinstall the operating system. IP addresses return to the provider's pool after deletion and can be reused.\n\nQuestion: How should a control plane establish and maintain trust in host keys of machines it does not fully control, including legitimate host key changes?\n\nCover: pinning at creation, trust on first use, SSH host certificates signed by a certificate authority, SSHFP records, fingerprints from provider console output or metadata, and any other method. For each: what attack it prevents (for example a man-in-the-middle or IP reuse), what happens when the customer changes the host key legitimately, how trust is re-established, and operational cost. Describe the concrete consequences for the company and its customers when a control plane connects to an impostor. Include what AWS, Google Cloud, Ansible, and other widely used systems do.\n\nEvidence rules: Cite RFCs, OpenSSH documentation at exact versions, and official provider documentation. Separate documented behavior from inference. Give counterexamples for each method.\n```\n"
}

## Assistant · 2026-09-14T22:00:32.267Z

I've committed everything as `5b4a2d7`. Checks and all 58 tests pass, and dev is redeployed.

**Live test on dev:** a server I created as its owner, with no membership row, registered its host key through `/ssh/host-keys`. It reached running, and deletion took 306 s. Hetzner then showed 0 servers and 0 Primary IPs, grants were back to 0 used, and no SSH access rows were left. Deliberately bad host key reports got 400/400/403, and the old path now returns 404.

**Stale dev data:** a grant row for your old, deleted Clerk user (`j975884kwjw34jvcxsqctce9y18eddaz`) is still in dev. It was left behind because deleting a user didn't delete their grant; it does now. You can delete that row in the dashboard.

## What changed

- **Admin:** "operator" is now "admin" everywhere, including the vocabulary.
- **The three gaps are closed:**
  - Host key reports have a rate limit per allocation (10 at once, 30 an hour).
  - Every list returns at most 100 items per page.
  - A server can have at most 100 members.
- **Error codes:** all codes are listed in `convex/errors.ts`. A client handles every failure by `code` in one of two ways:
  - A function that counted a rate-limit attempt returns `{ ok: false, code, field, message }`, because throwing would undo the count.
  - Everything else throws a `ConvexError` carrying `{ code, message }`.
- **Public API:** `docs/api.md` says every public Convex function is public API. It covers authorization, error codes, repeatable requests, page sizes, and which changes break clients. `AGENTS.md` links to it as a hard rule.
- **Ownership:** the owner no longer has a membership row; ownership already includes every permission. `servers/ownership.ts` holds `listMine`, `getOwner` and `transfer`. Deleting a user deletes their owned servers in batches.
- **Old docs removed:** the plan and audit docs are deleted, and the facts that still apply moved into `decisions.md`.

## Your questions

**`/bootstrap/ssh`.** It didn't fit how the other route is named. `/webhooks/clerk` is named for the system that sends events; this route receives one fact about one resource, so it's now `/ssh/host-keys`.
- **How it works:** a new server posts its host key once, with a random token valid for one allocation.
- **What was wrong:** the route checked the token only after it had parsed and processed the request.
- **Now:** it caps the body size, checks the format, and checks the token before any work or database write. Then it applies the rate limit. Invalid tokens return 403 and write nothing.

**Grants and limits.** I recommend two layers and no general limits module:
- **Deployment layer:** can this deployment create servers at all? Today that's a switch (creation is off when the Hetzner config is missing). A total capacity cap would go here if you want one.
- **Per-user layer:** the existing `serverGrants` table (`limit`, `used`). An admin sets it for now, and people email to ask for more. Billing will later set the same `limit`, so nothing gets thrown away.
- **Rate limits are a separate thing.** They cap how often you can do something; a grant caps how many servers you can hold at once. Don't merge them.

**"Built but not exposed".** The backend can read `authorized_keys`, write it safely, and remove selected keys (`read_file.ts`, `write_file.ts`, `remove_authorized_keys.ts`). "Not exposed" means no public function calls that code yet, and the `manageSsh` permission isn't checked anywhere. Nobody can use it until we add public functions for it. It's maintainable because it's small and has no second copy of the data, but option validation doesn't exist yet. That's what the research prompts are for.

**S1 (accounts and files).** Discover them live with `sshd -T -C user=…`, which reports the key file paths that apply to each account. If discovery fails, say so and let the user enter a path. Keep in mind that `sshd -T` reads the config on disk, which can differ from the running daemon.

**S2 (validation).** This needs research before I decide. The known facts: `sshd -t` doesn't check `authorized_keys` entries, and nothing on the machine validates them for us. Prompt 02 compares the candidate methods, from reimplementing the parser to a test login with a temporary key.

**S4 (management key).**
- **Recommendation:** list our key but refuse to remove it through the panel, and show clearly when it's missing. Putting it back silently fights the user's root access.
- **Principle:** yes, write "best effort, visible degradation" down as a rule. When the machine lacks something we need, the feature says what's missing and what still works; it never guesses or fails silently. It fits `AGENTS.md` next to the rule about production-ready features.
- **Recovery without SSH:** Hetzner has no agent inside the machine that we control.
  - **Rebuild:** a reinstall that wipes the disk; I understood from earlier research that it accepts new cloud-init data, so it can bootstrap our access again.
  - **Rescue mode:** can mount the disk and fix it, but only after a reboot.
  - **V2 hosts:** our own hypervisor could offer a real channel, such as a guest agent over virtio or vsock, though the user can disable that too.
  
  Prompt 08 covers this area.

**Naming.**
- **"Authorized key", not "credential":** I've added authorized key, key pair, host key and management key to the vocabulary, with "credential" rejected.
- **Env var:** `SSH_CREDENTIAL_KEY` still breaks this rule. It's tied to the key rotation work that's still open, so I'll rename it there.
- **Other names:** nothing else looks urgent.

**Permissions.**
- **"Connection details"** means the IP, port and host key fingerprint. They show where a server is, not how to get in. Every member sees them, and a member with no authorized key can never connect. That's correct, because server access and SSH access are separate.
- **Groups:** show them only as headings in the UI, with no dependencies between permissions. Dependencies create exploit paths, like your rename example.
- **A "change permissions" exception:** agreed that it's foolish. The existing ceiling is enough: nobody can grant or remove a permission they don't hold.
- **"Only my own keys":** this only means something if each member has their own non-sudo Linux account. With shared root, any key can edit the whole file. Document it for later and keep the model neutral now; the current design doesn't block it.

**Host key trust.** When we connect, the host key proves we reached the machine we created and not an impostor. The two realistic ways to reach an impostor are a network attacker in the middle, or an IP address Hetzner reused after deletion. If we trusted an impostor, we could send it the user's key changes, read its fake files as the truth, or tell the user a change worked when it didn't. That's why we pin the key at creation. If the user legitimately replaces the host key, we stop connecting and show that clearly until trust is set up again (prompt 09).

**Rebuild, rescue mode and snapshots.**
- **Rebuild:** reinstalls an image on the same server with the same IPs, and wipes the disk.
- **Rescue mode:** boots a temporary Linux in memory on the next reboot and leaves the disks untouched, so someone can mount and repair them. It's an advanced feature.
- **Snapshots:** save a disk image in Hetzner that you can restore or create from later. They need nothing inside the machine.

**Degradation.** Make it an agent rule in `AGENTS.md`, not just a doc. It applies to every feature that depends on machine state.

**Hostname (option B).** The condition "change the hostname only if it still equals the old name" is the right one: it respects a hostname the user set on purpose. "Needs management access" means we must be able to log in with our management key. It has nothing to do with member permissions. If that login fails, the rename still succeeds in the panel and we show that the machine's hostname wasn't updated. Creation sets the hostname through cloud-init; updating it on rename comes with the SSH operations work.

**Research prompts:** `docs/ssh-options-research-prompts.md` has 9 prompts, each self-contained:
1. The exact `authorized_keys` format and options for each OpenSSH version
2. How to check an entry is valid
3. Existing parsers and editors
4. How other providers manage keys on running machines
5. A test harness against real sshd builds
6. Finding the accounts and key files that apply
7. How to present options
8. Reaching a machine without SSH
9. Trusting host keys over time

They state facts and questions without suggesting an answer, and they require exact source versions, counterexamples, and a list of what couldn't be verified. I left out the agent setup topic because we deferred it.

## Decisions I need from you

1. **Grants:** keep the per-user grant table plus a deployment switch, with email for increases until billing sets the limit? And do you want a total capacity cap for the deployment too?
2. **Management key:** refuse removal and show clearly when it's missing, rather than hiding it and re-adding it?
3. **Degradation rule:** add "best effort, visible degradation" to `AGENTS.md`?
4. **Groups and "only my own keys":** permission groups as UI headings only, and only-my-own-keys documented for later rather than built?

16	## Naming rules
17	
18	Convex builds each function's path from its file path. Every rule below follows from that:

21	2. **Convex functions don't repeat their path.** You always call them through the path, so `api.servers.members.add` is right and `api.servers.members.addMember` repeats itself.
22	3. **Plain exports do carry the area name.** They're imported by bare name, so they have to make sense alone: `isReservedServerName`, `SshError`, `readSshFile`.
23	4. **A file is named after its main export**, minus the folder name.
24	5. **One definition per word.** Today "access" means three things: `userAccess` (account disabled), `server_access.ts` (permission checks), and `serverSshAccess` (a stored credential).

90	
91	## What the research shows
92	
93	Convex gives very little official guidance on structure:
94	- **File paths become API paths.** `convex/foo/bar.ts` is called as `api.foo.bar.fn`, and folders can nest.
95	- **"Thin" public functions.** The docs suggest keeping queries and mutations short and putting most logic in plain helper functions in a folder like `convex/model/`. That's all it says about layout.
96	- **Nothing on naming** modules or functions.
97	
98	Real projects don't agree with each other:
99	
100	| Project | Layout | Function names |
101	|---|---|---|
102	| chef (Convex) | Flat, about 30 top-level files | — |
103	| ai-town | One folder per area; each folder has its own `schema.ts`, merged into the root schema | File names repeat the prefix inside the folder (`aiTown/agentDescription.ts`) |
104	| Convex agent component | Flat modules | Repeats the module name (`threads.getThread`, `messages.addMessages`) |
105	| Convex workpool component | Flat modules | Doesn't repeat it (`lib.enqueue`, `lib.status`) |
106	
107	So there isn't one accepted "best" shape. What matters is picking rules we can apply the same way everywhere.
108	
109	## Was my first proposal the best? No
110	
111	- The "one word, one meaning" rule was too broad (see above).
112	- `listMine` didn't really belong in `members.ts`. It only landed there because I'd removed `servers.ts`.
113	- Splitting `users.ts` into a folder was symmetry for its own sake.
114	- Every folder-based layout has to answer "where do the functions for the server itself go?", and I dodged that by removing `servers.ts`.
115	- I missed that `server_model.ts` holds table validators, while Convex's docs use "model" for business logic.
116

119	| Shape | How calls read | Downside |
120	|---|---|---|
121	| **A. `servers.ts` next to `servers/`** | `api.servers.create`, `api.servers.members.add`, `api.servers.lifecycle.power` | The area lives in a file and a folder. A function can't share a name with a subfolder module. |
122	| B. Everything inside the folder | `api.servers.servers.create` | Repeats itself. Convex treats `index.ts` like any other file, so that doesn't help. |
123	| C. Split by job, no main file | `api.servers.names.rename`, `api.servers.members.listMine` | Some functions get forced into files where they don't fit. |
124	| D. Convex's `model/` pattern | `api.servers.create`, with logic in `model/servers.ts` | Every area gets two homes, and it's a logic refactor, not a rename. |
125	
126	**My pick is A, with one rule:** `<area>.ts` holds the functions for that area's main table, and `<area>/` holds everything else.
127	- `users.ts` stays a single file.
128	- `ssh/` has no main table, so there's no `ssh.ts`.
129	
130	The TypeScript types support a file and a folder with the same name, and the runtime paths (`servers:create` and `servers/members:add`) are different strings. I haven't pushed that to a dev deployment yet; I'd do that first.
131	
132	```
133	convex/
134	  auth.config.ts convex.config.ts crons.ts http.ts schema.ts   (spreads ...serverTables)
135	  rate_limits.ts
136	  users.ts            current, syncCurrent, Clerk sync; requireUser moves here
137	  servers.ts          list, getByName, create, rename, remove
138	  servers/
139	    schema.ts         server tables and their validators (replaces server_model.ts)
140	    access.ts         access checks and permission helpers
141	    names.ts  reserved_names.ts
142	    members.ts        list, add, setPermissions, remove, transferOwnership, removeAll, removeForUser
143	    lifecycle.ts      power, status, provision and delete helpers
144	    grants.ts         reserve, set
145	    worker.ts         sweep, claim, dispatch, authorizePower, record, retry, run
146	    inventory.ts  hetzner.ts
147	  ssh/                unchanged
148	```
149	
150	**Names inside files: qualify by distance.** A name that stays inside its folder doesn't repeat the area. For example, `isReservedName` inside `servers/` is clear. A name used from another area, or defined in a shared file, carries the qualifier: `SshError`, and `serverNameAttempt` in `rate_limits.ts`. This matches your point about context, and it keeps constants like `NAME_PATTERN` short.
151	
152	## Decisions for you
153	
154	1. **Where server functions live:** A, B, C, or D. I recommend A.
155	2. **Repeat the module name in function names?** (`members.add` or `members.addMember`.) I recommend not repeating it, because calls always include the path.
156	3. **Schema:** one root `schema.ts`, or a `schema.ts` per folder merged into the root (the ai-town approach). I recommend per folder for folders, and root for single-file areas like users.
157	4. **Table renames:** these are now free since there's no production data. For example, `serverInventory` holds scan cursors, so `serverInventoryScans` fits better.

174	## D: what the `model/` folder gets you, and what it costs
175	
176	D doesn't change what anyone sees from outside. The API calls and file names are the same as in A (`api.servers.create`, `api.servers.members.add`). The only difference is that most of each function's logic moves into a second, parallel tree under `model/`.
177	
178	**What Convex says it gets you, checked against this repo:**
179	- **Sharing logic inside one transaction.** You get this from any exported plain function, with or without a folder. The repo already does it: `requireServerAccess`, `provision`, `deleteServer`, `reserve`, `connectionForAllocation`.
180	- **A small public surface you can audit.** A folder doesn't enforce this. Any `mutation(...)` anywhere is callable by clients. What actually separates public from private is `mutation` vs `internalMutation`.
181	- **Easier refactors.** This helps a little when many entry points (public, internal, HTTP, cron) share one operation. Only `deleteServer` looks like that here, and it's already a helper.
182	
183	**What it costs:**
184	- **Two trees to keep in sync.** Every area exists twice (`servers/members.ts` and `model/servers/members.ts`). Every move or rename happens twice, and every change means opening two files.
185	- **Pointless wrappers.** Most handlers here are used once. Pulling their logic out produces one-to-one wrappers that add a hop and share nothing.
186	- **"Model" doesn't describe what's inside.** It means "not a Convex function", and says nothing about the area. `ssh/` would get split in half: `authorized_keys.ts` into `model/`, `bootstrap_state.ts` out of it.
187	- **Convex's own code doesn't use it.** chef, workpool, agent, workflow and r2 have no `model/` folder.
188	
189	**My recommendation is A.** I'd keep the useful part of D as a rule rather than a folder: when a second function needs some logic, move it into a plain helper exported from the file that owns the table it writes. A doesn't block D later, because the API stays the same either way.
190

211	**Same word, two meanings in one place**
212	- `inventory.record` uses `scan.kind` (`servers`/`primary_ips`) and `resource.kind` (`server`/`ipv4`) in the same function. The scan field needs a different name.
213	- `power` has `const limit = await rateLimiter.limit(...)` in the same file as `grant.limit`.

383	## 2. Splitting out allocations: now or later
384	
385	**What ties the backend to servers today** (from reading the code):
386	- **The backend deletes server data itself.** When deletion finishes, `server_lifecycle.record` deletes the `servers` row and schedules `servers.deleteMembers`.

388	- **Server code calls backend internals directly:**

390	  - `servers.remove` calls `deleteServer`
391	  - `transferOwnership` reads `serverAllocations.deleteRequested`
392	- **SSH depends on allocations, not servers.** `ssh/bootstrap*` reads `serverAllocations`, and its credentials are stored per allocation.
