````text
So I would attach a provenance to every answer:

```text
effective_config_basis = "current files parsed by OpenSSH 10.5p1"
running_daemon_verified = false
```

unless you have actually probed the listener.

## `AuthorizedKeysFile`: don't construct `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`

For OpenSSH 10.5p1, `AuthorizedKeysFile` may contain **multiple whitespace-separated entries**, each entry may contain glob wildcards, `none` disables file lookup, and relative entries are relative to the target user's home directory. The documented default in this version is `.ssh/authorized_keys .ssh/authorized_keys2`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

The permitted tokens for `AuthorizedKeysFile` are:

```text
%%   literal %
%h   target user's home directory
%U   target user's numeric UID
%u   target username
```

`AuthorizedPrincipalsFile` has the same token set. Commands have a much larger token set because their values may depend on the offered credential and connection. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

You should take the template returned by `sshd -T`, resolve the account through the system identity database, substitute these tokens, prefix the home directory when the result is relative, and then perform glob expansion **as the target user**. This mirrors the 10.5p1 authentication source: it expands `%h/%u/%U`, prefixes `pw_dir` for relative paths, temporarily assumes the user's identity, runs `glob()`, and checks every matching file until it finds the offered key. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth.c))

This means a configuration such as:

```text
AuthorizedKeysFile /srv/sshkeys/%u/*.keys .ssh/admin_keys
```

may resolve for `alice` to several files under `/srv/sshkeys/alice/` plus `/home/alice/.ssh/admin_keys`. Reporting only one path is wrong.

`sshd -T` deliberately prints the configuration templates rather than converting `%u`, `%h`, etc. into per-account filenames; the print path dumps the stored `authorized_keys_files` array directly. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/servconf.c))

## `StrictModes` requires more than checking `chmod 600`

When an authorized-keys or authorized-principals file is opened, 10.5p1 first requires it to be a regular file. With `StrictModes yes`, it then calls `safe_path_fd()`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c))

For the user file, `safe_path()` requires the owner to be the target user or an accepted system-directory UID, rejects group/other write bits (`022`), resolves the path with `realpath()`, then walks upward through the canonical parent directories. Those directories likewise must have acceptable ownership and must not be group/world writable. It stops at the canonical home directory when that is encountered, otherwise it can continue to `/`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/misc.c))

Several consequences matter for a discovery implementation:

```text
-rw------- alice alice ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
```

is not sufficient if `.ssh` or the relevant parent path is insecure.

Conversely, “Alice's home is writable by someone else, therefore every Alice key source is invalid” is also too broad. An absolute key source under `/etc/ssh/keys/alice`, whose canonical path does not traverse Alice's home, is checked along that other path.

And with `StrictModes no`, ownership/mode safety is skipped, but the file still has to be openable as the target user and must be a regular file. The source opens these files after temporarily switching to the account's credentials. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c))

The same user-file mechanism is used for `AuthorizedPrincipalsFile`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c))

Do not apply those exact rules to `AuthorizedKeysCommand`. Its executable has separate requirements: the command must use an absolute executable path, be owned by root, and not be writable by group or others. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

## Dynamic key commands are fundamentally not enumerable

`AuthorizedKeysCommand` is a **program**, not another filename. It runs only for valid users, normally after the file sources fail to authorize the offered key. Its output is parsed as `authorized_keys` data. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

The critical discovery problem is that its arguments may include:

```text
%f   offered key/certificate fingerprint
%k   offered key/certificate itself
%t   key/certificate type
%C   connection endpoints
%D   routing domain
%h %U %u
```

and the principals command has even more certificate-specific substitutions. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

Therefore, “run `AuthorizedKeysCommand` once and enumerate all of its keys” is not generally meaningful. A perfectly valid command can be:

```text
lookup-key --user=%u --fingerprint=%f --source=%C
```

and answer differently for every offered key, client address, database state, or time.

It may also have external side effects. For discovery, report it as a dynamic source:

```text
type: authorized_keys_command
command: ...
run_as: ...
enumerable: false
```

Do not execute it merely to populate the UI. Execute it only as part of an explicit test involving a real candidate credential.

A counterexample is a host with `AuthorizedKeysFile none` and an `AuthorizedKeysCommand` backed by LDAP. Scanning every filesystem key file yields “no keys”; actual key login succeeds.

## Certificates require two distinct CA models

There are two ways an OpenSSH user certificate may become trusted, and they should not be collapsed.

A `cert-authority` entry may live directly in an `AuthorizedKeysFile`—or in `AuthorizedKeysCommand` output. On such a line the `principals=` authorized-keys option may constrain which certificate principals are valid. `AuthorizedPrincipalsFile` is **not** consulted for this type of CA. The `sshd(8)` authorized-keys format explicitly supports `cert-authority` and `principals=`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd.8))

Separately, `TrustedUserCAKeys` names a system CA-key file. A certificate signed by one of those CAs may authenticate a user when the certificate has an acceptable principal. If neither `AuthorizedPrincipalsFile` nor `AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand` is configured, the target username itself must appear in the certificate principals. If either is configured, a certificate principal must match that source. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

`AuthorizedPrincipalsFile` may itself use `%h/%u/%U/%%` and wildcards; 10.5p1 actually performs `glob()` on the expanded path as the user. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

So a useful source report might look conceptually like:

```text
alice
  direct key files:
    /srv/keys/alice/a.keys
    /home/alice/.ssh/authorized_keys

  dynamic key source:
    /usr/local/libexec/ssh-key-lookup ...     [not enumerable]

  certificate source:
    trusted CA file: /etc/ssh/user_ca_keys
    principal files: /etc/ssh/principals/alice
    principal command: none
```

An account with no ordinary key lines can therefore still be fully usable through certificates.

The source ordering in 10.5p1 is also illuminating: it checks configured authorized-key files, then `TrustedUserCAKeys` certificate authorization, then `AuthorizedKeysCommand`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkey.c))

## Public-key enabled does not mean login allowed

`PubkeyAuthentication yes` only enables that authentication method; it is not an account verdict. Its upstream default is `yes` in 10.5p1. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

`AuthenticationMethods` is an easy-to-miss second gate. `any` permits a single enabled method. A setting such as:

```text
AuthenticationMethods publickey,password
```

means a public key can be accepted but does **not** complete login by itself. `publickey,publickey` requires two different public keys. If none of the allowed method sequences begins with or contains publickey in an applicable position, having `PubkeyAuthentication yes` does not make public-key login useful. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))
````

````text
```text
public_key_method_usable
public_key_alone_sufficient
```

rather than one Boolean.

Also look at `RefuseConnection`; in 10.5p1 it can unconditionally terminate a matching connection. `RevokedKeys`, algorithm restrictions, minimum RSA size, FIDO verification requirements, certificate validity, and per-key `from=` or `expiry-time=` conditions can make individual credentials fail even though the account-level configuration looks permissive. An unreadable `RevokedKeys` file is especially significant: the man page says that it disables public-key authentication for all users. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

## Root is special

Do not interpret `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password` as “root cannot use SSH.” In 10.5p1 it explicitly permits public-key authentication while disabling password and keyboard-interactive authentication. The source's `auth_root_allowed()` allows `publickey` in this mode. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

The statuses are approximately:

| `PermitRootLogin` | Public-key result |
|---|---|
| `yes` | ordinary rules |
| `prohibit-password` | public key may authenticate |
| `forced-commands-only` | conditional: only a key/certificate producing a forced command |
| `no` | root denied |

For `forced-commands-only`, you cannot classify root as generally key-login-capable merely because an authorized-keys file exists; the actual matching credential must carry the necessary restriction. The 10.5p1 source checks the effective authentication options for a forced command. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth.c))

## `AllowUsers`, `DenyUsers`, and identity enumeration

`AllowUsers` can contain `USER@HOST` forms and CIDR address restrictions; `DenyUsers` takes precedence. The actual account check also applies `AllowGroups` and `DenyGroups`, so a reliable implementation should not omit those just because the UI requirement mentions only users. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

This also explains why a bare “alice: yes” result is misleading: Alice might be allowed from `192.0.2.0/24` and denied from everywhere else.

Account discovery itself has a separate problem. Use NSS (`getpwnam`, `getpwent`, or `getent passwd`), not just `/etc/passwd`; OpenSSH itself uses the system account lookup functions. But **NSS enumeration is not guaranteed to list every resolvable account**. For example, SSSD explicitly supports operation with enumeration disabled; its documentation notes that `getent passwd` may display no domain users while named lookups such as `getent passwd alice` remain the appropriate test. ([SSSD](https://sssd.io/troubleshooting/basics.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Thus on a host with `passwd: files sss`, the honest result may be:

```text
local accounts enumerated: yes
all possible directory accounts enumerated: unknown
```

A UI claiming “these are all SSH accounts” from `getent passwd` alone is not reliable across enterprise Linux systems.

## Shells and “logged in” are different from authentication

OpenSSH 10.5p1's pre-auth account check rejects a non-chrooted user if its configured shell does not exist, is not a regular file, or has no execute bit. An empty shell becomes `/bin/sh`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth.c))

It does **not** ask whether the executable is semantically a “no login” program. Therefore an executable `/usr/sbin/nologin` passes this particular pre-auth check. Authentication can succeed, after which `nologin` terminates an attempted shell or command. OpenSSH's documented login processing invokes the user's configured shell after successful authentication. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd.8))

So report something like:

```text
key_authentication: potentially_allowed
interactive_session: shell_declares_nologin
```

rather than declaring the account incapable of key authentication.

`/etc/shells` is not part of the core check above. PAM can impose additional shell policy, e.g. through an appropriate PAM module.

There is also `/etc/nologin`: OpenSSH's documented post-auth login process checks it and quits for non-root users if present. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd.8))

With `ChrootDirectory`, even the pre-auth shell check differs: the core code skips the host-side shell existence check when chrooting because the execution environment is different. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth.c))

## PAM prevents a complete static answer

`UsePAM yes` is particularly important. OpenSSH 10.5p1 documents that PAM **account and session processing applies to all authentication types**, including public-key authentication. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

The source calls `pam_acct_mgmt()` and regards ordinary PAM account failures as denial. PAM modules may consult account expiry, time of day, host or source address, SSSD/LDAP policy, local files, network services, or arbitrary site-specific code. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth-pam.c))

Consequently:

```text
PubkeyAuthentication yes
valid authorized key
```

still does not imply successful login if:

```text
UsePAM yes
```

and the PAM account stack rejects the user.

Another interesting source detail: the OpenSSH-native “locked account” check is performed when `UsePAM` is off; with PAM enabled the result can instead depend on the PAM account policy. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth.c))

PAM session modules are also invoked. In 10.5p1, failure of `pam_open_session()` causes OpenSSH to restrict the session rather than being reducible to the same simple pre-auth Boolean. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/auth-pam.c))

Therefore `UsePAM yes` should normally lower a static result from “yes” to something like **“configuration permits; PAM account policy not evaluated”**. Parsing `/etc/pam.d/sshd` does not fix this generally because PAM modules are executable code.

## The smallest defensible command set

If the panel already has privileged command execution on the machine, this is about as small as I would make the external-command portion:

1. Identify the server that actually owns the SSH connection/listener, rather than assuming that an installed `/usr/sbin/sshd` is relevant:

   ```bash
   ss -H -ltnp
   ```

   Then inspect the relevant PID's `/proc/$pid/exe` and NUL-separated `/proc/$pid/cmdline`. Also inspect the ancestor chain of the panel's current SSH session, because inetd/systemd/socket-activated configurations may not have `sshd` itself owning the listening socket. Capture the implementation/version from that executable, e.g. the version option supported by that implementation.

2. Enumerate the identity database as far as the system permits:

   ```bash
   getent passwd
   ```

   Use named `getent passwd "$candidate"`/`getpwnam()` lookups for users discovered elsewhere. Treat enumeration as incomplete when an NSS directory backend can resolve non-enumerated users.

3. For every OpenSSH candidate account and every connection context you intend to answer for, invoke the **same implementation/binary** and replay its relevant `-f` and `-o` configuration arguments:

   ```bash
   /proc/$pid/exe -T \
     -f /the/actual/config \
     ...original -o overrides... \
     -C "user=$u,host=$h,addr=$a,laddr=$la,lport=$lp,rdomain=$rd"
   ```

   If this panel's current connection is the scope, `$SSH_CONNECTION` conveniently provides client IP/port and server IP/port. The hostname component still needs to be treated according to `UseDNS`/OpenSSH hostname resolution semantics.

4. Everything after that should preferably be program logic/syscalls, not more shell parsing: expand `%h/%u/%U/%%`, glob as the target user, `open`/`fstat`/`realpath` the files, reproduce the StrictModes path walk, evaluate `PermitRootLogin`, `AllowUsers`/`DenyUsers` and group rules, shell state, `AuthenticationMethods`, and attach `unknown/conditional` for PAM or commands. Do **not** execute dynamic key/principal commands merely to discover their contents.

That is not an exact query of the resident daemon. No inspection-only command sequence can provide that guarantee when the running process may have old configuration in memory or its policy delegates to arbitrary PAM/key-command code.

## How to report partial answers

I would make uncertainty first-class rather than squeezing the result into yes/no. A per-account result could carry:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| `scope` | `addr=203.0.113.8,laddr=10.0.0.4,lport=22` |
| `server` | `OpenSSH_10.5p1`, PID 123 |
| `config_basis` | `current_on_disk`, not runtime snapshot |
| `account_resolution` | resolved / enumeration incomplete |
| `pubkey_method` | enabled / disabled |
| `auth_completion` | key alone / key + password / conditional |
| `account_policy` | allowed / denied / conditional |
| `key_files` | expanded paths plus secure/readable/absent state |
| `key_command` | none / dynamic |
| `trusted_ca` | path and readability |
````

````text
I’ll treat “high fidelity” as “answers for the exact installed `sshd` binary, its compiled feature set/patches, and the effective server configuration—not merely upstream OpenSSH syntax.” I’ll compare static/source-derived approaches against experiments that actually drive the authentication path, and I’ll call out where a method can say “valid” while the daemon still rejects or gives different semantics.

The upstream code already shows why a “parser-only” answer is incomplete: parsing an option string is only one stage. Later stages perform context checks (`from=`, expiry, CA/principal consistency), merge key/certificate options, and then session code enforces command/forwarding/PTY/environment behavior. A validator has to decide which of those stages it is claiming to model.

**ChatGPT**

A useful version-drift example emerged: OpenSSH 10.5 (released August 11, 2026) fixed `restrict` so it actually restricts tunnel forwarding; 10.4 also fixed a regression where key options could be applied after a failed signature. Those are exactly the kinds of discrepancies a cloned parser or “what the man page says” validator can miss for a particular installed build.

**ChatGPT**

For this problem, “valid authorized_keys entry” is not one property. OpenSSH makes several distinct decisions: the line must parse; the key/certificate must be authorized in a connection context; a signed authentication may have to succeed; and, after authentication, the resulting options interact with server policy and session/channel code. In OpenSSH 10.5p1, the single-line routine `auth_check_authkey_line()` parses the key and options, compares the actual key/CA, performs context-dependent authorization, and merges certificate options; `from=` depends on the actual remote host/IP and `expiry-time` on the current clock. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c))

That distinction matters because a method can be an excellent **parser oracle** and still be a bad **behavior oracle**.

## Comparison

| Method | Exact installed build? | Entry syntax / key match | Context authorization | Signature/authentication | Option semantics | Machine risk | Maintenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reimplement OpenSSH parser | No, unless continuously matched | High for modeled version | Only what you model | No | Only what you model | Very low | **Very high** |
| Build OpenSSH's parsing code into helper | Only if built from exact source/patches | **Very high** | Potentially high if enough code is imported | No | No, unless much more of sshd is imported | Low | High |
| `sshd -t` / `-T` / current `-G` | Uses installed binary | **No authorized_keys validation** | No | No | Gives useful global/effective config only | Low | Low |
| `ssh -G` | Client only | No | No | No | No | Negligible | Low |
| `ssh-keygen -l` / `-L` | Installed utility, not sshd parser | Key/certificate blob only | No | No | No authorized_keys options | Negligible | Low |
| Exact installed `sshd`, isolated, unsigned public-key query | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes, for simulated connection context** | No signature | Does not activate/test session options | Moderate | Moderate |
| Exact installed `sshd`, isolated, signed login + behavioral probes | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes, for simulated context** | **Yes**, if exact private credential available | **Highest pre-production fidelity** | Moderate–high | Moderate–high |
| Authentication through live production sshd | **Yes; actual running service** | **Yes** | **Yes, for that connection** | Yes if signed | Yes if actively tested | **High operational risk** | Moderate |
| Production loopback with temporary key | Yes | Yes | Wrong context for `from=`/address-dependent `Match` | Yes for temporary key | High for what you probe | **High** | Moderate |
| `AuthorizedKeysCommand` alone | No; it is a key source, not validator | Its output is subsequently parsed by sshd | Only when invoked by sshd | No by itself | No by itself | Production use can be invasive | Low–moderate |
| Protocol-level unsigned public-key probe against live sshd | **Yes** | **Yes for the queried key** | **Yes for that connection** | No | No | Low–moderate | Moderate |
| ptrace/gdb/eBPF/LD_PRELOAD instrumentation | Exact process possible | Potentially | Potentially | Potentially | Potentially | **Very high** | Very high |

The two strongest techniques are therefore different: an **unsigned public-key query to an isolated copy of the exact installed sshd** is unusually good for asking “would this daemon authorize this exact public key/entry?”, while **a signed connection followed by explicit behavioral probes** is required if “apply its options as intended” is meant literally.

---

## 1. Reimplement the authorized_keys parser

This can give a fast, side-effect-free UI validator. If you reproduce `sshauthopt_parse()` and the surrounding key-line rules precisely, you can catch quoting, commas, option names, argument syntax and key decoding. At 10.5p1, `auth_check_authkey_line()` first attempts to read a key, otherwise skips the option field, reads the key, calls `sshauthopt_parse()`, compares the key/CA, then performs authorization checks. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c)) The current option parser sets fields such as the `restrict` flag and disables forwarding/PTY/etc. in its returned `sshauthopt`; malformed/unrecognised material eventually produces `unknown key option`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth-options.c))

What it **does not prove** is more important. It is not necessarily the code in the customer's executable. A distro may backport changes, apply downstream patches or build different features; a customer with root can replace sshd entirely. It also doesn't prove time/address/certificate conditions, signature behavior, or whether session/channel code enforces a parsed flag correctly.

There is a particularly strong real wrong-answer case. The OpenSSH 10.4p1 man page said `restrict` enabled “all restrictions”, including future restrictions. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_4_P1/sshd.8)) Its parser duly treated `restrict` as a restriction, but `server_request_tun()` in 10.4p1 checked `PermitTunnel` and global `DisableForwarding` without consulting the key's `restricted` flag. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_4_P1/serverloop.c)) Commit **`d322f2c`** fixed this, and OpenSSH 10.5's release notes explicitly say `restrict` was fixed to apply correctly to tunnel forwarding. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/commit/d322f2c))

**Reproducible experiment E1:** build OpenSSH `V_10_4_P1` and `V_10_5_P1` in disposable VMs/namespaces. Configure `PermitTunnel yes`; authorize a test key as `restrict <key>`. Authenticate and request a TUN device (`ssh -w ...`). On 10.4p1 the TUN authorization path lacks the `restricted` check; repeat against 10.5p1 to observe the fix. Do this only in a disposable namespace/VM because TUN setup has network side effects. This is a concrete case where a parser-derived interpretation and even the matching 10.4 documentation produce the wrong behavioral answer.

A parser clone remains valuable for explaining entries in the UI, but its maintenance burden is high: every OpenSSH release, vendor patch and semantic fix becomes your problem.

## 2. Compile or link OpenSSH's parser into a validator

This is stronger than reimplementation for syntax. Calling the same revision's `sshauthopt_parse()` eliminates many transcription differences. Importing `auth_check_authkey_line()` goes further: that function is specifically documented in source as checking one authorized_keys-format line, returning the options on success. It also applies contextual checks and handles certificate-option merging. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c))

But OpenSSH does not expose this as a stable validator ABI. `auth_check_authkey_line()` depends on OpenSSH internal types and more of sshd's authentication machinery. The further you pull the dependency graph, the closer you get to building a second sshd. A helper built from pristine upstream 10.5p1 does not prove the behavior of Ubuntu's, RHEL's, a vendor's, or the customer's locally patched 10.5p1 executable.

**Experiment E2:** build the helper from pristine `V_10_5_P1`, then change one option-recognition branch in an sshd build while retaining the same externally displayed version. Feed the changed option to both. The helper and daemon disagree. Repeat by rebuilding the helper from the exact patched tree; syntax agreement returns, while the helper still cannot reveal a bug such as the 10.4 tunnel-enforcement defect.

Security risk is much lower than starting a daemon, but build and packaging maintenance is significant. It is a very good *source-version parser oracle*, not an installed-binary semantics oracle.

## 3. `sshd -t`, `sshd -T`, and server `sshd -G`

These solve a different problem. In the 10.5p1 `sshd(8)` man page, `-t` checks configuration validity and host-key sanity. `-T` prints the effective server configuration and additionally performs the `-t` checks; `-C` supplies connection parameters such as user and source address so matching `Match` blocks can be evaluated. Current 10.5p1 also has `-G`, which parses and prints effective configuration. None is specified to parse authorized_keys. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/sshd.8))

They are extremely useful **adjuncts**, because option meaning depends on server configuration. For example, session code combines the per-key forwarding permission with `DisableForwarding` and `AllowTcpForwarding`; a key cannot make globally forbidden forwarding available. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/session.c)) Likewise, server `ForceCommand` wins over a key's `command=` option in 10.5p1 session code. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/session.c))

**Experiment E3:** create a syntactically valid sshd configuration and an authorized_keys line beginning with an unknown option, e.g. `this-option-does-not-exist <valid-key>`. `sshd -t`/`-T` still validate the server configuration; an actual authorization attempt using that line is rejected by `sshauthopt_parse()`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth-options.c)) This is the simplest demonstration that `-t`/`-T` are not authorized_keys validators.

Cost and risk are low, so they should be used to determine effective policy, but a successful exit is not evidence that an entry works.

## 4. `ssh -G`

`ssh -G` evaluates **client** `Host` and `Match` configuration and exits. That is exactly how the matching 10.5p1 `ssh(1)` describes it. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/ssh.1)) It says nothing about the server's authorized_keys file.

**Experiment E4:** run `ssh -G target` before and after replacing a server authorized_keys line with the unknown-option line from E3. Its output is unchanged. No server authentication is performed.

It is essentially irrelevant to server-side validation except when debugging the client parameters used by a separate end-to-end test.

## 5. `ssh-keygen`

`ssh-keygen -l` proves that it can obtain a public key and fingerprint it; the matching 10.5p1 man page says exactly that. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/ssh-keygen.1)) It is not an authorized_keys option parser.

This distinction is particularly dangerous because `ssh-keygen` intentionally accepts formats where material precedes a key. Its fingerprint path ultimately finds and reads a public key; it never substitutes for `sshauthopt_parse()`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/ssh-keygen.c))

**Experiment E5:**
```sh
ssh-keygen -q -t ed25519 -N '' -f /tmp/ak-test

{
    printf 'this-option-does-not-exist '
    cat /tmp/ak-test.pub
} >/tmp/candidate

ssh-keygen -lf /tmp/candidate
```

A fingerprintable key does not imply that sshd accepts the surrounding options. Feed `/tmp/candidate` to the 10.5p1 authorization path: the sshd option parser rejects the unknown option. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth-options.c)) `ssh-keygen -L` is similarly useful for inspecting a certificate's contents, but it cannot decide how an authorized_keys CA line, server policy and certificate options combine.

Risk is negligible and maintenance low. Keep it as a **key/blob sanity check**, not the verdict.

## 6. Run the exact installed sshd under a temporary configuration

This is the first method that can give high fidelity to an arbitrary patched build without reproducing its source.

`sshd -d` uses the daemon itself in debug mode, stays in the foreground, does not fork and handles one connection; `-D` also prevents detaching. These properties are documented in the matching 10.5p1 man page. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/sshd.8)) You can launch the exact executable on a loopback-only high port with a temporary host key and temporary configuration.

A particularly useful way to inject the candidate without modifying the customer's authorized_keys is:

```text
AuthorizedKeysFile none
AuthorizedKeysCommand /root-owned/path/emit-candidate
AuthorizedKeysCommandUser dedicated-user
```

The 10.5p1 man page requires the command to be absolute, root-owned and not group/world-writable, and specifies that it writes authorized_keys-format lines. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5)) More importantly, the 10.5p1 source shows that stdout from `AuthorizedKeysCommand` is passed to **the same `auth_check_authkeys_file()` used for ordinary keys**, with the candidate key and connection's remote IP/hostname. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkey.c))

That gives you the exact installed parser and authorization code.

However, there are two substantially different tests you can perform against this daemon.

### Unsigned public-key query

SSH public-key authentication supports a request without a signature. In OpenSSH 10.5p1, the unsigned branch calls `mm_user_key_allowed()` on the key and sends `SSH2_MSG_USERAUTH_PK_OK` if the key is allowed. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkey.c)) The signed branch separately requires both `mm_user_key_allowed()` and a successful cryptographic signature check. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkey.c))

This is almost tailor-made for the panel's pre-write problem: you possess the public key but normally should not possess the customer's private key.

It proves that the **exact executable** recognizes the entry and authorizes that public key for the supplied user/address/time/certificate context. `user_key_allowed()` also rejects revoked keys before scanning sources. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkey.c)) `auth_check_authkey_line()` checks `from=`, expiration and certificate relationships before declaring a candidate key usable. For `from=`, the actual remote host and IP are passed through `match_host_and_ip()`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c))

It does **not** prove that the signature will work, that a FIDO authenticator will satisfy its requirements, that a multi-factor `AuthenticationMethods` chain completes, or that session restrictions are subsequently enforced.

**Experiment E6:** use a tiny SSH protocol test client or instrumented OpenSSH client to issue the `publickey` method with the signature-present flag false. Against the isolated sshd and candidate from its AuthorizedKeysCommand, observe `SSH2_MSG_USERAUTH_PK_OK`. Then send the same request with a deliberately invalid signature: the signed branch fails. This reproduces the exact distinction visible in the 10.5p1 source. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkey.c)) A second variant configures `AuthenticationMethods publickey,password`: the key can receive PK_OK while public-key authentication alone cannot complete the configured authentication sequence.

I would implement the unsigned probe at protocol/library level rather than make parsing `ssh -vvv` output part of the panel API.

### Signed login plus behavioral probes

If you possess a matching test private key, a complete authentication goes through signature verification and activates the returned key options. It is then possible to actually request a PTY, forwarding, a forced command, environment variables, agent/X11 forwarding or a tunnel.

That is the only general way to catch bugs in **enforcement**, such as the 10.4 `restrict`/TUN defect.

For arbitrary customer-supplied public keys you normally do not have the private half. You can substitute a panel-generated key while preserving the options field, which tests the option behavior but no longer proves key/certificate-specific properties of the original entry.

**Experiment E7:** emit
```text
restrict,command="/controlled/test-program" <panel-test-key>
````

````text

## 7. Loopback authentication against the live sshd

This executes the real production listener and therefore gets the real config, libraries, PAM/account policy, filesystem and running daemon. It is excellent evidence for the **particular loopback connection you made**.

It is nevertheless not a universally correct oracle. `from=` is explicitly evaluated using the actual remote host/IP. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c)) The same is true for address-dependent `Match` configuration, which `sshd -T -C` exists partly to model. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/sshd.8))

A straightforward wrong-answer case is:

```text
from="127.0.0.1" ssh-ed25519 AAAA...
```

**Experiment E8:** authenticate from `127.0.0.1`; then authenticate with the same credential from a second VM/network namespace with a non-loopback source. The former succeeds and the latter is denied by `auth_authorise_keyopts()`. Reverse the CIDR and a loopback test can become a false negative instead. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c))

Temporarily adding a generated root key to the production file is operationally worse: a crash can leave a credential behind, another administrator can race your edit, forced commands/PAM/audit hooks may run, and a session probe can alter the machine. Given that your customers already have root, the threat model is unusual, but your control panel still should not introduce an unnecessary long-lived credential.

## 8. AuthorizedKeysCommand as a “validator”

By itself, it is not one. It is merely another authorized-key **source**. The man page says it is tried after ordinary AuthorizedKeysFile files and isn't run if a matching key was already found there. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/sshd_config.5))

Changing a customer's production sshd configuration just to install a validator command would therefore be a poor fit. It changes production behavior and can be bypassed by an earlier file match.

Its value is as an **injection mechanism for the isolated exact-daemon experiment**. The source confirms that its stdout is parsed by the same authorization path, making it much better than inventing a separate parser. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkey.c))

A safe experiment helper should literally read the candidate from a root-controlled file descriptor/file and emit the bytes to stdout. Do not construct:

```sh
/bin/sh -c "printf '$USER_SUPPLIED_AUTHORIZED_KEYS'"
```

because values such as `command="..."` are untrusted text and must never acquire shell semantics in the validator machinery.

It also won't test `StrictModes` or the ownership/mode of the customer's actual authorized_keys path, because you have deliberately replaced that source.

## 9. An after-write unsigned probe to the production sshd

This deserves separate treatment from a full loopback login. After writing the real entry, an unsigned public-key query to the actual listener asks the real running sshd whether that **exact public key** is allowed in the connection context without possessing or using its private key.

The relevant 10.5p1 server branch calls `mm_user_key_allowed()` and returns PK_OK but does not verify a signature. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkey.c)) This is a strong post-write sanity check.

**Experiment E9:** write a valid entry, send the unsigned query and observe PK_OK. Change only the line to an unknown option and repeat: no PK_OK. Change it to `from="127.0.0.1"` and compare a loopback probe with a probe originating from the control panel's normal network path. The differing result is intentional and demonstrates that the answer is connection-context-specific.

Its side effects are much smaller than an authenticated session, but it is not completely inert: it is an authentication attempt, so expect logging and potentially rate/penalty mechanisms. It still cannot prove signature or session semantics.

## 10. Binary instrumentation and provenance

Hashing the running sshd executable, recording package provenance and `sshd` version are useful for caching results and choosing an explanatory parser. They are not validation themselves. With root customers, neither a package version nor upstream tag establishes that the binary wasn't replaced or patched.

You could attach a debugger, inject a library, trace functions with eBPF/uprobe machinery, or arrange to call internal functions inside the process. In principle that can observe the exact implementation. In practice it is much more dangerous than starting a private sshd: attaching to the production authentication daemon can perturb or crash it, crosses distro/kernel hardening boundaries, and is exceptionally version-dependent. I would reserve such methods for engineering diagnostics.

A useful maintenance technique is differential CI: for every supported upstream tag and important distro build, feed a corpus/fuzzer into your explanatory parser and into an isolated real sshd. That detects parser drift early, but it still is not a per-machine oracle.

---

## What “meaning” actually requires

Even after a line has been accepted, the options don't constitute an isolated policy language. In 10.5p1:

- `restrict` sets per-key forwarding/agent/X11/PTY/user-rc flags in the parser. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth-options.c))
- Runtime forwarding combines those flags with global forwarding policy. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/session.c))
- `command=` can be superseded by server `ForceCommand`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/session.c))
- `from=` is evaluated against connection address/hostname and can reject a perfectly parseable key. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c))
- `expiry-time` is checked against `time(NULL)`, so acceptance changes over time without the file changing. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c))
- Certificate options are separately parsed/authorized and merged with the authorized_keys options, so the meaning of a CA line cannot always be established from that line alone. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_5_P1/auth2-pubkeyfile.c))

The 10.4→10.5 `restrict` fix demonstrates that even understanding all those fields from the parser does not guarantee that runtime enforcement has no bug. ([OpenSSH](https://www.openssh.org/txt/release-10.5))

## Recommendation after comparing the methods

There is **no single method that can, in general, prove both “this exact entry will authenticate” and “every option will have its intended production effect” without actually exercising the relevant authentication/session behavior in an equivalent production context**. In particular, if you do not possess the customer's private credential, full signed-authentication fidelity is impossible; and address-dependent options make a loopback result inherently contextual.

For a control panel, I would use a layered result rather than one “valid/invalid” boolean:

1. **Use the installed binary as the authority.** Record the actual executable/hash and use `sshd -T -C ...` to obtain the effective configuration for the intended user/address context. Version/package information is advisory and useful for explanations/cache invalidation, not proof.
2. **For pre-write acceptance, launch the exact installed sshd in a tightly isolated one-connection configuration and inject the exact candidate through AuthorizedKeysCommand. Send an unsigned public-key query for the exact key.** This is the best combination of exact-build fidelity, no need for customer private keys, and avoiding modification of the real authorized_keys.
3. **Maintain a parser/model for explanations, not authority.** Use it to turn the accepted line plus effective configuration into statements such as “PTY denied”, “TCP forwarding limited to…”, or “only valid from…”. Test that model differentially against real OpenSSH builds.
4. **For options whose actual enforcement matters, use isolated signed behavioral probes with a disposable panel-controlled key carrying the same option string.** This is especially warranted for forwarding, TUN, forced-command, PTY, environment and future options whose semantics extend outside the parsing code. Mark this as an option-semantics test, not proof about the customer's original cryptographic credential.
5. **After writing, optionally issue an unsigned query to the production listener using the original public key.** This gives a very strong “the running daemon currently authorizes this key from this source/context” check without inserting another private credential or opening a session.
6. Expose the evidence level to the customer: e.g. **“parsed by exact daemon”**, **“authorized for simulated source 203.0.113.x”**, **“authorized by running production daemon from panel source”**, **“signed authentication tested”**, and **“session restrictions actively verified.”** That is more accurate than pretending OpenSSH exposes a comprehensive authorized_keys lint mode.

I would specifically **not** make `sshd -t/-T`, `ssh-keygen`, a version-keyed parser, or a temporary production root key the authoritative validator. The first three provably miss classes of failures; the last obtains fidelity by taking considerably more operational/security risk than the isolated-daemon + unsigned-query design.
````

```text
The first important distinction is already clear: **“the IP address” must not be the durable identity**. ## Conclusion

For a control plane that manages customer-owned VPSs, the safest model is:

**Bind SSH trust to a durable control-plane instance identity, not to an IP address; pin the initial host identity through an authenticated bootstrap path; fail closed on unexplained changes; and provide a separate authenticated re-enrolment mechanism for reinstalls or loss of the old host key.**

That distinction—**rotation with continuity** versus **re-enrolment after continuity is lost**—is fundamental. SSH itself cannot determine whether an unexpected new key means “the customer reinstalled” or “an attacker now owns this IP/path.” RFC 4253 explicitly says the client must verify that the presented host key really belongs to the server, for example using a certificate or local database; accepting it without verification makes SSH insecure against active attacks. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4253.html))

The current upstream release as of September 2026 is OpenSSH **10.5/10.5p1, released August 11, 2026**; the OpenSSH behavior below refers specifically to its 10.5p1 documentation. ([OpenSSH](https://www.openssh.com/releasenotes.html))

### Threat model first

A host key authenticates an SSH endpoint. It does **not** establish that the operating system is trustworthy. In your scenario the customer legitimately has root, so they can replace `sshd`, replace every host key, modify any agent you installed, or deliberately run a hostile SSH service. Your control plane therefore needs to answer a narrower question:

> “Is this SSH endpoint the endpoint currently authorized to represent control-plane resource X?”

The IP address is unsuitable for that purpose. Google Cloud's security documentation makes exactly the relevant point: VM names and IP addresses can be reassigned or reused, and attackers can exploit such reassignment to impersonate a VM. It recommends obtaining host keys through a trusted side channel before the first SSH connection. ([Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/connect/ssh-best-practices/credentials?authuser=6))

I would make the authoritative identifier something like:

`provider / account / resource_id / incarnation`

where `incarnation` changes when a deleted resource is recreated, and perhaps on a destructive reinstall depending on your semantics. IP addresses are merely current routing attributes of that identity.

## Methods compared

| Method | What it prevents | Legitimate host-key change | How trust returns | Operational cost | Important counterexample |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Authenticated pinning at creation** | First-connection MITM and IP-reuse attacks, provided the registration channel really identifies the new instance | Unexpected SSH connection fails | New key must be authenticated through old trusted state or independent re-enrolment | **Low–medium** | If pins are indexed only by IP, deleting A and assigning its IP to B breaks the identity model |
| **TOFU / `accept-new`** | MITM *after* an uncompromised first connection | Changed key is rejected | Human/admin removes old pin and accepts a new one | **Low initially; high incident toil** | Attacker present at the first connection gets permanently pinned |
| **OpenSSH host certificates / CA** | MITM and IP reuse without storing every host key, if CA issues correct principals | New host key simply gets another valid host certificate | Sign new key after authenticated enrolment | **Medium/high setup; low steady-state** | Compromised CA, or an enrolment service allowing a VM to request somebody else's principal, compromises the model |
| **DNSSEC + SSHFP** | First-use MITM when DNSSEC validation is trustworthy | Securely replace/add SSHFP | Secure DNS update; overlap old/new during planned rotation | **Medium–high** | Unsigned SSHFP is not a trust anchor; RFC 4255 explicitly says not to trust it |
| **Provider console/API fingerprint** | Network MITM and IP reuse, assuming lookup is against expected provider instance identity | Obtain new fingerprint from same authenticated provider channel | Operator or automation approves provider-observed replacement | **Low–medium, provider-specific** | Comparing the SSH prompt with `ssh-keyscan` over the same attacked network gives no independent evidence |
| **Guest metadata / guest attributes** | External network attacker if provider API associates data with expected resource | Guest republishes new key | Query provider API again | **Low, cloud-specific** | On GCP, *any process in the VM* can write guest attributes; therefore it does not protect against a malicious/compromised guest |
| **Signed cloud instance identity + enrolment protocol** | Strongly binds re-enrolment to a provider resource | New key submitted during authenticated enrolment | Verify cloud identity plus challenge and bind that proof to the key | **Medium engineering effort; strong option** | Verifying an instance token and receiving a host key in separate, unbound transactions allows substitution/replay |
| **`UpdateHostKeys`** | Safe *planned* key transition while an existing trusted key remains | Old server advertises replacements over authenticated SSH | Automatic | **Very low** | Does not solve a reinstall where every old private key vanished |
| **`ssh-keyscan` alone** | Essentially nothing against an on-path adversary | Re-scan obtains whatever answers | None securely | **Very low** | OpenSSH explicitly warns an interceptor can substitute its own key |

### 1. Pinning at creation: the right baseline

Your existing creation procedure is already a strong foundation. If the freshly booted instance generates its host key and sends its public key or fingerprint to the panel over a channel that the panel has independently authenticated as belonging to *that exact resource*, store that binding.

For automated SSH, use `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes`. OpenSSH 10.5p1 documents that this mode never automatically adds a new host key and refuses hosts whose key changed; OpenSSH describes it as providing its maximum MITM protection. By contrast, `accept-new` automatically records previously unseen hosts but still rejects changed keys, while `no`/`off` can permit changed keys subject to restrictions. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/ssh_config.5))

Do not key that database as:

`203.0.113.12 → key K`

Use something conceptually closer to:

`instance-7f32, generation 4 → {K1, K2}`
```

```text
and separately:

`instance-7f32 → current IP 203.0.113.12`.

OpenSSH's `HostKeyAlias` is useful here: 10.5p1 explicitly lets an alias replace the real hostname when looking up/saving host keys and when validating host certificates. Thus the panel can connect to a changing or reusable IP while verifying a stable synthetic identity such as `vps-7f32-g4.internal.example`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/ssh_config.5))

For a centrally managed registry, either generate an ephemeral `known_hosts` file for each job, or use `KnownHostsCommand`. OpenSSH 10.5p1 permits that command to emit normal known-host lines dynamically, and terminates the connection if the command fails abnormally. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/ssh_config.5))

**Counterexample:** if a machine is deleted, its IP returns to the pool, and your software deletes the corresponding known-host entry and then uses TOFU on the next machine at that IP, you have discarded the main security property your authenticated creation channel gave you.

### 2. TOFU is useful for humans, weak for a control plane

TOFU solves a different problem: “I don't currently know the server key, but remember the first one I see.”

It protects subsequent connections if the first connection was genuine. It does not authenticate the first connection. Google explicitly calls out that a MITM on first use can cause the client to trust the wrong VM. ([Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/connect/ssh-best-practices/credentials?authuser=6))

`StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new` is a reasonable OpenSSH implementation of automatic TOFU: new destinations are added, changed keys are rejected. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/ssh_config.5))

For your service, it is inferior to creation-time pinning because you already possess a better trust source.

**Counterexample:** attacker controls routing during the first management connection. The control plane TOFUs the attacker's key. Thereafter it will faithfully reject the real server.

A subtler VPS-pool counterexample is IP reuse: removing the old IP's pin because “the old VPS no longer exists” and then automatically TOFUing the new occupant turns every reassignment into another vulnerable first-use event.

### 3. Host certificates are the cleanest solution at fleet scale

OpenSSH host certificates replace a large collection of individually trusted host keys with trust in one or more host CAs. In OpenSSH 10.5p1 a certificate contains a public key, identity information, principals and options, signed by a CA; clients can trust the CA instead of every host key individually. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/ssh-keygen.1))

The control plane can place an `@cert-authority` entry in its trusted-host database; OpenSSH's known-host format explicitly supports this marker. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/sshd.8))

The critical design point is the **principal**. Do not issue a certificate merely saying “this key is valid somewhere in the VPS fleet.” Give it a principal such as:

`vps-7f32-g4.hosts.example`

OpenSSH host certificates encode hostnames as principals, and `HostKeyAlias` can supply the name against which the certificate is validated. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/ssh-keygen.1))

When the customer regenerates a host key, there is no client-side pin update: the new key gets a new host certificate for the same authorized principal.

But certificates do **not eliminate enrolment**. They move it to the signer. The CA/signing service must establish that the requester is entitled to `vps-7f32-g4` before signing its new key.

**Counterexample:** suppose any VPS can call `POST /sign-host-key` with `principal=vps-1234`. Then compromising one customer's VPS lets it obtain a certificate for another customer's machine. Cryptography is working perfectly; authorization is broken.

The operational trade-off is favorable at scale but increases blast radius. Protect host-CA private keys in an HSM/KMS or isolated signing service, issue short-lived certificates where feasible, log issuance, and tightly constrain principal issuance. A CA compromise can impersonate every principal in its scope.

Teleport provides a useful production example of the lifecycle. Its documented CA rotation is phased: create a new CA, move clients into a state trusting the transition, update servers/certificates, and eventually retire the old CA; its current documentation exposes an `update_clients` phase specifically for that dual-trust transition. ([Teleport](https://goteleport.com/docs/zero-trust-access/management/security/ca-rotation/))

### 4. SSHFP works, but only with authenticated DNS

RFC 4255 defines publishing SSH host-key fingerprints as DNS `SSHFP` records. Its security requirement is unusually explicit: a host key verified by SSHFP **must not be trusted if the SSHFP record was not authenticated by a trusted DNSSEC signature**. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4255.html))

RFC 6594 defines fingerprint type 2 as SHA-256 and says SSHFP implementations supporting SHA-256 must prefer it to SHA-1. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6594.html))

With DNSSEC and a stable machine name, this can provide secure first-use discovery. For a planned rotation, publish fingerprints for both old and new keys, deploy the new key, wait through DNS caches as necessary, then withdraw the old record.

For an unplanned reinstall, however, something still has to authorize the DNS update. You've simply moved the re-enrolment problem into your DNS-management path.

RFC 4255 also says that without comparison against a fingerprint obtained over a secured channel, the connection remains MITM-vulnerable; overall SSHFP security depends in part on the SSH and DNS administrators transferring the fingerprint securely. ([RFC Editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4255.html))

**Counterexample:** publish an unsigned SSHFP record and configure clients to accept it. An attacker who can spoof DNS can spoof the fingerprint and SSH endpoint together.

Operationally, SSHFP is attractive if you already operate signed DNS correctly. Introducing DNSSEC solely for internal VPS host-key management is often more complex than a direct registry or CA.

### 5. Provider console output and metadata make good independent channels

A provider's authenticated control plane is a natural second trust root because it knows the cloud resource independently of SSH routing.

AWS documents retrieving an EC2 instance's SSH host-key fingerprint from its console output and comparing that value with the SSH client's prompt; AWS says a mismatch may indicate MITM. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/connection-prereqs-general.html))

The useful security property is not “console text” itself. It is:

**authenticated AWS account → exact EC2 instance ID → that instance's console output → fingerprint.**

This defeats the IP-reuse problem because the query identifies the expected resource, not merely whoever owns the current IP.

**Counterexample:** run `ssh-keyscan 203.0.113.12`, see key X, then compare it with the SSH prompt from `203.0.113.12`. Both observations traversed the same attackable path, so they are not independent. OpenSSH 10.5p1 expressly warns that `ssh-keyscan` cannot verify authenticity and that an interceptor can substitute keys; its output should be verified out of band or used directly only on a trusted network. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openssh/openssh-portable/V_10_5_P1/ssh-keyscan.1))

### 6. AWS demonstrates explicit re-enrolment rather than auto-accept

AWS's EC2 Instance Connect browser client has a particularly relevant behavior. AWS says that if you rotate an instance's host keys, **the new keys are not automatically uploaded to the AWS trusted-host-key database**, causing host-key validation to fail. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/TroubleshootingInstancesConnecting.html))

AWS's documented recovery is to run `eic_harvest_hostkeys` on the instance to upload the new host keys, after which browser-based Instance Connect works again. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/TroubleshootingInstancesConnecting.html))

That is a valuable design precedent: unexpected replacement produces failure, followed by an explicit mechanism that re-establishes the binding. AWS does not solve legitimate rotation by saying “host keys change sometimes, so accept whatever appears.”

### 7. Google Cloud uses a provider back channel—but note its trust boundary

Google's documentation goes further and explicitly recommends obtaining a host key through a trusted side channel. Compute Engine can expose host keys through guest attributes so tooling can obtain them through Google's API before opening SSH. ([Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/connect/ssh-best-practices/credentials?authuser=6))

That helps significantly against an external MITM or recycled IP. But its internal threat model is weaker than a hardware/provider-generated attestation: Google documents that **any process running in the VM can write guest attributes, even without sudo**, although outside users cannot write them. ([Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/metadata/manage-guest-attributes))

So guest attributes answer:

> “What host key is software inside this particular Google VM advertising?”

They do not answer:

> “Has the customer-controlled OS remained trustworthy?”

For your customer-root model that may be perfectly acceptable—you already allow the customer to control the guest—but you should document the boundary.

Interestingly, the `gcloud compute ssh` command itself documents a default of `StrictHostKeyChecking=no` on the first connection and `yes` on subsequent ones. ([Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/ssh)) That default should not be copied blindly into an unattended high-privilege control plane, particularly when you possess a stronger authenticated registration path.

### 8. Signed provider identity is an excellent re-enrolment primitive

A robust approach after reinstall is to make the fresh guest prove its cloud-resource identity independently of its SSH key.

Google Compute Engine can issue a Google-signed VM identity JWT. Google documents that the token confirms instance identity, expires within an hour, can be treated as single-use by the receiver, and contains fields including project, zone, instance ID and creation timestamp. ([Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/verifying-instance-identity?authuser=0&hl=en))

AWS likewise supplies an EC2 instance identity document, and AWS documents verifying its signatures using AWS public certificates to establish the document's origin and authenticity. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/us_en/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/instance-identity-documents.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
```

```text
## Executive conclusion

There are four materially different models in the market:

| Model | Examples | Who is authoritative? | Treatment of manual guest edits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Provisioning-only keys** | DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Linode/Akamai, OVHcloud, Vultr | The VM | Provider deliberately does not synchronize account keys into an existing VM. Users edit `authorized_keys` themselves. |
| **One-shot guest mutation** | Azure VMAccess; broadly Forge/Ploi/RunCloud | The VM after the operation | Control plane asks something inside/with access to the VM to add/remove a key. There generally is no continuous desired-state reconciliation. |
| **Continuously reconciled external desired state** | Google metadata SSH keys | Metadata/control plane | Guest agent writes the control-plane state into `authorized_keys`; direct edits to managed files can be overwritten. |
| **Authenticate at login without persistent `authorized_keys` entries** | AWS EC2 Instance Connect, Google OS Login, Fly.io | IAM/access service at login time | Local `authorized_keys` is either an independent second path or not part of the managed mechanism at all. |

For a VPS product whose **instance must remain the source of truth**, the closest precedents are **Azure VMAccess plus the server-management products**, not Google metadata SSH keys or OS Login. The strongest VPS providers go further: DigitalOcean and Hetzner explicitly refuse to pretend that an account-level SSH-key list is synchronized with an existing root-controlled machine. ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/extensions/vmaccess-linux?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

# AWS

### EC2 Instance Connect

**Mechanism.** EC2 Instance Connect does **not normally append the customer's key to `authorized_keys`**. `SendSSHPublicKey` puts the public key into EC2 instance metadata for **60 seconds**. On the VM, the EC2 Instance Connect package configures OpenSSH's `AuthorizedKeysCommand`; when `sshd` authenticates the user, AWS's helper retrieves and validates the temporary key from IMDS. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-instance-connect-tutorial.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The official package source is unusually useful here. AWS documents three components: `eic_run_authorized_keys`, `eic_curl_authorized_keys`, and `eic_parse_authorized_keys`; the wrapper enforces a five-second timeout so a broken metadata lookup does not indefinitely block `sshd`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/aws/aws-ec2-instance-connect-config?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) The Debian installer adds an `AuthorizedKeysCommand` override but contains checks intended to avoid trampling an already configured `AuthorizedKeysCommand`/service override. ([GitHub](https://github.com/aws/aws-ec2-instance-connect-config/blob/master/debian/postinst?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Post-creation.** Yes, inherently. A new ephemeral key can be pushed for any connection; there is no need to have chosen that public key at instance creation. It expires from metadata after 60 seconds, although an already established SSH session persists. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/us_en/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-instance-connect-methods.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Options exposed.** The documented interface selects the instance, OS username and public key. AWS does **not expose first-class OpenSSH per-key restriction fields** such as `command=`, `from=`, `restrict`, `no-pty`, or forwarding controls.

**Manual guest edits.** Ordinary local `authorized_keys` entries remain a separate OpenSSH authentication path. Editing them does not update IAM/EIC state. Conversely, changing `sshd_config`, replacing the `AuthorizedKeysCommand`, disabling the helper, or breaking IMDS access can disable EC2 Instance Connect even though the EC2 control plane still permits `SendSSHPublicKey`. The package's source specifically reflects awareness of `AuthorizedKeysCommand` conflicts. ([GitHub](https://github.com/aws/aws-ec2-instance-connect-config/blob/master/debian/postinst?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Failures/recovery.** Control-plane failures appear as EC2 Instance Connect/API or client errors; guest lookup failures are `sshd`/helper-side failures. AWS's helper intentionally fast-fails on metadata trouble. There is no “merge conflict” UI because EIC is not reconciling a persistent guest file. A separate recovery route is Systems Manager when configured, or EC2's other console/recovery facilities.

### Systems Manager Session Manager

This is important because AWS deliberately offers an access system that is **not SSH-key management at all**. Native Session Manager uses SSM Agent plus IAM to provide an interactive shell without opening inbound ports or maintaining SSH keys. IAM is the access authority; SSM Agent creates the bidirectional channel. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
```

## Assistant · 2026-09-15T01:53:15.169Z

Read them. Here's what they settle, and what they change.

## 1. Is our add-key flow standard?

Yes, but it puts us in a specific camp. The provider comparison found four models:

| Model | Who does it | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| **Provisioning-only keys** | DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Linode, OVH, Vultr | The machine. They *deliberately refuse* to change keys after creation |
| **One-shot guest mutation** | Azure VMAccess, Laravel Forge, Ploi, RunCloud | The machine, after each edit |
| **Continuously reconciled state** | Google metadata keys | The control plane; it overwrites the file |
| **Authenticate at login, no file entries** | AWS Instance Connect, GCP OS Login, Fly | An access service |

We are the second: connect with our own key, edit the file, done. That is exactly Azure VMAccess and the server-management products, and it is the only model compatible with "the server is the source of truth". The third would make us overwrite what customers do by hand, and the fourth needs an agent or a lookup hook installed in the guest.

Worth knowing: Hetzner and DigitalOcean **choose not to do this at all** — they won't pretend an account key list matches a root-controlled machine. We are doing the thing they avoid, honestly, by reading the file live every time instead of keeping a copy.

## 2. Expiry, rotation, and the prompt: two different clocks

They are separate, and only one of them is short:

- **The enrollment token in the prompt** is short-lived and single-use. It authorizes adding one key. Once the agent has used it, it is spent, and it expires on its own if nobody does.
- **The key it adds has no expiry by default.** It sits in the file until somebody removes it. Nothing to refresh, nothing to rotate, no background machinery.

So the default flow is frictionless: copy prompt → agent adds its key → connected forever, until you revoke it by removing the entry.

If you *want* time-limited access, OpenSSH has it natively: `expiry-time="…"` on the entry, enforced by sshd whether or not we are reachable. That is one optional field on the add form (and one optional checkbox in the agent flow: "this access expires in 24 hours"). Not a default, not a knob anyone must touch.

The research adds one caution for display: a date-only `expiry-time` means midnight at the *start* of that day, and without a `Z` suffix it uses the server's timezone. We serialize UTC with `Z` and show both.

## 3. Certificates versus what we are building

|  | Keys in the file (us) | Certificates |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | None | A CA, one `@cert-authority` line trusted on each machine, and an issuing service |
| Granting | Write one line — needs the machine reachable | Sign a certificate — no contact with the machine |
| Revoking | Remove the line — needs the machine reachable | Stop issuing (takes effect at expiry), or publish a revocation list |
| Expiry | Optional per entry, native | Inherent: short lifetimes are the point |
| Client friction | Paste a public key once, then plain `ssh` | Each person fetches a fresh certificate into their agent, repeatedly |
| If we cannot reach the machine | Cannot grant or revoke | Can still grant; revocation happens by expiry |
| Blast radius | One line, one key | A compromised CA impersonates every machine in its scope |
| Customer can undo it | Removes the line | Removes the CA line |

Two things I got wrong earlier and should correct: we *do* have real expiry (native `expiry-time`) and real revocation (we edit the file). What certificates add is that neither operation needs the machine to be reachable, and that access is short-lived by default.

The research's judgement matches: certificates win at fleet scale and cost a real enrolment problem of their own (the signer must prove the requester owns that principal before signing, or one compromised machine gets a certificate for someone else's). For us they are **additive later** — a CA is one more native line in the same file we already edit.

## 4. Codex round two

All four findings are real. Two fixed, two accepted with reasons (`4a234d2`):

- **Fixed — the locale bug (P1).** Genuinely dangerous: SFTP addresses paths as UTF-8 while Python encodes them with the locale, so on a non-UTF-8 locale we could read one file and write a different one. The helper now runs in UTF-8 mode, so both encode identically.
- **Fixed — the staging file after a signal (P3).** The cleanup now unlinks before any close, so a signal during cleanup cannot leave a full copy of the candidate behind.
- **Accepted — the concurrent-write window (P1).** This one is the documented model, not a slip: `decisions.md` already says the write is "not compare-and-swap against independent editors". `flock` is advisory, so nothing we do on Linux can exclude a person editing the file by hand at that exact moment; the alternative is a lock protocol the customer's own tools would have to honour, which contradicts "the server is the source of truth". What I will do is state the consequence plainly in the docs, including that we restore the metadata we observed, so a permission change made in that window is reverted.
- **Accepted — extended attributes the helper cannot see (P2).** Reproducing it needed a non-root helper; we always connect as root, where `trusted.*` attributes are visible. Worth a line in the docs, not a change.

Also noted: you deleted the parser test, so `bun test` currently has nothing to run.

## 5. S1, accounts and files: settled

The report kills the naive version ("read `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`") in several ways at once. `AuthorizedKeysFile` can list several patterns with globs and `%h %u %U` tokens, can be `none`, and the default is actually two files. So:

**What we do per server, in one session:**
1. Find the listener (`ss -H -ltnp`, then `/proc/<pid>/exe` and `cmdline`) so we use *that* binary and *its* config arguments, not an assumed `/usr/sbin/sshd`.
2. `getent passwd` for accounts, marked "enumeration may be incomplete" (directory backends need not enumerate).
3. For each account, run that binary with `-T -C user=…,addr=…,laddr=…,lport=…` — passing only user/host/addr gives wrong answers when the config has `Match LocalPort`, which is a one-line counterexample in the report.
4. Expand the tokens, glob as the account, and stat the results.

**What we show, and never overstate:**
- Real key files, each marked readable / unsafe permissions / absent (StrictModes checks the whole parent path, not just the file).
- `AuthorizedKeysCommand` shown as a **dynamic source, not enumerable** — it can answer differently per key, address and time, and we must never run it just to fill a list.
- Certificate sources (`TrustedUserCAKeys`, principals files) shown separately: an account with no key lines can still be fully usable.
- Two separate flags instead of one: *public-key authentication is enabled* and *a key alone completes login* (`AuthenticationMethods publickey,password` breaks the second).
- `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password` still allows key login — an easy thing to get backwards.
- An executable `/usr/sbin/nologin` shell passes authentication and then kills the session, so "can authenticate" and "gets a shell" are reported separately.
- Every answer is labelled **"config on disk, as parsed now"**, because the running daemon keeps its own copy until it is reloaded.

**V1 scope:** we edit *file* sources. Dynamic and certificate sources are shown, explained, and left alone.

## 6. S2, validation: settled, and it is layered

There is no lint mode for `authorized_keys`. `sshd -t`/`-T` do not look at the file at all, and `ssh-keygen -l` happily fingerprints a line whose options sshd will reject. Cloning the parser is a maintenance trap: OpenSSH 10.5 (August 2026) *fixed* `restrict` so it finally restricts tunnel forwarding, so a clone matching 10.4's documentation would have been confidently wrong about a real machine.

So, three layers, each with an honest label:

1. **Before writing:** our own parser must be able to represent the entry losslessly, and `ssh-keygen -l` on the target machine proves the key blob parses with *its* OpenSSH. We claim nothing about the options.
2. **After writing: an unsigned public-key query to the running daemon.** SSH lets a client ask "would you accept this public key?" without a signature and without the private key. The real listener answers with its real config, its real file, its real permissions. This is the strongest check available to us and it needs nothing installed. It is context-specific — a `from=` entry can answer differently for our address than for the customer's — so the result is labelled with the source we probed from.
3. **Explanations,** from our parser plus the effective config: "PTY blocked by this entry", "server policy may restrict this further".

Explicitly not doing: starting a second sshd on a customer machine with an `AuthorizedKeysCommand` (highest fidelity, far too invasive for V1), and signed behavioural probes (needs a private key we do not have).

One thing to verify before I build layer 2: whether `ssh2` can send a signature-less publickey request, or whether that needs a few lines at the protocol level. I'll find out from the library, not from a model.

## 7. S5, host key changes: settled

Our current design already matches the best practice — pin at creation through an authenticated channel, and key the pin to the **allocation**, never to the IP, which is what stops a recycled address from impersonating a deleted server.

The rest follows:
- **A changed host key fails closed, always.** No trust-on-first-use, ever, and no "ssh-keyscan and compare" — both observations travel the same attackable path.
- **Legitimate changes need an explicit re-enrolment**, exactly as AWS does it (a changed key breaks Instance Connect until you run `eic_harvest_hostkeys` on the instance). Ours is the mechanism we already have: mint a **new short-lived bootstrap token** and give the user one command to run on their machine, which posts the new host key to the same endpoint. They prove control by being able to run it. A rebuild is the other path, since cloud-init pins afresh.
- **Hetzner gives us no signed instance identity** (AWS and GCP do), so the user-run command is the practical re-enrolment, not a provider attestation.
- **Free win available later:** OpenSSH's `UpdateHostKeys` lets a server hand us its new host keys over the already-authenticated channel, which covers planned rotation with no user action. Worth adding if `ssh2` supports the request.

## What I'll build next

The SSH slice, backend only: discovery as above, list, add, update, remove — one blanket keys permission, no presets, all native options accepted, every answer labelled with what it does and does not prove. Then the re-enrolment mutation for S5.

**Decisions I need before writing it:**
1. **V1 edits file sources only** (dynamic and certificate sources shown, not editable) — agreed?
2. **The post-write unsigned probe** is part of the first version, not a later addition — agreed?
3. **Re-enrolment by user-run command** (new short-lived token), with rebuild as the other path — agreed?

## Next prompt

The parser is what the entire feature rests on, and the format report gives an exact standard to check it against:
