53	| [Google, Software Engineering at Google: Testing Overview](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html), March 2020 | **Engineering handbook / stated Google practice** | The “Beyoncé Rule”: test every behavior you do not want to break. But think in **behaviors**, not coverage percentages. | Code review, static analysis, human exploratory testing, larger tests, canaries and monitoring. Google explicitly warns that a bad/brittle suite can be worse than none. ([Abseil](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html)) |
54	| [SQLite, How SQLite Is Tested](https://www3.sqlite.org/testing.html), current page; figures mostly snapshot SQLite 3.42.0, 16 May 2023 | **Project policy + project-reported quantitative data** | SQLite core maintains 100% branch coverage and MC/DC and adds a regression test for every reported bug. | Assertions, fuzzing, fault injection, mutation testing, static/dynamic analysis, independent harnesses and release checklists. SQLite explicitly says this level of effort is probably not cost-effective for a typical application. ([SQLite](https://www3.sqlite.org/testing.html)) |
55	| [OpenSSL Testing Policy](https://openssl-library.org/policies/technical/testing/), current policy accessed 15 Sep 2026 | **Explicit project policy** | New functionality and fixes to functional behavior require tests. | Refactoring, performance changes, comments, internal naming and several other categories **do not require new tests**. A test may also be exempted when its cost is disproportionate. The exemption is visible and reviewed. ([OpenSSL Library](https://openssl-library.org/policies/technical/testing/)) |
56	| [LLVM Testing Infrastructure Guide](https://llvm.org/docs/TestingGuide.html), current guide accessed 15 Sep 2026 | **Explicit project guidance** | Compiler transformations and analyses are primarily covered by small regression tests; bugs normally get a minimized reproducer. | LLVM deliberately reserves unit tests mainly for support libraries and generic data structures rather than unit-testing every compiler component. ([LLVM](https://llvm.org/docs/TestingGuide.html)) |
57	| [GitLab Testing Strategy](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/testing_guide/testing_strategy/), current docs accessed 15 Sep 2026 | **Explicit project strategy** | Start at the lowest useful level; test important behavior without duplicating evidence. | “Every test should earn its keep”; unreliable tests should be fixed or deleted. If unit/feature/integration coverage is sufficient, GitLab explicitly says an E2E test is unnecessary. ([GitLab Docs](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/testing_guide/testing_strategy/)) |
58	| [curl, Verify](https://curl.se/docs/verify.html), current docs accessed 15 Sep 2026 | **Stated project practice** | Ideally each functionality is tested, with extensive failure-path testing. | Human review, complexity limits intended to keep code readable, compiler warnings as errors, static analysis, sanitizers, Valgrind, fuzzing, reproducible releases. curl acknowledges that its billions of build configurations make exhaustive testing impossible. The project says no code change bypasses proof validation. ([seL4](https://sel4.org/About/fact-sheet.html)) |

61	So there are strong, reputable counterexamples to a literal “test everything” policy. OpenSSL is perhaps the cleanest one: it writes the distinction into governance. A refactor need not come with a new test merely because code changed, and even a behavioral test can be explicitly exempted on cost grounds. LLVM makes a different distinction: it certainly tests heavily, but says **the right unit of testing for compiler transformations is normally a regression example, not a unit test of each implementation object**. GitLab goes further in explicitly treating duplicate tests as waste.
62	
63	That is materially different from simply having poor coverage.
64	
65	## The high-coverage argument
66	
67	There are two somewhat different versions.
68	
69	Google's 2020 handbook is close to “cover all important behavior,” but decidedly **not** “hit every line.” Its rule is that if a property matters, there should be an automated check for that property. Google explicitly argues against a numerical coverage target: executing a line says nothing about whether the test made a meaningful assertion, and an 80% target can readily turn into an 80% ceiling. ([Abseil](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html))
70	
71	The motivation is mostly **change over time**. Google says a piece of code may be modified dozens of times, including by other teams and automated tools; a test written by the original author becomes shared executable knowledge for all those later editors. Its unit-testing chapter therefore says the ideal test changes only when the required behavior changes: a pure refactoring should not require test edits, while a bug fix should normally add the previously missing regression case. ([Abseil](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html))
72	
73	Google gives one piece of **self-reported operational data**, rather than a controlled experiment. Its Web Server project had reached a point around 2005 where, according to the handbook, more than 80% of production pushes contained user-affecting bugs requiring rollback. After requiring new changes to carry automated tests and continuously running them, emergency pushes reportedly halved within a year despite increasing change volume. That is suggestive before/after operational evidence, but many things could have changed at the same time; it is not causal experimental evidence. ([Abseil](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html))
74	
75	SQLite represents a more literal high-coverage position. Its current documentation reports 100% branch coverage of core SQLite in the deployed configuration, MC/DC coverage, millions of cases, simulated OOM and I/O failures, crash testing, fuzzing and thousands of assertions. For the 3.42.0 snapshot, SQLite reported about 155.8 KSLOC of library code versus 92,053.1 KSLOC of test code/scripts—about 590 times as much. Those are **project-reported quantitative data**, not an independent measurement. ([SQLite](https://www3.sqlite.org/testing.html))
76	
77	Its reasoning is illuminating: SQLite says full coverage lets developers make substantial changes with confidence that unrelated branches have not silently changed. But the same page says maintaining 100% MC/DC is laborious and “probably not cost effective” for a normal application; SQLite considers it justified because it is extraordinarily widely deployed infrastructure and a database can preserve the consequences of an old bug indefinitely. ([SQLite](https://www3.sqlite.org/testing.html))
78	
79	Robert C. Martin states the stronger philosophical version. In his 6 March 2017 article [“Testing Like the TSA”](https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2017/03/06/TestingLikeTheTSA.html), he argues that 100% should be an **asymptotic goal** and that there is no principled lower number at which one should stop trying to increase coverage. He also says roughly 1:1 production-to-test LOC feels appropriate. That is **commentator opinion**, not empirical evidence. Interestingly, even Martin says there is generally no reason to retest trusted framework functionality, which shows that “high coverage” still involves decisions about where responsibility resides. ([Clean Coder Blog](https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2017/03/06/TestingLikeTheTSA.html))
80	
81	What this school buys is durable, machine-readable memory. The original programmer can leave, comments can rot and reviewers can misunderstand the implementation, but a well-chosen behavior test continues objecting when that behavior changes.
82	
83	Its characteristic failure is **false contracts**. If tests pin implementation details, mock call sequences or incidental output rather than externally meaningful behavior, they make legitimate change expensive. Google's own handbook describes this as a serious problem: brittle tests can make teams afraid to refactor, and Google specifically reports trouble from excessive mocking. ([Abseil](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html))
84	
85	And coverage itself is not the cure. A suite can execute every line while checking the wrong things.
86	
87	## The deliberately-selective argument
88	
89	David Heinemeier Hansson is one of the clearest proponents. His 11 April 2012 [“Testing like the TSA”](https://signalvnoise.com/posts/3159-testing-like-the-tsa.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) explicitly says not to aim for 100% and argues that tests have writing, reading and maintenance costs, so preventing sufficiently improbable or cheap bugs can cost more than the bugs. He says the hard skill is deciding what **not** to test. That is **commentator opinion**.
90	
91	His practice was not “no tests.” In January 2012 he described his approach as “less testing than the average”: test things with enough logic to be worthwhile, and let functional/integration testing cover the rest rather than directly testing trivial framework declarations. ([Signal v. Noise](https://signalvnoise.com/posts/3094-code-statistics-for-basecamp-next)) His 2014 Basecamp write-up reported a model suite with 3,333 assertions, all hitting the real database, and a whole suite taking about 4½ minutes with roughly a 1:1 test/code ratio. Those are **self-reported practice data**; they show that his dispute was substantially about *granularity, duplication, isolation and architecture*, not an absence of automated tests. ([DHH](https://dhh.dk/2014/slow-database-test-fallacy.html))
92	
93	His 29 April 2014 [“Test-induced design damage”](https://dhh.dk/2014/test-induced-design-damage.html) makes the deeper argument relevant to your stated philosophy: code can become **less clear** if it acquires repositories, interfaces, command objects and mocks primarily so that everything can be unit-tested in isolation. His preference is to let system design determine test boundaries: intricate model logic gets direct tests, controllers can be integration-tested and UI behavior system-tested. Clarity of production code comes before the convenience of isolated tests. Again, this is a **commentator's position**, not data. ([DHH](https://dhh.dk/2014/test-induced-design-damage.html))
94	
95	Kent C. Dodds makes a TypeScript-specific version in his 13 July 2019 [“Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.”](https://kentcdodds.com/blog/write-tests). He argues that TypeScript and linting already supply substantial confidence, so tests should address confidence they *cannot* supply—especially business behavior. He opposes blanket 100% application coverage and warns that reaching the last few percent often induces tests of implementation detail. He also says many of his small reusable libraries do reach 100%, because the cost is low and the blast radius of a break is high. This is explicitly **commentator opinion**; he even flags one numerical diminishing-return threshold in the article as something he made up rather than scientific evidence. ([Kent C. Dodds](https://kentcdodds.com/blog/write-tests))
96	
97	This school buys less duplicate specification and greater freedom to simplify or refactor implementation. Its costs become visible when some “obvious” fact was obvious only to the original author.
98	
99	A future engineer cannot query the absent test to discover why a particular odd condition mattered. If the substitute was “David would notice this in review,” the substitute leaves with David.
100	
101	## What can legitimately substitute for a test?
102	
103	“Not tested” only works as an engineering strategy when there is some other oracle. The examples above use several.
104	
105	**Types and static analysis** are particularly attractive because they automatically survive refactoring. If the property is “this function cannot receive this variant without handling it,” a good discriminated union plus exhaustive checking may provide stronger, cheaper evidence than several examples. But the type checker does not tell you that `rename(2)` behaves as you expect across filesystems, that a remote user's permissions are correct, or that your business rule is the intended one. Dodds's TypeScript argument draws exactly that line. curl similarly combines tests with compiler warnings-as-errors and several static analyzers. ([Kent C. Dodds](https://kentcdodds.com/blog/write-tests))
106	
107	**Assertions and invariants** make reasoning assumptions executable. SQLite currently reports 6,754 `assert()` statements checking preconditions, postconditions and loop invariants; some are disabled in production for performance but active in debug/testing builds. Its `ALWAYS`/`NEVER` machinery deliberately turns supposedly impossible states into assertion failures during testing. ([SQLite](https://www3.sqlite.org/testing.html)) This works well for “if control reaches here, X must be true”; it does not help with a case that is never exercised.
108	
109	**Human review** handles properties that are easy for a knowledgeable reader to verify and expensive to encode. OpenSSL turns this into an explicit governance mechanism: every PR gets a testing-status label, exemptions are visible, and disagreements over whether tests are needed go through normal review. curl says every PR is reviewed and separately imposes complexity ceilings specifically to keep functions understandable. ([OpenSSL Library](https://openssl-library.org/policies/technical/testing/)) Review's weakness is repeatability: the next reviewer may not possess the same history or notice the same issue.
110	
111	**Higher-level tests instead of lower-level ones** are another substitute. LLVM does not conclude that a compiler transformation is safe merely because it lacks a unit test; it uses minimized IR regression examples. GitLab says not to add an E2E test when lower-level coverage already settles the behavior. These are really arguments about finding one durable test at the right abstraction, not minimizing the test count for its own sake. ([LLVM](https://llvm.org/docs/TestingGuide.html))
112	
113	**Manual exploratory testing** is used for things whose failure modes are not known in advance. Google's 2020 handbook explicitly retains it, particularly for discovering surprising paths and qualitative problems, but says defects found this way should generally become automated regression tests afterward. ([Abseil](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch14.html))
114	
115	**Staged rollout and monitoring** cover the unavoidable gap between laboratory and production. Google's 2018 SRE Workbook says test environments are not identical to production and tests cannot cover every possible scenario; a canary exposes only a fraction of traffic to a candidate and evaluates production metrics before widening rollout. This is a **stated SRE practice**, not an argument that tests are unnecessary. It limits the cost of omissions rather than proving them absent. ([Google SRE](https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/))
116	
117	The weakness is obvious but important: by the time a canary tells you about a semantic bug, some real workload has exercised it. It also catches only faults reflected in the measurements you chose.
118	
119	**Formal proof** is the most radical replacement. seL4's current project material says verified configurations have machine-checked proofs that the C implementation conforms to a formal specification, with proof validation required for code changes. The project still tests machine/hardware assumptions, unverified configurations, integration and whether the *formal specification itself* captures what developers actually intended. ([seL4](https://sel4.org/About/fact-sheet.html))
120	
121	The seL4 project reports **field-history data** of no functional-correctness defect in verified code since the proof was completed in 2009, while defects have been seen in unverified configurations and unverified assumptions. That is remarkable project-reported evidence, but it is not a controlled comparison with an otherwise-identical conventionally tested kernel. And it illustrates formal verification's boundary very well: a proof is only as comprehensive as its specification and assumptions. ([seL4](https://sel4.com/Verification/proofs.html))
122	
123	## The “someone else changes it a year later” test
124	
125	This thought experiment exposes what each strategy is optimizing.
126	
127	With a good behavior-oriented automated test, the new engineer does not need to know *why* the old author cared. They make a change; CI presents a counterexample. This is the central Google/SQLite benefit. The useful test is an executable historical fact.
128	
129	With a badly chosen automated test, precisely the opposite happens. The new engineer makes a harmless internal change and encounters twenty failures explaining implementation details nobody actually cares about. They must either reconstruct obsolete architecture or mass-update tests. Eventually people stop trusting failures. Google reports that at scale, flakiness and brittleness can make an otherwise impressive suite lose its value. ([Abseil](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html))
130	
131	With **types**, the future engineer gets very good protection against exactly those properties encoded in the type system, usually without needing to understand the old implementation at all. But an unwritten semantic condition remains unwritten.
132	
133	With **clear code plus review**, the year-later experience can be excellent when correctness really is local. A five-line transformation whose complete invariant is visible in those five lines may be easier to verify afresh than to understand 50 lines of test setup. The failure mode is hidden context: what was “obvious” may have depended on a production incident, an odd customer configuration or an undocumented external-system behavior.
134	
135	With **integration-first tests**, the future maintainer has good protection against observable system behavior and considerably more implementation freedom. The cost is weaker localization: when a broad test fails, it may take more work to discover which component violated the contract.
136	
137	With **canaries and monitoring**, a future engineer is protected even against some failure modes nobody predicted. But the oracle operates late, potentially after customer impact, and silently misses anything outside the metrics.
138	
139	With **formal proof**, the new engineer cannot land a change to a verified property without restoring the proof. That is an exceptionally strong form of institutional memory. Its price is the specification/proof engineering itself, and properties outside the proof remain ordinary software-engineering problems.
140	
141	## Coverage data does not resolve the argument
142	
143	There is actual empirical work here, but it is considerably less decisive than testing rhetoric often implies.
144	
145	Inozemtseva and Holmes's ICSE 2014 study, [“Coverage Is Not Strongly Correlated with Test Suite Effectiveness”](https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~rtholmes/papers/icse_2014_inozemtseva.pdf), generated **31,000 test suites for five Java systems up to 724,000 LOC** and used mutation faults to measure fault detection. This is **empirical experimental data**. After controlling for the number of tests, coverage had only low-to-moderate correlation with effectiveness, and stronger coverage criteria did not provide much more information. The authors concluded that coverage is useful for locating undertested areas but not a good standalone quality target. ([Computer Science at UBC](https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~rtholmes/papers/icse_2014_inozemtseva.pdf))
146	
147	Kochhar, Lo, Lawall and Nagappan's large-scale study, published in IEEE Transactions on Reliability in 2017, examined **100 large open-source Java projects and their actual post-release bug reports**. This is **empirical observational data**. They found an insignificant correlation between coverage and post-release bug count at project level and no such correlation at file level. ([Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/code-coverage-and-post-release-defects-a-large-scale-study-on-open-source-projects/))
148	
149	That does **not** establish that adding a good test has no causal benefit. Cross-project coverage is entangled with project type, difficulty, engineering culture and the quality of the assertions, and the 2014 study used mutants rather than actual field failures. What these studies do undermine is the shortcut “90% is demonstrably better than 70% merely because it is 90%.”
150	
151	Martin Fowler's 17 April 2012 [“Test Coverage”](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestCoverage.html) reaches a similar conclusion as **commentator opinion**: he expects thoughtful suites often to produce high coverage, regards very low coverage as a useful warning, but is suspicious of a numeric target—particularly 100%—because the number is easy to game. ([martinfowler.com](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestCoverage.html))
152	
153	That position is compatible both with “write lots of tests” and “delete low-value tests.”
154	
155	## Applying those schools to the TypeScript/SSH system you described
156	
157	Your “correctness should be visible by reading; tests are for what reading cannot settle” principle has respectable precedents. It is close to DHH's emphasis on clarity, OpenSSL's distinction between behavior and implementation, and LLVM's preference for testing compiler behavior at the useful boundary rather than every internal object.
158	
159	The important question is what **reading actually can settle**.
160	
161	For pure TypeScript logic with a small state space, strong types, exhaustive switches and explicit invariants can move a surprising amount into that category. A thin function that converts one validated value into another may genuinely acquire little from a separately maintained example test. Tests written solely to prove that TypeScript assignment or a trusted library's trivial forwarding method works resemble exactly the duplication the selective camp objects to.
162	
163	SSH and a customer-owned Linux machine move in the opposite direction. Whether a file operation behaves correctly can depend on process credentials, permissions, symlinks, filesystem semantics, quoting/argument boundaries, existing file state, interrupted operations and what actually happens when the remote process dies halfway through. Those facts are not all present in the TypeScript source, however readable it is.
164	
165	Because this team can cheaply start **real Linux servers in containers**, an integration test using a real SSH daemon and real filesystem is unusually attractive. It need not imply hundreds of mock-heavy unit tests. In fact it fits DHH's argument for using the real database and Google's preference for real dependencies when feasible: put the executable evidence at the boundary where the uncertainty actually exists. Google explicitly notes that larger/local-machine tests are appropriate when integration with real processes and resources is the behavior being checked. ([Abseil](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html))
166	
167	The selective interpretation would therefore be something like: let the compiler settle static structural facts; let simple, reviewable code settle genuinely local facts; use assertions for invariants that should be impossible; use a small number of real-server tests for Linux/SSH/filesystem behavior; turn escaped bugs into regression cases; and rely on rollout/observability for production-specific conditions you cannot reproduce. The high-coverage interpretation would use those same mechanisms but add substantially more executable examples around each behavior so that less depends on future readers reconstructing the reasoning.
168	
169	Neither eliminates the other's failure mode. The sparse version can lose an undocumented assumption. The dense version can accumulate a second codebase of stale or implementation-coupled tests.
170	
171	There is one separate issue with **no CI**. Every project above that treats automated tests as durable protection also treats **running them automatically** as part of the mechanism. Google says automated tests get their value from being run frequently and its current workflow uses CI; LLVM says unit/regression tests should be run before every commit; curl reports more than 200 CI jobs for every commit and PR and refuses unexplained failures. ([Abseil](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html))
172	
173	So without CI, a test can still be useful as executable documentation and as a local debugging tool, but it is much weaker answer to the “new engineer a year later” problem: that engineer can simply not run it. That observation applies whether the project chooses ten tests or ten thousand.
174	
175	The durable dividing line in these examples is therefore less **“pro-testing versus anti-testing”** than **“where do we want the proof obligation to live?”** SQLite deliberately puts an extraordinary amount into executable tests. OpenSSL divides it between tests and review. DHH is willing to put more into simple design, framework trust and broader integration checks. Google combines a broad behavioral test contract with review, static checks, exploratory work and production safeguards. seL4 moves selected obligations into formal proofs. Each buys confidence in a different place, and each pays maintenance cost—and admits failures—at the boundaries of the evidence it chose.
176	
```

61	
62	## Real defects and incidents: what could tests actually have prevented?
63	
64	The unusually valuable study here is **Yuan et al. 2014**, because it starts with production failures rather than test metrics. The researchers randomly examined 198 user-reported failures from five mature distributed data systems. Despite the scale of those systems, almost all failures required three nodes or fewer to reproduce. Many needed particular *sequences* of events, and catastrophic cases were dominated by bad handling of otherwise non-fatal errors. ([Usenix](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi14/technical-sessions/presentation/yuan?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
65	
66	That argues for tests around **failure semantics**—timeouts, corrupt responses, retries, partial writes, exception paths, recovery after an earlier error—rather than merely replaying the normal implementation structure. An error-handler test with three nodes might technically be an “integration test”, but its value comes from the scenario and oracle, not the taxonomy.
67	
68	The OpenStack study is an interesting hybrid. Marques et al. first manually analyzed **2,048 real Nova bug reports**, extended the classification of 512 of them, and used those data to construct a realistic Python/OpenStack fault model. They then injected 11,309 faults and ran more than 245 million test executions. ([Scribd](https://www.scribd.com/document/1071706402/Martins-et-al-2022-Injecting-software-faults-in-Python-applications?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) In *that particular architecture*, local unit tests were extraordinarily effective, while the integration suite detected very few of the injected faults. Yet the authors still found complementary value from functional tests, and timing/serialization failures remained difficult at every level. ([Scribd](https://www.scribd.com/document/1071706402/Martins-et-al-2022-Injecting-software-faults-in-Python-applications?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
69	
70	So this is evidence for **putting a defect check at the cheapest level capable of reproducing it**, not evidence for deleting integration tests.
71	
72	There is also counter-evidence against interpreting the mere *presence* of unit tests as protection. Chioteli, Batas & Spinellis analyzed more than **2 million Eclipse crash reports**, reducing them to 126,026 unique stack traces, and related crashes to test coverage. Unit-tested code was not associated with fewer crashes. The authors explicitly discuss selection effects—the difficult, fault-prone code may be exactly the code developers choose to test—so this should not be read as “unit testing doesn't work.” It does demonstrate how poor a proxy “this method has unit tests” can be for field reliability. [ACM study record, 2021](https://research.tudelft.nl/en/publications/does-unit-tested-code-crash-a-case-study-of-eclipse/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.04055?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
73	
74	Formal retrospective studies saying “this exact incident would have been prevented by test X” are surprisingly scarce. Many company postmortems recommend a missing regression test afterward, but those anecdotes suffer severe hindsight bias. The OSDI work is considerably stronger because prevention/reproduction was itself the subject of systematic analysis.
75	
76	## Coverage and test quantity are weak proxies
77	
78	Two studies deserve to shape team policy here.
79	
80	In **ICSE 2014**, Inozemtseva & Holmes generated 31,000 suites across five substantial Java systems. After controlling for the number of test cases, statement, decision and MC/DC coverage had only low-to-moderate relationships with mutation effectiveness. Their recommendation is unusually clear: coverage is useful for identifying **untested regions**, but should not be a test-suite quality target. ([Computer Science at UBC](https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~rtholmes/papers/icse_2014_inozemtseva.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
81	
82	Then Kochhar et al. looked at **real post-release defects** in 100 projects and found essentially no useful coverage/defect relationship. ([Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/code-coverage-and-post-release-defects-a-large-scale-study-on-open-source-projects/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
83	
84	That does **not** mean coverage is useless. “0% coverage” is excellent evidence that a path is not dynamically tested. “95% coverage” is poor evidence that the tested behavior is correct.
85	
86	A test such as:
87	
88	```text
89	call calculateInvoice()
90	assert result != null
91	```
92	
93	may execute every branch while being nearly useless against wrong prices. Coverage can tell you the code ran; it cannot tell you whether anyone noticed the wrong answer.
94	
95	The automated-test-generation study makes this oracle problem concrete. Even sophisticated tools that obtain substantial coverage frequently failed to detect the actual Defects4J bug because the bad internal state either did not propagate to an observed value or the generated assertions did not distinguish correct from incorrect behavior. ([ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281640540_Do_Automatically_Generated_Unit_Tests_Find_Real_Faults_An_Empirical_Study_of_Effectiveness_and_Challenges?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
96	
97	## Assertions and test oracles matter at least as much as test inputs
98	
99	This is one of the more consistent empirical themes.
100	
101	Memon, Banerjee & Nagarajan's **ASE 2003** experiment constructed 11 different GUI oracle strategies, 100 faulty versions of each of four applications, and performed roughly 660,000 runs per application. Richer oracles detected faults earlier and needed fewer test cases, though each test was more expensive. [Study, 2003](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~atif/papers/MemonASE2003-abstract.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ([UMD Computer Science](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~atif/papers/MemonASE2003-abstract.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
102	
103	Zhi & Garousi's **2013** empirical study of three open-source suites used mutation and state coverage to examine “inadequate assertions”; they found the problem widespread—on their measure, roughly 55–65% in some sampled suites—and associated with more complex test code. The important limitation is that their definition of assertion adequacy is mutation/state based, not observed real-bug prevention. [IEEE study record, 2013](https://pure.qub.ac.uk/en/publications/on-adequacy-of-assertions-in-automated-test-suites-an-empirical-i/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ([ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/261092581_On_Adequacy_of_Assertions_in_Automated_Test_Suites_An_Empirical_Investigation?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
104	
105	A newer **FSE 2026** study across 12 real projects reached a complementary result: human-written assertions often observe much less program state than is available. More systematic choices about which state to observe improved regression detection by an average 35.7%. Crucially, exhaustive state capture was not always necessary: carefully selected observable state could provide much of the benefit with vastly less oracle material. [FSE 2026 study](https://spideruci.org/publication/du-spectra-2026/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ([ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/408291756_Revealing_Regressions_A_Comparative_Study_of_State-Capture_Strategies_in_Validating_Program_Behavior?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
106	
107	There is also older Microsoft evidence concerning **runtime/software assertions**, rather than specifically xUnit assertions. Kudrjavets, Nagappan & Ball (**2006**) studied two commercial components and found higher assertion density associated with lower fault density; assertions also exposed many recorded faults. Because this is observational and only two components, causal claims should be restrained. [Microsoft Research, 2006](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/assessing-the-relationship-between-software-assertions-and-code-qualityan-empirical-investigation/?locale=zh-cn%2Fbibtex%2F&utm_source=chatgpt.com) ([Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/assessing-the-relationship-between-software-assertions-and-code-qualityan-empirical-investigation/?locale=zh-cn%2Fbibtex%2F&utm_source=chatgpt.com))
108	
109	So the useful principle is not “add lots of asserts.” It is **make the oracle sensitive to the ways the contract could be wrong**.
110	
111	## Mutation testing: useful microscope, poor KPI
112	
113	Mutation testing has some of the best evidence of any test-quality technique, but the nuanced conclusion matters.
114	
115	Earlier work found encouraging relationships between mutants and real defects. The stronger corrective came from Papadakis et al. (**ICSE 2018**): after controlling for test-suite size, mutation score itself was only weakly predictive of real-fault detection. Nevertheless, when comparing suites of the **same size**, suites selected for higher mutation scores detected significantly more real faults. ([IEEE Xplore](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8453121/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
116	
117	That makes mutation particularly useful in this form:
118	
119	> “Here is a concrete change that your existing tests fail to notice. Is that something they ought to notice?”
120	
121	It is much less defensible in this form:
122	
123	> “Our mutation score is 91.7%, therefore our software is safe.”
124	
125	Google provides unusually strong industry evidence. Its **ICSE 2021** longitudinal study examined almost 15 million mutants over six years. Developers exposed to mutation feedback added more and better tests, and retrospective analysis of high-priority real defects found surviving mutants that would have signaled inadequate testing at the defect-introducing change. ([2021.icse-conferences.org](https://2021.icse-conferences.org/details/icse-2021-papers/70/Does-mutation-testing-improve-testing-practices-?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
126	
127	But mutation has substantial cost. Google's separate **TSE 2021/2022** work says conventional whole-codebase mutation simply did not scale. Their practical system mutates only changed code, filters unhelpful mutants and selects operators based on historical usefulness. It was used across more than 24,000 developers and 1,000 projects and reduced mutant volume by orders of magnitude. [Practical Mutation Testing at Scale](https://research.google/pubs/practical-mutation-testing-at-scale-a-view-from-google/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ([Google Research](https://research.google/pubs/practical-mutation-testing-at-scale-a-view-from-google/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
128	
129	That is probably the best-supported implementation policy: **mutation-test changed/high-risk code as a diagnostic, rather than making global mutation score a gate.**
130	
131	## “Test the contract, not the implementation”
132	
133	This slogan is primarily **design/practitioner literature**, not the conclusion of a controlled trial. But there is empirical evidence underneath part of it.
134	
135	Martin Fowler's **2007** *Mocks Aren't Stubs* explicitly distinguishes tests that inspect resulting state from tests that specify the precise sequence of collaborator interactions. He points out that interaction-heavy/mockist tests are more coupled to implementation and therefore more likely to break under refactoring. He also presents the advantages of mockist testing rather than claiming mocks are simply wrong. [Mocks Aren't Stubs, 2007](https://martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
136	
137	Google's **2014–2015** Testing on the Toilet pieces are likewise practitioner guidance, **not empirical studies**. They advocate testing through public APIs and call tests that mechanically mirror code “change-detector tests.” One example asserts that collaborator A must be called and then collaborator B; rearranging the implementation while preserving its output makes the test fail. [What Makes a Good Test, 2014](https://testing.googleblog.com/2014/03/testing-on-toilet-what-makes-good-test.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [Change-Detector Tests Considered Harmful, 2015](https://testing.googleblog.com/2015/01/testing-on-toilet-change-detector-tests.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
138	
139	The important empirical support comes from Spadini et al.'s mock study. Across three open-source projects and one industrial system, production changes frequently forced mock changes; keeping fake expectations synchronized and the additional test/production coupling were prominent maintenance problems. ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-018-9663-0?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
140	
141	So “contract” should be interpreted carefully. It does **not** mean “only test the public HTTP endpoint.” A meaningful contract can be quite local:
142	
143	- `sort(xs)` returns the elements ordered, without caring which sorting algorithm ran.
144	- A payment operation emits **one** charge, not merely the right return value. Here an interaction is genuinely part of the contract.
145	- A retry component must stop after three attempts. Number/timing of calls may therefore be behavior, not implementation detail.
146	- A protocol adapter must emit a particular wire representation. Exact bytes may be the contract.
147	
148	The question is: **would a legitimate consumer notice the difference?** If yes, the test can justifiably observe it.
149	
150	## What brittleness looks like empirically
151	
152	Brittleness is best thought of as a high probability of a **false maintenance alarm**: the test requires editing even though the behavior relevant to its purpose has not become wrong.
153	
154	Kashiwa et al.'s **ICSME 2021** study is particularly useful because it looked at 615,196 test cases around real refactorings. Most refactorings rarely broke tests, which argues against caricatures of unit suites as intrinsically fragile. But renaming attributes/classes and changes such as adding parameters or changing return types had materially higher breakage/edit costs. ([Waseda University Pure](https://waseda.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/does-refactoring-break-tests-and-to-what-extent/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
155	
156	Spadini et al.'s **ICSME 2018** analysis of more than one million test cases across 221 releases found that tests containing recognized “test smells” were more change- and defect-prone. Indirect Testing, Eager Test and Assertion Roulette were particularly associated with change-proneness. This is observational evidence: smelly tests may occur disproportionately in difficult code, so it does not prove that removing the smell will eliminate defects. [ICSME 2018 study](https://research.tudelft.nl/en/publications/on-the-relation-of-test-smells-to-software-code-quality/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ([TU Delft Research Portal](https://research.tudelft.nl/en/publications/on-the-relation-of-test-smells-to-software-code-quality/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
157	
158	Even the individual-smell evidence is contested. A **2022** experiment with 42 students found only modest effects from Assertion Roulette, while a **2023** experiment with 96 students found that Assertion Roulette/Eager Test slowed troubleshooting, especially Assertion Roulette. Both use students and artificial tasks. ([Researcher Conference Management](https://conf.researchr.org/details/vlhcc-2022/vlhcc-2022-vl-hcc-main-conference/11/Is-Assertion-Roulette-still-a-test-smell-An-experiment-from-the-perspective-of-testi?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) That is a good example of an area where the evidence is too weak to justify rigid lint rules.
159	
160	Concrete refactor-only breakages include an exact mock sequence failing because `A(); B()` became `B(); A()` even though the result is identical; dozens of tests requiring constructor edits because an irrelevant dependency was added; a test reaching into a private helper failing when the helper is inlined or extracted; an exact SQL-string assertion failing because the query was equivalently rewritten; or a DOM snapshot changing because a wrapper, CSS class, generated identifier or attribute ordering changed while user-visible semantics did not. The first two are represented directly in the practitioner literature and are consistent with the empirical mock/refactoring results. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2014/03/testing-on-toilet-what-makes-good-test.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
161	
162	## Snapshot tests: criticism is plausible, but the evidence base is thin
163	
164	The evidence here is noticeably weaker.
165	
166	Cruz, Rocha & Valente's **Journal of Systems and Software 2023** paper is peer-reviewed, but its underlying data are a **grey-literature review** of 50 practitioner documents—not experiments showing how many real bugs snapshots catch. Practitioners most often praised ease of creation and regression detection; the dominant criticism was fragility and constant updating of the golden snapshot. The authors explicitly noted the scarcity of prior academic evidence. [Snapshot Testing in Practice, 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0164121223001929?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0164121223001929?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
167	
168	That makes the common snapshot failure mode credible but not strongly quantified:
169	
170	```text
171	expected.html changed
172	```
173	
174	The developer sees a 400-line diff, decides it looks unsurprising and updates it. If a genuine regression is buried among 399 intentional changes, the nominally very rich oracle has become a poor human oracle.
175	
176	The newer FSE 2026 state-observation work gives the debate more substance. Broad snapshot-like state capture really can expose regressions, but carefully choosing observable state can retain substantial detection power while producing dramatically less oracle data. ([ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/408291756_Revealing_Regressions_A_Comparative_Study_of_State-Capture_Strategies_in_Validating_Program_Behavior?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This supports a **signal-to-noise** criticism of huge snapshots rather than “snapshots cannot catch bugs.”
177	
178	Snapshots are genuinely appropriate when the *whole deterministic artifact* is itself a useful contract: compiler output, generated source/configuration, serialization formats, protocol messages, rendered visual output, complex error diagnostics, or a large stable data structure where enumerating individual assertions would merely reproduce the same information less readably. They work best when snapshot changes are uncommon, reviewable and meaningful.
179	
180	They are poor when the captured representation contains lots of incidental churn: random IDs, timestamps, ordering with no semantics, internal DOM structure, object addresses, whitespace or formatting that consumers do not depend upon.
181	
182	## Characterisation tests: intentionally different from correctness tests
183	
184	Characterisation testing has an even weaker empirical defect-detection literature. Its principal source is Michael Feathers' legacy-code work; his **2016** explanation is explicit that the purpose is to record **what the program currently does**, not to establish that what it does is correct. [Feathers, Characterization Testing, 2016](https://michaelfeathers.silvrback.com/characterization-testing?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ([michaelfeathers.silvrback.com](https://michaelfeathers.silvrback.com/characterization-testing?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
185	
186	That distinction resolves much of the apparent contradiction with “don't write change-detector tests.”
187	
188	A characterization test is appropriate when:
189	
190	> “I am about to replace/refactor code whose real behavior I don't fully understand, and accidental behavior changes are currently riskier than preserving some questionable behavior.”
191	
192	For example, before replacing a 20-year-old pricing parser, capturing 500 representative input/output pairs can be enormously valuable even if some outputs seem odd. It gives you a behavioral perimeter within which you can refactor.
193	
194	It becomes harmful when the team subsequently treats every captured accident as a permanent requirement. Characterisation suites should normally lead to investigation: identify which behaviours are genuine contracts, write clearer contract tests for those, deliberately change known bugs where appropriate, and delete obsolete characterization checks.
195	
196	So characterization testing is **a migration/refactoring technique**, whereas ordinary regression tests aspire to be statements about correctness. Conflating the two is the source of much snapshot controversy.
197	
198	## What I would infer for the team
199	
200	The evidence supports a policy more like this than a fixed testing pyramid:
201	
202	1. **Start from failure modes and contracts.** Ask what can be wrong from a consumer/system perspective, including error and recovery behavior. Put each check at the cheapest test boundary capable of creating that condition and observing the right outcome. Production-failure studies support this much more strongly than arbitrary ratios of unit/integration/E2E tests. ([Usenix](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi14/technical-sessions/presentation/yuan?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
203	2. **Treat coverage as a searchlight, not a score.** Uncovered critical code is actionable; 100% coverage is not proof of a good suite. ([Computer Science at UBC](https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~rtholmes/papers/icse_2014_inozemtseva.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
204	3. **Review the oracle, not merely the setup.** For important tests ask, “What plausible bug would execute this test and still pass?” Mutation testing is one of the better-supported ways of answering that. ([IEEE Xplore](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8453121/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
205	4. **Prefer observations stable under implementation substitution.** If replacing an algorithm, extracting classes, changing helper calls, or swapping persistence technology leaves the contract intact, most corresponding tests should remain green. Make exceptions where the interaction itself is contractually significant.
206	5. **Audit churn.** A particularly useful local metric may be “tests edited because behavior changed” versus “tests edited merely because implementation changed.” The latter is direct evidence of brittleness in *your* system, often more informative than generic arguments about testing schools.
207	6. **Keep a small number of boundary/E2E checks for failures that genuinely require boundaries.** Neither the OpenStack result nor the unit/integration comparison establishes that integration tests are generally waste; different levels can expose complementary faults. ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0164121219301955?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
208	7. **Use snapshots and characterization deliberately.** Snapshot a stable artifact when the artifact is the contract; characterize legacy behavior when preserving it temporarily is the goal. Do not confuse either technique with independently specifying correctness.
209	
210	The clearest empirical warning sign is therefore not “too many unit tests” or “too many snapshots.” It is a suite where **large amounts of test code can be changed mechanically in parallel with a refactor without anyone having to reconsider an expected behavior**. That is very close to the phenomenon Google's “change-detector” terminology describes, and the mock/refactoring studies show that this kind of coupling has measurable maintenance consequences. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2015/01/testing-on-toilet-change-detector-tests.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
211	
212	The clearest positive sign is the opposite: a test survives arbitrary implementation rewrites but reliably fails under realistic mutations, historical regressions or reconstructed production failure conditions. That is the closest the available evidence gets to the team's stated goal: **tests that fail because the system is wrong rather than because the code is different.**
213	
````

39	## Comparison
40	
41	| Strategy | What it actually proves | What it tends to miss | Run / maintenance cost | When the other side releases a new version | How drift is detected |
42	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
43	| **Run the real software in containers / VMs** | Your code interoperates with that **actual implementation, configuration and version**. Protocol parsing, error behavior, real query/parser semantics, real daemon state machines and many filesystem effects are exercised. | Anything not represented in the matrix: other versions, distro patches, customer configuration, proxies/bastions. Containers also share the host kernel; they do not reproduce a whole guest OS, whereas a VM has its own kernel. ([Docker Documentation](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/)) | Usually moderate. Containers are cheap enough for PR CI; VMs are slower and operationally heavier. Testcontainers explicitly targets throwaway real PostgreSQL/MySQL/Oracle/browser instances, including known initial state. ([GitHub](https://github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-java/blob/main/docs/index.md)) | A **pinned** image keeps tests reproducible but learns nothing about the release until you update the image. Detect that through scheduled latest-version lanes and support-matrix review. |

The most dangerous failures are where the fake gives a plausible but incorrect answer. | Very cheap to execute; potentially very expensive to maintain. The fake effectively becomes another implementation of the external system. | Nothing necessarily happens. A cassette is historical evidence, not a current compatibility test. | Very cheap replay; moderate fixture/cassette maintenance. Secrets and nondeterministic fields need scrubbing. | Usually completely invisible until rerecording. VCR.py explicitly says changed APIs require deleting/rerecording cassettes. ([vcrpy.readthedocs.io](https://vcrpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html)) | Periodic forced rerecords, cassette-age limits, or a small live lane. There is no simulator-fidelity question. | Hard-to-trigger failures, destructive scenarios, precise state setup, reproducibility, exhaustive edge cases. Literal testing in customers’ production machines is particularly hazardous for mutating software. | Highest variable cost and usually slowest feedback. Terraform AWS Provider acceptance tests create real AWS resources and explicitly warn that they cost real money; some are marked long-running. ([hashicorp.github.io](https://hashicorp.github.io/terraform-provider-aws/running-and-writing-acceptance-tests/)) | SaaS changes are observed immediately—the advantage and the danger. Tests can start failing without your repository changing. | No stand-in can drift, but you instead need to distinguish genuine incompatibility from environmental flakiness and external outages. Terraform therefore separates ordinary CI from explicitly enabled AWS acceptance tests. ([hashicorp.github.io](https://hashicorp.github.io/terraform-provider-aws/running-and-writing-acceptance-tests/)) |
48	
49	The key distinction is that **“real” does not mean “production customer data.”** Terraform's acceptance suite talks to the real AWS control plane and creates real resources, but it requires credentials and explicit `TF_ACC=1`; it is a controlled acceptance environment, not “try destructive tests against somebody's important account.” Its tests apply Terraform and then verify results using the provider API. ([hashicorp.github.io](https://hashicorp.github.io/terraform-provider-aws/running-and-writing-acceptance-tests/))
50	
51	## Real software: where fidelity matters most
52	
53	Database projects are a useful comparison because SQL is similar to SSH in one respect: a seemingly well-defined interface still has implementation-specific semantics.
54	
55	Microsoft's EF Core testing guidance, last updated **30 January 2023**, explicitly warns that a test double does not guarantee production behavior. Its concrete example is SQL Server's normally case-insensitive string comparison versus SQLite's case-sensitive behavior: the same LINQ test can pass on SQLite and fail on SQL Server, or vice versa. Raw SQL, provider-specific functions and transactions introduce more differences. Microsoft consequently recommends substantial coverage against the actual production database system; EF Core itself has more than 30,000 SQL Server tests that it says run in CI on every commit and complete in minutes. ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/testing/choosing-a-testing-strategy))
56	
57	That is the main argument for your OpenSSH container: when starting the real dependency is cheap, **a fake often buys surprisingly little**.
58	
59	The same pattern exists in browser testing. Playwright runs real browser engines, maintains explicit browser-version coupling, supports Chromium, Firefox, WebKit and branded Chrome/Edge, and tells users to update regularly so the suite sees new browser versions. ([Playwright](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers)) It accepts the cost of real implementations because browser compatibility is precisely the thing being tested.
60	
61	For SSH, Teleport's repository gives a directly analogous example. Its integration test contains a function whose comment says it “checks if Teleport and OpenSSH behave in the same way when executing commands”; the test covers stdin piping, shell invocation, TTY behavior and file effects. That is **test-code evidence**, rather than merely a statement in documentation. ([GitHub](https://github.com/gravitational/teleport/blob/master/integration/integration_test.go))
62	
63	### Containers versus VMs for an SSH backend
64	
65	A container is sufficient when the relevant oracle is primarily `sshd` plus users/files/filesystem and process behavior. Docker's own documentation makes the boundary explicit: containers are isolated processes sharing the host kernel; a VM has an entire OS and its own kernel. ([Docker Documentation](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/))
66	
67	So a VM becomes materially better when correctness involves things such as PAM stacks, full `systemd` login/session behavior, kernel/security-module differences, mount behavior, reboot persistence, kernel-enforced filesystem semantics, or a distro setup that is awkward/artificial inside a container. You do not need to pay that price for every test.
68	
69	## Fakes: fast, controllable, and capable of lying convincingly
70	
71	Paramiko gives an unusually clean example.
72	
73	**What its current test code does:** `tests/test_transport.py` repeatedly calls `setup_test_server()` and then drives Paramiko client channels against a Paramiko server transport. It tests exec, shells, forwarding, rekeying, unauthenticated requests and many other behaviors inside its own implementation. ([GitHub](https://github.com/paramiko/paramiko/blob/main/tests/test_transport.py))
74	
75	That is extremely useful for Paramiko's internal behavior, but it is partly **self-interoperability**: Paramiko client and Paramiko server can share the same mistaken assumption.
76	
77	**What happened against reality:** Paramiko issue #1175, opened **13 March 2018** and associated with CVE-2018-7750, investigated whether a server should accept connection-level requests before authentication. The maintainer then ran the test client against Ubuntu/OpenSSH 7.2 in a Docker container. OpenSSH returned a protocol error/`SSH_MSG_UNIMPLEMENTED`; Paramiko's server had been willing to dispatch the request. The issue explains that OpenSSH changes its dispatch table according to protocol phase, whereas Paramiko's dispatch model behaved differently. ([GitHub](https://github.com/paramiko/paramiko/issues/1175))
78	
79	That is not merely “a mock was incomplete.” It is the more dangerous case: **the project's own server implementation supplied false confidence about the behavior of the reference server**.
80	
81	There are parallel examples elsewhere:
82	
83	Microsoft explicitly documents SQLite/in-memory database fakes producing different query semantics from SQL Server. ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/testing/choosing-a-testing-strategy))
84	
85	A jsdom issue opened **6 June 2023** showed `getComputedStyle()` returning an empty CSS custom property under jsdom 22 while equivalent browser code returned `red`; the issue was labelled as having a failing upstream Web Platform Test. ([GitHub](https://github.com/jsdom/jsdom/issues/3563))
86	
87	A LocalStack issue opened **14 January 2025** showed Step Functions/S3 error handling returning different status/cause information from real AWS under LocalStack 4.0.3. ([GitHub](https://github.com/localstack/localstack/issues/12139))
88	
89	Those are exactly why a simulator needs an external oracle.
90	
91	LocalStack's own repository has a good calibration model: a test can be switched to `TEST_TARGET=AWS_CLOUD`; once it has been shown to work against AWS, AWS's response is captured as a snapshot and LocalStack is compared with that snapshot. Its documentation says these AWS-validated snapshot tests are preferred because they increase parity confidence. ([GitHub](https://github.com/localstack/localstack/blob/main/docs/testing/integration-tests/README.md)) Moto's documented approach is different but similar in intent: run a subset of Terraform's AWS tests against MotoServer on every PR. ([docs.getmoto.org](https://docs.getmoto.org/en/4.2.4/docs/contributing/development_tips/tests.html))
92	
93	An independent DynamoDB conformance project illustrates how measurable drift can remain even in mature simulators. Its **3 September 2026** run executes the same suite against live DynamoDB first and uses that as the baseline. In that particular 1,251-test suite, LocalStack 2026.8.1 had 95.3% coverage and **8.1% divergent behavior**; AWS itself is the 0% baseline. The project's authors explicitly warn that these are point-in-time, suite-specific measurements rather than certification. ([GitHub](https://github.com/paritysuite/dynamodb-conformance)) That number should therefore not be read as “LocalStack is 8.1% wrong in general”; it demonstrates that measurable emulator divergence is a normal engineering phenomenon.
94	
95	## Record/replay is a cache of reality, not a simulation of reality
96	
97	VCR.py describes the attraction well: record HTTP interactions on the first execution, replay them later, and obtain offline, deterministic, faster tests. Its documentation says that if the server API changes, cassettes can be deleted and generated again. ([vcrpy.readthedocs.io](https://vcrpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html))
98	
99	The logical limitation follows directly: until you do that rerecord, **the old test cannot know the remote system changed**.
100	
101	That makes record/replay particularly good where obtaining a realistic response is expensive but replaying the response exercises valuable client parsing or business logic. It is less convincing for an SSH protocol compatibility test. SSH has negotiation, authentication state, channels, flow control, PTYs, exit statuses and encrypted transport; raw packet replay can quickly stop representing a valid conversation.
102	
103	For your application, recording **above** that layer could still be useful: e.g. “command issued → stdout/stderr/exit status” or “SFTP operation → result.” I would regard those fixtures as application test data, not evidence that you still interoperate with OpenSSH.
104	
105	A well-run replay suite therefore has a deliberately expiring notion of truth: rerecord on a cadence, or maintain a small live acceptance suite that makes stale cassettes visible.
106	
107	## Contracts solve a different problem
108	
109	Contract testing is most valuable when the “other system” has an owner you can coordinate with.
110	
111	Pact's model illustrates why it is different from an ordinary fake. On the consumer side, the expected interaction is registered with a mock provider and the real client code makes its request to that mock. On the provider side, the provider is independently verified against those interactions. ([Pact Docs](https://docs.pact.io/getting_started/how_pact_works)) The fake therefore is not supposed to be a freehand reimplementation of the provider: it is an executable statement of the consumer's requirement, checked later against the provider.
112	
113	The idea predates Pact. Ian Robinson's “Consumer-Driven Contracts: A Service Evolution Pattern,” published **12 June 2006**, argued for exposing the obligations a provider must preserve as it evolves. ([martinfowler.com](https://martinfowler.com/articles/consumerDrivenContracts.html)) Pact itself arose at realestate.com.au in 2013 from problems with slow/brittle integration testing, according to Pactflow's **14 October 2019** history; the Pact Broker subsequently became the mechanism for exchanging contracts and verification results. ([Pactflow Contract Testing Platform](https://pactflow.io/blog/everything-you-didnt-even-know-you-wanted-to-ask-about-pactflow/))
114	
115	A ThoughtWorks GeekNight talk, **“Microservices: Contract Testing Using PACT,” 4 March 2021**, provides a dated practitioner treatment covering integration testing, contract testing, Pact and its code workflow.
116	
117	[Microservices: Contract Testing Using PACT — GeekNight ThoughtWorks, 4 Mar 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yaAe0aR1G-U&utm_source=chatgpt.com)
118	
119	
120	For arbitrary customer-owned SSH servers, though, there is a fundamental mismatch: **you have nobody on the provider side who has agreed to run your contract before changing `sshd`, PAM, sudoers, the filesystem or shell configuration**.
121	
122	You can still create a **conformance profile**—“these are the behaviors our product requires”—and execute it against supported servers. That is very useful, but it is not consumer-driven contract testing in the Pact sense.
123	
124	## “Only test the real system” is the other extreme
125	
126	Terraform AWS Provider is a useful example because it genuinely exercises the external production implementation. Its contributor guide says acceptance tests are end-to-end interactions with AWS that create, read and destroy real resources; it also warns explicitly that those tests cost real money. ([hashicorp.github.io](https://hashicorp.github.io/terraform-provider-aws/running-and-writing-acceptance-tests/))
127	
128	The test harness makes that expensive activity deliberate. `TF_ACC=1` must be supplied; credentials and regions are configured; some tests exceed 300 seconds and are separately treated as long-running. An acceptance step applies Terraform configuration and checks results using the provider/API. ([hashicorp.github.io](https://hashicorp.github.io/terraform-provider-aws/running-and-writing-acceptance-tests/))
129	
130	That approach has maximum provider fidelity but would be a poor *only* test suite. It is costly, slow, harder to isolate, and bad for exercising failures like “the connection vanishes exactly between temporary-file write and rename.”
131	
132	For your software, “production only” is worse still if production means **customers' real machines**. A product whose job is rewriting configuration files should not need destructive experiments on customer hosts to find out whether its update algorithm is safe. Production telemetry and carefully designed non-destructive probes can be useful evidence; they should not replace reproducible integration tests.
133	
134	## What I would use for your SSH backend
135	
136	I would treat the external behavior as a **compatibility envelope** rather than claiming correctness against “Linux over SSH” in general. Customer machines can be changed arbitrarily, so no finite test suite can establish that universal guarantee.
137	
138	A practical hierarchy would be:
139	
140	- **Every PR:** run the actual backend against real `sshd` in Docker. Use several pinned OpenSSH/distro combinations representing supported environments. Exercise the real shell/SFTP path and real filesystem operations, not an SSH mock.
141	- **The same black-box conformance suite against every target:** login/authentication, exec semantics, stdout/stderr and exit codes, PTY/no-PTY, SFTP operations, ownership/mode preservation, symlinks, atomic replace/rename, `sudo` where supported, disconnects, malformed/partial files, permission denial, disk-full-like failures and concurrent modification. This is the suite you can also point at a VM or customer-like test host.
142	- **A small local fake:** only where it gives you something real OpenSSH cannot conveniently provide—precise timeout points, packet loss, forced disconnect during a write, impossible-to-reproduce server errors. Make it obvious that these tests establish your recovery logic, not SSH compatibility.
143	- **Scheduled VM tests:** use them for PAM/systemd/security-module/kernel/filesystem cases where sharing Docker's host kernel makes the container materially unlike a customer's Linux host. Docker itself documents that architectural distinction. ([Docker Documentation](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/))
144	- **Scheduled moving-version lane:** alongside pinned CI images, regularly test the newest distro/OpenSSH packages you intend to support. A pinned container is reproducible; a moving lane tells you reality moved.
145	- **Differential tests for any fake:** every behavior implemented by your fake should ideally have the same black-box test runnable against real OpenSSH. Paramiko #1175 is the reason.
146	- **Record/replay only above SSH**, where useful for deterministic application fixtures; do not make encrypted SSH transcript replay the compatibility oracle.
147	- **No reliance on customer production as the test environment.** If production evidence is needed, prefer read-only capability probes and explicit compatibility diagnostics, plus controlled canary hosts.
148	
149	The most useful architectural rule is: **the test that guards an external-system guarantee should have an oracle independent of the code implementing that guarantee.** Paramiko-client-against-Paramiko-server lacked that independence in the problematic case. LocalStack's AWS snapshots have it. Pact provider verification has it. Playwright running actual browsers has it. Terraform's AWS acceptance tests have it.
150	
151	Because Docker is already available to your developers and `sshd` is cheap to start, your case sits unusually far toward the “run the real dependency” side of the trade-off. I would need a concrete reason *not* to put real OpenSSH integration tests in the normal CI path.
152	
```

42	Infrastructure systems usually do **not** test “idempotency” as one property. They split it into several different properties:
43	
44	1. **Fixed-point idempotency:** once desired state is reached, running again makes no change.
45	2. **Replay safety:** if the caller cannot tell whether an operation completed, retrying the same logical operation cannot perform it twice.
46	3. **Ambiguity containment:** if replay cannot be made safe, record “outcome unknown” and refuse to repeat it.
47	4. **Compensation:** after a partially completed workflow, clean up the pieces that must not survive.
48	5. **Convergence:** repeated reconciliation, once failures cease and observations catch up, eventually reaches the desired state and then stops mutating it.
49	
50	Those require different tests. A “run it twice” test exercises only the first.
51	
52	## How the major systems approach it
53	
54	| System | Documented contract | What its own tests actually exercise |
55	|---|---|---|
56	| **Terraform / providers** | An apply may partially succeed. Terraform records completed changes but does **not** automatically roll back the apply; the user fixes the error and applies again. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/docs/resource-instance-change-lifecycle.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Provider acceptance tests execute plan → apply → refresh → final plan; a non-empty final plan normally fails. `CheckDestroy` can query the real API after destruction and fail if anything remains. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/testing/testing-patterns?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) The repository's `ExpectEmptyPlan` literally asserts that there are no output or resource changes.  That repository snapshot is from August 31, 2026.  |

Molecule's idempotence phase reruns the converge playbook and fails when the second run reports changes; its `side_effect` facility can deliberately introduce things such as a network partition. ([GitHub](https://github.com/ansible/molecule/blob/main/docs/workflow.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Ansible's own integration tests often repeat a module and assert `is not changed`. ([Crossplane Docs](https://docs.crossplane.io/v1.20/concepts/managed-resources/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | `crossplane-runtime` has explicit reconciler cases named `ExternalCreatePending`; their stated reason is that it “might have leaked a resource and don't want to create another.”  The expected status is Creating plus a reconciliation error, rather than a second Create.
