64	
65	## Idempotency tests: fixed point versus safe retry
66	
67	Terraform's normal provider test is a good example of a **fixed-point** test. Provision the resource, refresh it from the real API, then plan again. If the provider is correctly modeling the remote object, the last plan is empty. `plancheck.ExpectEmptyPlan()` makes the same assertion explicitly. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/testing/testing-patterns?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This catches perpetual diffs, normalization mistakes, and many create/update implementations that don't settle.
68	
69	Ansible's equivalent is even more literal: execute the same desired-state operation twice and assert that the second invocation reports `changed=false`. The Ansible repository's `deb822_repository` test additionally varies argument ordering, which is a useful way of checking semantic rather than textual equality. ([GitHub](https://github.com/ansible/ansible/blob/devel/test/integration/targets/deb822_repository/tasks/test.yml?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) A real 2019 bug demonstrates the value of this rudimentary test: Ansible issue #57541, opened **June 7, 2019**, reported that Molecule's idempotence phase caught `yum_repository` reporting a change on the second run. ([GitHub](https://github.com/ansible/ansible/issues/57541?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
70	
71	But neither test proves **at-most-once external side effects**. A defective module could, for example, rewrite a file or issue an API PUT on every run and still report `changed=false`. For customer infrastructure, the stronger test instruments the external boundary: run the operation twice and assert both the resulting state **and the number/identity of mutating API calls**. For a non-idempotent POST protected by a request token, the test should deliberately discard the first response, resend the request with the same token, and assert that only one remote object exists.
72	
73	EC2 documents exactly the semantic result such a test ought to verify: the original and retried request with the same token complete the logical operation only once. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/devguide/ec2-api-idempotency.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
74	
75	## Testing a truly unknown result
76	
77	Crossplane is unusually explicit about this state. Its protocol is effectively a small write-ahead log:
78	
79	`pending → external create → succeeded/failed`
80	
81	The dangerous crash window is between the external create and writing `succeeded`. On restart, `pending > succeeded,failed` means **“maybe created.”** The assertion is therefore *not* “retry succeeds.” It is “Create is not called again, the managed object visibly enters an indeterminate/error condition, and reconciliation stops until the ambiguity is resolved.” ([Crossplane Docs](https://docs.crossplane.io/v1.20/concepts/managed-resources/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) The repository's `ExternalCreatePending` test exercises exactly that branch. 
82	
83	This pattern is appropriate when the underlying creation operation is not safely replayable. If the external resource has a deterministic name or another stable lookup key, the controller can instead observe by that identity and turn “unknown” back into “known.” Crossplane has an explicit test for proceeding after a pending create when the name is deterministic. 
84	
85	AWS takes the opposite approach: it makes the ambiguous request **replayable** at the API boundary using a stable `ClientToken`. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/devguide/ec2-api-idempotency.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) These are the two clean solutions to the classic “request committed; reply lost” problem: either make retry safe, or make uncertainty durable and prohibit retry.
86	
87	Terraform is less expressive at this level. It does preserve successful portions of a failed apply and deliberately avoids automatic rollback, but if a provider has created a resource and cannot return enough identity/state to Terraform, the resource can fall outside state. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials/cli/apply?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
88	
89	A concrete example occurred in the AzureRM provider. Issue #24517, opened **January 17, 2024**, described an Azure Function App whose base resource was successfully created, after which zip deployment failed because of a transient network/DNS error. Terraform treated creation as failed, the app was not in state, and the next apply found that the Azure resource already existed; users had to delete it manually. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-azurerm/issues/24517?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) A normal happy-path “apply, refresh, empty plan” test would not exercise this. A targeted acceptance test could: inject failure *after Azure creation but before Create returns success*, then assert that either the ID remains in Terraform state and is tainted/recoverable, or cleanup removes the external app.
90	
91	## Partial failure and rollback
92	
93	There are three distinct test philosophies here.
94	
95	**Terraform** is explicitly incremental rather than transactional. The guarantee is that after an error it records completed resource changes and exits; it does not promise to restore the pre-apply world. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials/cli/apply?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Thus a partial-failure test should assert the exact *intermediate* state, not expect a rollback that the product never promises. Then it should remove the injected fault, run again, and prove convergence to an empty plan.
96	
97	Terraform's provisioner behavior shows how non-repeatable substeps alter the assertion. A creation-time provisioner failure taints the resource because it may be only partly configured. A failed destroy-time provisioner is run again on the next apply, so such a provisioner must itself be safe to replay. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/provisioners?optInFrom=terraform-io&utm_source=chatgpt.com))
98	
99	**CloudFormation** exposes rollback as part of the contract. A test of `ROLLBACK` should therefore verify not only stack status but the inventory of resources remaining afterward. The `RetainExceptOnCreate` flag is particularly telling: it defines whether resources *newly introduced by the failed operation* are expected to survive. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/APIReference/API_CreateStack.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
100	
101	**Nova and Kubernetes-style controllers** usually use compensation/reconciliation rather than an all-or-nothing transaction. The Nova server-build path spans scheduler, Placement accounting, database state, messaging and compute. Its bug #1859496 showed why checking only the primary server record is insufficient: a server build interrupted after its resource claim could be deleted while leaving its Placement allocation behind. The fix says AMQP problems or a conductor restart could create that condition, and added the functional regression test that interrupts the build and checks the allocation disappears. ([OpenDev](https://opendev.org/openstack/nova/commit/f35930eef8fa27ee972e87366abb38596839fdba?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) That is a model test for partial failure: fail at a deliberate phase boundary and enumerate **all secondary resources and reservations**, not just the headline object.
102	
103	## How controllers prove they do not act twice
104	
105	Kubernetes's controller expectations are essentially a short-lived local record of “writes I have issued but have not yet observed through my read path.” ReplicaSet records expected creations before firing the creates.  `TestControllerExpectations` verifies that the controller is considered unsatisfied until those observations arrive, including concurrent notifications and the TTL escape hatch. 
106	
107	The newer `ConsistencyStore` attacks a related race at a lower level. Kubernetes controllers commonly write directly to the API server but read through asynchronous informer caches. On **April 28, 2026**, the Kubernetes project documented the v1.36 mitigation: remember the resource version a controller has written, and skip reconciliation until the cache's resource version has caught up. ([Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/04/28/kubernetes-v1-36-staleness-mitigation-for-controllers/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) That turns “read-your-own-write” into an assertion that can be tested.
108	
109	Why that matters is visible in Kubernetes issue #140217, opened **July 3, 2026**. Under rapid scale-out of 6,000–10,000 DRA pods, a ResourceClaim could be created, its entry evicted from a fixed-size mutation cache before the informer Add arrived, and the controller would later see NotFound and create the claim a second time. ([GitHub](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140217?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) A small ordinary reconciliation test would probably miss it. A deterministic regression test can catch it by creating more entries than the cache capacity while deliberately delivering the Pod update before the ResourceClaim add event, and then asserting the create-call count stays at one.
110	
111	This illustrates an important rule for reconciliation tests: **event ordering and stale observations have to be inputs to the test**, not merely implementation details.
112	
113	## What should be asserted about leftovers?
114	
115	“Cleanup succeeded” cannot mean only “the control-plane record disappeared.” Terraform's `CheckDestroy` is intended to query the infrastructure API itself and fail when a real object still exists. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/sdkv2/testing/acceptance-tests/testcase?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Ansible's repository tests assert that the files corresponding to removed repositories are actually absent. ([GitHub](https://github.com/ansible/ansible/blob/devel/test/integration/targets/deb822_repository/tasks/test.yml?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Nova's regression test checks Placement allocations, because the leaked object in that incident was resource accounting rather than the VM object itself. ([OpenDev](https://opendev.org/openstack/nova/commit/f35930eef8fa27ee972e87366abb38596839fdba?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
116	
117	Crossplane is a useful exception: in an ambiguous create the correct test may explicitly permit **one possible leaked resource**. The safety property is that the controller exposes the possibility and creates *no more* until someone establishes what happened. Trying to assert “zero resources remain” would force the controller to take another potentially unsafe action.
118	
119	Terraform has historical evidence of why independent external inventory matters. Issue #9592, opened **October 25, 2016**, reported `unexpected EOF` during apply causing an existing Elastic Beanstalk environment to disappear from state; subsequent runs attempted to create it again. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/9592?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Terraform issue #1783, opened **May 3, 2015**, is an even cleaner acted-twice example: the second plan reported no changes, but applying resulted in another resource. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/1783?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) An empty-plan assertion alone is therefore not a complete duplicate-action test; reproducing #1783 requires performing the second execution—or instrumenting provider calls—and asserting that no mutating action occurs.
120	
121	## Testing reconciliation for convergence
122	
123	A good reconciler test is not “call `Reconcile` once and compare an object.” It is a small state-machine test.
124	
125	The property to test is:
126	
127	> Starting from any reachable partial state, once injected failures stop and observations eventually reflect successful writes, repeated reconciliations reach a fixed point matching desired state; after that point, further reconciliations issue no mutations.
128	
129	That decomposes into **safety** (“before convergence, don't create/delete more than allowed”), **liveness** (“temporary failures or stale caches do not leave the controller stuck forever unless the product deliberately chooses an indeterminate/manual state”), and **quiescence** (“after convergence, another reconcile is a no-op”).
130	
131	Kubernetes expectations tests cover part of that: they verify that reconciliation remains gated while observations are outstanding and becomes eligible again when observations arrive or expectations expire.  Crossplane exercises a deliberately *non-convergent without intervention* state for ambiguous creates, which is a safety tradeoff rather than a liveness bug. The distinction matters: Crossplane issue #340, opened **July 14, 2022**, showed a provider pod being killed during a long create, leaving `external-create-pending` stuck and requiring manual removal. ([GitHub](https://github.com/crossplane/crossplane-runtime/issues/340?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) That behavior is inconvenient, but it is consistent with preferring “stop” over “possibly create twice.”
132	
133	There is also a failure on the other side of that tradeoff. Crossplane issue #4099, opened **May 24, 2023**, describes a GCP ServiceAccount that had been created successfully; later the provider failed to observe it, attempted creation again, received GCP's `409 already exists`, and eventually entered the create-pending safety state. ([GitHub](https://github.com/crossplane/crossplane/issues/4099?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) A provider-level reconciliation regression test could simulate “resource exists, Observe temporarily returns false” and assert that the controller recovers via stable identity/grace logic rather than issuing another create. The generic Crossplane runtime tests cannot prove that every provider's `Observe` implementation is correct.
134	
135	## The fault matrix I would use for a customer-infrastructure control plane
136	
137	The strongest test suite places a fault at every point where durable knowledge can diverge from the external side effect:
138	
139	| Fault point | Required assertion |
140	|---|---|
141	| Fail **before request send** | No external object; retry may act once. |
142	| Send request, service rejects it definitively | Durable `failed` result; retry according to normal policy. |
143	| **Service commits, response is lost** | Either same idempotency key is safely replayed and exactly one object exists, or operation becomes durable `unknown/pending` and no retrying mutation occurs. |
144	| Response received, crash **before local state/ID is persisted** | On restart, recover by idempotency key/deterministic identity, or halt as ambiguous. Never blindly create again. |
145	| First of several subresources succeeds, later step fails | Assert the documented compensation policy and inventory every surviving primary object, attachment, allocation, credential, file, reservation and metadata record. |
146	| Rollback itself fails halfway | Record rollback as incomplete; retries must resume compensation without repeating already-completed destructive work. |
147	| Write succeeds but reads are stale | Feed stale observation deliberately and assert no second action; then advance the observer and prove progress. |
148	| Process dies and restarts | Reload only durable information; outcome should not depend on an in-memory “already did that” flag. |
149	| Reconcile is invoked repeatedly and concurrently | Count external mutations, verify per-resource serialization/deduplication, eventually expose the latest observed state, then reach zero mutations. |
150	| Cleanup/destroy finishes | Query the authoritative external systems, not just the controller database, and assert exactly the resources the retention policy permits remain. |
151	
152	The central lesson from these projects is that **“second run is a no-op” is the floor, not the ceiling**. The hard test is the one Crossplane, Kubernetes and idempotent cloud APIs point toward: manufacture the exact window where the external world has changed but the control plane does not yet know that it has changed. Then assert either **safe replay with a stable operation identity**, or **durable uncertainty plus refusal to act twice**. Terraform's and Nova's historical leaks, and Kubernetes's 2026 duplicate ResourceClaim race, are all variants of failing to test that window strongly enough.
153	
```

2	
3	Source: https://chatgpt.com/share/6aa92dba-a428-83ed-a89d-fa0f9a627ff6
4	
5	---
6	
7	**User**
8	
9	Context: A TypeScript repository has product code and a small number of deliberately chosen tests. Some tests are pure and instant; some start a container and take a minute. The team has not decided where test files live, how they are named, or how the slow ones are kept out of the fast path.
10	
11	Question: How do well-regarded repositories arrange their tests, and what follows from each arrangement?
12	
13	Cover: tests beside the code versus a separate tree; naming conventions; splitting by speed, by layer, by domain, or not at all; how slow suites are separated and when they run; shared fixtures and helpers and how they are prevented from becoming a second untested framework; and how a repository keeps a suite honest when it cannot be run on every change.
14	
15	Include examples from at least one large monorepo, one widely used library, and one infrastructure tool, and say how many tests each has relative to its size.
16	
17	Evidence rules: cite the repositories directly with dates. Say which conventions are enforced by tooling and which are habit. Include arrangements that the projects themselves later changed, and why.
18	
19	---
20	
21	**ChatGPT**
22	
23	I’ll ground this in repository layouts and CI/config files, not style-guide summaries. I’ll also distinguish “the runner makes this true” from “contributors usually do this,” because that is where many test-layout recommendations become misleading.
24	
25	---
26	
27	**ChatGPT**
28	
29	One useful distinction is already visible in the examples: mature repos rarely encode “unit/integration/e2e” only in directory names. They usually make the expensive boundary executable—via Bazel targets/tags, a dedicated command/config, or an opt-in environment variable—so “fast by default” cannot silently regress into “sometimes starts Docker.”
30	
31	---
32	
33	**ChatGPT**
34	
35	The library case has an instructive wrinkle: date-fns has recently become a monorepo root, so I’m treating layout claims as dated observations rather than timeless rules. That also gives a concrete example of why copying a famous repository’s current folder names without copying its runner configuration is unsafe.
36	
37	---
38	
39	**ChatGPT**
40	
41	The strongest pattern is not “put unit tests here and integration tests there.” It is to treat **ownership/layout** and **execution cost** as separate design problems. Mature repositories tend to organize tests physically by the code or domain they belong to, while making “may contact the network / start a service / take much longer” an explicit runner or CI boundary. Directory names help humans; the command that selects the suite is the real control.
42	
43	For scale, I used a deliberately crude but comparable measure: conventional test files divided by all primary-language files at a dated repository snapshot. It is **test-file density, not test-case count**—parameterization and large test files make case counts misleading. At Angular commit `c60c41e` (committed September 13, 2026), GitHub finds 711 `_spec.ts` files among 6,016 TypeScript files; at Zod `59bbc03` (September 13), 195 `.test.ts` files among 425 TypeScript files; at Terraform `4c9023a` (September 15), 658 `_test.go` files among 1,752 Go files.         
44	
45	| Repository | Physical arrangement | Operational split | What is actually enforced | Test-file density |
46	|---|---|---|---|---:|
47	| **Angular** — large monorepo | Mostly package-local test trees such as `packages/core/test/acceptance/component_spec.ts`; also distinct repository-level `integration/` and other specialized areas. ([GitHub](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/main/packages/core/test/acceptance/component_spec.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Bazel targets. Ordinary CI deliberately excludes `//integration/...` and several other suites; `integration-tests:ci` selects `//integration/...` separately. ([GitHub](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/main/package.json?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | **Enforced:** Bazel target/CI selection. **Mostly convention:** `_spec.ts` and finer folder taxonomy; a file matters because a BUILD target includes it, not because its English label says “acceptance.” | 711 / 6,016 TS = **11.8%** |
48	| **Zod** — widely used TS library | A middle ground: tests are in `tests/` directories *inside* implementation/domain slices, e.g. `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/tests/lazy.test.ts`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/packages/zod/src/v4/classic/tests/lazy.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Core tests are simply `pnpm test`/Vitest; the project does not invent a fast/slow taxonomy for a largely fast library suite. Separate resolution/integration packages get their own jobs. ([GitHub](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | **Enforced:** the commands/hooks/CI that invoke Vitest. **Documented convention:** create tests in each workspace's `tests` directory; `.test.ts` is the prevailing discoverable naming pattern. ([GitHub](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | 195 / 425 TS = **45.9%** |
49	| **Terraform** — infrastructure tool | Ordinary tests sit with their Go packages as `_test.go`; a few genuinely cross-cutting systems have separate areas such as `testing/equivalence-tests`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/HashiCorp/terraform?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Default unit suite is offline/self-contained. Tests hitting external systems are explicitly enabled with `TF_ACC=1`, normally scoped to the affected package. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | **Hard-enforced:** Go only treats `_test.go` as test source. **Hard operational boundary:** acceptance behavior is opt-in through `TF_ACC`. “Acceptance” as a conceptual label is secondary. | 658 / 1,752 Go = **37.6%** |
50	
51	## Beside the code or a separate tree
52	
53	For a **small, deliberately selected suite**, exact or near colocation has an important advantage: tests participate in the same mental unit as the implementation. A rename or deletion makes the associated test conspicuous; reviewers looking at a domain see its tests; and there is no second directory hierarchy that gradually stops matching the product hierarchy.
54	
55	Zod illustrates the useful compromise. It does not require every `foo.ts` to have `foo.test.ts` next to it, but it keeps `tests/` inside the implementation slice. Angular does something similar one level higher: `packages/core/src/...` and `packages/core/test/...` belong to the same package, while truly cross-package integration work gets a repository-level boundary. ([GitHub](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/packages/zod/src/v4/classic/tests/lazy.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
56	
57	A top-level mirror such as `tests/unit/domainA/...` becomes attractive when test code has a **different operational environment**—large fixture trees, an assembled application, deployment manifests, certificates, Docker Compose files, browser projects. Its cost is indirection. A product move now needs a corresponding test-tree move, and stale tests can look perfectly tidy while having lost their obvious owner.
58	
59	So the practical rule is: **organize physically by the most durable thing, usually domain/ownership. Split physically only when the harness itself is cross-cutting.** “Fast” and “slow” are usually not durable enough to deserve the primary directory hierarchy.
60	
61	## Naming and what the name should encode
62	
63	The least surprising TypeScript convention is one ordinary suffix, normally `*.test.ts` or `*.spec.ts`, throughout the repository. Pick one rather than assigning philosophical meaning to both. Angular strongly prefers `_spec.ts`; Zod prefers `.test.ts`. Neither choice carries useful semantics by itself.
64	
65	If one class of tests has a concrete operational property that must never enter the inner loop, adding one modifier is useful. In the repository you described, `repository.test.ts` versus `repository.container.test.ts` is clearer than `unit` versus `integration`: “container” tells you exactly why it is expensive. Then make the runner use that distinction. A naming rule that CI does not parse is only a comment.
66	
67	Layer labels such as `unit`, `integration`, and `e2e` work when the architecture has genuine layer contracts, but they decay surprisingly quickly. A test can exercise five modules yet be pure and take 3 ms; another can test one adapter but launch PostgreSQL and take a minute. For developer feedback, **resource requirement and duration matter more than the textbook layer name**.
68	
69	That gives four reasonable axes with different jobs: domain should normally drive directories; layer can describe test intent where genuinely useful; speed/resource class should drive runner selection; and no classification at all is best when the entire suite is fast. Zod is a good example of the last case rather than creating categories merely because categories sound mature. ([GitHub](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
70	
71	## Slow tests: separate execution, not merely separate prose
72	
73	Angular makes this concrete. Its current root scripts define normal CI as a Bazel selection that explicitly subtracts `//integration/...` and several other specialized targets, while `integration-tests:ci` explicitly selects `//integration/...`. That is much safer than “developers know not to run that folder.” ([GitHub](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/main/package.json?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Angular's contributor guide also says Bazel is the primary build/test system, contributors should run package tests before submission, affected tests run on CI, and a PR cannot merge unless the tests pass. ([GitHub](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/main/contributing-docs/building-and-testing-angular.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
74	
75	Terraform makes the same separation without moving the files. Unit tests remain colocated and offline; external-service tests stay in their natural packages but are inert unless `TF_ACC=1` is set. The contributor guide recommends enabling them only for the relevant package, both to shorten the run and to avoid failures caused by unrelated external-system drift. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This is an important counterexample to the idea that a slow suite must live in `tests/integration/`.
76	
77	For your particular numbers, a test taking **one minute** is slow for an edit–test loop but not necessarily slow for pull-request CI. I would keep it out of the default local `test` command while still running the container suite as a separate, visible CI job on every PR if the total is only a few minutes and reasonably reliable. “Not in the fast path” and “not on every change” are different decisions.
78	
79	If eventually it becomes too expensive for every PR, use targeted/path-aware execution for relevant changes plus an unconditional backstop on main or the merge queue and a scheduled clean-environment run. Do not let “nightly” become the *only* place it runs: that turns failures into archaeology.
80	
81	## Fixtures and helpers
82	
83	The healthiest test support code is deliberately boring. Static fixture data can be widely shared. Factories can remove irrelevant setup. A container lifecycle wrapper can standardize start/stop and readiness. The warning sign is when the helper starts containing branching business logic, retries, implicit state, its own object model, or a mini-DSL that makes test code unreadable without learning another framework.
84	
85	At that point it should be treated like product code: narrow API, explicit owner, and tests of its own. A useful threshold is not a specific line count but **whether a bug in the helper could make many tests pass incorrectly**. If yes, leaving it untested defeats the suite.
86	
87	Angular has a very recent example of pruning this kind of support structure. Its September 13, 2026 commit moved animation acceptance tests away from a bespoke `fakeAsync` frame utility toward async/await and a shared animation-frame helper, then removed the obsolete helper and its Bazel dependency.  The lesson is not “always centralize helpers”; it is that shared test abstractions should be removable when the platform or test style makes them unnecessary.
88	
89	For a small TypeScript suite, I would therefore start with local factories and fixtures. Promote something to `test/support` only after multiple tests genuinely need the same behavior. Keep container support as a thin adapter over the underlying container library rather than creating your own orchestration API.
90	
91	## Keeping a suite honest when it cannot run everywhere
92	
93	There are two different failure modes: a slow suite can **fail**, or it can silently stop being meaningful. The latter is worse. A credible setup therefore needs selection integrity and freshness: the slow command should fail if it unexpectedly discovers zero tests; scheduled/main runs should have an owner and visible last-success status; quarantined tests should have explicit owners/expiry rather than becoming permanent skips; and release policy should say how recent a successful slow run must be when that suite is not a per-PR gate.
94	
95	External dependencies need an additional distinction between **signal** and **gate**. Zod has a particularly clean recent example. On July 13, 2026, issue #6185 documented that every PR had been red since TypeScript 7.0.2 became npm's `latest`, including documentation-only changes—the bleeding-edge compiler leg was breaking the build for an external/toolchain reason. ([GitHub](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/issues/6185?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Its current release workflow now says explicitly that the publishing matrix is deliberately narrower than `test.yml`: stable TypeScript versions gate publishing, while `test.yml` carries the TypeScript 7 signal, because a bleeding-edge compiler regression must not block a release. ([GitHub](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
96	
97	That is a useful model for slow or environmentally fragile tests too: **do not suppress valuable signal just because it is unsuitable as a universal gate. Give it a separate lane with a clear escalation policy.**
98	
99	Terraform's guide describes the other half of the problem: acceptance tests against external systems can fail because those systems drift. It recommends first running the existing acceptance tests against an unchanged worktree before blaming a new change. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) That is essentially a control experiment, and it is especially valuable for container/service tests whose environment may move independently of the product.
100	
101	## What I would adopt for the TypeScript repository you described
102	
103	With only a handful of intentionally chosen tests, I would **not** create `tests/unit`, `tests/integration`, `tests/e2e`, and a parallel copy of the source tree. Keep ownership local. Put pure tests beside their subject as `foo.test.ts`; put a container test beside its subject as `foo.container.test.ts` unless it genuinely tests several domains, in which case a small top-level `test/container/` area is justified.
104	
105	Then make the distinction executable: the normal `test`/watch command explicitly excludes `*.container.test.ts`; `test:container` explicitly includes it; CI shows them as separate jobs. Imports of your container library can even be lint-restricted to `*.container.test.ts` or `test/container/**`, which turns “fast tests must stay pure” from tribal knowledge into an enforceable invariant.
106	
107	The resulting policy is small enough to remember: **location says who owns the test; the filename says that it is a test and, only when necessary, what expensive resource it needs; runner configuration determines what executes; CI determines when.** Angular, Zod, and Terraform differ substantially in directory layout, but all three point toward that separation of concerns rather than toward one canonical `tests/` tree.
108	
```

The hard parts are lifecycle across process interruption, isolation, deterministic nondeterminism, and failure diagnostics—not `test()` itself.

Separately, Node users specifically called out Jest’s partial-object matcher and easy class/module mocking as things they missed.

40	
41	A minimal runner is usually enough. What a serious project needs beyond it is not another framework so much as a **small test-support layer plus an execution policy**: resource ownership, isolation, deterministic control of time/randomness, a few domain-aware assertions, and failure diagnostics. The useful dividing line is whether those pieces remain ordinary imported code. Once the project starts reimplementing module interception, source transforms, browser environments, worker pools, snapshots, or a reporter/plugin architecture, it is effectively building a test framework.
42	
43	### What to add, and what not to add
44	
45	| Need | Framework-free form | Key rule |
46	|---|---|---|
47	| Fixtures/resources | Factories plus a per-test cleanup stack | Acquisition and cleanup belong together |
48	| Interrupted-run cleanup | Run IDs + external reaper/lease/TTL/scavenger | In-process hooks cannot clean up after a dead process |
49	| Parallelism | A tiny file sharder / CI matrix spawning separate runner processes | Parallelise isolated units rather than sharing mutable state |
50	| Isolation | Unique temp dirs, DB/schema names, ports, namespaces | Isolation is mostly a resource-naming problem |
51	| Parameterised tests | A loop that declares one named test per row | Prefer visible individual tests to a `test.each` clone |
52	| Time | Injected `Clock` for business time; focused fake-timer library when scheduling itself is under test | Do not make the whole suite depend on patched globals |
53	| Randomness | Explicit seed, deterministic PRNG, seed in failure output | Every random failure must be replayable |
54	| Assertions | Native assertions plus a very small domain helper module | Add an assertion only when it improves meaning or diagnostics |
55	| Reporting | Failure context + captured logs/artifacts + reproduction command; JUnit adapter only if CI requires it | Optimise output for the person diagnosing the failure |
56	
57	That is roughly the model used by Node core itself. Its current test guide has a project-owned `common` support module and fixture module; `common` also detects leaked globals. It uses helpers such as `mustCall`/`mustSucceed` for asynchronous invariants, closes resources explicitly, recommends OS-assigned port `0` for safe parallel execution, and says tests should be written to make failures easy to debug. Test stdout/stderr is normally suppressed but included with a failed assertion, specifically because it can reveal where a CI hang occurred. ([GitHub](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/doc/contributing/writing-tests.md))
58	
59	## Fixtures and lifecycle: make ownership the abstraction
60	
61	The useful fixture primitive is not “fixture injection”. It is **scoped ownership**. A helper that creates a database, server, temporary directory or mock installation should either return its disposer with the resource or register that disposer immediately with the current test's cleanup scope. Register cleanup *before* doing the next fallible setup operation, execute cleanup in reverse order, and make disposers idempotent.
62	
63	That handles ordinary failure well. If setup creates A and then creation of B throws, A is already registered. If the assertion throws, teardown still happens. If teardown itself fails, preserve the original test error and attach/report the cleanup error; only make cleanup the primary failure when the test itself succeeded.
64	
65	This is also where small project-specific abstractions are valuable. Markpad provides a good recent example. Its Svelte stores can own effects and browser listeners that are correct to keep alive for the whole application but leak between tests in a shared jsdom environment. Its test guidance therefore says `SettingsStore.dispose()` must be paired automatically with the test-finished hook rather than relying on every test author to remember it. An abandoned store can otherwise react to a later test's `flushSync()` or storage event. ([GitHub](https://github.com/sftwrdotdev/Markpad/blob/master/AGENTS.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) The relevant migration/fix was made on **12 August 2026**. [Markpad's 12 Aug 2026 migration commit](https://github.com/sftwrdotdev/Markpad/commit/d1615e5b10fe0b87f174635f67ba353bd12c3b4a?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
66	
67	An interrupted process is a different problem. `afterEach`, `finally`, shutdown handlers and disposers work only while code is still being allowed to run. `SIGKILL`, a crashed worker, machine loss, and many IDE/debugger “Stop” operations give your process no cleanup opportunity. Testcontainers-node's **11 September 2020** Ryuk request describes exactly this failure mode: a test starts containers in setup, the developer stops the debugger, no `afterEach`/`afterAll` runs, and containers accumulate. The solution class is an external reaper/watchdog rather than a better hook. ([GitHub](https://github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-node/issues/118))
68	
69	For non-container resources, the same idea can be simpler: tag every externally created thing with a test-run ID; use a lease/expiry where the service supports one; remove stale run-owned temp directories on the next startup; or have a parent process own child resources and destroy them when workers disappear. Signal cleanup is worth having as a best effort, but it should never be your only interrupted-run guarantee.
70	
71	## Parallelism: solve isolation first
72	
73	A minimal runner does not need an internal worker pool. A small script can discover test files, partition them across N workers, and start N independent runtime processes; CI can do the same with a matrix. **File/process isolation is usually the least surprising concurrency boundary.** Tests that mutate process-wide environment variables, current working directory, global monkey patches or module state then cannot contaminate another worker.
74	
75	Inside each worker, external resources still need unique ownership. Use a fresh temp directory, unique database/schema/tenant name, unique queue/topic prefix, and let the OS allocate network ports rather than “finding” a supposedly unused one and releasing it before use. Node core's guide explicitly recommends listening on port `0` because it permits safe parallel tests. In the **18 July 2023** Node 18.17.0 release, several inspector/debugger tests were changed to random/port-0 allocation and then moved from the sequential set into the parallel set. ([GitHub](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/doc/contributing/writing-tests.md))
76	
77	That is an instructive ordering: the fix was not “turn concurrency on”; it was **remove the shared resource collision, then turn concurrency on**.
78	
79	Some tests should remain serial. A test of a single global lock, a fixed OS service, a process-wide installation, or a scarce physical device can legitimately be marked/partitioned into a serial lane. Trying to manufacture parallelism around intrinsically singleton state usually creates worse tests.
80	
81	## Parameterised cases do not need a feature
82	
83	For finite cases, ordinary language constructs are generally better than reproducing `test.each`:
84	
85	```js
86	for (const c of cases) {
87	  test(`${c.name}: ${c.input}`, () => {
88	    assert.equal(transform(c.input), c.expected);
89	  });
90	}
91	```
92	
93	The important part is that each row declares a separate, well-named test. That preserves filtering and gives the failure a useful identity. A five-line `cases()` helper can standardise naming if this pattern occurs everywhere, but once it has format strings, argument unpacking rules, `.only`, `.skip`, nesting, typing tricks and its own error wrapping, it has stopped paying for itself.
94	
95	For a large combinatorial space, do not create a more sophisticated table helper. That is where a focused property-testing package can make sense independently of the test runner.
96	
97	## Time: distinguish “what time is it?” from scheduling
98	
99	Most application time should be controlled through an ordinary application seam:
100	
101	```text
102	Clock.now()
103	```
104	
105	Production gets a system clock; tests get a fixed or manually advanced clock. This is especially clean for expiry, billing periods, cache freshness, token validity and date calculations. The downside is that the clock dependency becomes part of the production design, but that is often desirable: dependence on wall-clock time is a real dependency whether the code admits it or not.
106	
107	When the thing being tested is **timer machinery**—timeouts, debouncing, retry delays, intervals—a focused fake-clock package is appropriate without adopting its surrounding testing framework. `@sinonjs/fake-timers`, for example, can install only the timer/time globals, advance the clock deterministically, count leaked timers, and uninstall to restore the originals. ([GitHub](https://github.com/sinonjs/fake-timers?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
108	
109	The project rule should be that global fake time is always registered for restoration at the moment it is installed. For ordinary business logic, prefer the injected clock because it does not affect unrelated code in the process.
110	
111	Real sleeping should be rare. Node core's own test guidance says to avoid timers unless timers are actually the subject because they are a source of flakiness. ([GitHub](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/doc/contributing/writing-tests.md))
112	
113	## Randomness: randomness is fine; irreproducible randomness is not
114	
115	Give a run one explicit seed. Feed all test-data randomness from a deterministic PRNG, ideally derive a stable per-test seed from the root seed plus test identity so reordering or parallel scheduling does not change a test's values. On failure, print the root/test seed and provide a simple environment variable or command-line route for replay.
116	
117	A focused package can do more without replacing the runner. fast-check is explicitly designed to run inside existing test blocks; it reports a seed for failed runs, supports exact replay with `seed` plus `path`, and shrinks the generated input to a smaller counterexample. Its current documentation describes the seed as replayable and its August 2026 examples show failure reports containing seed, path and the reduced counterexample. ([Fast Check](https://fast-check.dev/docs/api/interfaces/Parameters/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
118	
119	The practical rule is that `Math.random()`/equivalent should not directly generate correctness-critical test data. A nightly fuzz lane may deliberately choose a fresh seed, but that seed still has to be printed and retained when it fails.
120	
121	## Assertion helpers: add semantics, not vocabulary
122	
123	Native strict/deep/throws assertions should remain the default. A custom assertion earns its existence when it captures a recurring **domain invariant** or produces materially better evidence than several generic assertions.
124	
125	Node's `common.mustCall` is a good example. Its value is not prettier syntax: it detects the otherwise easy-to-miss case where an expected asynchronous callback never happened. `mustSucceed` additionally refuses to ignore the error-first argument. Those helpers encode failure modes that normal end-of-test equality checks can silently miss. ([GitHub](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/doc/contributing/writing-tests.md))
126	
127	A project-specific `assertHttpProblem`, `assertNoLeakedJobs`, `assertSameDomainRecord`, or `assertEventuallyConsistent` can similarly be worthwhile if its error tells the maintainer *why* the invariant failed and exposes useful actual values.
128	
129	What is usually not worth building is a fluent matcher DSL merely to recover framework syntax. There is real ergonomic loss here: on **25 October 2023**, a Node user migrating from Jest specifically requested a native equivalent of `toMatchObject`, saying partial deep matching on large objects was one thing they missed. ([GitHub](https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/50399?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) If a codebase repeatedly needs that operation, one well-tested `assertMatchObject()` is reasonable. Recreating dozens of `expect(...).toX()` matchers is not.
130	
131	## Reporting: diagnostic context matters more than reporter architecture
132	
133	A failing test should leave enough information that someone who was not watching it run can begin diagnosis. That normally means the full test name and file; actual/expected values and native diff; parameterised-case inputs; seed/replay information; relevant resource/run IDs; bounded stdout/stderr or a path to a retained log/artifact; and a copyable command for rerunning that test.
134	
135	Do not catch a native assertion and replace it with `"test failed"`; that destroys the useful stack, diff and cause. If setup talks to a subprocess/service, capture its logs but reveal them primarily on failure—Node core follows exactly that pattern. ([GitHub](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/doc/contributing/writing-tests.md))
136	
137	CI machine formats are a separate concern. When nodejs.org proposed moving from Jest on **16 November 2023**, it explicitly intended to keep generating JUnit reports even while removing Jest's reporter/coverage dependency stack. ([GitHub](https://github.com/nodejs/nodejs.org/issues/6123)) That is a good architecture: human-readable diagnostics live close to the tests; JUnit or similar is a thin transport adapter for CI.
138	
139	## What people miss after leaving Jest/Vitest—and what they do not
140	
141	The clearest migration record is nodejs.org's November 2023 proposal. The reasons for leaving Jest were fewer dependencies, substantially less test tooling, native ESM, speed, and the fact that the project did not need snapshots or other richer Jest features. It expected to remove Jest-related reporters and coverage generators while retaining JUnit output. The notable migration pain was module mocking: Jest's module-name mapping and `__mocks__` convention could not simply carry over and the mocks had to become explicit. ([GitHub](https://github.com/nodejs/nodejs.org/issues/6123))
142	
143	The community reports line up with that. Besides partial-object matching, a **7 August 2023** Node help issue from a Jest user specifically struggled with replacing a class instantiated inside the module under test—common with SDK-style dependencies—and contrasted that with Jest's easy class mocking. ([GitHub](https://github.com/nodejs/help/issues/4220?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This is often a useful design signal: if replacing a dependency requires loader magic, consider making that dependency injectable before adding loader magic to every test.
144	
145	The migration is not confined to early adopters. Wretch's **19 October 2025** 3.0.0 changelog records “Remove jest in favour of node:test”. ([GitHub](https://github.com/elbywan/wretch/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Commander 15, released **29 May 2026**, switched its tests from Jest to `node:test` in the same release that made the library ESM-only; its notes explicitly call out test frameworks/bundlers as a potential ESM compatibility issue. ([GitHub](https://github.com/tj/commander.js/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
146	
147	So what teams are glad to lose is fairly consistent: dependency weight, configuration, transforms they do not require, framework-specific APIs, ESM friction, and integrated features they were not actually using. What they miss is also consistent: convenient module mocking, a few rich matchers, watch/coverage/reporting in one command, and—in UI/build-heavy projects—the ability to reproduce the application's transformed execution environment.
148	
149	## When teams go back to a framework
150	
151	There are important counterexamples, and they give a good boundary.
152	
153	**Markpad, 12 August 2026**, deliberately ended up with **Vitest alongside `node --test`, not instead of it**. Plain TypeScript stays on the native runner. Svelte-runes modules and real-DOM tests use Vitest with the Svelte compiler and jsdom. The reason was correctness: the native-runner tests had hand-written `$state`/`$derived`/`$effect` shims whose semantics differed from compiled Svelte—most importantly, effects did not actually re-run—so a behavior test could pass against the imitation while the real application was wrong. The project explicitly says moving an ordinary passing TypeScript test to Vitest “buys nothing.” ([GitHub](https://github.com/sftwrdotdev/Markpad/blob/master/AGENTS.md))
154	
155	**Wanta, by June 2026**, also moved tests from `node --test` back to Vitest in a build-related change. Its current decision record says an endpoint became a Vite `define` compile-time constant and the tests moved in the same change because Vitest gave them the native Vite transformation; otherwise they needed a runtime-injection hack. ([GitHub](https://github.com/oomol-lab/wanta/blob/main/docs/key-decisions.md)) That is almost the canonical case for adopting the framework: the framework is part of reproducing the production module/build semantics.
156	
157	A third useful contrast is GEOLYTIX/xyz's current migration from its small Codi test framework to Vitest. Its stated reasons were not `describe` or assertions; Codi already had those. The server-side suite lacked dependency mocking, automatic discovery, coverage, watch mode and CI integration, and some tests were effectively un-runnable without a browser/live server. Vitest supplied that bundle and the project decided the bundle was worth having. ([GitHub](https://github.com/GEOLYTIX/xyz/blob/main/TESTING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
158	
159	That suggests a practical stopping rule: **do not adopt a framework because you need fixtures, tables, seeded randomness, a clock or better assertions. Those are small composable tools. Consider the framework when faithful testing requires the application's compiler/loader/browser transform environment, or when your home-grown support layer has accumulated mocking transforms, discovery, workers, watch mode, snapshots and reporter infrastructure.**
160	
161	For the repository in your premise, I would keep the built-in runner and make `test/support/` an intentionally boring library: a cleanup scope, resource factories, clock/RNG helpers, a parameter-case helper if repetition warrants it, a handful of domain assertions, and a diagnostic recorder. Put parallel file execution in a separate script/CI layer. That gives most of what teams actually use from a framework without turning the test suite into a second application platform.
162	
````

1	# Testing External Format Rewriters
2	
3	Source: https://chatgpt.com/share/6aa92c85-b398-83eb-b2c1-4a9c969d25a1
4	
5	---
6	
7	**User**
8	
9	Context: A project parses and rewrites a configuration format defined by another program, which is authoritative and changes between its own releases. The project must preserve bytes it does not intend to change, and must never widen what an entry permits.
10	
11	Question: How do projects test a parser or rewriter for a format they do not own?
12	
13	Cover: round trip and idempotency testing; differential testing against the authoritative implementation; corpus based testing and where corpora come from; fuzzing, including structure aware fuzzing; property based testing of preservation; golden files and their failure modes; and how projects detect that the upstream grammar changed in a new release.
14	
15	Also cover how projects decide what to do with input they cannot parse, and how that decision is tested.
16	
17	Use named examples such as configuration file rewriters, code formatters, linters, and protocol libraries.
18	
19	Evidence rules: cite repositories and papers with dates. Where a project publishes its corpus or fuzzing setup, describe how it is run and how failures are triaged. Include examples of bugs these methods found.
20	
21	---
22	
23	**ChatGPT**
24	
25	I’ll treat this as an engineering survey rather than a single best-practice recipe: I’ll separate invariants you can test without an oracle from oracle-based checks against upstream, then use concrete repositories and fuzzing/paper evidence to show how mature projects combine them.
26	
27	---
28	
29	**ChatGPT**
30	
31	Two useful patterns are already visible in the repositories: `gix-config` explicitly promises lossless Git-config round trips, while Ruff treats idempotency, syntax validity, and compatibility against Black/real-world projects as separate checks. That separation is important: a single “golden output” test cannot prove all three.
32	
33	---
34	
35	**ChatGPT**
36	
37	The strongest design is “layered oracles”: byte-level preservation properties first, semantic comparison to upstream second, and fuzz/corpus tests to explore cases neither suite anticipated. For safety-sensitive rewrites, the write path should have a stricter acceptance gate than the read/diagnostic path.
38	
39	---
40	
41	**ChatGPT**
42	
43	For a parser or rewriter of somebody else’s format, the most effective approach is to treat the upstream program as a **versioned executable specification**, and then test several different contracts independently: syntactic compatibility, semantic compatibility, byte preservation, rewrite safety, and robustness. No single oracle—especially not golden files—is strong enough by itself.
44	
45	### Round trips and idempotency
46	
47	For a lossless configuration rewriter, the first test should be stronger than the usual `parse → print → parse` check. A no-op operation should satisfy **byte identity**:
48	
49	`rewrite_noop(x) == x`
50	
51	That includes comments, blank lines, quoting choices, whitespace, line endings, ordering, and unknown-but-preservable material. `gix-config`, for example, explicitly describes its goal as lossless Git-config round trips, retaining comments and whitespace and changing only affected lines. ([GitHub](https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/blob/main/crate-status.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
52	
53	For an actual edit `e`, useful properties are:
54	
55	`R_e(R_e(x)) == R_e(x)` — applying the same edit twice is idempotent.
56	
57	`upstream_parse(R_e(x)) succeeds` — you never emit something the owner rejects.
58	
59	`semantic_upstream(R_e(x)) == intended_edit(semantic_upstream(x))` — the edit means what you intended according to the owner, not merely according to your parser.
60	
61	For a permission-like entry, add the security property explicitly. If `Allowed(x)` is the behavior permitted by the authoritative implementation, a restriction-only rewrite should establish something like
62	
63	`Allowed(R_e(x)) ⊆ Allowed(x)`
64	
65	and, more generally, `Allowed(R_e(x))` must be no larger than the set authorized by the requested edit. This catches the particularly dangerous class of bug where an unknown flag, negation, qualifier, or ordering rule gets lost and the rewritten entry becomes more permissive.
66	
67	Formatters use the same idea without byte preservation: canonicalization should satisfy `F(F(x)) = F(x)`. Rustfmt's test infrastructure deliberately checks not only source→expected-output goldens but also that files already in the expected `tests/target` tree remain unchanged and that formatting does not require multiple passes to converge. ([GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/blob/main/Contributing.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Ruff similarly runs stability checks for a second formatting pass, syntactic validity of the result, and panics. ([GitHub](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/main/crates/ruff_python_formatter/CONTRIBUTING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
68	
69	These checks find real defects. On June 3, 2024, Ruff reported an idempotency failure found by its `ruff_formatter_idempotency` fuzz target: a multiline string changed differently on the first and second formatting passes. ([GitHub](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/11724?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
70	
71	### Differential testing against the owner
72	
73	When one implementation is authoritative, differential testing is unusually valuable. McKeeman's 1998 paper describes the core method: feed mechanically generated cases to comparable implementations and investigate disagreements, crashes, and hangs. ([DBLP](https://dblp.org/rec/journals/dtj/McKeeman98.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
74	
75	For a configuration format, I would compare more than “accepted/rejected.” For every corpus or generated file, record the authoritative program's observable interpretation: resolved keys, boolean values, effective permissions, include expansion, precedence, normalization, or whatever commands expose the semantics. Then compare those observations with your implementation.
76	
77	Gitoxide does this directly. Its Git-config `includeIf` work was tested against a Git baseline so the two implementations had to agree on conditional inclusion behavior. ([GitHub](https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/discussions/468?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This is preferable to comparing two ASTs because Git's internal AST is not the contract; Git's externally visible interpretation is.
78	
79	Ruff provides another good example. Its parser work has used fuzz results comparing Ruff with CPython's parser/compiler, and a 2025 tracking issue lists semantic syntax errors discovered from those disagreements. ([GitHub](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/17412?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) A protocol analogue is BoringSSL's TLS suite: it intentionally uses a second TLS implementation—a patched Go `crypto/tls`—to construct both valid and deliberately malformed handshakes. Rustls runs that BoGo suite against itself. ([BoringSSL](https://boringssl.googlesource.com/boringssl/%2B/master/ssl/test/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
80	
81	Differential testing does need an “allowed differences” layer. Versions differ; some errors are implementation-specific; diagnostics may change without semantics changing. Compare the narrowest externally meaningful result you can, and version the exceptions rather than silently updating expected output.
82	
83	### Corpora: where useful tests actually come from
84	
85	A mature corpus is usually an amalgam rather than something invented from scratch. The highest-yield sources are upstream's own conformance/regression tests; real files taken from open-source projects, package repositories, operating-system images, and customer installations where licensing permits; every user bug reproducer; minimized fuzzer crashes; files exercising each historical syntax version; and hand-written pathological cases involving quoting, continuation, encodings, duplicate entries, nesting, comments, and boundary sizes.
86	
87	Real-world code is particularly useful because grammar documents rarely describe all accepted quirks. Ruff copied most of Black's formatter fixtures into its own suite to expose output differences, and separately runs ecosystem checks on selected real projects; its documentation cites projects such as Django and Zulip when quantifying compatibility. ([GitHub](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/main/crates/ruff_python_formatter/CONTRIBUTING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Rustfmt's `tests/source`/`tests/target` pairs are another classic repository corpus. ([GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/blob/main/Contributing.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
88	
89	Fuzzing corpora should be cumulative. OSS-Fuzz recommends starting fuzz targets with good sample inputs, continually evolves the corpus through coverage-guided mutation, permits downloading the accumulated corpus, and recommends examining coverage to see which grammar areas remain unreachable. ([GitHub](https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz/blob/master/docs/getting-started/new_project_guide.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Gitoxide publicly maintains fuzz-corpus directories, including for `gix-config`, and runs continuous fuzzing through OSS-Fuzz. ([GitHub](https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/discussions/1308?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
90	
91	The practical rule is: **a fixed regression suite remembers bugs you have already seen; a living corpus gives mutation-based tools useful places from which to search for bugs you have not seen.**
92	
93	### Fuzzing: raw, structured, and differential
94	
95	Raw byte fuzzing remains worthwhile. It is very good at lexer failures, invalid UTF-8 handling, integer/pathological-length cases, crashes, hangs, recursion explosions, and accidental assumptions about terminators or allocation sizes.
96	
97	But highly structured formats need structure-aware fuzzing as well. Godefroid, Kiezun and Levin's 2008 grammar-based whitebox work showed why: random malformed input tends to die in early parsing stages; adding grammar knowledge increased code-generation-module coverage in their IE7 JavaScript experiment from 53% to 81% while using fewer tests. ([Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/?p=153167&utm_source=chatgpt.com)) LangFuzz, published at USENIX Security in 2012, combined grammar-aware generation with fragments from existing programs and bug-triggering inputs; the authors reported 105 new severe Mozilla JavaScript vulnerabilities and 18 PHP crash defects. ([Usenix](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity12/technical-sessions/presentation/holler?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
98	
99	For a configuration rewriter, structure-aware fuzzing can generate a document AST plus an **edit operation**, not merely a document. Useful mutation dimensions include duplicate sections, quoted/unquoted representations, escaped separators, comments in every legal position, alternative line endings, include chains, version-specific constructs, and an edit targeting an arbitrary occurrence.
100	
101	Google's libprotobuf-mutator is a concrete implementation of this general technique: describe a structured input using a protobuf representation, mutate the tree rather than arbitrary bytes, then convert it into the real syntax. Its documentation describes this for SQL and other grammars and records bugs found in Chromium and Envoy. ([GitHub](https://github.com/google/fuzzing/blob/master/docs/structure-aware-fuzzing.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
102	
103	The best setup normally combines both approaches. Keep one byte-oriented target for hostile malformed input, one structure-aware target for deep semantic paths, and one **differential target** that feeds the same generated input to the upstream implementation and your own.
104	
105	Gitoxide's experience illustrates the value of the first category: after expanded `gix-config` fuzzing was put onto Google's infrastructure, a stack-overflow vulnerability was found within about a day; another fuzzer exposed unbounded recursive behavior in `gix-glob`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/discussions/1261?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
106	
107	### Property-based testing for preservation
108	
109	Property-based testing is particularly well suited to rewriters because the strongest requirements are invariants rather than specific expected outputs. QuickCheck's original 2000 paper framed exactly this model: define properties and generate large numbers of inputs, with custom generators where ordinary random generation is insufficient. ([DBLP](https://dblp.uni-trier.de/rec/conf/icfp/ClaessenH00.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
110	
111	For a lossless rewriter, I would make these properties executable:
112	
113	* no requested edit ⇒ exact byte identity; requested edit ⇒ all known untouched token spans remain byte-identical and in the same order; repeated edit ⇒ identical bytes; output is accepted by the targeted upstream version; authoritative semantics after rewriting equal the intended semantic transformation; and, for security restrictions, the authoritative permitted set never exceeds the intended permitted set.
114	
115	The important detail is that the last two properties must use an independent oracle where possible. Testing `my_parser(my_writer(my_parser(x)))` can establish internal consistency while both parser and writer share the same misunderstanding.
116	
117	Shrinking is valuable here. The ideal failing artifact is not a 400 KB configuration but the smallest file containing, say, “negated option + escaped quote + trailing comment” that still causes the permission-widening error.
118	
119	### Golden files: valuable, but not a proof
120	
121	Goldens are excellent for reviewability. A test author can see exactly which byte changed, and unusual syntax remains permanently represented in the repository. Rustfmt's source/target fixtures and Ruff's snapshot tests are good examples. Ruff even copied Black test fixtures and removes a snapshot once Ruff and Black no longer differ on that input. ([GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/blob/main/Contributing.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
122	
123	Their failure mode is oracle circularity. If `expected.conf` was produced by the same implementation under test, a bug can simply become the blessed answer. A broad “update all snapshots” operation can turn a regression into the new specification. Goldens can also bake in platform line endings, upstream-version quirks, nondeterministic ordering, or an accidental normalization that violates byte-preservation requirements.
124	
125	Therefore I would treat a golden as **one readable example of an invariant**, never as the invariant itself. A preservation golden should also be accompanied by an assertion identifying which byte spans were permitted to change. A semantic golden should ideally also be checked against the owner.
126	
127	### Detecting an upstream grammar change
128	
129	Projects that do this reliably do not wait for user reports. They maintain an upstream compatibility job.
130	
131	Run the differential/conformance suite against at least the oldest supported upstream, the current release, and a preview/nightly or upstream main branch. For each version, retain an acceptance matrix. A particularly valuable alarm is:
132	
133	`new_upstream accepts input && our_current_parser rejects input`
134	
135	because that is often a newly introduced grammar feature.
136	
137	Ruff has concrete examples. On April 23, 2024, a contributor adding PEP 696 syntax to CPython noticed that Ruff began failing in CPython CI; that exposed missing Ruff parser support for the new Python 3.13 syntax. ([GitHub](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/11099?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) In June 2025, Python 3.13.4 changed f-string behavior in a way that made Ruff's formatted output syntactically invalid; Ruff subsequently changed its formatter and documented the grammar-related compatibility fix. ([GitHub](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/18632?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
138	
139	Baseline tests can detect subtler changes as well. Gitoxide records a baseline failure caused by a behavior change in Git 2.47's `rev-parse`; such a failure is exactly what should trigger investigation rather than automatic fixture regeneration. ([GitHub](https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/blob/main/etc/plan/bug-fixes.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
140	
141	Protocol suites make this process especially explicit. Rustls documents that updating its vendored BoGo suite is expected to expose new failures. Maintainers triage those into changed upstream error expectations versus newly added test-runner options; genuinely unsupported options are marked `NYI` rather than silently pretending to support them. ([GitHub](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/main/bogo/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) That is a good model for configuration grammar evolution too: “new upstream construct that we deliberately do not understand” should be a named state, not an accidental parse error.
142	
143	### What to do with input you cannot parse
144	
145	For a security-sensitive rewriter, the safest default is **fail closed and do not write**. The original bytes remain untouched, the user gets a diagnostic saying which upstream versions you support, and no partially understood document is normalized.
146	
147	There are valid alternatives, but they need explicit contracts. A lossless parser may represent an unknown construct as an opaque byte span if it can determine its boundaries without guessing; then unrelated edits can proceed while the opaque span is copied exactly. What it should not do is interpret half an entry, drop the unknown half, and serialize the portion it thinks it understands. That is precisely how a restrictive entry can become permissive.
148	
149	Error recovery is appropriate for linters and editors, where showing later diagnostics is useful. It is much more questionable as the basis for an on-disk rewrite. A sensible architecture is therefore **permissive read for diagnostics, strict write for mutation**: before committing an edit, require a complete safe parse or safe opaque segmentation, generate the output, and run the targeted authoritative parser/evaluator over the result.
150	
151	Ruff's fix machinery illustrates the final validation step. In reported cases where a lint fix generated invalid Python, Ruff prints “Fix introduced a syntax error. Reverting all changes” rather than leaving the broken rewrite in place. ([GitHub](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/16472?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
152	
153	Test this policy as aggressively as successful parsing. Feed truncated files, future-version syntax, invalid encodings, embedded NULs, malformed quoting, and random bytes; kill the process during the write; and inject errors between temp-file creation and rename. On every rejected case, assert that the original file's bytes and metadata are unchanged. For opaque preservation, mutate something before and after the unknown construct and assert exact identity of the unknown range. For any successful rewrite, rerun the authoritative implementation before declaring the test passed.
154	
155	### A practical hierarchy
156	
157	For the project in your context, I would make the release gate conceptually:
158	
159	**byte preservation → syntactic validity → upstream semantic equivalence → non-widening safety → idempotency**, with corpus and fuzzing supplying the inputs.
160	
161	The core CI suite would contain hand-written and regression examples plus property tests. A compatibility job would compare against supported upstream releases. A scheduled job would run against upstream prerelease/main and its latest test suite. Fuzzing would have separate raw-byte, structured-document/edit, and differential targets. Every minimized fuzz failure would become a permanent regression input; every upstream divergence would be classified as “our bug”, “new upstream behavior”, “unsupported but safely preserved”, or an explicitly documented intentional difference.
162	
163	That combination is much more robust than trying to reconstruct the owner's grammar perfectly. In practice, successful reimplementations such as Gitoxide, Ruff, rustfmt, and rustls assume that their understanding will sometimes be incomplete, and build tests specifically to discover when that happens. ([GitHub](https://github.com/gitoxidelabs/gitoxide?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
164	
```

First, “more tests” is not monotonic with better signal: Google found large tests far flakier than small ones, while Meta got high regression recall running a selected subset. Second, several seemingly sensible fixes—especially simply lengthening timeouts—have published cases where they did not fix the failure rate.
