```text
34	
35	The strongest evidence points to a fairly specific design for a test suite that is meant to survive two years of change: **keep most tests small, deterministic and close to stable behavioural contracts; treat end-to-end tests as a scarce resource; measure flakiness and runtime as properties of the suite itself; use coverage to find gaps rather than as a quality score; and keep deployment safeguards independent of the test suite.**
36	
37	I would distinguish three evidence levels below: **Measured** means an empirical study or quantitative production report; **case report** means an organisation or practitioner describing one system without a controlled comparison; **guidance** is informed practice but not evidence that the intervention caused an improvement.
38	
39	### Flaky tests: large organisations have measured this, and the numbers are not small
40	
41	| Organisation / source | What was measured | What they did | Evidence that the intervention works / fails |
42	|---|---|---|---|
43	| **Google, 27 May 2016 — Measured production data.** [Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them](https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/05/flaky-tests-at-google-and-how-we.html?hl=de_AT&utm_source=chatgpt.com) | About **1.5% of all test executions** produced a flaky result; almost **16% of tests had some flakiness**. More strikingly, **84% of observed pass→fail transitions involved a flaky test**. Google listed concurrency, nondeterministic/undefined behaviour, third-party failures and infrastructure as causes. Its flake insertion rate was roughly equal to its fix rate. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/05/flaky-tests-at-google-and-how-we.html?hl=de_AT)) | Selective/automatic retries; tests marked flaky could require three consecutive failures; automated quarantine plus a bug; monitoring changes in each test's flakiness. | Google explicitly says these mitigations are imperfect. Three retries can turn a 15-minute test into **45 minutes** before a real regression is recognised; quarantine can conceal a real race or product bug; repeated false alarms caused developers to dismiss genuine failures. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/05/flaky-tests-at-google-and-how-we.html?hl=de_AT)) |
44	| **Google, 17 Apr 2017 — Measured.** [Where do our flaky tests come from?](https://testing.googleblog.com/2017/04/where-do-our-flaky-tests-come-from.html?hl=it_IT&utm_source=chatgpt.com) | Among ~**4.2 million tests**, ~63,000 had a flaky execution in a week. Flakiness was **0.5% for small, 1.6% for medium and 14% for large tests**. Some technologies looked worse—Android-emulator tests 25.46%, Python WebDriver 18.72%—but test size was a major confounder. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2017/04/where-do-our-flaky-tests-come-from.html?hl=it_IT&utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Push functionality toward smaller tests rather than assuming that choosing a different test runner fixes the problem. | This is correlation, not an experiment proving that shrinking any particular test will cure it. But Google later published a concrete migration with measured before/after results, discussed below. |
45	| **Microsoft, ICSE 2020 — Measured study of six proprietary projects.** [A Study on the Lifecycle of Flaky Tests](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/a-study-on-the-lifecycle-of-flaky-tests/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) | Researchers identified **2,089 flaky tests**, of which 1,040 had been fixed. Among categorized fixes, **Async Wait was 78%**, network 14%, with concurrency, resource leaks, randomness, I/O and time also represented. ([Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/LamETAL20FaTB.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) The operational impact varied enormously: one project had only 176 flaky tests yet they would have affected **35.7% of builds**; another had 1,453 but affected only **0.4% of builds**. ([Department of Computer Science](https://cs.gmu.edu/~winglam/Lam21PhD.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Microsoft built tooling around identifying/suppressing known flakes and experimented with **FaTB**, which derives appropriate waits for asynchronous tests instead of guessing. | On five flaky tests, FaTB made tests **up to 78% faster without increasing their observed flaky-failure rate**. Crucially, the authors also reran tests where developers claimed to have fixed flakiness by increasing waits and found cases where the longer waits **did not reduce flakiness at all**. ([Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/a-study-on-the-lifecycle-of-flaky-tests/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
46	| **Meta, 10 Dec 2020 — Measured production system, though no controlled before/after flake-rate experiment.** [Probabilistic flakiness at Facebook](https://engineering.fb.com/2020/12/10/developer-tools/probabilistic-flakiness/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) | Meta calculates a probabilistic flakiness score for **millions of tests** from normal CI history. It reports an irreducible framework-dependent floor: well below 1% for unit-test frameworks, but as high as **~10% for some end-to-end frameworks**. ([Engineering at Meta](https://engineering.fb.com/2020/12/10/developer-tools/probabilistic-flakiness/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Retries; continuous per-test flakiness measurement; owner tickets when reliability regresses; sufficiently bad/unfixed tests become ineligible for change-based CI selection. | Meta calls retries its most powerful tool but explicitly calls them **resource-intensive**. PFS became widely used internally, but the post does not give a clean experimental “before X%, after Y%” result. Its strongest finding is organisational: continuous ownership/incentives make flakiness visible rather than normalising it. ([Engineering at Meta](https://engineering.fb.com/2020/12/10/developer-tools/probabilistic-flakiness/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
47	
48	The most defensible intervention from these reports is therefore **not “retry flaky tests until green.”** Retries are useful diagnostically and to keep CI moving, but Google documents how they delay recognition and create alarm fatigue. Better-supported changes are to reduce test size and dependencies, explicitly await asynchronous work rather than guessing sleeps, measure each test's reliability, and give flaky tests an owner and an expiry path rather than letting “known flaky” become permanent.
49	
50	### Suites that became too slow to run
51	
52	This failure mode is plainly documented. GitLab says its full suite, without parallelisation, **takes hours**. Its measured profiling identified recurring sources: unnecessary database-persisted factories and factory cascades, full browser tests where HTML-level tests suffice, widely included slow shared examples, waits for elements expected to be absent, and invoking real external operations such as compilation or Git commands. GitLab now collects timings centrally, profiles tests, and automatically raises work for tests above thresholds. ([GitLab Docs](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/testing_guide/best_practices/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [GitLab testing best practices](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/testing_guide/best_practices/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
53	
54	There are two unusually useful measured interventions. First, **Meta's predictive test selection**, published 21 November 2018 after more than a year in production, ran only about **one-third of transitively affected tests**, while reporting over **99.9% of faulty changes** and cutting change-testing infrastructure cost by a factor of two. Meta had to account explicitly for flaky failures, including aggressive retries in training data. This is compelling evidence that “run everything on every edit” is not a necessary endpoint for a very large suite. It is, however, evidence from Facebook's monorepo and workload rather than proof that ML selection is worthwhile for a 20-person product team. ([Engineering at Meta](https://engineering.fb.com/2018/11/21/developer-tools/predictive-test-selection/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [Predictive test selection at Facebook](https://engineering.fb.com/2018/11/21/developer-tools/predictive-test-selection/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
55	
56	Second, a Google team replacing a brittle legacy system reported a much simpler architectural intervention. Their old end-to-end tests started many external services and took about **30 minutes**. After moving functional checking toward unit-level RPC-stub tests, the replacement suite took about **3 minutes**; the client-side tests were reported as **0% flaky**, and after comparing the new and old suites Google judged them equally effective at finding bugs. They consequently retained E2E mainly for service-configuration problems. That comparison was made once about 80% of tests had been converted. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/11/what-test-engineers-do-at-google.html?hl=sk&utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [Google: Building Test Infrastructure, 18 Nov 2016](https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/11/what-test-engineers-do-at-google.html?hl=sk&utm_source=chatgpt.com)
57	
58	There are important failures in the same Google case. Trying simply to split the existing large tests was **impossible without refactoring the entire legacy system and its dependencies**. A second attempt—mocking unnecessary services in the large tests—merely shifted the burden into maintaining mocks and a dependency graph of more than 200 services. That is unusually valuable evidence because the source reports the failed interventions as well as the successful one. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/11/what-test-engineers-do-at-google.html?hl=sk&utm_source=chatgpt.com))
59	
60	### Tests that become liabilities during refactoring
61	
62	The empirical literature has much less clean “we rewrote 4,217 tests during refactor X” data than it has flakiness data. The best large-company evidence is therefore the Google case above: inappropriate coupling between tests and system structure made existing tests difficult to decompose; migration to a different testing boundary took **months and migration of all existing unit tests** to the new framework. That is a **case report with measurements**, not a controlled study. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/11/what-test-engineers-do-at-google.html?hl=sk&utm_source=chatgpt.com))
63	
64	A useful counterexample shows what survives a refactor. In a 2024 InfoQ practitioner presentation, a team described roughly **8,000 outside-in contract tests** around a service. When a new requirement invalidated the database design, the team rewrote the service's entire internal implementation while keeping its external contracts; the old tests still passed. This is **a practitioner case report, not independently measured research**, but it illustrates the architectural distinction cleanly: a test tied to a stable observable contract can survive a wholesale implementation replacement; a test tied to internal collaborators, call sequences or object layout often cannot. ([InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/microservices-outside-in/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [Production Comes First — InfoQ case report](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/microservices-outside-in/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
65	
66	So “unit test” versus “integration test” is not quite the durable distinction. **Coupling to volatile implementation detail versus stable behaviour is.** Small tests still win strongly on speed and flakiness, but small tests that mock every internal call can be extremely refactor-sensitive.
67	
68	### Coverage targets: useful measurement, weak quality objective
69	
70	The strongest direct experiment remains Inozemtseva and Holmes, ICSE 2014. They generated **31,000 test suites** for five Java systems, up to **724,000 LOC**, measured statement, decision and modified-condition coverage, and used mutation testing for effectiveness. Once they controlled for the number of tests, coverage had only **low-to-moderate correlation with effectiveness**, and stronger coverage criteria did not give greater insight. Their conclusion is unusually explicit: coverage is useful for finding under-tested code, but **should not be used as a test-suite quality target**. ([Computer Science at UBC](https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~rtholmes/papers/icse_2014_inozemtseva.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [Coverage Is Not Strongly Correlated with Test Suite Effectiveness — ICSE 2014](https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~rtholmes/papers/icse_2014_inozemtseva.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
71	
72	Google's industrial practice is consistent with that result, though not a replication of it. Its 2019 FSE paper reports computing coverage for roughly **one billion lines of code every day** and emphasizes making it actionable at **changelist/code-review level**. Google had voluntary levels—60/70%, 75/80%, 90/90% project/change coverage—but **did not mandate a single threshold across the codebase**. ([Google Research](https://research.google/pubs/code-coverage-at-google/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [Code Coverage at Google — FSE 2019](https://research.google/pubs/code-coverage-at-google/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
73	
74	Google's 2020 guidance makes the caveat stronger: there is no ideal universal percentage; top-down targets can become a checkbox, and teams should not obsess about moving from 90% to 95%. Its 60/75/90 labels are internal guidelines, not empirical boundaries at which software suddenly becomes safe. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2020/08/code-coverage-best-practices.html?hl=fr&utm_source=chatgpt.com))
75	
76	**Practical implication:** a coverage floor can be an organisational nudge, but don't make “85% coverage” the definition of done. More defensible uses are “show me what this change leaves unexercised” and “why is this critical path untested?”
77	
78	### False confidence: a green validation pipeline can precede a severe production incident
79	
80	The July 2024 CrowdStrike incident is an unusually clear documented example. CrowdStrike's official post-incident report describes an extensive sensor QA process including unit, integration, performance and stress testing and staged sensor rollout. The relevant IPC template type passed a **5 March 2024 stress test**, and four earlier template instances subsequently operated successfully in production. On **19 July 2024**, however, a buggy Content Validator accepted problematic content; CrowdStrike says trust in the prior tests, validator and previous successful deployments contributed to the decision to release it. On affected Windows systems it triggered an out-of-bounds read and a BSOD. ([CrowdStrike.com](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/falcon-content-update-preliminary-post-incident-report/)) [CrowdStrike Preliminary Post Incident Review, 24 Jul 2024](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/falcon-content-update-preliminary-post-incident-report/)
81	
82	This isn't evidence that automated tests are ineffective. It is evidence that **passing the tests only establishes the properties represented by those tests and their oracle**. Here the validating component itself was wrong, and the production path contained a failure mode the existing checks had not exercised.
83	
84	CrowdStrike's announced interventions were broader Rapid Response Content testing—including rollback tests, fuzzing, fault injection, stability and interface tests—additional validator checks, better interpreter error handling, and, importantly, **canary/staggered deployment plus monitoring before expanding rollout**. ([CrowdStrike.com](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/falcon-content-update-preliminary-post-incident-report/)) These are sensible incident-derived interventions, but they should be labelled correctly: CrowdStrike announced or implemented them after the incident; the PIR is **not a controlled study demonstrating their subsequent effectiveness**.
85	
86	A subtler green-suite failure has been measured academically. A 2021 study examined roughly 100 mature projects in **each of Java, Pharo and Python** for “rotten green tests”: tests that pass because some or all assertions never execute. Researchers found them in all three ecosystems and found **actual program bugs hidden by rotten tests in Pharo and Python**. ([ETS Research Portal](https://pure.etsmtl.ca/en/publications/rotten-green-tests-in-java-pharo-and-python-an-empirical-study/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [Rotten Green Tests — Empirical Software Engineering, 2021](https://pure.etsmtl.ca/en/publications/rotten-green-tests-in-java-pharo-and-python-an-empirical-study/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
87	
88	That suggests two independent controls: test the testing machinery itself where practical, and do not make pre-production tests your only protection. Canary releases, runtime observability and rollback are safeguards against classes of defect that a suite simply never represented.
89	
90	### A test can faithfully preserve a bug
91	
92	There is both measured and practical evidence for this.
93	
94	A 2017 Defects4J study of automated program repair demonstrates the oracle problem directly. Regression-test generators ran the **currently buggy program** and therefore sometimes generated “bug-exposing tests” whose expected result was the program's incorrect output. In one bug, Math 53, all 30 repair runs produced a correct patch, yet the generated suite contained on average **1.1 tests that failed against that correct patch**; naïvely trusting those tests would therefore tend to reject the fix. The broader study covered 224 bugs and found that its attempted automated handling of this oracle problem was not very successful—only one additional correct patch was obtained—so this is also evidence of an intervention **failing to solve the problem generally**. ([ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/314152764_Test_Case_Generation_for_Program_Repair_A_Study_of_Feasibility_and_Effectiveness?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [Test Case Generation for Program Repair, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.00198?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
95	
96	Snapshot frameworks expose the same risk in everyday engineering. Deno's current documentation, updated **25 June 2026**, explicitly warns that its snapshot-update command will record bugs as the new expected output and that snapshots prove that output is unchanged, **not that it is correct**. It therefore recommends human diff review and precise assertions where practical. That is **tool-author guidance rather than an experiment**, but it describes the exact mechanism. ([Deno](https://docs.deno.com/runtime/test/snapshots/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [Deno snapshot-testing guidance](https://docs.deno.com/runtime/test/snapshots/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
97	
98	The durable rule is: **never derive the normative oracle solely from the implementation you are trying to check.** Characterisation tests and snapshots are useful while preserving legacy behaviour, but someone has to classify that observed behaviour as “contract” or “bug” before it becomes permanent specification.
99	
100	### Fixtures and helpers really do acquire maintenance cost—but be careful with simplistic “test smell” rules
101	
102	Bavota et al.'s 2015 empirical study found at least one defined test smell in **86% of the JUnit tests** they examined across open-source and industrial systems; in a controlled comprehension experiment, comprehension was about **30% better when test smells were absent**. “General Fixture”—setup that constructs substantially more context than individual tests need—is one of the established fixture smells. ([SciSpace](https://scispace.com/papers/are-test-smells-really-harmful-an-empirical-study-4m3nh359qn?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [Are test smells really harmful? — 2015](https://scispace.com/papers/are-test-smells-really-harmful-an-empirical-study-4m3nh359qn?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
103	
104	A broader 2018 study of **221 releases, ten systems and more than one million test cases** found tests containing smells to be more change- and defect-prone, with Indirect Testing, Eager Test and Assertion Roulette particularly associated with change-proneness. This is **observational correlation**, not proof that removing a helper automatically reduces defects. ([TU Delft Research Portal](https://research.tudelft.nl/en/publications/on-the-relation-of-test-smells-to-software-code-quality/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [On the Relation of Test Smells to Software Code Quality — ICSME 2018](https://research.tudelft.nl/en/publications/on-the-relation-of-test-smells-to-software-code-quality/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
105	
106	There is an important counter-result. A 2022 validation study manually checked hundreds of suites and found that conventional automated smell detectors badly mismatch genuine maintainability problems; one older detector **misclassified more than 70%** of cases. So “run a test-smell linter and eliminate every fixture” is not evidence-based either. ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-022-10207-5?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
107	
108	The recent **ICSE-SEIP 2026 Hamster study**, covering about **1.7 million developer-written Java tests**, helps put fixtures in perspective: 43.1% of test classes had setup methods and 16.2% teardown methods. The authors explicitly observe both benefits—reuse and modularity—and costs from layered inheritance and shared state. ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3786583.3786857?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) [Hamster, ICSE-SEIP 2026](https://doi.org/10.1145/3786583.3786857?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
109	
110	For helpers, the best large-company material is guidance rather than an intervention trial. Google's “DAMP, not excessively DRY” advice is to tolerate duplication where it makes the test's cause, action and assertion locally understandable; helpers are useful for irrelevant construction detail, but abstractions that hide the behaviour being tested make tests harder to audit. Microsoft independently recommends explicit helper methods over broad setup/teardown because setup tends to create too much context and hidden shared state. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2019/12/testing-on-toilet-tests-too-dry-make.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
111	
112	### What I would choose for a suite you still want in 2028
113	
114	The evidence supports a **layered but strongly bottom-heavy** strategy:
115	
116	1. Make the default test small, deterministic, independently runnable and expressed against observable behaviour. Treat network, wall-clock time, real databases, browsers and whole service graphs as dependencies that require justification. Google's 0.5% versus 14% small/large flakiness difference and its 30→3 minute migration are unusually strong reasons for that choice. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2017/04/where-do-our-flaky-tests-come-from.html?hl=it_IT&utm_source=chatgpt.com))
117	2. Keep a smaller set of integration/contract/E2E tests for risks that small tests genuinely cannot expose. Do **not** implement every business rule a second time through an E2E path.
118	3. Give the test suite its own SLOs: runtime distribution, flaky-failure rate, retry rate and number/age of quarantined tests. A test repeatedly needing retries is a defect in the engineering system, not “normal CI.”
119	4. Make quarantine temporary and owned. Google explicitly documents the danger that retry/quarantine turns genuine failures into ignored alarms. ([Google Testing Blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/05/flaky-tests-at-google-and-how-we.html?hl=de_AT))
120	5. Use coverage as a **map**, not a score. Look at missing change coverage and critical untested paths; do not infer reliability from 90%.
121	6. Keep test data and helpers boring and local. Extract construction detail when it clarifies intent; don't build a second application framework underneath the tests.
122	7. For snapshots/characterisation tests, require review of the expected output and distinguish “current behaviour” from “required behaviour.”
123	8. Finally, keep production risk controls—canaries, monitoring and rollback—outside the suite. CrowdStrike is a concrete demonstration of why “CI is green” cannot safely mean “deployment is safe.” ([CrowdStrike.com](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/falcon-content-update-preliminary-post-incident-report/))
124	
125	The recurring pattern across Google, Microsoft, Meta and the empirical literature is that the long-term enemy is less “too few automated tests” than **loss of signal**: flaky failures that people ignore, a suite too expensive to run, assertions coupled to yesterday's implementation, coverage that becomes a target rather than evidence, and abstractions that make nobody quite sure what a green test actually proved.
126	
```

```text
11	Question: How do teams handle tests that create real infrastructure, and what do they run instead in everyday development?
12	
13	Cover: how often such tests run and who triggers them; how resources are guaranteed to be cleaned up, including after a crashed run; how cost is bounded; how credentials are handled; what is asserted in those tests that cheaper tests cannot assert; and what teams report about whether the expense was worth it.
14	
15	Include the practice of testing against a provider's own emulator or a local API implementation, and evidence on how faithful those are.
16	
17	Evidence rules: cite documentation, repositories and engineering write-ups with dates. Include reports of these suites being removed or reduced, with the stated reason.

28	
29	The pattern is already fairly consistent across mature provider projects: cheap deterministic tests are the default PR loop; live-cloud tests are a gated “confidence layer,” not the inner loop. I’m checking the less obvious parts now—crash cleanup, credential isolation, and cases where teams decided the live suite was not earning its keep.
30	
31	---
32	
33	**ChatGPT**
34	
35	One important caveat from the evidence: “cleanup is guaranteed” is too strong if it means “the test’s `defer` always runs.” Mature systems treat cleanup as **eventual and out-of-process**: normal teardown first, then CI `always` cleanup and/or a sweeper that inventories the dedicated test account. GitLab’s 2025 experience shows even sophisticated destroy jobs can lose to corrupt state and orphaned resources, so inventory-based cleanup matters.
36	
37	---
38	
39	**ChatGPT**
40	
41	Teams that do this successfully usually treat **real-cloud infrastructure tests as acceptance tests, not as the everyday development loop**. The common architecture is a three-level test stack: fast code-level tests, a local/mock/emulator integration layer, and a deliberately gated live-cloud layer.
42	
43	| Layer | Typical cadence / trigger | Credentials & cost | What it proves |
44	|---|---|---|---|
45	| Unit / provider logic | Every edit, push and PR | None | Schema logic, serialization, diff/plan behavior, validation, helper functions |
46	| Fake API / emulator / recorded API | Local development and every PR | Usually none | Full client/provider request paths, CRUD wiring, error handling, import/state transformations |
47	| Real cloud acceptance | Targeted before merge, PR label/manual trigger, nightly, or release gate | Dedicated test credentials; real spend | The provider/service really creates, updates and destroys resources; real API semantics, defaults, asynchronous behavior, eventual consistency and upstream API changes |
48	
49	The Terraform AWS provider is a good representative example. Its current contributor guide, checked **15 September 2026**, says ordinary CI on every PR does linting, compilation, unit tests and static analysis, whereas acceptance tests interact end-to-end with AWS and create real billable resources. Acceptance tests require the explicit `TF_ACC=1` opt-in, can be targeted down to one resource or one test, and tests longer than five minutes can be excluded with `-short` during intermediate development. The guide recommends rerunning the affected long tests before submitting the PR. ([HashiCorp](https://hashicorp.github.io/terraform-provider-aws/running-and-writing-acceptance-tests/))
50	
51	### How often live tests run, and who triggers them
52	
53	There is no universal “nightly” rule. The cadence is proportional to both cost and the value of detecting provider drift.
54	
55	For API-provider projects, nightly can be justified because the service can change even when the client code does not. A HashiCorp engineer described on **22 August 2020** how provider teams ran acceptance tests manually while developing and also nightly, specifically so that a remote API change would be detected. The current Google provider process still reflects that model: its Release Shepherd page, edited **2 March 2026**, makes triaging both GA and Beta nightly-test failures a daily responsibility and also has the shepherd check the nightly VCR record/replay suite. ([HashiCorp Discuss](https://discuss.hashicorp.com/t/dynamic-test-environments/13200))
56	
57	Expensive suites are more often human-gated. MongoDB Atlas changed its acceptance workflow in **September 2020** from running on PRs to running only when a collaborator added a `run-testacc` label; the change was merged **28 September 2020**. The PR documents the gating change but does **not** claim cost as the reason, so it should not be read as evidence of a cost-driven change. ([GitHub](https://github.com/mongodb/terraform-provider-mongodbatlas/pull/319))
58	
59	A current example is the Redpanda Terraform provider repository, checked **15 September 2026**: its PR process exposes separate labels such as `ci-ready`, `ci-ready-byoc`, and `ci-ready-serverless` to request real-cloud suites, while its recommended local workflow is unit and credential-free colocated integration tests. Its README explicitly warns that the manual cluster commands create real resources and may incur costs. ([GitHub](https://github.com/redpanda-data/terraform-provider-redpanda))
60	
61	So in practice, “every PR” means cheap tests. Real infrastructure tends to mean **changed-resource acceptance tests, a maintainer/PR-label gate, a nightly drift detector, or a release gate**, depending on price.
62	
63	### Cleanup: the important part is surviving a dead test process
64	
65	Normal teardown is straightforward but insufficient. Terraform’s AWS acceptance harness automatically destroys what it created and then calls the actual AWS API to verify deletion; if the object is still present, the test reports a dangling resource. That catches broken delete implementations rather than merely trusting Terraform state. ([HashiCorp](https://hashicorp.github.io/terraform-provider-aws/running-and-writing-acceptance-tests/))
66	
67	But `defer`, `finally`, `t.Cleanup`, or even the test harness’s destroy phase cannot guarantee cleanup if the process is killed, the runner disappears, Terraform state becomes corrupt, or the provider API is unavailable. The Google provider documentation says explicitly that panics, failed deletes and interrupted post-test destruction leave dangling resources. Its answer is an independent **sweeper**: list resources in the dedicated test project, decide which are test leftovers, and delete them. CI sweepers run after nightly tests, with project deletion deferred until other builds are finished. That page’s relevant sweeper guidance was expanded in the wiki history on **27 November 2024**. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-google/wiki/Developer-Best-Practices))
68	
69	A useful two-layer variant appears in Redpanda’s current testing design: package-level cleanup after the test process, plus an `always-runs` CI postscript that invokes cloud cleanup commands specifically as protection against failed `TestMain` execution or crashed test processes. Resources are tagged/suffixed with the commit SHA so cleanup can distinguish this run from another concurrent run. ([GitHub](https://github.com/redpanda-data/terraform-provider-redpanda/blob/main/TESTING.md))
70	
71	Even that is not an absolute guarantee. GitLab documented the failure mode vividly in an MR opened **4 November 2025** and edited **10 November 2025**: despite increasingly sophisticated destroy handling and cleanup scripts, flaky pipelines left corrupt Terraform state and orphaned AWS/GCP resources; cleanup fell behind, quotas were hit, and people eventually had to enter the accounts and clean them manually. Their mitigation included reusing resources per merge request instead of creating a fresh set for every pipeline, graceful SIGINT rather than SIGKILL, serialization, and cloud-specific cleanup scripts. ([GitLab](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/ci-cd/runner-tools/grit/-/merge_requests/302))
72	
73	That leads to a practical rule: **cleanup that must survive crashes cannot depend solely on the state file or the process that created the resource**. Use normal destroy first, but also make resources discoverable from outside the run—dedicated account/project, predictable prefixes/tags/run IDs and timestamps—and have an independent janitor/sweeper. “Guaranteed” realistically means bounded-time eventual cleanup, not a mathematical guarantee during a cloud outage.
74	
75	### How teams bound the bill
76	
77	The first bound is opt-in. HashiCorp’s `TF_ACC=1` exists partly to stop an innocent `go test ./...` from provisioning AWS. The second is **scope**: run one changed resource/service instead of the provider’s entire acceptance suite. The third is **lifetime**: create, assert, destroy within the same test. The fourth is **reuse**: exercise many mutations and dependent objects against one expensive base resource rather than repeatedly provisioning it. Google’s provider best practices, edited **5 June 2025**, specifically recommend putting many field create/update cases into one acceptance test to reduce total test time. ([HashiCorp](https://hashicorp.github.io/terraform-provider-aws/running-and-writing-acceptance-tests/))
78	
79	The economics can be stark. Redpanda’s current testing analysis estimates a real cluster at roughly **30–50 minutes and $10–15**, which is why its proposed methodology consolidates multiple resource/datasource scenarios around one cluster and reserves live runs for explicit labels. Whether that exact number applies elsewhere is immaterial; the useful pattern is making the expensive object the reusable fixture rather than the unit of every assertion. ([GitHub](https://github.com/redpanda-data/terraform-provider-redpanda/blob/main/TESTING.md))
80	
81	Quotas also act as a safety ceiling, though relying on them as the primary cost control is a mistake: GitLab’s 2025 report shows that reaching cloud quotas simply converts leaked-resource spend into broken CI. ([gitlab.com](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/ci-cd/runner-tools/grit/-/merge_requests/302))
82	
83	### Credentials and blast radius
84	
85	Live suites are normally pointed at a **test account/project**, not production, with credentials injected at runtime rather than committed to the test. The AWS provider accepts an AWS profile or environment credentials and even supports alternate-account credentials for cross-account tests. HashiCorp’s 2020 description of its AWS acceptance setup mentioned a pair of dedicated AWS accounts because some provider capabilities require two accounts. ([HashiCorp](https://hashicorp.github.io/terraform-provider-aws/running-and-writing-acceptance-tests/))
86	
87	More recent Google-provider guidance shows the direction credentials have moved. Its **5 June 2025** development guide recommends Application Default Credentials for developers and supports service-account impersonation via `GOOGLE_IMPERSONATE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`, with the developer granted `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator`, instead of treating a long-lived downloaded service-account key as the default workflow. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-google/wiki/Developer-Best-Practices?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
88	
89	The operational pattern is therefore: dedicated low-blast-radius test identity and project/account; only the permissions needed by that suite; secrets supplied by CI or the developer’s credential mechanism; and, where supported, impersonated/short-lived credentials rather than persistent keys. Local emulator/fake tests should need no cloud credentials at all.
90	
91	### What the expensive tests buy that mocks cannot
92	
93	The valuable assertion is not merely “my program issued a Create call.” Terraform AWS acceptance tests apply actual configuration and then query the **provider API directly** to establish that the remote object really exists. After destruction they query AWS again to prove it is gone. They also exercise create/read/update/delete/import, external disappearance and recreation, and computed values returned by the service. ([HashiCorp](https://hashicorp.github.io/terraform-provider-aws/running-and-writing-acceptance-tests/))
94	
95	Real services also expose timing semantics that are intrinsically difficult to fake accurately. Google’s provider guide documents cases where an API reports successful creation but subsequent operations temporarily return 404/403 or “operation in progress” because the service is eventually consistent. A fake can test that your retry code reacts correctly to a scripted sequence; only the real service tells you whether the sequence, duration and newly introduced service behavior are actually what production does. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-google/wiki/Developer-Best-Practices))
96	
97	That is also why nightly live suites can find bugs with **no corresponding code change**: the upstream API, default behavior, regional implementation or asynchronous timing changed. ([HashiCorp Discuss](https://discuss.hashicorp.com/t/dynamic-test-environments/13200))
98	
99	### Provider emulators and local API implementations: useful, but deliberately incomplete
100	
101	Provider-supplied emulators are one of the strongest alternatives to live infrastructure because they generally speak the real SDK/API protocol. They are still not replicas of the production control plane.
102	
103	Google’s Firestore emulator documentation, updated **8 September 2026**, says it attempts to reproduce production faithfully but explicitly does not mimic production transaction concurrency, all timeout/size limits, or composite-index enforcement. Google tells users to test against real Firestore where those behaviors matter. ([Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/native/docs/emulator?hl=en))
104	
105	The Pub/Sub emulator docs, updated **17 July 2026**, list missing IAM operations, unsupported update RPCs, no real subscription expiry/retention behavior, and incomplete BigQuery-subscription behavior. That means it is excellent for publisher/subscriber protocol tests but cannot establish that your production IAM and several lifecycle features work. ([Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/emulator?hl=en))
106	
107	Microsoft’s Azurite documentation, updated **26 August 2025**, similarly says there are functional differences from Azure Storage: it covers Blob, Queue and Table but not Azure Files or Data Lake Storage Gen2; it offers no production performance/scaling guarantee; and even where error status codes align, messages can differ. ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-use-azurite))
108	
109	AWS’s DynamoDB Local documentation, checked **15 September 2026**, is especially explicit. It ignores provisioned throughput, lacks account/region separation, performs most control-plane changes immediately, makes eventually consistent reads often appear strong because everything is local, does not raise real `TransactionConflictException`s, lacks tagging and vector indexes, and tells users to test vector-index behavior against the actual service. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DynamoDBLocal.UsageNotes.html))
110	
111	So emulator fidelity is **feature-specific, not binary**. A good test strategy reads the emulator’s documented differences and reserves live cases specifically for those gaps.
112	
113	There is useful industry evidence that this trade pays. AppsFlyer’s engineering write-up of **30 June 2022** describes moving Terraform VPC tests to LocalStack: their feedback cycle went from minutes to seconds, cloud charges disappeared, developers no longer contended for shared cloud resources, and many Terraform apply failures became locally reproducible. But they retained real AWS tests for things LocalStack did not adequately support—EKS was their cited example. ([Medium](https://medium.com/appsflyerengineering/how-we-sped-up-our-aws-infrastructure-testing-using-localstack-58ce1b1d2856))
114	
115	### Do teams think the live-cloud expense is worth it?
116	
117	The evidence says **yes when real-provider behavior is the product; much less clearly for broad application/system testing**.
118	
119	HashiCorp’s Martin Atkins described both sides in **August 2020**. At a previous company his team spent months creating disposable dynamic environments, then abandoned the approach: duplicating infrastructure was expensive and slow, failures were hard to diagnose, destroys sometimes failed and left money-burning resources, and the extra monitoring/cleanup machinery increased human cost. A long-lived shared copy of the environment ended up cheaper overall. In contrast, he said HashiCorp’s provider acceptance-test infrastructure—with years of cleanup automation—was worth the investment because provider correctness against remote APIs was the core product, while questioning whether the same investment made sense for most other situations. ([HashiCorp Discuss](https://discuss.hashicorp.com/t/dynamic-test-environments/13200))
120	
121	There are also concrete examples of suites being reduced rather than merely tolerated. GitLab’s **November 2025** GRIT change reduced per-pipeline cloud-resource generation after quota pressure and orphan cleanup became operationally painful, and it **removed its GKE Windows E2E test** because it was consistently flaky, extremely slow, and required so many retries that engineers stopped investigating failures—making the test ineffective. ([GitLab](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/ci-cd/runner-tools/grit/-/merge_requests/302)) MongoDB Atlas’s **27 March 2024** changelog records deletion of “outdated integration tests” and corresponding dependency cleanup; the stated reason there is simply that those integration tests were outdated, not cost. ([GitHub](https://github.com/mongodb/terraform-provider-mongodbatlas/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
122	
123	The resulting rule of thumb is fairly strong: **keep a small live suite whose assertions are inherently about the real provider, and make everything else cheaper**. If a test is proving serialization, Terraform plan behavior, error propagation, CRUD orchestration, or application logic, it belongs in unit/fake/emulator/VCR tests. If it is proving “AWS/GCP/Azure really accepted this, reached the expected asynchronous state, returned these actual defaults, and really deleted it,” that is where paying for the real infrastructure is justified.
124	
```

```text
function docker(args: string[], input?: string) {
	const result = spawnSync("docker", args, {
		encoding: "utf8",
		input,
		maxBuffer: maxOutputBytes,
	});
	if (result.status !== 0) {
		throw new Error(
			`docker ${args[0]} failed: ${result.stderr || result.stdout}`,
		);
	}
	return result.stdout.trim();
}
```

```text
export function renderCloudInit({

}: {
	publicKey: string;
	bootstrapFile: SshBootstrapFile;

}) {

			},
		],

	};
	// biome-ignore-end lint/style/useNamingConvention: cloud-init requires snake_case keys
	// JSON is a subset of YAML, so no value can become cloud-config structure.
	return `#cloud-config\n${JSON.stringify(config)}\n`;
}
```

## Assistant · 2026-09-15T12:11:57.165Z

Decompacted from the session jsonl (179 messages, the full back and forth), plus `docs/decisions.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `docs/vocabulary.md`, the `/refactor` skill, and all nine research reports. Tree is clean at `99b5b76`. 65 pure tests pass in 63 ms; 16 container tests exist.

## First, a correction

The tenth link was not a duplicate. It was prompt **04, on concurrency and state-machine defects**: deterministic simulation, property-based and model-based testing, fault injection, TLA+, idempotency and replay testing. Its share page returns no conversation data, so the import fails rather than skipping:

```
error: https://chatgpt.com/share/6aa92d9e-... contains no conversation data.
```

That is the one report I most wanted, because it is the only one aimed at the worker. Worth re-sharing if the conversation still exists.

## Where the question is: I never asked it

You are right to call this out. I wrote "the open question you have not answered: the testing policy" as though it were sitting in your court. It was not. I listed it as open and never posed it. Here it is, properly, now that I have read the research instead of writing prompts about it.

## What the research actually found, about our suite

Not abstract. Five things that apply to code we have:

**1. Half of `authorized_keys.test.ts` has no independent oracle.** Report 06 names this exactly: testing `my_parser(my_writer(my_parser(x)))` establishes internal consistency while parser and writer share the same misunderstanding. Report 03 gives the case that proves it costs real money: Paramiko's suite drove a Paramiko client against a Paramiko server for years, and a 2018 security bug only surfaced when someone ran it against real OpenSSH 7.2 in Docker, which rejected what Paramiko's own server accepted. Our round-trip tests are that shape. The authoritative oracle exists and we already run it in a container.

**2. The property we care about most is not tested at all.** Report 06 states it for exactly our case: for a restriction-only rewrite, `Allowed(R_e(x)) ⊆ Allowed(x)`. In our words: an edit must never widen what an entry permits. Our tests check that bytes are preserved. Nothing checks that sshd's interpretation did not widen. Only sshd can answer that.

**3. Every bug Codex found in the worker is a named row in report 10's fault matrix.** Stale result completing a replacement operation is "write succeeds but reads are stale". Cleanup unable to recover an uncertain resource is "crash before local state is persisted". Admin retry undone by an outstanding run is the same row. Crossplane's `external-create-pending` is our "uncertain", and its runtime has a test named for precisely the branch we implemented by hand. Codex found ours by extracting handler bodies and running them against a mocked database, and told us so. That is a test we do not have, in the place where we have had the most real defects.

**4. `bun test` is green on a machine without Docker.** Sixteen tests report as skipped and the run exits 0. Report 05 names this as the worse of the two failure modes: not that a slow suite fails, but that it silently stops being meaningful. Report 08 measures the neighbouring case, "rotten green tests" that pass because assertions never execute, in three ecosystems.

**5. The container leaks if the process dies.** We clean up in `afterAll`. Report 09 is blunt that in-process hooks cannot clean up after a dead process, and Testcontainers built an entire reaper for this. A Ctrl+C at the wrong moment leaves an Ubuntu container running. A label plus a sweep at startup fixes it in about five lines.

And on your instinct about freeze tests: report 02 states the warning sign independently, as the single clearest empirical signal of a bad suite. *"A suite where large amounts of test code can be changed mechanically in parallel with a refactor without anyone having to reconsider an expected behavior."* That is your "blanket freeze the state" objection, arrived at from Google's change-detector work and the mock-maintenance studies rather than from taste.

## The question I owe you

The policy itself I do not think you need to decide. The research converges hard on one sentence, and it is already our house style applied to tests:

> A test earns its place when a behavior could plausibly regress and no cheaper, more durable mechanism already makes the mistake impossible or conspicuous. Its oracle must not be the code under test: where another system defines the truth, ask that system.

That rule, applied to what we have, keeps the container suite, keeps the address parser tests, and puts the round-trip tests on probation until they gain a real oracle. I can write it into `AGENTS.md` as one rule without asking.

**The decision that is actually yours is whether we build the third suite: the worker interleaving tests.**

It is where every real defect has been found. It is also the only one that costs something architecturally. To manufacture "Hetzner committed the create and the response was lost", the worker has to be able to take a substituted provider. Today it imports one. `/refactor` warns in one line against adding a production seam so that mocking becomes convenient, and in another says a seam is justified at a true external boundary. Hetzner is a true external boundary. So the honest question is not "do we want tests" but:

**Should the Hetzner API become an interface the worker is given, rather than a module it imports?** If yes, the fault matrix becomes testable and the next Codex audit has less to find. If no, those paths stay verified by reading and by paid audits, and I will say so plainly rather than pretending the container suite covers them.

A smaller one, which I will decide myself unless you object: I will re-point the preservation tests at sshd as the oracle, asserting non-widening rather than byte identity alone.

## The exact remaining surface

**Built and settled.** Clerk sync, ownership and memberships and permissions, name claims, quotas at both levels, rate limits, allocations with the Hetzner worker (epochs, leases, uncertain outcomes, inventory findings), SSH access with the address-bound pin and the renewal command, discovery, key list/add/update/remove, hostname on rename, the closed error-code set, `docs/api.md`.

**Built but unproven.** The probe. Writing the file proves the bytes landed; only an unsigned publickey query to the running daemon proves sshd will use them. The container harness is where it belongs.

**Decided, not built.** Preinstall at creation: you corrected me and you were right, and `cloud_init.ts` still has no `packages:` list. What goes in it is a small open question (python3 and curl are ours; node and an agent CLI are the delighter). Also the encryption-key rotation path.

**Not decided, needs grounding first.** The app naming scheme and DNS, which is the gate on certificates, and which you correctly said should not be picked from the SSH side. Snapshots. Billing. Production environments. Support surface.

**My recommended order:** the worker seam question above, then the probe, then the server UI, then the agent flow, which the UI unblocks.

```text
1	# Compare concurrency testing methods
2	
3	Source: https://chatgpt.com/share/6aa92d9e-0fdc-83ed-a8a5-956a00600e7c
4	
5	---
6	
7	**User**
8	
9	Context: A control plane records intent, then a worker performs provider calls and records the outcome. Runs can overlap, responses can be lost, and a late result can arrive after the work it belonged to was replaced. Defects here are rare in normal use and severe when they occur.
10	
11	Question: How do teams find defects in concurrent workflows and state machines, and what does each method actually catch?
12	
13	Cover: deterministic simulation testing; property based and model based testing; fault and latency injection; chaos testing; formal specification such as TLA+ or Alloy; randomized interleaving tools; idempotency and replay testing; and plain example based tests of specific interleavings.

64	## The most informative cases where one technique found what another had missed
65	
66	**DynamoDB/TLA+, 2015** is probably the clearest design-level example. The data-loss error required a shortest counterexample of 35 high-level steps. It had already survived extensive design review, code review and testing. This is almost the archetype for “rare in ordinary use, catastrophic if reached.” ([Leslie Lamport's Home Page](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/tla/amazon-excerpt.html))
67	
68	**Microsoft CHESS, OSDI 2008** is the clearest implementation-scheduling example. Ordinary stress testing had seen the defect only once in months; CHESS systematically controlled scheduling and found it in seconds, then made it immediately reproducible. ([Usenix](https://www.usenix.org/event/osdi08/tech/full_papers/musuvathi/musuvathi_html/index.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
69	
70	**Riak Poolboy/QuickCheck, January 2012** is a good example of semantic state-space exploration beating coverage. The code already had 85% unit coverage, yet state-machine generation produced a five-step timeout sequence that leaked a worker, plus several EXIT/death bookkeeping defects. None caused the existing unit suite to fail. ([Riak](https://riak.com/posts/technical/quickchecking-poolboy-for-fun-and-profit/index.html))
71	
72	**MongoDB Mobile/TLA+-generated tests, experiment in 2020, retrospective June 2025** is unusually useful because MongoDB has comparison numbers. Faithfully translating roughly 1,000 lines/21 merge rules into TLA+ exposed an actual infinite-recursion bug involving one participant swapping array elements while another moved one. The finite model then generated 4,913 behaviors and reached 100% branch coverage, against 21% handwritten and 92% from millions of AFL executions. ([MongoDB](https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/engineering/conformance-checking-at-mongodb-testing-our-code-matches-our-tla-specs))
73	
74	**TigerBeetle/Jepsen, reported June 2025** shows the reverse lesson: even extremely serious deterministic fuzzing can have a workload blind spot. Jepsen found a query-engine correctness error in a component covered by four fuzzers, including TigerBeetle's deterministic VOPR. The generator had accidentally arranged records so the problematic multi-index “probing” situation never arose. After replacing the constrained workload with arbitrary inputs plus a richer reference model, TigerBeetle's deterministic test trivially reproduced the bug. That is a particularly good demonstration that a powerful exploration engine cannot compensate for an impoverished generator or oracle. ([TigerBeetle](https://tigerbeetle.com/blog/2025-06-06-fuzzer-blind-spots-meet-jepsen/))
75	
76	There is an analogous lesson inside **TigerBeetle's own DST**. In July 2023 it split its simulator into safety and liveness modes because temporary faults would eventually heal and conceal permanent-livelock situations. The new mode exposed a “resonance” bug in which repair requests alternated between precisely the replicas that lacked the requested log entries, forever. Their earlier safety-mode simulation would eventually reset the condition and miss it. ([TigerBeetle](https://tigerbeetle.com/blog/2023-07-06-simulation-testing-for-liveness/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
77	
78	## What matters specifically for your control-plane pattern
79	
80	The key is to distinguish **deduplication** from **authority**.
81	
82	Suppose intent generation 41 creates run A. A asks the provider to mutate something. The provider performs the mutation but its response is delayed. The control plane then records generation 42 and starts run B. B completes correctly. Finally A's response arrives.
83	
84	An idempotency key prevents **A being executed twice**. It does not prevent **A from being accepted after B**. Those are different correctness properties.
85	
86	The core safety invariant should be something close to:
87	
88	> A worker outcome may update the current projection only while the intent/run generation that authorized the work is still current.
89	
90	Operationally, that generally means each run carries an immutable **intent generation / fencing token**, and the outcome write is conditional on ownership still matching—for example conceptually, “update current state where generation = 41.” Once generation 42 exists, A's update affects zero rows. A may still be recorded as an historical or obsolete outcome, but it must not become current.
91	
92	A second invariant is monotonicity: **a visible current generation can never decrease**, regardless of completion order.
93	
94	A third belongs at the provider boundary: all retries of one logical provider mutation use the **same provider idempotency key**, while a genuinely new intent gets a new key. That handles the “provider committed but response was lost” ambiguity described by both Stripe and AWS. ([Stripe](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
95	
96	The fourth is subtler: cancellation does not revoke causality. Once a provider request has escaped your process, “cancelled” should normally mean “we no longer wait for it,” not “we know it did not happen.” A later provider observation/callback can therefore be valid historical evidence without being authorized to overwrite the current generation.
97	
98	## The test stack I would use here
99	
100	I would not start by building a FoundationDB-scale simulator. For this particular architecture, the highest return is a layered approach:
101	
102	1. **Write the state-machine invariants first**, preferably in a small TLA+ model. Model `record intent`, `start run`, `send provider request`, `provider commits`, `lose/delay reply`, `replace intent`, `retry`, `receive reply`, and `record result`. This is cheap enough to explore whether your generation/fencing rules are logically sufficient before spending heavily on implementation machinery. AWS's experience is strong evidence for this kind of design problem, while the MongoDB experience is a warning not to make the spec implementation-shaped or commit immediately to expensive trace conformance. ([Leslie Lamport's Home Page](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/tla/amazon-excerpt.html))
103	
104	2. **Turn every known dangerous sequence into a barrier-controlled ordinary test.** One essential regression is: A/provider effect occurs → withhold A reply → replace with B → complete B → release A → assert A cannot change current state. Repeat with A's reply lost and retried, duplicated, and delivered before/after each durable state transition. Thread Weaver's principle—explicit control points rather than sleeps—is the right shape. ([Google Open Source Blog](https://opensource.googleblog.com/2009/10/testing-race-conditions-in-java.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
105	
106	3. **Add model/property-based sequence generation around the real state machine.** Commands should include create/replace intent, lease/start, timeout, provider success/failure/ambiguous success, retry, worker crash, duplicate delivery and result arrival. Shrinking makes the failures practical to debug. The Poolboy results illustrate why this finds mistakes that coverage-oriented unit testing does not. ([Riak](https://riak.com/posts/technical/quickchecking-poolboy-for-fun-and-profit/index.html))
107	
108	4. **Make the fake provider fault-capable at semantic boundaries.** Especially support “perform effect but never return the response” and “perform effect, hold response until released.” Generic random HTTP latency is much less useful. Jepsen and Netflix's results show the value of deliberately exploring failure semantics rather than merely load. ([InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2016/03/failure-testing-netflix/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
109	
110	5. **Use a controlled/randomized scheduler if your important race is inside one worker/control-plane process.** If most nondeterminism is in queues/provider responses rather than threads, model those as scheduler events. Save the exact schedule. CHESS/PCT show why scheduler control is dramatically better than “run the test 100,000 times and hope.” ([Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/a-randomized-scheduler-with-probabilistic-guarantees-of-finding-bugs/?lang=ja&utm_source=chatgpt.com))
111	
112	6. **Continuously test idempotency and workflow replay separately.** Idempotency tests should deliberately lose replies after provider commitment and verify retries do not duplicate effects. If you have durable workflow histories, replay old production/test histories through new orchestration code in CI. But keep a separate fencing assertion, because idempotency alone does not provide newest-intent-wins semantics. ([Amazon Web Services, Inc.](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
113	
114	7. **Use chaos later, as a reality check rather than the primary race detector.** Once the invariants above are exercised deterministically, chaos is excellent for discovering that your real queue has different delivery behavior, your timeout is wrongly configured, a failover path does not work, or a dependency you thought was redundant is not. It is a poor first instrument for finding a five-event stale-result sequence because a failure is harder to reproduce and the oracle usually sees less internal state.
115	
116	The evidence does not support a single “best” technique. It supports **cross-checking different search spaces**. FoundationDB and TigerBeetle are perhaps the strongest advocates of deterministic simulation, yet TigerBeetle explicitly added real-system nondeterministic testing, and Jepsen subsequently found a correctness bug its deterministic fuzzers had projected out of their generated state space. ([TigerBeetle](https://tigerbeetle.com/blog/2025-02-13-a-descent-into-the-vortex/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Likewise, AWS's TLA+ work found errors testing had missed, but AWS explicitly did **not** claim that checking the specification proved the implementation. ([Leslie Lamport's Home Page](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/tla/amazon-excerpt.html))
117	
118	For the failure you described, the best discriminator is therefore: **TLA+/model checking for whether your ownership protocol is sound; model/property-based generation plus deterministic fault/schedule control for whether the implementation really preserves it; idempotency testing for ambiguous provider outcomes; and a few explicit interleaving tests as permanent regression locks.** Chaos comes after those, to show that your abstraction of the real deployment was not wishful thinking.
119
```

The cause is in `scripts/research/chat-gpt.ts:135`. The reader pulled the payload out with a pattern for a quoted JavaScript literal, `("(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*")`. That alternation backtracks. On the 394 KB payload of a normal share it matches. On this conversation's **1.64 MB** payload it exceeds the regex engine's limit and returns **no match at all**, rather than throwing. The empty result then hit our own `contains no conversation data` check, and the reader confidently reported that the source was empty.

I confirmed it differentially: a linear scan over the same bytes recovers 2 chunks and a 1,641,039-character first line from the page the regex read as zero.

So this was the failure mode we keep designing against, in our own tooling: a silent wrong answer wearing the costume of a legitimate diagnosis. And I passed it on to you as fact.

## Fixed

Replaced the pattern with a linear scan that walks the literal and respects escapes. The comment records why, since the code cannot say it:

```ts
/**
 * Reads every string the page hands to its stream. The literals are scanned rather than matched,
 * because a pattern for a quoted literal backtracks past the engine's limit on a long conversation
 * and then reports no match instead of an error, which cannot be told apart from an empty page.
 */
```

Verified it is behaviour-preserving, not just working: re-imported two of the nine that already succeeded, and git reports **no byte difference** in either file. `bun run check` is clean. The tenth report is now at `docs/research/2026-09-15-compare-concurrency-testing-methods.md`.

## It was worth recovering, and it answers my own question

This is the report aimed squarely at our worker, and it names our exact situation before giving the rule:

> An idempotency key prevents **A being executed twice**. It does not prevent **A from being accepted after B**. Those are different correctness properties.

It calls the first deduplication and the second **authority**, and prescribes: each run carries an immutable generation, and the outcome write is conditional on that generation still being current. That is precisely what our epoch does, and precisely the Codex P1 we fixed, where a late result could complete the operation that had replaced it. Independent confirmation that the fix was the right shape, and now we have the vocabulary for it.

It also settles the question I put to you last turn, in the direction I suspected but could not justify. Its step 2 is the exact regression test:

> A/provider effect occurs → withhold A reply → replace with B → complete B → release A → assert A cannot change current state.

and its step 4 says the fake provider must be fault-capable **at semantic boundaries** — specifically "perform effect but never return the response" — because generic random latency is much less useful. That is the seam I asked about, and this is a much stronger argument for it than "tests would be convenient": the fault class is unreachable without it, and it is where every real defect we have found lives.

It also warns against overreach in both directions. AWS found a DynamoDB data-loss bug whose shortest counterexample was 35 steps, after design and code review had passed it. MongoDB spent 10 weeks on trace conformance and abandoned it because the spec and the implementation modelled transitions differently. And TigerBeetle's own deterministic fuzzer missed a bug Jepsen found, because the generator had quietly arranged the data so the bad case never arose. A powerful search does not rescue a weak generator or a weak oracle.

So my recommendation firms up: **yes to the seam and the barrier-controlled interleaving tests, no to a simulator**, and the small TLA+ model is optional since the invariant is already written down and now independently corroborated.

Two things I have deliberately not done. I have not committed (the reader fix plus the new report are sitting in the working tree), and I have not added a test for the reader, though under the policy I proposed it is the strongest candidate we have: a silent, size-dependent wrong answer that no type or review would make conspicuous. Both are yours to say go on.

```text
export async function callHetznerCloud(
	path: string,
	method = "GET",
	body?: unknown,
): Promise<Record<string, unknown> | null> {
	if (!env.HCLOUD_TOKEN) {
		throw new HetznerCloudError("token_missing", {
			status: httpStatus.unauthorized,
		});
	}
	let response: Response;
	try {
		response = await fetch(`${apiUrl}/${path}`, {
			method,
			headers: {
				// biome-ignore lint/style/useNamingConvention: HTTP defines the Authorization header name
				Authorization: `Bearer ${env.HCLOUD_TOKEN}`,
				"Content-Type": "application/json",
			},
			body: body === undefined ? null : JSON.stringify(body),
			signal: AbortSignal.timeout(requestTimeoutMs),
		});
	} catch {
		throw new HetznerCloudError("transport_uncertain");
	}
	if (response.status === httpStatus.notFound && method === "GET") {
		return null;
	}
	if (response.status === httpStatus.noContent) {
		return {};
	}
	let data: Record<string, unknown>;
	try {
		data = requireObject(await response.json());
	} catch {
		throw new HetznerCloudError("invalid_response", {
			status: response.status,
		});
	}
	if (!response.ok) {
		const hetznerErrorCode = requireObject(data.error).code;
		throw new HetznerCloudError("request_rejected", {
			status: response.status,
			retryAfterMs: toRetryAfterMs(response),
			...(typeof hetznerErrorCode === "string" &&
			hetznerErrorCodePattern.test(hetznerErrorCode)
				? { hetznerErrorCode }
				: {}),
		});
	}
	return data;
}
```

## Assistant · 2026-09-15T12:29:20.938Z

Committed as `7d5c09c`. Now the real answers.

## 1. The Hetzner question, in plain terms

Forget testing for a moment. Here is what the code looks like today.

`api.ts` exports one function:

```ts
callHetznerCloud(path, method, body)
```

That is a *transport*. It knows how to send an HTTP request with a token and parse a JSON body. It does not know what a server is, or a Primary IP.

So all the knowledge of *what Hetzner's API actually looks like* lives in `worker.ts`, mixed line by line with our state machine:

```ts
const labelQuery = new URLSearchParams({
  label_selector: `controller-id=${controllerId},allocation-id=${allocationId},...`,
  per_page: lookupPageSize,
});
const labeled = await callHetznerCloud(`${collection}?${labelQuery}`);
const found = requireObject(response[resourceKeys[kind]]);
```

`worker.ts` is 653 lines that are supposed to be about epochs, leases, uncertainty and recovery. Instead it also knows Hetzner's URL paths, label-selector syntax, pagination parameter names, and which key to unwrap each response from.

**The objective answer is yes, and the reason has nothing to do with tests.** `/refactor` calls this a shallow module: a wrapper whose interface is nearly as complicated as the thing it wraps, because every caller still has to reinterpret it. Two things that change for completely different reasons (Hetzner changing their API; us changing our recovery policy) are interleaved in one file. The fix is that `api.ts` should own *operations* rather than transport: `findResource`, `createResource`, `deleteResource`, `getAction`, `sendPowerCommand`. Then `worker.ts` is only the state machine.

I want to be careful here, because `/refactor` explicitly says **do not add a production seam just to make mocking convenient**, and I nearly sold you this on testing grounds. The correct framing: the design pressure exists on its own, the shape is better on its own, and testability falls out as a consequence rather than as the justification.

The honest cheaper alternative: leave the structure alone and just let the worker be *handed* `callHetznerCloud` instead of importing it. That unlocks the same fault injection for a fraction of the work, and leaves the knowledge spread out. I would not choose it, but it is a legitimate answer and it is the one that gets you to the UI sooner.

## 2. "Preservation tests" was jargon, sorry

I meant four specific tests in `convex/ssh/authorized_keys.test.ts`: *"an unchanged plan preserves arbitrary bytes"*, *"ordered options retain duplicates, case, quoted separators, and backslashes"*, *"a no-op update retains all original separators and line endings"*, and *"arbitrary byte sequences round-trip through the public boundary"*.

They all check that our writer gives back what our parser read. That proves our two halves agree with each other. It does not prove either half agrees with **sshd**, which is the only thing that actually decides whether a key works. That is the Paramiko failure exactly. The fix is not to delete them; it is to add the assertion only sshd can make: after our edit, does sshd still accept the keys it accepted before, and does it now refuse the one we removed. The property is "never widens what an entry permits", and it needs the container.

## 3. A landmine in our own rules that I want to flag

I went and read Convex's bundler to find out why our test files are not deployed. It is not a test-file rule. It is this:

```js
} else if ((base.match(/\./g) || []).length > 1) {
  logVerbose(`Skipping ${fpath} that contains multiple dots`);
}
```

Convex skips any file whose name has **more than one dot**. `addresses.test.ts` is excluded because it has two dots, not because it is a test.

Now combine that with our own casing rule, which says Convex file names are `snake_case`. A future agent "fixing" `addresses.test.ts` into `addresses_test.ts` would satisfy our rule and silently add a file importing `bun:test` and `node:child_process` to the production deployment. That is a real trap we built ourselves. It needs a line in `docs/decisions.md` and probably an explicit carve-out in the casing rule.

## 4. The things I will just decide, and why

**Bun stays the runner.** It already is, via `verify`. It gives declaration, assertions, lifecycle and filtering, and the research is clear that what projects actually need beyond that is a small support layer, not a framework. You already ruled out vitest and convex-test.

**`scripts/` keeps its own tsconfig.** It is the only place with `types: ["bun"]` and no DOM lib. Without it, scripts would typecheck against Next's DOM types and `Bun.file` would not resolve. It earns its place. Three tsconfigs for three genuinely different runtimes is not ceremony.

**Test files keep `/// <reference types="bun" />` at the top** rather than adding bun types to `convex/tsconfig.json`. Adding them globally would let production Convex code reference Bun globals and still typecheck, then fail at deploy. The per-file directive is the narrowest possible suppression, which matches how we handle everything else.

**I will add a reaper for the container** (label it, sweep stale ones at startup), because `afterAll` cannot run if you press Ctrl+C, and right now that leaves an Ubuntu container running.

**I will add a test for the research reader**, with a synthetic oversized payload. Today's bug was silent, size-dependent, and no type or review would have caught it.

## 5. Is anything blocking? No, after these four

The only genuine blocker was the worker shape, and the recovered report settled the design question. Everything else I was holding back on because you told me once, correctly, that I added tests before we had agreed what tests were for. I did not want to repeat that. But you have now said you want the surface properly covered and designed, which is the answer, so after these four I will build rather than ask.

```text
"use node";

import { createCipheriv, createDecipheriv, randomBytes } from "node:crypto";
import { v } from "convex/values";
import ssh2 from "ssh2";
import { internal } from "../_generated/api";
import type { Doc, Id } from "../_generated/dataModel";
import { type ActionCtx, action, env } from "../_generated/server";
import { toConvexError } from "../errors";
import {
	bootstrapLifetimeMs,
	isSshAccessEncryptionKey,
	toBootstrapTokenDigest,
} from "./access_state";
import { toSshBootstrapCommand } from "./bootstrap_command";
import type { SshBootstrapFile } from "./cloud_init";
import type { SshConnectionOptions } from "./connection";

const { utils } = ssh2;

const bootstrapTokenBytes = 32;
const nonceBytes = 12;
const authTagBytes = 16;
const sshPort = 22;
const connectionTimeoutMs = 30_000;

type AllocationSshAccess = Doc<"allocationSshAccess">;
type SshAccessSecrets = { privateKey: string; token: string };

export class SshAccessError extends Error {
	readonly code:
		| "allocation_unavailable"
		| "bootstrap_expired"
		| "bootstrap_url_insecure"
		| "encryption_key_invalid"
		| "encryption_key_missing"
		| "host_key_missing"
		| "secrets_unreadable";

	constructor(code: SshAccessError["code"]) {
		super(code);
		this.name = "SshAccessError";
		this.code = code;
	}
}

function getEncryptionKey() {
	const value = env.SSH_ACCESS_ENCRYPTION_KEY;
	if (!value) {
		throw new SshAccessError("encryption_key_missing");
	}
	if (!isSshAccessEncryptionKey(value)) {
		throw new SshAccessError("encryption_key_invalid");
	}
	return Buffer.from(value, "base64");
}

// Binding the allocation ID as authenticated data prevents moving secrets to another allocation.
function toAuthenticatedData(allocationId: string) {
	return Buffer.from(`allocationSshAccess:${allocationId}`);
}

function encrypt(allocationId: string, secrets: SshAccessSecrets) {
	const nonce = randomBytes(nonceBytes);
	const cipher = createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", getEncryptionKey(), nonce);
	cipher.setAAD(toAuthenticatedData(allocationId));
	const data = Buffer.concat([
		cipher.update(JSON.stringify(secrets), "utf8"),
		cipher.final(),
	]);
	return Buffer.concat([nonce, cipher.getAuthTag(), data]).toString("base64");
}

function decrypt(sshAccess: AllocationSshAccess): SshAccessSecrets {
	try {
		const bytes = Buffer.from(sshAccess.encryptedSecrets, "base64");
		const dataStart = nonceBytes + authTagBytes;
		const decipher = createDecipheriv(
			"aes-256-gcm",
			getEncryptionKey(),
			bytes.subarray(0, nonceBytes),
		);
		decipher.setAAD(toAuthenticatedData(sshAccess.allocationId));
		decipher.setAuthTag(bytes.subarray(nonceBytes, dataStart));
		const secrets: unknown = JSON.parse(
			Buffer.concat([
				decipher.update(bytes.subarray(dataStart)),
				decipher.final(),
			]).toString("utf8"),
		);
		if (
			secrets === null ||
			typeof secrets !== "object" ||
			!("privateKey" in secrets) ||
			!("token" in secrets) ||
			typeof secrets.privateKey !== "string" ||
			typeof secrets.token !== "string"
		) {
			throw new Error("The secrets have an unexpected shape.");
		}
		return { privateKey: secrets.privateKey, token: secrets.token };
	} catch (error) {
		if (error instanceof SshAccessError) {
			throw error;
		}
		throw new SshAccessError("secrets_unreadable");
	}
}

export async function requireSshConnection(
	ctx: ActionCtx,
	allocation: Doc<"serverAllocations">,
): Promise<SshConnectionOptions> {
	if (allocation.deleteRequested || allocation.ipv4 === undefined) {
		throw new SshAccessError("allocation_unavailable");
	}
	const sshAccess: AllocationSshAccess | null = await ctx.runQuery(
		internal.ssh.access_state.get,
		{ allocationId: allocation._id },
	);
```
