/** Only an expired bootstrap without a registered host key needs new access. */
export function canReuseAllocationSshAccess(
	sshAccess: AllocationSshAccess | null,
) {
	return (
		sshAccess !== null &&
		(sshAccess.bootstrapExpiresAt > Date.now() ||
			sshAccess.hostKey !== undefined)
	);
}

export async function generateAllocationSshAccess(
	allocationId: Id<"serverAllocations">,
) {
	const keyPair = utils.generateKeyPairSync("ed25519");
	const token = randomBytes(bootstrapTokenBytes).toString("base64url");
	return {
		allocationId,
		publicKey: keyPair.public,
		encryptedSecrets: encrypt(allocationId, {
			privateKey: keyPair.private,
			token,
		}),
		bootstrapTokenDigest: await toBootstrapTokenDigest(token),
		bootstrapExpiresAt: Date.now() + bootstrapLifetimeMs,
	};
}

/**
 * Opens one more bootstrap window and returns the command that completes it, for a member whose
 * server no longer accepts Composery. The command must run on the server itself: the report
 * that it sends is refused from any other address.
 */
export const renewBootstrap = action({
	args: { serverId: v.id("servers") },
	returns: v.object({ command: v.string() }),
	handler: async (ctx, { serverId }): Promise<{ command: string }> => {
		const allocation: Doc<"serverAllocations"> = await ctx.runQuery(
			internal.servers.permissions.requireSshAccess,
			{ serverId },
		);
		const allocationId = allocation._id;
		const sshAccess: AllocationSshAccess | null = await ctx.runQuery(
			internal.ssh.access_state.get,
			{ allocationId },
		);
		if (sshAccess === null) {
			throw toConvexError("server_busy");
		}
		const token = randomBytes(bootstrapTokenBytes).toString("base64url");
		await ctx.runMutation(internal.ssh.access_state.storeBootstrap, {
			allocationId,
			encryptedSecrets: encrypt(allocationId, {
				privateKey: decrypt(sshAccess).privateKey,
				token,
			}),
			bootstrapTokenDigest: await toBootstrapTokenDigest(token),
		});
		return {
			command: toSshBootstrapCommand(
				{
					...toSshBootstrapFile(sshAccess),
					token,
				},
				sshAccess.publicKey,
			),
		};
	},
});

function toSshBootstrapFile(sshAccess: AllocationSshAccess): SshBootstrapFile {
	const url = `${env.CONVEX_SITE_URL}/ssh/host-keys`;
	// The token travels in this URL's request body, so a plain HTTP report would expose it.
	if (!url.startsWith("https://")) {
		throw new SshAccessError("bootstrap_url_insecure");
	}
	return {
		allocationId: sshAccess.allocationId,
		token: decrypt(sshAccess).token,
		url,
	};
}

export function requireSshBootstrapFile(
	sshAccess: AllocationSshAccess,
): SshBootstrapFile {
	if (sshAccess.bootstrapExpiresAt <= Date.now()) {
		throw new SshAccessError("bootstrap_expired");
	}
	return toSshBootstrapFile(sshAccess);
}
```

import { type Infer, v } from "convex/values";
import type { Doc, Id } from "../_generated/dataModel";
import { internalQuery, type QueryCtx } from "../_generated/server";
import { requireServerAllocation } from "../allocations/operations";
import { toConvexError } from "../errors";
import schema from "../schema";
import { requireUser } from "../users";
import { serverPermissions } from "./schema";

export type ServerPermissions = Infer<typeof serverPermissions>;
export type ServerPermission = keyof ServerPermissions;

export type ServerAccess = {
	isOwner: boolean;
	permissions: Readonly<ServerPermissions>;
};

export const allServerPermissions: Readonly<ServerPermissions> = Object.freeze({
	rename: true,
	power: true,
	manageMembers: true,
	manageSsh: true,
	delete: true,
});

export const ownerAccess: Readonly<ServerAccess> = Object.freeze({
	isOwner: true,
	permissions: allServerPermissions,
});

export const serverSummary = v.object({
	_id: v.id("servers"),
	name: v.string(),
	isOwner: v.boolean(),
	permissions: serverPermissions,
});

/** A delegate cannot grant or remove authority outside their own permissions. */
export function hasServerPermissions(
	available: Readonly<ServerPermissions>,
	requested: Readonly<ServerPermissions>,
) {
	return Object.entries(requested).every(
		([permission, isGranted]) =>
			!isGranted || available[permission as ServerPermission],
	);
}

export async function getServerMembership(
	ctx: QueryCtx,
	serverId: Id<"servers">,
	userId: Id<"users">,
) {
	return await ctx.db
		.query("serverMemberships")
		.withIndex("by_server_id_and_user_id", (q) =>
			q.eq("serverId", serverId).eq("userId", userId),
		)
		.unique();
}

export async function requireServerMembership(
	ctx: QueryCtx,
	membershipId: Id<"serverMemberships">,
) {
	const membership = await ctx.db.get("serverMemberships", membershipId);
	if (membership === null) {
		throw toConvexError("membership_not_found");
	}
	return membership;
}

/** Returns null for a user who neither owns the server nor has a membership. */
export async function getServerAccess(
	ctx: QueryCtx,
	server: Doc<"servers">,
	userId: Id<"users">,
): Promise<ServerAccess | null> {
	if (server.ownerId === userId) {
		return ownerAccess;
	}
	const membership = await getServerMembership(ctx, server._id, userId);
	return membership === null
		? null
		: { isOwner: false, permissions: membership.permissions };
}

export function toServerSummary(
	server: Doc<"servers">,
	access: ServerAccess,
): Infer<typeof serverSummary> {
	return {
		_id: server._id,
		name: server.name,
		isOwner: access.isOwner,
		permissions: access.permissions,
	};
}

async function requireServerChangeable(ctx: QueryCtx, serverId: Id<"servers">) {
	if ((await requireServerAllocation(ctx, serverId)).deleteRequested) {
		throw toConvexError("server_deleting");
	}
}

/**
 * Access alone allows reads. A change also needs its permission, and a server
 * that is being deleted accepts no change.
 */
export async function requireServerAccess(
	ctx: QueryCtx,
	serverId: Id<"servers">,
	permission?: ServerPermission,
) {
	const user = await requireUser(ctx);
	const server = await ctx.db.get("servers", serverId);
	const access =
		server === null ? null : await getServerAccess(ctx, server, user._id);
	// A server that the user cannot access looks the same as one that does not exist.
	if (server === null || access === null) {
		throw toConvexError("server_not_found");
	}
	if (permission !== undefined) {
		if (!access.permissions[permission]) {
			throw toConvexError("permission_denied");
		}
		await requireServerChangeable(ctx, serverId);
	}
	return { user, server, ...access };
}

/** The allocation of a server whose SSH access the caller may change. */
export const requireSshAccess = internalQuery({
	args: { serverId: v.id("servers") },
	returns: schema.doc("serverAllocations"),
	handler: async (ctx, { serverId }) => {
		await requireServerAccess(ctx, serverId, "manageSsh");
		return await requireServerAllocation(ctx, serverId);
	},
});

export async function requireServerOwner(
	ctx: QueryCtx,
	serverId: Id<"servers">,
) {
	const access = await requireServerAccess(ctx, serverId);
	if (!access.isOwner) {
		throw toConvexError("permission_denied");
	}
	await requireServerChangeable(ctx, serverId);
	return access;
}
```

## Assistant · 2026-09-15T12:47:24.736Z

Fair on `/refactor`. I was quoting it like scripture when it is an input written for a different repo before our rules existed. It should probably be rewritten against this repo's vocabulary and the no-mocks decision, or folded into `AGENTS.md`. I'll stop citing it as authority.

And you are right that the worker finding is a symptom, not the disease. I went looking. Here is the first pass.

## The pattern

I mapped every import in `convex/` and then deep-read three files. The recurring fault is not coupling. It is that **a file's name announces one concept while the file holds three or four that change for different reasons.** Everything else follows from that.

**`ssh/access.ts`** (224 lines) is named for one thing and contains four: the AES-GCM envelope, the connection builder, bootstrap issuance, and a public API action. Inside it I found a real wart that only exists because those live together:

```ts
command: toSshBootstrapCommand(
  { ...toSshBootstrapFile(sshAccess), token },   // <- token immediately overwritten
  sshAccess.publicKey,
)
```

`toSshBootstrapFile` decrypts the row to read the **old** token, which the spread then discards. We decrypt a secret, materialize it in memory, and throw it away, in a repo with an explicit rule about not letting secrets linger. Nobody wrote that on purpose. It happened because a function that should build a small record also owns decryption.

**`servers/permissions.ts`** (152 lines) holds permission constants, membership lookup, access resolution, a *view model* (`serverSummary`), and an SSH-specific `internalQuery`. Two consequences:

- `requireSshAccess` reads the allocation twice per call, once through `requireServerAccess` and once directly.
- `requireServerAccess(ctx, id)` and `requireServerAccess(ctx, id, "power")` differ by more than a permission check. Passing a permission *also* asserts the server is not being deleted. The name does not say that, so every caller has to know it. That is the same class of problem as the worker: knowledge that should live in one place is something callers must carry.

**`allocations/hetzner_cloud/api.ts`** is named for Hetzner's API but is a transport, so `worker.ts` carries Hetzner's URL paths, `label_selector` syntax, `per_page`, and response-key unwrapping inside the state machine.

One thing I want to correct before you act on it: I nearly reported `operations.ts` importing `hetzner_cloud/` as a violation. It is not. The `switch` over `backend` is exactly our own exhaustive-kind rule, and `allocationBackend` being a single-member literal means a second backend breaks compilation everywhere it must. That one is right. The open question is only whether four separate switches should be one `Record` keyed by backend.

There is also no import cycle. `ssh/` and `allocations/` reference each other at folder level, but `addresses.ts` is a leaf, so the module graph is acyclic. I checked rather than assumed.

I have not yet read `worker_state.ts`, `keys.ts`, `lifecycle.ts`, `memberships.ts`, `clerk.ts`, `users.ts` or `src/` closely. Based on three-for-three, I expect more of the same, and I would rather find it while doing the work than write a longer report first.

## Where I was wrong: the dots

I raised a false alarm. Our rule says Convex **file names** are snake_case. In `authorized_keys.test.ts` the name is `authorized_keys`; `.test.ts` is the suffix. Nothing in the rule tells anyone to write `authorized_keys_test.ts`, and you are right that nobody underscores a test. The rule is fine and needs no carve-out.

What is real and worth recording is the Convex fact I found in its bundler, because the code cannot explain it:

```js
} else if ((base.match(/\./g) || []).length > 1) {
  logVerbose(`Skipping ${fpath} that contains multiple dots`);
}
```

That is *why* our test files are never deployed. Not a test rule, a two-dots rule. It belongs in `docs/decisions.md` as a fact we rely on.

## "container" is my invention, and I think it is the wrong word

It is not a standard test type. The standard taxonomy is unit/integration/e2e, and the research argues that decays fast, because a test can touch five modules in 3 ms or one adapter in a minute. The suggestion to name by resource came from one report, not from industry.

But your question cuts deeper: **Docker is the mechanism, not the requirement.** What the test actually needs is *a real OpenSSH server*. Docker is one way to get one; Podman takes the same arguments, WSL has one, Linux and macOS can run one natively. If we name the file after Docker we have to rename it the day we support Podman.

So the honest axis is **what external thing must exist for this test to mean anything**, which gives us exactly four classes:

| needs | examples | cost |
|---|---|---|
| nothing | parser, address parsing, the research reader | instant |
| a real `sshd` | discovery, write, remove, the probe | ~1 min, needs Docker or Podman |
| real Hetzner | create, delete, quota release, uncertain outcomes | minutes, real money |
| a Convex deployment | mutations and queries | we have no answer yet |

That last row is the gap nobody has grounded. We rejected convex-test, so how we exercise mutations honestly is genuinely undecided, and it is where the worker's fault matrix lives.

## `bun test` with no script: yes, and I grounded it

You are right and it is cleanly possible. `bun test` is a native verb, `bun run check` is ours, so there is no drift as long as we **never add a `test` script**. `verify` already calls `bun test` directly.

I also found Bun 1.4.2 has more than I expected, which changes what we need to build ourselves:

```
--parallel=N        --isolate        --shard=1/3 --timings
--changed[=ref]     --randomize      --seed
--bail  --retry  --rerun-each        --reporter=junit
--path-ignore-patterns
```

`--changed` is the fast inner loop with no script. `--shard` and `--timings` are what CI would use later. `--reporter=junit` is the CI adapter the research said to keep thin. `--seed` and `--randomize` give us replayable randomness without a library.

And I verified exclusion works from config rather than from a script:

```toml
[test]
pathIgnorePatterns = ["**/*.container.test.ts"]
```

I tested it: plain `bun test` ran 1 of 2 files. A positional filter does **not** override it, but `bun test --path-ignore-patterns=` does run everything. So excluding by default is available if we want it. My inclination is not to use it: let `bun test` mean everything, and let a missing sshd be a failure rather than a silent skip.

## Live Hetzner: my three options were badly worded

There was only ever one question, and it is **who starts it**. You, a schedule, or every push. You have answered: real Hetzner yes, no silent daily job. That settles it. What matters technically is that resources carry a run id and a sweeper removes leftovers, so a crashed run cannot quietly bill you. Our inventory scan is already most of that.

## What I need from you

Almost nothing, which is the honest answer to "why haven't you started".

1. **A test policy document.** I think yes: `docs/testing.md` next to `vocabulary.md` and `decisions.md`, plus one line in `AGENTS.md`. Say no if you want it inside `decisions.md` instead.
2. **The suffix word.** Naming by what must exist, not by Docker. My preference is `authorized_keys.sshd.test.ts` and later `worker.live.test.ts`, because `sshd` stays true if we switch to Podman. `.container.` is the alternative if you prefer the resource over the program.
3. **More research: I would say only one prompt, not ten.** The nine reports cover strategy, oracles, organization, runners, rewriters, infrastructure and failure modes well, and more general testing research now mostly risks polluting first-principles thinking, as you put it. The single genuine gap is the fourth row of that table: **how people test a Convex-style backend when they have rejected the framework's own test harness.** If you want, I will write that one prompt carefully and you can send it while I refactor.

Then I start the hard refactor, file by file, beginning with the three I have already read and working outward, rewriting the tests from scratch rather than preserving any of the three we have.

## Assistant · 2026-09-15T13:24:16.910Z

Taking the correction first, because I earned it.

## I overstepped on Hetzner

You reasoned out loud, dictation caught it, and I turned your thinking-aloud into "you have answered: no silent daily job" and wrote it down as settled. That is me manufacturing a decision from your uncertainty, which is worse than asking. There is no CI, no GitHub remote, and therefore nothing that could run daily. I should have said "this isn't answerable yet" instead of closing it.

And my three options were bad because **they were not the real question.** Here is the real one, which I only saw properly after thinking about what a Hetzner test can actually prove:

> You cannot ask Hetzner to lose your response.

Every dangerous path in the worker is "Hetzner committed the change and we never found out": lost reply, crash before we persisted the id, a late result arriving after its operation was replaced. Those are exactly the defects Codex found, and **a real Hetzner test cannot produce a single one of them**, because the failure is in the network and the clock, not in Hetzner.

So real-Hetzner tests and fault tests prove disjoint things:

- **Real Hetzner** proves the boring-but-essential facts nothing else can: that Hetzner accepts our create body, that our labels come back the way we read them, that a delete really deletes, that `resource_limit_exceeded` looks how we think it looks.
- **A substituted provider** proves the interesting failures, and only locally.

Neither replaces the other, and only one of them costs money. Everything else about Hetzner — who starts it, how often, whether CI — depends on the test shape we have not designed yet. You were right that it comes after. I am dropping it until then.

## What kinds of tests: the pyramid is wrong for us, and here is why

You kept asking this and I kept answering about filename suffixes. Sorry. Here is the actual answer.

Unit / integration / e2e classifies tests by **how much of our own code runs**. For us that is not the interesting variable. A parser test touches one file; a discovery test touches five; both could be fast or slow, and neither fact tells you anything about whether the test can be *wrong*.

The variable that actually matters here is **who decides the right answer.** Our system has four different authorities, and we have already been burned by getting this wrong once:

| Authority | What it settles | What it needs to run |
|---|---|---|
| **Us** | the format, the arithmetic, the parse | nothing |
| **sshd** | whether a key works, whether an edit widened access | a real OpenSSH server |
| **Our own recorded contract** | error codes, permissions, repeatability, the state machine under adversarial ordering | a real Convex backend + a provider we control |
| **Hetzner** | that the provider really did it | money |

That is not a taxonomy I read anywhere. It falls out of this system. And it is the *useful* one, because a test's value is exactly whether it consulted the right authority. Our four `authorized_keys` round-trip tests fail on this axis: they ask *us* a question only *sshd* can answer. That is the same defect as Paramiko testing itself.

The suffix then stops being a naming debate and becomes a consequence: the filename says which authority the test needs, because that is the thing that determines whether it can run. I will stop relitigating the word.

## Convex: I was unclear, and you were right

By "the framework's own test harness" I did mean `convex-test`, and your instinct is correct: it is a simulation of Convex written in JavaScript, so it is the Paramiko trap again in a different costume.

What I did not know, and now do, is that there is a real alternative. The `convex` package downloads and runs an actual backend binary:

```
convex-local-backend-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip
convex-local-backend-{aarch64,x86_64}-unknown-linux-gnu.zip
convex-local-backend-{aarch64,x86_64}-apple-darwin.zip
```

`convex dev --configure --dev-deployment local` selects it, and there is a deployment kind called **anonymous** that needs no account at all. So the third row is not a mock and not the cloud: it is the real backend, running locally, disposable. That is almost certainly the thing you remembered from the other projects, and I have a subagent checking exactly how they wired it up, under the no-verbatim rule.

## Module graph or policy?

Policy, not a graph. A drawn graph rots the moment someone adds an import and nobody notices.

But this repo already has the better pattern: a short rule plus a script that enforces it, the way `scripts/characters.ts` enforces the character rule. I would add one rule about dependency direction and one about a file having a single reason to change, then a `check:imports` that fails when they are broken. Prose nobody can run is how we got here.

## Assistant · 2026-09-15T13:29:17.962Z

The subagent came back. Both sibling projects rejected the pyramid, and they disagree with each other about almost everything else.

## What it found

**composery-1** used `convex-test` (the mock) with Vitest. Its categories were `behavior/` `invariants/` `system/`, and — unusually — those were genuinely enforced by meta-tests that assert the layout, not just documented. Docker appeared only in `system/`, never for Convex.

The valuable part is that the project measured its own mock and wrote down what it found: workflow bodies could be observed **failing but never succeeding** under the mock, and certain mutants were unkillable because the mock's ordering comparison treats anything that is not ascending as descending. That is a project discovering, with a controlled experiment, that its oracle was lying to it in a specific direction. It is the strongest argument against `convex-test` I have seen, and it comes from someone who shipped it rather than from me.

**composery-2** ran a **real anonymous local Convex backend per suite**, and explicitly banned both `convex-test` and Vitest — which matches what you told me you wanted here. The mechanism, all verified in its harness code rather than its docs:

- copies the backend package into a fresh temp workspace, symlinks `node_modules` (junction on Windows) instead of reinstalling
- reserves free cloud and site ports explicitly
- **pins the backend server build to a version**, because a restart once re-fetched the latest release and left a detached executor process behind
- forces anonymous mode so no account is reachable
- deletes every Convex CLI variable from the child environment, plus every name read from the backend's env example — the deny-list is *derived from that file*, not hand-maintained
- redirects `TEMP`/`TMP`/`TMPDIR` into the workspace
- keeps state in a per-test `mkdtemp` under a gitignored repo-local `tmp/`, not system temp
- `beforeAll`/`afterAll` via async-dispose, with recorded budgets of 180 s per stage, 300 s suite start, 60 s teardown
- on Windows, hunts detached executor processes by matching their command line against the exact workspace path

Its categories were `logic/` `backend/` `web/` plus a non-test `harness/`, and unlike composery-1 **nothing enforced them**.

Neither has CI. The agent was explicit about which claims it verified in code versus which were only prose, and flagged that it could not confirm either suite currently passes.

## What that actually changes for us

**Three things, and none of them is "copy composery-2".**

First, the local-backend path is real, and someone has already paid for the sharp edges. That list above is a hazard inventory: the backend auto-updates unless pinned, it leaks processes on Windows, it inherits environment variables that will silently point your test at your real deployment, and the system temp directory is not where you want its state. I would not have predicted most of those.

Second, **it is expensive.** Three CLI invocations and budgets measured in minutes. That settles a design point: the "our own contract" row cannot be per-test. It is one deployment per run, or it is unusable.

Third, both projects invented their own categories and neither used unit/integration/e2e. Untrusted repos, so it is weak evidence — but it is consistent with the research, and it is two more data points that the pyramid gets abandoned by people who actually have to organize a real suite. What I take from composery-1 is not its categories but its habit: **every rule named its enforcer.** That is exactly this repo's style, and it is the argument for `check:imports` I made earlier.

## The three prompts

You said feel free, so here they are rather than asking again.

**1 — How test suites are actually categorized**

```text
Context: A team is organizing a small, deliberately chosen automated test suite for a backend system. They have not decided what categories of test to have, or whether to have categories at all.

Question: What schemes do real projects use to categorize their tests, and what follows from each?

Cover the unit/integration/end-to-end pyramid, but treat it as one option among several rather than as the default. Include projects that use a different scheme entirely, projects that deliberately have no categories, and projects that changed their scheme and said why. Cover schemes organized by speed, by resource required, by which system decides whether the result is correct, by risk, by lifecycle stage, and any others you find.

For each scheme: what decision it helps someone make, what it fails to capture, whether it is enforced by tooling or only by convention in that project, and what happens to it as the codebase grows.

Also cover the published criticisms of the test pyramid and the responses to those criticisms.

Evidence rules: cite repositories, documentation, talks and papers with dates. Distinguish a project's stated scheme from what its test directories and CI configuration actually do. Do not conclude that one scheme is correct. Where a project abandoned a scheme, say what it replaced it with and whether the replacement is reported to have worked.
```

**2 — Running a real backend process for tests**

```text
Context: A project's correctness depends on a backend server it does not want to simulate. The developers can run the real server locally as a separate process. They have no continuous integration.

Question: How do projects run a real server process for their tests, and what goes wrong?

Cover: starting one disposable instance per test run versus per test file versus sharing a long-lived one; how the instance is isolated from the developer's own working environment, including environment variables, configuration files, ports, temporary directories and credentials; how it is guaranteed to be shut down, including after a crash, an interrupted run, or a debugger stop; how the version of the server binary is controlled and what happens when it updates unexpectedly; how long startup costs in practice and what projects do about it; and how state is kept from leaking between tests.

Use named examples across several ecosystems: databases, message brokers, provider emulators, headless browsers and application backends. Include at least one project that abandoned this approach, and say what it moved to.

Evidence rules: cite repositories, issues and documentation with dates. Prefer evidence from harness code and CI configuration over prose in a README. Include concrete reports of leaked processes, port collisions, cross-contaminated state, or a test accidentally running against a developer's real environment.
```

**3 — The Bun test runner in practice**

```text
Context: A TypeScript project uses Bun's built-in test runner and does not want to add a separate test framework.

Question: As of late 2026, what does Bun's test runner provide, what do serious projects actually use from it, and what do they still build themselves?

Cover its current feature set and how recently each part arrived, including file discovery and filtering, lifecycle hooks, concurrency and isolation between test files, sharding and timing data, watch and changed-file selection, snapshots, mocking, coverage, reporters, randomization and seeding, and any configuration available through bunfig.toml rather than command-line flags.

Then cover practice rather than documentation: named repositories that use it for a non-trivial suite, what they configure, what helpers they wrote themselves, and what they report missing. Include projects that adopted it and later left, with the stated reason, and projects that run it alongside another runner rather than instead of one.

Evidence rules: cite the Bun repository, its changelogs and release notes, and third-party repositories, with dates and version numbers. Distinguish what is documented from what the repositories actually do. Where a feature is recent or unstable, say so. Do not assume the runner is sufficient or insufficient.
```

## Where I am

Starting the backend refactor now, as authorized: `api.ts` gains real operations and `worker.ts` loses Hetzner's URL syntax, then `access.ts` and `permissions.ts` get split along their actual reasons to change. Tests come after that lands, because rewriting them against the shape we are about to delete would be wasted work.

Still open and genuinely yours: the `AGENTS.md` fold, which I want to show you rule by rule rather than perform silently.

HBase is a useful demonstration that “medium” need not mean “integration” or vice versa. | **Strongly tool-enforced.** Bazel can filter by size and timeout; HBase requires annotations and changes which Maven phase executes them. As suites grow, these labels become scheduling contracts. The danger is semantic drift: a test can still be mis-sized even though the label itself is enforced. |
60	| **Required resource / capability** | **CPython** treats resources such as `network`, `cpu`, GUI, large files, and URL fetching as capabilities that the test runner may enable. Tests call `requires()` / `requires_resource()`; disabled resources cause a controlled skip rather than an attempt to reinterpret the test as “unit” or “integration.” Current CI modes deliberately enable different resource sets. Actual tests use these markers—for example exhaustive Unicode work is conditioned on the CPU resource and some data fetching on network availability. ([GitHub](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/test/support/__init__.py?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) **Apache Airflow** similarly distinguishes DB tests, database backends, external-integration tests, and `long_running` tests. ([GitHub](https://github.com/apache/airflow/blob/main/contributing-docs/testing/unit_tests.rst?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | “Can this test run in this environment?” “What infrastructure must be provisioned?” “Which subset can we safely run locally or on this CI worker?” | Granularity and importance. A network test may be tiny; an in-memory test may be computationally huge. | **Machine-enforced.** Airflow goes further: CI detects a DB-using test that is missing the DB marker. At scale, resource classification tends to become multi-dimensional—Airflow has DB/non-DB, backend, external integration, long-running, quarantine and product-area dimensions rather than one hierarchy. Its current developer commands expose those divisions directly. ([GitHub](https://github.com/apache/airflow/blob/main/contributing-docs/testing/unit_tests.rst?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
61	| **Who/what supplies the oracle; dependency ownership** | **Spotify’s microservice testing practice**, published **11 January 2018**, distinguishes *integration* tests from *integrated* tests using J. B. Rainsberger’s terminology. An “integrated test” can pass or fail because some other nontrivial system is correct or incorrect. Spotify advocated many service-level integration tests with controlled collaborators, few implementation-detail tests, and ideally very few cross-system integrated tests—the “testing honeycomb.” ([Spotify Engineering](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2018/1/testing-of-microservices)) **SQLite** separates independent test harnesses whose notions of correctness differ. SQL Logic Test compares millions of SQL results with other database engines; TH3 checks the deployed C library and configurations; fuzzers largely use crash/invariant properties; the Tcl suite carries conventional expected-results tests. ([SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/testing.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | “If this fails, whose correctness is implicated?” “Should the external system be real, simulated, or used as a differential oracle?” “Are we checking examples, agreement with another implementation, or invariants?” | Usually says little about speed or business priority. An oracle based on another implementation can also share the same bug or differ legitimately. | Spotify’s distinction is principally an **architectural convention** reported from internal services; its internal CI cannot be independently inspected from the article. SQLite’s distinction is much more structural: separate harnesses embody separate oracle/failure strategies. At scale this axis tends to multiply rather than form a pyramid: new fault models, target configurations and independent implementations add new forms of evidence. |
62	| **Artifact / compiler phase / observable** | **rustc**’s `compiletest` suites are arranged as `ui`, `incremental`, `debuginfo`, `codegen-*`, `assembly`, `mir-opt`, `coverage`, `crashes`, `run-make`, and others. A UI test, for example, compares compiler output against checked-in `.stdout`/`.stderr` files; `--bless` updates them for human inspection. ([Rust Compiler Development Guide](https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/tests/compiletest.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | “Which artifact or compiler property is being checked, and which harness understands it?” | Whether a test is “unit” or “integration” is almost beside the point. The suite name also does not automatically encode risk or execution cost. | **Strong structural/tool enforcement:** directory determines harness behavior, normalization and expected artifacts. Growth produces additional specialized suites and directives rather than an attempt to squeeze everything into three levels. |
63	| **Risk / criticality → how strongly a test gates delivery** | **Slack** changed to this model in **2021**, describing the change in a **18 February 2022** engineering article (updated 23 August 2022). Previously, most E2E testing was pre-merge. With test execution growing about 10% month over month for three years, a typical PR could trigger dozens of E2E suites and compound flake probability. The replacement put fewer than 1% of E2E tests—the highest-criticality set—pre-merge; under 10% medium-criticality tests post-merge but before deployment; the remainder ran in a bi-hourly regression tier. ([Slack Engineering](https://slack.engineering/balancing-safety-and-velocity-in-ci-cd-at-slack/)) | “Which failures justify stopping a merge or deployment?” and “How much latency should we buy for this risk?” | It deliberately says almost nothing about test construction. A blocking test might be unit-sized or E2E-sized; a nonblocking regression might still test a critical subsystem indirectly. | **Pipeline-enforced once classified; risk classification is human judgment.** This scheme was created *because* the suite grew. Slack reports p95 CI latency falling from >30 minutes to <18, PR flakiness from roughly 50% to <5%, with no measurable increase in customer-reported defects. That is one of the clearer published cases where a replacement is reported to have worked. ([Slack Engineering](https://slack.engineering/balancing-safety-and-velocity-in-ci-cd-at-slack/)) |
64	| **Change risk / development lifecycle stage** | **Chromium** has CQ modes rather than merely test types. Normal dry runs and full runs use a curated presubmit set; **Mega-CQ** invokes a substantially larger set for particularly risky changes and enables CI-only tests. Generated CQ configuration and recipes implement these distinctions, so this is not just prose guidance. ([Chromium Git Repositories](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/%2B/HEAD/docs/infra/cq.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | “How much evidence should this particular change obtain before submission?” | It does not identify test scope or oracle. Two identical tests can be treated differently depending on the change/pipeline context. | **Tool-enforced.** Growth leads to curation: the ordinary set is kept practical while exceptional changes can spend substantially more CI budget. A February 2026 Chromium change, for example, explicitly added CI-only coverage to certain Clang rolls, showing that this classification is actively adjusted as risk changes. ([Chromium Git Repositories](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/tools/%2B/f067649e2ef4c812d42703dde34a65237cbf0823?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
65	| **Product/API lifecycle maturity and conformance** | **Kubernetes** uses conformance testing as a public-contract gate. In 2018 only about 11% of stable endpoints were covered by conformance tests; policy subsequently required stable APIs to carry conformance coverage. APISnoop automated visibility into gaps, and Kubernetes reported reaching **100% conformance-tested eligible endpoints in 1.27 (2023)**. ([Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/10/05/sig-architecture-conformance-spotlight-2023/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | “May this API graduate?” “Can an implementation claim the portability/conformance promise?” | Internal quality, speed and component granularity. Conformance can be complete for the defined public surface while other failure modes remain. | **Policy plus automation.** This grew from sparse coverage into a lifecycle gate. The published “worked” result is specifically endpoint-conformance coverage—11% to 100%—not evidence that all defect classes disappeared. |
66	| **Ownership/product area and test health** | **Airflow** also divides CI tests into areas such as Core, API, CLI, Operators, WWW, Providers and Other, primarily for selective execution and parallelism. It separately marks `quarantined` tests and gives them different CI semantics. ([GitHub](https://github.com/apache/airflow/blob/main/contributing-docs/testing/unit_tests.rst?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | “Whose change should cause this to run?” “Who should investigate?” “Is this result trusted enough to gate?” | Neither semantic scope nor resource use follows necessarily from ownership. “Quarantined” describes the test’s reliability state, not what it tests. | These are **operational labels**, used by tooling. They are characteristic of growth: once a suite is too large for every test to run identically, selection, ownership and test-health state become classifications of their own. |
67	| **Deliberately blurry / no unit-vs-integration categories** | **Oppia’s backend suite** is unusually explicit. Its backend-testing guide, edited **4 December 2025**, says: “we don't distinguish clearly between unit and integration tests.” They are written the same way and differ mainly in how much is mocked; developers are encouraged not to mock merely to preserve a category. ([GitHub](https://github.com/oppia/oppia/wiki/Backend-tests?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Oppia **does** separately have E2E/acceptance testing, so it would be inaccurate to call the entire project category-free. ([GitHub](https://github.com/oppia/oppia/wiki/End-to-End-Tests?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Avoids making developers resolve an ambiguous “unit or integration?” question when that distinction does not drive the backend workflow. The practical choice becomes “what should be real versus mocked in this test?” | It no longer tells you, from a nominal category, how isolated or slow a particular backend test is. | The lack of a crisp unit/integration distinction is **deliberate convention**; the runner does not enforce that semantic split. As the suite grew, operational organization appeared elsewhere—runtime-based CI sharding and a separate E2E suite. This is illustrative of a recurring phenomenon: declining one taxonomy does not mean declining all operational structure. |
68	
69	There is therefore a meaningful difference between **“we call these categories”** and **“the build system acts on these categories.”** Bazel size, HBase size, CPython resources, Airflow DB markers, rustc suite directories and Chromium CQ modes have executable consequences. GitLab is mixed: CI understands the levels, but deciding that a regression *belongs* at the lowest practical level remains a review/design judgment. Spotify and Slack are published accounts of real internal practice, but the underlying private repositories cannot be checked against those accounts in the way the open-source examples can.
70	
71	### The pyramid is one economic model, not merely three nouns
72	
73	The modern “test pyramid” descends from Mike Cohn’s **2009** unit/service/UI pyramid. Martin Fowler’s **1 May 2012** article popularized the formulation of many small, focused tests and progressively fewer broad-stack tests; Fowler revised the article in **2016 and 2017**. Importantly, Fowler makes the underlying premise fairly explicit: broad-stack tests tend to be slower, more brittle and more expensive to diagnose and maintain. He also says that where higher-level tests are fast, reliable and cheap to modify, the economic reason for duplicating their coverage with lower-level tests is much weaker. ([martinfowler.com](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestPyramid.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
74	
75	GitLab is a strong example of a project where that model remains an intentional policy. It asks developers to put regressions at the lowest practical test level, and its actual population is pyramid-shaped. Google’s Mike Wacker made a similar case in **“Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests,” 22 April 2015**, suggesting 70% unit / 20% integration / 10% E2E as a *first guess*, not a universal constant. The reason given is feedback quality: lower runtime, less flakiness and easier failure isolation. ([GitLab Docs](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/testing_guide/testing_levels/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
76	
77	Ham Vocke’s **26 February 2018** “Practical Test Pyramid” is already a response to taking Cohn’s original picture too literally. Vocke calls the simple three-layer rendering overly simplistic for modern systems and discusses service integration, contract, UI and E2E testing while retaining the weaker rule: test at different granularities and generally have fewer of the most expensive broad-scope tests. ([martinfowler.com](https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html))
78	
79	### Published criticisms—and how the responses differ
80	
81	One criticism attacks the pyramid’s **choice of architectural unit**. Spotify’s **2018** “Testing of Microservices” argues that, in a microservice architecture, the deployable service is often the more useful “unit.” Heavy mocking of individual classes can make tests follow implementation details while missing the service’s actual interaction boundaries. Its proposed honeycomb therefore emphasizes service integration tests rather than implementation-detail tests, with very few cross-system “integrated” tests. Spotify reports that on a simple service, running the database and service and testing through the real API yielded a small suite and easier refactoring, at the price of seconds rather than milliseconds and sometimes less precise failure localization. ([Spotify Engineering](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2018/1/testing-of-microservices))
82	
83	That argument inherited terminology from J. B. Rainsberger’s **“Integrated Tests Are A Scam,” originally 5 April 2009**. His point was not “never test integration”; it was that tests whose results depend on several uncontrolled nontrivial components rapidly acquire combinatorial coverage and diagnosis problems. He later emphasized the distinction between **integration tests** and **integrated tests**, and in the **10 October 2023** talk *Beware the Integrated Tests Scam: A Retrospective And An Apology* explicitly softened the slogan: integrated tests are not always a scam, though he still argues that excessive dependency coupling creates the underlying problem. ([The Code Whisperer](https://blog.thecodewhisperer.com/permalink/integrated-tests-are-a-scam?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
84	
85	A second criticism attacks the pyramid’s **cost assumptions**. Kent C. Dodds’ **13 July 2019** “Testing Trophy” argues, mainly for frontend applications, that modern integration tests can provide substantially more confidence per test than very narrow unit tests without carrying the historical cost of browser-level E2E. The resulting “trophy” puts most weight in integration tests. But Dodds’ **3 June 2021** follow-up is an important qualification often lost when the diagram is copied: he says the trophy was aimed at his frontend context, not as a universal prescription for backend/microservice systems, and argues that debates over exactly where “unit” ends and “integration” begins can become less useful than asking whether tests are expressive, fast, reliable and valuable. ([Kent C. Dodds](https://kentcdodds.com/blog/write-tests?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
86	
87	Fowler’s response to this kind of objection is largely to concede the premise rather than defend a fixed shape. His article says the pyramid follows when broad tests have worse economics; change those economics and the desired distribution can change. He also notes that some apparent disputes about “more integration, fewer unit tests” are disputes over what people mean by *unit*. ([martinfowler.com](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestPyramid.html))
88	
89	A third criticism attacks the idea of a **geometric distribution at all**. Karl Evard and Rebecca Wirfs-Brock’s *Flow Focused Testing Strategies: Working Towards a Pattern Language Alternative to the Test Pyramid*, presented at PLoP **12–15 October 2025** and appearing in the **2026 ACM proceedings**, argues that choosing a suite by a shape—pyramid, trophy, honeycomb, etc.—can itself be the wrong abstraction. They propose reasoning from important flows and the testing strategies appropriate to them. This is a proposal/pattern-language paper, not a published report of a large project abandoning its pyramid and demonstrating better production-defect outcomes, so its evidential status is different from Slack’s before/after account. ([PlopCon](https://plopcon.org/proceedings/plop/2025/15.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
90	
91	The strongest defense of the pyramid therefore is not “70/20/10 is scientifically correct.” It is the weaker observation found in Fowler, Google and Vocke: **when broader tests systematically cost more to execute, maintain and diagnose, duplicating everything at the broadest level produces poor feedback economics**. The strongest criticism is correspondingly not “integration tests are always superior”; it is that scope labels are an unreliable proxy when architecture and tooling have changed the cost curve.
92	
93	## Projects that actually changed what categories control
94	
95	Slack is the clearest migration in this set because it publishes a cause, replacement and measured outcome. The old organization effectively made “E2E” imply “run before merge.” As the repository and suite grew, that mapping broke down: many independent flaky tests multiplied the probability that a PR would encounter at least one unrelated failure, while the infrastructure cost and queue latency grew. Slack did **not** report solving this by replacing E2E with unit tests. It replaced **test-type-driven timing with risk-driven timing**: a tiny critical set before merge, a somewhat larger deployment gate after merge, and broad regression asynchronously after that. The reported latency/flakiness improvements were large, and Slack says it observed no measurable customer-defect increase. ([Slack Engineering](https://slack.engineering/balancing-safety-and-velocity-in-ci-cd-at-slack/))
96	
97	Kubernetes is a different sort of change. Conformance initially described an aspirational portability property while only a small fraction of stable API endpoints had matching tests. The community turned it into a **lifecycle rule**—stable APIs should not advance without conformance coverage—and added APISnoop automation to expose gaps. The reported result, reaching 100% of eligible stable endpoints in Kubernetes 1.27 in **2023**, supports the claim that the new process improved *conformance-test completeness*. It should not be inflated into a claim that Kubernetes thereby achieved complete behavioral testing. ([Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/10/05/sig-architecture-conformance-spotlight-2023/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
98	
99	GitLab illustrates a third path: **keep the old taxonomy but add more taxonomies around it**. The pyramid remains documented, while modern CI additionally reasons about progressive tiers, change prediction, resource efficiency, E2E critical journeys and product/lifecycle areas. Its growth from roughly 59,000 classified tests in 2019 to roughly 289,000 in the 2025 snapshot did not force it to choose between “pyramid” and “risk”; those schemes now answer separate questions. ([GitLab](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-foss/-/blob/b7c7d91c86ec62b204eca9c41a4e00a1800e68ca/doc/development/testing_guide/testing_levels.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
100	
101	## What follows for the design space of a small backend suite
102	
103	These projects expose several genuinely different choices rather than variants of one universal hierarchy.
104	
105	A team can make categories describe **semantic scope**, as GitLab does; the payoff is guidance about where a behavior should be asserted. It can make them describe **run cost**, as HBase and Bazel do; the payoff is a predictable local/CI feedback budget. It can label **capabilities and dependencies**, as CPython and Airflow do; the payoff is environment-aware execution. It can classify by **oracle or dependency ownership**, as Spotify and SQLite effectively do; the payoff is clearer interpretation of failures. It can classify by **risk and gate position**, as Slack and Chromium do; the payoff is deciding what is worth blocking delivery for. It can classify by **public-contract maturity**, as Kubernetes does; the payoff is governing API evolution. Or, as Oppia does within its backend suite, it can deliberately decline a crisp unit/integration distinction when that name would not drive a useful operational decision.
106	
107	The growth evidence also argues against expecting categories to remain purely descriptive. Small suites can get by with names. Large suites tend to turn useful distinctions into **control surfaces**: selectors, markers, timeouts, sharding keys, required environments, ownership rules, quarantine states and merge/deployment gates. Conversely, distinctions that do not change any behavior can remain fuzzy for years without necessarily causing a problem—Oppia documents exactly that for unit versus integration.
108	
109	So the schemes are not mutually exclusive competitors. A single test can coherently be **“integration” by scope, “medium” by runtime, “database/postgres” by required resource, “payments” by ownership, “critical” by risk, and “pre-merge” by lifecycle placement**. Real projects increasingly look like that as they grow. The substantive choice is not which label system is universally correct, but **which decisions the suite needs its taxonomy to make visible or enforce**.
110

54	### The three useful lifetimes
55	
56	| Lifetime | Where it appears | Advantages | Characteristic failures |

68	
69	A good harness treats the developer's shell and home directory as hostile input.
70	
71	**Environment variables and credentials.** Do not simply inherit everything and override `SERVER_URL`. Both Firebase's and Playwright's launchers currently spread `process.env` into child processes before adding their own variables. Firebase then injects emulator endpoint variables and project configuration; its own source has explicit warnings for commands where an emulator variable is set but the operation will nevertheless affect production. ([GitHub](https://github.com/firebase/firebase-tools/blob/main/src/emulator/commandUtils.ts))

73	The danger is demonstrated rather than hypothetical. 75	So for a local-only project I would create the server environment from a **whitelist**: `PATH` only if required, locale variables, the harness-created temp directory and port, deliberately fake/test credentials, and whatever test flags are necessary. 87	A shared-broker setup makes collisions and cross-use easier. RabbitMQ's `amqp091-go` integration tests take `AMQP_URL`, but otherwise silently default to `guest:guest@127.0.0.1:5672`. Consequently, whatever RabbitMQ happens to own the developer's standard port becomes the test broker. ([GitHub](https://github.com/rabbitmq/amqp091-go/blob/main/integration_test.go)) Kafka-go's Compose setup similarly fixes host ports 9092/9093 and ZooKeeper 2181, although it at least pins Kafka 2.3.1 and creates explicit test topics. ([GitHub](https://github.com/grafana/segmentio-kafka-go/blob/main/docker-compose.yml))
88	
89	**Temporary directories.** Give every run a newly created root; put data directories, Unix sockets, logs, PID files, browser profiles and generated configuration underneath it. For parallel workers, create a subdirectory per worker. Deleting the run root then becomes both cleanup and an orphan detector: if the previous run left a root plus live PID, you know something went wrong.
90	
91	### Shutdown is not something `finally` can guarantee
92	
93	Normal shutdown is straightforward: context manager / fixture finalizer → graceful server shutdown → wait with a deadline → kill the whole process tree if necessary.
94	
95	Playwright's web-server harness shows a fairly mature implementation. Setup tears down if startup fails; normal teardown invokes the stored process killer. It can send SIGINT or SIGTERM to the entire Unix process group and wait for a configured grace period. Its launcher also checks whether the target URL is already occupied and, unless `reuseExistingServer` is enabled, refuses to proceed rather than silently attaching to somebody else's process. ([GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright/src/plugins/webServerPlugin.ts))
96	
97	But **a finalizer cannot run after `SIGKILL`, a runner crash, power loss, or many IDE “Stop” operations**. Signal handlers cover Ctrl-C only when the process is allowed to handle the signal. Firebase registers shutdown handling for SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP and SIGQUIT and keeps PID/locator information, yet its code also contains logic to print PIDs of emulator subprocesses that “may still be running.” ([GitHub](https://github.com/firebase/firebase-tools/blob/main/src/emulator/commandUtils.ts))
98	
99	And bugs happen. Firebase issue #2477, **21 July 2020**, reproduced `firebase emulators:exec --only firestore 'cat'`; Ctrl-C killed the test command but left the Java Firestore emulator alive, and the next invocation failed because its port was taken. ([GitHub](https://github.com/firebase/firebase-tools/issues/2477)) Playwright issue #26980, **9 September 2023**, reported Chromium processes accumulating after developers repeatedly Ctrl-C'd test runs, eventually driving laptop CPU usage up. ([GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/26980))
100	
101	The only way to get substantially stronger guarantees is to move cleanup **outside the test runner**. Testcontainers does this with the Ryuk resource-reaper process; testcontainers-python explicitly integrated Ryuk for “better container cleanup” in release 4.1.0 on **19 March 2024**. A June **10, 2026** issue is revealing by exception: its `ComposeContainer` path lacked equivalent Ryuk cleanup, so containers could remain after crashes or force-stops. ([GitHub](https://github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-python/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md))
102	
103	For direct processes, the analogous design is an OS-level job/process group plus a tiny supervisor/watchdog. On Windows, a Job Object with kill-on-job-close is stronger than ordinary parent/child tracking. On Linux, a wrapper can use parent-death semantics; elsewhere a watchdog can observe the test runner PID. On the next test start, also reap any process carrying your run marker/PID file. You need both mechanisms: parent-death cleanup for abrupt termination and next-run recovery for cases it misses.
104	
105	### Version control is part of test isolation
106	
107	Using “whatever server is installed” makes the operating system's package manager part of your test input.
108	
109	`pytest-postgresql`, unless configured otherwise, searches configured paths, `pg_config --bindir`, Windows PostgreSQL installations and finally `PATH` for `pg_ctl`. Convenient locally, but an OS/Postgres upgrade can silently change the server version used by the tests. ([GitHub](https://github.com/dbfixtures/pytest-postgresql))
110	
111	Kafka-go documents the consequences directly: later Kafka versions caused subtle behavioural changes that broke historical tests, hence its examples use Kafka **2.3.1** and its Compose file pins a corresponding image. ([GitHub](https://github.com/segmentio/kafka-go))
112	
113	Browsers are an especially good counterexample. Playwright couples each Playwright release to specific browser binaries and tells users to reinstall those browsers after Playwright upgrades. ([GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/docs/src/browsers.md)) When people opt out and use system Chrome, the system updater returns as an uncontrolled dependency: issue #41883, opened **20 July 2026**, reports Chrome auto-updating around July 17 from roughly 129 to 150.0.7871.125; without test/config changes, browser startup, navigation and OAuth flows became noticeably slower. ([GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/41883?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
114	
115	For your case, I would therefore pin the server binary as an ordinary development dependency: exact version plus checksum, or an immutable image digest if containers are acceptable. A versioned tag is better than `PATH`; an image digest is better than a moving tag such as `latest`. Make upgrades explicit pull requests/commits, not consequences of `brew upgrade`.
116	
117	### Startup cost is real, and it drives the lifecycle choice
118	
119	The numbers vary enormously. A bare local daemon can start in tens or hundreds of milliseconds; JVM/provider emulators and complicated database images can take seconds to more than a minute.
120	
121	A Testcontainers/Postgres report from **11 July 2020** had a custom Postgres image taking **1 minute 20 seconds**, already longer than the library's one-minute readiness timeout. A Testcontainers user on **1 July 2023** was experimenting with container reuse specifically to avoid waiting “about a minute” for MySQL during development. ([GitHub](https://github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-java/issues/2990))
122	
123	Firebase issue #3594, **21 July 2021**, measured the first Firestore-emulator query at **8.4 seconds**, a hot repeat at 36 ms and a new test app at about 3 seconds; the reporter ended up issuing a warm-up request before the real test because otherwise the suite cost roughly `number of tests × 3s`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/firebase/firebase-tools/issues/3594))
124	
125	Even headless browser launch is material: a Playwright proposal opened **3 March 2026** measures **2–5 seconds of heavy CPU per browser launch** and proposes pre-warming a browser pool. Playwright's normal answer at the test level is more elegant: keep the actual browser running and give every test a cheap new `BrowserContext`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/39499))
126	
127	Projects consequently amortize startup rather than pretending it does not exist. `pytest-postgresql` creates an expensive initialized template once and clones it per test. Grafana starts its server in the background while Playwright browsers install, then polls `/health` for up to 60 seconds instead of sleeping a fixed interval. ([GitHub](https://github.com/dbfixtures/pytest-postgresql/blob/main/CHANGES.rst))
128	
129	The readiness probe matters: “process exists” or “TCP port opened” is often earlier than “server can correctly serve tests.” Poll an application-level health operation with a hard timeout and capture logs on failure.
130	
131	### State leakage is usually the harder problem than launching the process
132	
133	The rule is: **share the expensive process, not mutable test identity**.
134	
135	For a database, allocate a database/schema per test, clone a template, or recreate it. Transactions alone are insufficient when background workers or separate connections write outside the transaction. `pytest-postgresql` has historical scar tissue here: its changelog records a bug where a random test subprocess could reconnect before a database was dropped, causing the drop to fail and cascading into many later setup failures. ([GitHub](https://github.com/dbfixtures/pytest-postgresql/blob/main/CHANGES.rst)) It also added an option to drop a leftover test database at the beginning of a new run specifically for cases where an earlier run ended before cleanup. ([GitHub](https://github.com/dbfixtures/pytest-postgresql/blob/main/CHANGES.rst))
136	
137	For brokers, use a run/test prefix for **every** topic, queue, consumer group, exchange and durable subscription. RabbitMQ's integration suite performs explicit close/delete cleanup because the broker itself is shared. A fixed name on a long-lived broker is latent cross-test state; cleanup of a queue with a generic name is also capable of deleting a developer's own object.
138	
139	For provider emulators, prefer a unique fake project/account per run or test plus an explicit clear/reset API. Firebase's emulator hub itself warns that multiple suites using the same project may cause “unexpected behavior.” ([GitHub](https://github.com/firebase/firebase-tools/blob/main/src/emulator/hub.ts))
140	
141	For browsers, Playwright's isolation model is the archetype: one browser can be expensive and shared, while every test gets a fresh context containing its own cookies, local/session storage and other profile state. Its documentation specifically argues that trying to clean a reused environment is easy to get wrong—some state, such as visited-link state, is not realistically scrubbed—and recommends starting from a clean context. ([Playwright](https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
142	
143	For application servers, backend data has to receive the same treatment. Grafana's current Playwright configuration explicitly serializes two test projects because they toggle the **same backend fixture**; the second declares a dependency on the first so they cannot modify it concurrently. ([GitHub](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/main/playwright.config.ts)) That is a real example of browser-level isolation not being enough when the shared server has external state.
144	
145	### An instructive abandonment
146	
147	OpenTable's `otj-pg-embedded` is a particularly useful history because it **abandoned the native local-process form of this approach**. Pre-1.0 releases unpacked and ran native PostgreSQL tarballs. Version 1.0, released **31 January 2022**, moved to Docker/Testcontainers and the official PostgreSQL image. The maintainers cite Apple/Windows/Linux ARM, the disappearance of universal PG10+ Linux binaries, maintenance/security costs and cross-platform consistency as reasons. Earlier issue #142, **2 April 2020**, is representative of the native-process pain: an integration test inside Jenkins/Docker failed because `initdb` refused to run as root. ([Maven Repository](https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/com.opentable.components/otj-pg-embedded/1.0.0))
148	
149	It was not a free win. OpenTable says the container approach is **2–5× slower** than its old tarball launcher and explicitly observes that increasing the server lifetime improves speed but can make tests non-reproducible when they modify the same tables. ([GitHub](https://github.com/opentable/otj-pg-embedded/blob/master/README.md)) In other words, they traded native-process speed for packaging and lifecycle isolation.
150	
151	### What I would build for a project with no CI
152	
153	I would make the ordinary `test` command own a **single disposable server for the complete run**, with no dependency on a separately started developer instance. The developers may still be able to opt into a long-lived server for fast exploratory work, but that should be a visibly different command/mode.
154	
155	The harness contract would be:
156	
157	- Resolve an **exact pinned server binary** from the project/tool cache, not from an unqualified `PATH`; record its version in test output.
158	- Create one unique run root containing data, generated config, logs, PID/ownership metadata and any socket files; bind only to loopback and obtain an ephemeral port.
159	- Construct a minimal child environment and test credentials from scratch. Reject non-loopback production-style URLs before doing anything destructive.
160	- Start the server once, poll a real readiness operation, and expose the resulting endpoint only through the test fixture—not through the developer's normal configuration.
161	- Give each test a fresh logical namespace: database/schema, broker prefix, emulator project ID, browser context or application tenant. For expensive database setup, snapshot/template once and clone.
162	- On normal completion or Ctrl-C, gracefully terminate the whole process tree, wait with a short deadline, then force-kill it. Add an external watchdog/OS parent-death mechanism because a test finalizer alone cannot cover debugger force-stop or runner crashes.
163	- At the beginning of the next run, inspect ownership metadata and reap stale servers/directories from previous interrupted runs. Never kill a process merely because it happens to occupy “your” conventional port.
164	- Make reuse an explicit `--reuse-server` development optimization, never the default. If enabled, verify a run/test marker and exact server version before attaching; do not interpret “something answers on localhost:5432/5672/3000” as sufficient identity.
165	
166	That arrangement gives most of the fidelity of a real backend while keeping the failure domain close to the test run. The biggest lesson from the projects above is that **process launch is the easy part**. The engineering work is establishing ownership: ownership of the environment, endpoint, filesystem state, credentials, server version, mutable server data and, crucially, the process after the test runner itself stops behaving normally.
167	
```

70	So the execution model is worth making explicit:
71	
72	**`bun test` ≠ Jest/Vitest-style per-file isolation by default.** A normal run shares process, JS global and module state across test files. `--isolate` changes the realm/module isolation, while `--parallel` is what introduces multiple OS processes. `test.concurrent` is a third and separate thing: concurrency among tests *inside one file*. 
73	
74	That distinction explains a lot of real-world Bun test behavior around `mock.module`, environment variables, singleton caches and leaked resources.
75	
76	### How stable are the new isolation features?
77	
78	They are usable, but I would not mentally group them with `expect()` or `beforeEach()` yet. File isolation and multiprocessing only landed in April 2026. During the following months Bun received reports involving memory retention between isolated files, Linux resource/epoll flakes, and a Bun 1.4.0 regression combining `--isolate`, `mock.module()` and spawned processes. In other words, the design is now there, but 2026 has still been a stabilization cycle rather than years of battle-testing. ([GitHub](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/31771))
79	
80	## `bunfig.toml` matters more than it first appears
81	
82	The current `[test]` configuration is not just a place to persist CLI switches. Bun documents `root`, `preload`, `pathIgnorePatterns`, `smol`, `concurrentTestGlob`, `randomize`, `seed`, `retry`, `rerunEach`, the coverage settings, and `[test.reporter] junit`. 
83	
84	The especially interesting configuration-only or configuration-richer pieces are:
85	
86	- **`root`** — a single discovery root. There is no corresponding multi-root facility; the docs explicitly say an array is unsupported.
87	- **`concurrentTestGlob`** — lets only selected files opt into concurrent tests. CLI `--concurrent` is all-or-nothing.
88	- **Coverage policy** — `coverageThreshold`, `coverageSkipTestFiles`, `coveragePathIgnorePatterns`, `coverageIgnoreSourcemaps`; CLI is much more oriented around “turn coverage on / choose output”.
89	- **Persistent randomization** — `randomize` plus a fixed `seed`.
90	- **JUnit destination** through `[test.reporter]`.
91	
92	Many others simply persist CLI options: preload, path-ignore, retries, reruns, coverage reporters/directories, etc. Current coverage documentation also contains an implementation wrinkle worth knowing: `statements` can be supplied as a threshold key but is not currently enforced, and historically some threshold enforcement has differed depending on reporter/mode. 
93	
94	## What substantial repositories actually do
95	
96	The repositories tell a more useful story than the API checklist.
97	
98	| Repository | Actual practice |
99	|---|---|
100	| **oven-sh/bun itself** | Bun naturally uses `bun:test`, but **does not simply run one giant `bun test` command for its own CI**. Current `scripts/runner.node.mjs` says explicitly that it launches `bun test` processes itself, including separate processes “to catch crashes”; the wrapper has its own shard/max-shard model, CI retries, include/exclude rules, time budgets, JUnit handling, Buildkite integration and PR-file selection.  Its global `test/harness.ts`, loaded throughout the repository, additionally supplies platform/CI predicates, deterministic environment normalization, executable/process helpers and substantial fixture infrastructure.  |
101	| **elysiajs/elysia 1.4.30** | Uses plain **`bun test` for the functionality suite**, but its top-level `test` also runs a TypeScript type-check suite and separate Node CJS/ESM compatibility checks.  It builds small domain helpers itself: HTTP `req`/`post`, multipart upload fixtures and timing helpers live in `test/utils.ts`.  This is a good example of “use Bun for test semantics, own the application fixture layer.” |
102	| **honojs/hono 4.13.8** | Does **not** treat Bun as the universal runner. Its main suite remains `tsc … && vitest --run`; coverage is Vitest. A separate `test:bun` command runs Bun-specific runtime tests with `bun test`, alongside Deno and other runtime lanes.  This is a clear example of running Bun's runner **alongside**, not instead of, another framework. |
103	| **gruntwork-io/runbooks** | Backend unit tests use Bun directly and manually exclude web/docs/e2e/integration paths. Web tests are Vitest/jsdom, Node integration tests use Vitest, and end-to-end tests use Playwright. The repository comment records why its integration lane was separated: at the time, **Bun 1.3.x lacked a Node TLS API it needed**.  That statement is historical, not a claim that every 1.4.x build still lacks the API. |
104	| **mweinbach/agent-coworker** | A 2026 test-suite audit reports a suite on the order of **658 files / 7,500+ tests**. The project had introduced a per-file subprocess runner after encountering Bun crashes and cross-file module-mock leakage; that wrapper was later removed, while the audit still calls out extensive `mock.module`, DOM-global and environment-state usage as sources of suite coupling. This is unusually useful evidence of the boundary between Bun's primitives and the isolation discipline a large suite still needs. ([GitHub](https://github.com/mweinbach/agent-coworker/blob/main/test-suite-audit.md)) |
105	
106	That Bun itself still has a substantial orchestration script is not proof that `--parallel` or `--shard` are inadequate. Much of that infrastructure predates the native 2026 features and also covers Bun-specific requirements such as runtime crash detection, Node compatibility testing and Buildkite topology. But it is strong evidence for a narrower claim: **a serious test suite normally needs more than a runner API**.
107	
108	### A project that backed away from `bun test`
109	
110	**TideWatch** gives a particularly clean stated reason. During its December 2025 migration to Bun for runtime/package-management work, project guidance started saying to run `bun test`, while the project still had a Vitest/jsdom test setup. In **3.5.6 on 15 December 2025**, its changelog records CI failures with `document is not defined`: `bun test` was not consuming the `vite.config.ts` test/jsdom configuration, so the project changed CI and its coverage script back to **Vitest**. ([GitHub](https://github.com/homelabforge/tidewatch/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md))
111	
112	That should not be interpreted as “Bun cannot test DOM code”. Bun can run DOM libraries when you establish the environment explicitly. The practical lesson is that Bun does **not** magically consume another runner's configuration model. Migrating `vitest` → `bun test` means porting setup/environment configuration, not just changing the command.
113	
114	## What projects tend to rely on Bun for, versus build themselves
115	
116	In the repositories above, the stuff people happily take directly from Bun is the **testing language**: `test`/`describe`, `expect`, hooks, spies/mocks, snapshots, filtering, retries, Bun-native TypeScript execution, and—where applicable—coverage. The brand-new `--changed`, `--parallel`, `--shard` and timing machinery is much less entrenched simply because almost all of it is less than five months old.
117	
118	What they still commonly own is a different layer: **test infrastructure**. That means database/schema creation and teardown, unique ports and temp directories, HTTP/request builders, fake services, Docker/service lifecycle, DOM/global installation, deterministic environment normalization, cross-runtime compatibility lanes, type-level tests, crash containment, CI matrix logic, and—in difficult suites—process-level isolation around tests that mutate global module state.
119	
120	That is particularly relevant to Bun's module mocking. `mock.module()` is capable, but module mocks mutate the running module graph. In a default shared-process suite, that makes cleanup and architecture matter more than it does in an automatically per-file-isolated runner. Native `--isolate` is the 2026 answer, but the ecosystem evidence predates and overlaps its stabilization period.
121	
122	## What is still conspicuously absent or limited
123	
124	I would classify the remaining gaps into three groups rather than saying “Bun lacks serious-testing features.”
125	
126	First, there are concrete feature gaps: Jest-style **automatic `__mocks__`**, branch/full statements coverage semantics comparable with Istanbul, collect-coverage-from-unimported-files behavior, and richer mature reporter integrations are not equivalent to Jest/Vitest today. Bun's current docs themselves explicitly temper the old “Jest-compatible” label by saying compatibility is an aim and not everything is implemented. 
127	
128	Second, there is **configuration ecosystem compatibility**. A Vite/Vitest `test.environment = "jsdom"` setting is not Bun configuration; projects such as TideWatch had to discover that explicitly. Likewise, framework-specific plugins and reporter ecosystems do not transfer automatically. ([GitHub](https://github.com/homelabforge/tidewatch/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md))
129	
130	Third, the big-suite scheduling layer is **new rather than obviously deficient**. Native process parallelism, isolation, sharding and Git-aware selection arrived in 1.3.13, and timings in 1.4.0. The latter already has a live report around parallel timing distortion. It is reasonable to use these features, but equally reasonable for a production CI setup to keep its sharding simple and validate the new modes against its own suite before deleting mature custom orchestration. ([Bun](https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.3.13))
131	
132	## Bottom line for a TypeScript project that wants no second test framework
133	
134	On **Bun 1.4.2**, avoiding Jest/Vitest is no longer synonymous with giving up snapshots, module mocks, coverage, watch mode, randomization, CI reports, file isolation or sharding. Bun has all of those categories now.
135	
136	The trade is elsewhere: **you are choosing Bun's testing primitives plus your own project-specific harness**, rather than buying into the broader Jest/Vitest ecosystem. For a server/library TypeScript project, that can be a perfectly coherent arrangement. The repository evidence suggests keeping expectations realistic: use Bun for assertions, hooks, mocks, snapshots and execution; expect to own service/database fixtures, environment setup, resource allocation and cross-runtime checks; and treat the **1.3.13–1.4 large-suite features as recent infrastructure worth validating**, not as long-settled behavior.
137	
138	The most misleading description in either direction would therefore be “Bun test is just a lightweight runner” or “Bun test is now a drop-in Jest/Vitest replacement.” In late 2026 it is closer to **a substantial native test framework with a young orchestration layer and a deliberately smaller ecosystem around it**.
139	
```

````text
export default crons;
```

- You can register Convex functions within `crons.ts` just like any other file.
- If a cron calls an internal function, always import the `internal` object from '\_generated/api', even if the internal function is registered in the same file.

## Testing guidelines

- Use `convex-test` with `vitest` and `@edge-runtime/vm` to test Convex functions. Always install the latest versions of these packages. Configure vitest with `environment: "edge-runtime"` in `vitest.config.ts`.

Test files go inside the `convex/` directory. You must pass a module map from `import.meta.glob` to `convexTest`:

```typescript
/// <reference types="vite/client" />
import { convexTest } from "convex-test";
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { api } from "./_generated/api";
import schema from "./schema";

const modules = import.meta.glob("./**/*.ts");

test("some behavior", async () => {
  const t = convexTest(schema, modules);
  await t.mutation(api.messages.send, { body: "Hi!", author: "Sarah" });
  const messages = await t.query(api.messages.list);
  expect(messages).toMatchObject([{ body: "Hi!", author: "Sarah" }]);
});
```

The `modules` argument is required so convex-test can discover and load function files. The `/// <reference types="vite/client" />` directive is needed for TypeScript to recognize `import.meta.glob`.

- Only add the `/// <reference types="vite/client" />` directive at the top of test files that call `import.meta.glob`; do NOT add it to non-test files.
- Do NOT add a `compilerOptions.types` allowlist to `tsconfig.json` for type packages you have not installed (e.g. `"node"` without `@types/node`, or `"vite/client"` without vite). Any unresolved entry in `types` fails typechecking with TS2688. Leave `types` unset unless a package genuinely requires it and is installed.

## File storage guidelines

- The `ctx.storage.getUrl()` method returns a signed URL for a given file. It returns `null` if the file doesn't exist.
- Do NOT use the deprecated `ctx.storage.getMetadata` call for loading a file's metadata.

Instead, query the `_storage` system table. For example, you can use `ctx.db.system.get` to get an `Id<"_storage">`.
````
