### Tink: the clearest example of a staged distributed rotation

Tink is unusually explicit about the part that many “previous keys” examples omit. The project says there is almost never an atomic switch across all machines and ciphertexts. Its recommended lifecycle is therefore: add the new key as enabled but **not primary**, roll that keyset everywhere, and only when every binary knows the key promote it to primary. ([Google for Developers](https://developers.google.com/tink/design/keysets?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That point explains why Tink deprecated APIs such as `rotate-keyset` that added and immediately promoted a key. The earlier convenience operation was precisely wrong for a rolling deployment: once one new instance encrypts with K2, an old instance carrying only K1 cannot decrypt that write. ([GitHub](https://github.com/tink-crypto/tink/blob/master/java_src/src/main/java/com/google/crypto/tink/integration/android/AndroidKeysetManager.java?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The key-ID prefix also turns retirement into a measurable database migration when Tink prefixes are used. It is important, though, that Tink explicitly says the prefix is unauthenticated. A program must not treat “ID 1234” as authorization to use some key without subsequently authenticating the AEAD ciphertext. ([Google for Developers](https://developers.google.com/tink/wire-format?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### AWS Encryption SDK: rotation by wrapping data keys rather than fields directly

This is structurally different from replacing an AES-GCM field key. Each message gets a unique data key; the configured Raw AES key protects that data key. The ciphertext message therefore contains the encrypted field plus one or more **encrypted data keys**. The AWS Encryption SDK itself does not require an AWS account, and Raw AES keyrings exist specifically for caller-supplied AES wrapping keys, although AWS recommends stronger durable protection for those wrapping keys than an ordinary process secret when available. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/encryption-sdk/latest/developer-guide/introduction.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

There are two interesting overlap strategies. A service can encrypt new values only with K2 while using a decrypt-only multi-keyring containing K2 and K1. That resembles Rails/Tink. Alternatively it can encrypt each data key under both K2 and K1; then either wrapping key can decrypt that message. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/encryption-sdk/latest/developer-guide/faq.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) The latter reduces availability coupling but also means that, during the overlap, possession of the old key still opens newly created data. That distinction matters especially when rotation is responding to suspected compromise rather than routine hygiene.

AWS's own migration history is a warning against treating the ciphertext format as incidental. The move to key commitment required staged compatibility policies; turning on new-format encryption before all readers understood it could make rollback impossible without rewriting ciphertexts. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/encryption-sdk/latest/developer-guide/migration-guide.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Rails: close to the environment-variable model, with an optional escape from trial decryption

Rails' standard rotation mechanism is perhaps the most direct analogue to “an env var becomes a list of env vars.” A key provider accepts several keys; current Rails uses the **last** one for new encryption and can try all of them for decryption. ([Ruby on Rails Guides](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_encryption.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

There is an interesting documentation discrepancy. The Rails 7.1.5.2 API prose said `encryption_key` returned the **first** key, while the source code directly underneath used `@keys.last`. Current Rails 8.1 API documentation and the guide say **last**, agreeing with the implementation. ([Ruby on Rails API](https://api.rubyonrails.org/v7.1.5.2/classes/ActiveRecord/Encryption/KeyProvider.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

`store_key_references` converts the scheme from “try all keys” into “select by header.” Rails' key reference is quite short: `Key#id` is only four hex characters of SHA-1 of the secret. ([Ruby on Rails API](https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/Encryption/Key.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) That is an addressing hint rather than a cryptographic identity, much like Tink's prefix. Authentication still comes from AES-GCM.

Rails also demonstrates that key rotation is not the only compatibility axis. Its 7.0→7.1 digest changes produced reports where an upgraded application could read some old data but rollback could no longer read ciphertext newly created by the upgraded version. Rails added compatibility settings specifically around those digest changes. ([GitHub](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/guides/source/upgrading_ruby_on_rails.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Django: useful rotation semantics, but not the same encryption problem

Django's built-in mechanism is worth studying mainly because it is a clean example of **fallback validation without ciphertext key IDs**. The new `SECRET_KEY` is used to create new signatures; `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` permits old signatures, sessions and password-reset tokens to remain valid temporarily. Django explicitly warns that fallback verification costs increase with the number of keys. ([Django Project](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/ref/settings/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Its most instructive criticism is the rolling-deployment ticket. A user pointed out that changing the primary secret and fallbacks in one deployment can produce:

old instance → signs K1  
new instance → signs K2  
old instance → cannot validate K2.

The proposed correction was two phases: distribute knowledge of K2 everywhere while still signing K1, then switch the primary. Django closed the ticket as invalid because its documentation does not generally try to cover distributed deployment considerations; the response did not claim that mixed fleets somehow avoid the described problem. ([Django](https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/35400)) Tink, by contrast, has made essentially that two-phase rule part of its formal rotation documentation.

For actual encrypted Django model fields, a third-party package such as `django-fernet-encrypted-fields` applies a similar previous-key idea and explicitly says existing records can be re-encrypted by loading and saving them. ([GitHub](https://github.com/jazzband/django-fernet-encrypted-fields?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Vault Transit: the strongest built-in migration lifecycle

Vault makes the ciphertext's key version overt: `vault:v17:...`. The service owns the entire historical keyring, so callers never send the raw AES key alongside their process configuration. A rotation only changes which version new encrypt operations use; all allowed historical versions remain readable. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/tutorials/encryption-as-a-service/eaas-transit?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

`rewrap` is the notable feature. An application or batch worker can submit an old ciphertext and receive one under the latest key without ever receiving the plaintext. HashiCorp explicitly suggests that this can happen slowly in a background process to control database load. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/tutorials/encryption-as-a-service/eaas-transit-rewrap?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

It also separates **“stop ordinary decryption”** from **“destroy the key.”** Raising `min_decryption_version` archives older versions outside the working set and rejects their ciphertexts, but administrators can lower that threshold again if necessary. That is a safer retirement test than immediately deleting K1. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/transit?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The downside of putting all versions into a managed key object is that key history itself becomes state that has to scale. Vault has both an old real-world performance report involving extremely frequent rotations and current documentation warning that the archived version structure can grow beyond some storage backends' limits. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/issues/925?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### libsodium: the primitives deliberately leave this protocol to you

A libsodium construction often looks deceptively simple because the AEAD API itself has no concept of K1 versus K2. The library expects the protocol/application to store what it requires alongside the ciphertext, particularly the nonce. ([GitHub](https://github.com/jedisct1/libsodium-doc/blob/master/quickstart/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) A robust application may therefore invent a record format with a format version and key identifier, but that format is the application's protocol, not “the libsodium format.”

`crypto_secretstream`'s references to automatic key rotation can be misleading in this context. Its rekeying changes the running state of **one ordered encrypted stream**; it does not mean that calling libsodium somehow manages historical database master keys. ([GitHub](https://github.com/jedisct1/libsodium-doc/blob/master/secret-key_cryptography/secretstream.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This is also where nonce management and master-key rotation can become conflated. Sodium warns that constructions with short nonces require more application-level coordination and rotation and describes this as tricky; it generally encourages longer-nonce constructions where possible. ([GitHub](https://github.com/jedisct1/libsodium-doc/blob/master/secret-key_cryptography/encrypted-messages.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### MultiFernet and Laravel: the simple fallback-list pattern

Both expose the basic pattern many applications independently invent: a distinguished current key plus an ordered sequence of previous keys, with trial authentication/decryption.

`MultiFernet` adds one particularly useful operation: `rotate(token)`, which returns a token under the current key while retaining the original timestamp. But it has no idea which tokens exist in a database, so scheduling and completeness remain an application concern. ([Cryptography](https://cryptography.io/en/48.0.1/fernet/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Laravel 11 made essentially the same policy first-class in environment configuration: `APP_KEY` plus `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS`. New data uses `APP_KEY`; old keys are attempted only during decryption. ([Laravel](https://laravel.com/framework/docs/12.x/encryption?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This is operationally simple, but the absence of a key identifier is exactly why the operator cannot distinguish “old-key ciphertext remains” from “this key is no longer needed” without TTL knowledge, a full migration, or separate metadata.

### ASP.NET Core: treating the key ring itself as durable infrastructure

ASP.NET Core's Data Protection system represents the other extreme from an environment-variable list. Every ciphertext says exactly which GUID-labelled key produced it, while the shared repository stores key lifecycle metadata. It even creates replacement keys with a default **two-day activation delay** so other machines get time to observe the new key before it starts encrypting. ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/data-protection/implementation/key-management?view=aspnetcore-10.0&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Microsoft's advice about deletion is revealing: it generally says don't. Expired keys stop being used for new protection but remain available for old data; removing them makes matching payloads permanently inaccessible. ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/ga-ie/aspnet/core/security/data-protection/configuration/default-settings?view=aspnetcore-8.0&utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This is appropriate for a subsystem that often has no knowledge of whether its caller used `Protect` for a 20-minute cookie or a secret intended to live for ten years.
```

# OpenAPI Contract Practices

Source: https://chatgpt.com/share/6aaa268b-5c0c-83eb-a140-7e7733009709

---

**User**

Teams sometimes commit a trimmed copy of a third-party API's OpenAPI description into their repository and check two things against it: the requests their own code sends, and the replies their in-repo fake of that vendor returns. Survey how this is actually done in the wild. Where does the pinned file live relative to tests and to the generator that produces it; how is drift from the vendor detected and reviewed; what is this practice called and how does it relate to consumer-driven contract testing tools like Pact, Prism, Schemathesis and Microcks; and — most importantly — how do teams record a justified difference between what a vendor's description claims and what the vendor's service actually does, including whether a recorded exception that is no longer needed is treated as a failure. Give concrete public examples with sources, and report where the practice is considered a bad idea.

---

**ChatGPT**

I’ll look for public repos that pin or generate a reduced OpenAPI schema, then trace how they validate outbound requests, fake responses, drift, and exception lifecycle. I’ll also separate this from broader “contract testing” terminology so the comparison to Pact/Prism/Schemathesis/Microcks stays precise.

---

**ChatGPT**

A useful distinction is emerging: there are really two layers. The vendored/trimmed OpenAPI file is usually treated as a **test fixture or generated artifact**, while disagreements with upstream are better kept as a **patch/overlay/waiver layer** rather than silently editing the fixture; that separation is what makes vendor drift reviewable.

---

**ChatGPT**

I found one unusually complete public example worth drilling into rather than just citing its README: an unofficial dev.to client keeps the upstream spec, a machine-readable overlay of corrections, recorded fixtures, and CI drift checks separately. I’m checking whether its exception entries are merely documented or actively proved/removable in CI.

---

**ChatGPT**

Yes. This is a recognizable practice in public repositories, but it does **not** have one universally agreed name. The most accurate description is usually **vendored/pinned OpenAPI + schema-based contract/conformance tests**. When the spec is reduced to the operations a client uses, “curated” or “trimmed OpenAPI” also appears. It is importantly different from Pact-style **consumer-driven contract testing**.

The strongest pattern I found is:

> **verbatim upstream snapshot → deterministic filter/overlay → composed test contract → client/fake tests**, with a separate job that checks both **upstream-description drift** and, where feasible, **live-service drift**.

The important refinement is that a vendor discrepancy should normally be represented as a *small, reviewable, falsifiable exception* layered over the upstream snapshot—not baked invisibly into a forked copy.

## What public repositories actually do

| Example | Where the spec lives | Generator / transformation | Tests and drift |
|---|---|---|---|
| **svyatov/devto-client** (third-party dev.to/Forem client) | `spec/api_v1.json` is the pinned upstream; `spec/overlay.json` holds corrections; `spec/composed.json` is generated | `scripts/compose-spec.ts`, then `openapi-typescript` | Recorded live replies are in `tests/fixtures/recorded`; tests live in `tests/`. A daily job fetches Forem's current spec, structurally diffs it against the pin, and reports stale recordings; a separate manual “reality check” re-records dev.to replies and runs them against the composed spec. ([GitHub](https://github.com/svyatov/devto-client?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **openintegrations/openSDKs / Slack** | Both `slack.orig.oas.json` and the derived `slack.oas.json` sit at the SDK package root | `src/slack.oas.ts` imports the original and post-processes it; generated types are next to the spec | The `download` command is the networked acquisition step; generation is intentionally offline. The transform removes Slack's per-operation `token` parameter and derives scope metadata. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openintegrations/openSDKs?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **StackQL OpenAI provider** | Vendor spec is pinned by commit and hash in `provider-dev/config/spec_pin.json`; filtered artifacts remain under `provider-dev/` | `provider-dev/scripts/clean_specs.mjs`, normalization, then provider generation | `npm run fetch-spec -- --check` is a non-writing drift check; refreshes are explicitly reviewed diffs. Exclusions are deterministic and reason-coded in code plus `filter_report.csv`. It also has mock integration tests and live smoke tests. ([GitHub](https://github.com/stackql-registry/stackql-provider-openai/blob/main/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **Tectalic public OpenAI PHP client** | A copy lives directly under `tests/openapi.yaml` | No elaborate transform layer in the documented test setup | CI starts `prism mock tests/openapi.yaml`, then runs the integration tests against the generated fake rather than OpenAI. This is the “test fixture colocated with tests” variant. ([GitHub](https://github.com/tectalichq/public-openai-client-php/blob/main/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |

The layouts cluster into two styles. In SDK-generator repositories the OpenAPI tends to live with the **generation inputs** (`spec/`, `api_reference/`, `provider-dev/`, or package root), with tests referring into that area. In repositories where the spec exists only to drive an integration fake, putting it under `tests/` is common. The former scales better once you need provenance, filtering and vendor-drift review.

A useful producer-side analogue is OpenAI's own Python/CLI repositories: the transformed OpenAPI is under `api_reference/`, while test scripts live separately. The Python mock launcher even compares the checked-in transformed spec's hash with generation metadata and refuses to start if they disagree. ([GitHub](https://github.com/openai/openai-python/blob/main/scripts/mock))

## Drift: there are actually three kinds

A mature setup distinguishes **upstream-description drift**, **derived-artifact drift**, and **service-reality drift**.

For upstream-description drift, the robust pattern is to pin a commit/hash, periodically fetch the current vendor document, regenerate/filter deterministically, and expose the resulting diff for review rather than silently taking the update. StackQL states this explicitly: refreshes are “reviewed diffs, never silent regenerations.” ([GitHub](https://github.com/stackql-registry/stackql-provider-openai/blob/main/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) The dev.to client runs its upstream check daily and creates or refreshes one issue containing the structural changes and stale-fixture “shot list”; a clean run closes it. 

Derived-artifact drift is simpler: rerun the generator in CI and require `git diff --exit-code`, or record a hash tying generated output to its input. The dev.to client has a `check:drift` script that regenerates signatures/schemas/routing and fails on a Git diff. 

Service-reality drift is the one a spec-only job cannot see. The dev.to project explicitly calls this out: the spec can remain unchanged while the server behavior changes, so its manual reality job re-records real dev.to responses into an ephemeral `tests/fixtures/recorded` tree and reruns the conformance tests. A failure raises a “Server reality drift detected” issue.  That extra independent oracle is important; without it, the client and fake can both agree with the same wrong document.

## Recording “the vendor's spec is wrong”

This is where the dev.to repository is unusually instructive. Its `spec/overlay.json` entries aren't simply arbitrary patched schema fragments. An entry contains:

```json
{
  "target": "/some/json/pointer",
  "expect": { "...the upstream shape this patch assumes..." },
  "reason": "why the upstream description is wrong",
  "patch": { "...the observed/corrected shape..." },
  "provenance": {
    "instrument": "devto-fixture | local-forem | forem-source | spec-structure",
    "forem": "optional pinned commit",
    "corroborated": true
  }
}
```

Those semantics are enforced in the composer: `expect` is asserted against the unmodified upstream node before applying the patch; `null` means “this node must currently be absent.” A changed or dangling upstream target therefore fails composition instead of allowing the patch to slide onto some new meaning. Each correction also carries a non-empty reason and provenance identifying whether the evidence came from an actual dev.to recording, a pinned local Forem, source code, or inspection of the spec itself. 

That is very close to what I would call a **falsifiable contract waiver** rather than a normal patch.

Most importantly, that repository also implements the stale-exception check you asked about. During composition, if the upstream node already equals the patch value, the entry is classified as `deletable`; the real-spec test asserts that the current overlay contains **no deletable entries**. In other words, “upstream now agrees with our correction but we forgot to remove the correction” makes the test suite fail. 

There are two distinct stale cases worth handling:

1. **The upstream document changed under the waiver.** The `expect` precondition should fail. A human decides whether the upstream fix supersedes the waiver, conflicts with it, or merely rearranged the schema.
````

## Tool · 2026-09-16T13:02:41.327Z

**Tool result: toolu_01XQmURcbbgLmcjYevRzqHpY**

````text
1. **The upstream document changed under the waiver.** The `expect` precondition should fail. A human decides whether the upstream fix supersedes the waiver, conflicts with it, or merely rearranged the schema.
2. **The vendor has incorporated exactly your correction.** Applying your patch is now a no-op. Treat that as a stale waiver and fail CI with “remove this exception.”

The OpenAPI ecosystem now has a standardized mechanism for the transformation half of this design: **OpenAPI Overlay 1.0** defines a separate JSON/YAML document containing repeatable `update`/`remove` actions applied to a base OpenAPI description. ([OpenAPI Initiative Publications](https://spec.openapis.org/overlay/v1.0.0.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) The standard itself doesn't provide the dev.to project's `expect`, evidence, or stale-waiver semantics, so a team wanting those properties needs conventions/extensions or a wrapper around the overlay processor.

Keeping the modification separate is increasingly explicit guidance for third-party specs. Aklivity, for example, says directly that hand-patching a vendored/third-party document means forking something that is supposed to remain synchronized, requiring every upstream update to be manually reapplied; it uses an overlay instead. ([Aklivity Docs](https://docs.aklivity.io/latest/ai-gateway/mcp-gateway/openapi-overlay/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

## Should an exception that stops being necessary fail?

For a **deterministic targeted waiver, yes**. There is good precedent beyond OpenAPI. The Model Context Protocol conformance suite has an expected-failures YAML baseline where all four states are explicit: expected failure continues to fail → success; new failure → failure; normal pass → success; and, importantly, **an expected failure that starts passing → failure, because the baseline is stale and must be removed**. ([GitHub](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/conformance?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This is essentially `xfail(strict=true)` semantics.

Schemathesis deliberately makes a finer distinction. It supports a committed baseline of known API failures, and `--baseline-prune` removes an entry only when its operation was actually exercised and the failure failed to reproduce. An *unobserved* entry is not automatically declared stale because property-based input generation is randomized—the run may simply not have generated the witness again. ([Schemathesis](https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/guides/baseline/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That gives a useful rule: **fail on stale exceptions only when you have deterministically retested the exact condition the exception covers**. For a Schemathesis fuzz finding, “not seen today” isn't proof. For a specific `/users/{id}` field discrepancy with a saved response/reproduction case, it can be.

## Relation to Pact, Prism, Schemathesis and Microcks

These tools occupy overlapping but different positions.

**Pact** is the odd one out conceptually. Pact calls itself code-first, consumer-driven contract testing: executing the consumer tests creates concrete request/response interactions, and the provider verifies those interactions. It explicitly contrasts Pact contracts with a static OAS document. Pact's FAQ goes as far as saying that generating a Pact contract from Swagger/OpenAPI defeats the point and is like “marking your own exam.” ([Pact Docs](https://docs.pact.io/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) So a pinned vendor OpenAPI checked against your client is **not Pact-style CDC**. In Pact's vocabulary, checking a provider against OpenAPI is closer to *provider contract testing*; Pact notes that this alone does not prove consumers are using the provider correctly. ([Pact Docs](https://docs.pact.io/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Prism** is almost exactly the mechanical tool for the OpenAPI approach. Its mock mode turns the description into a fake server; its validation proxy examines both requests going to an implementation and responses coming back, reporting discrepancies with the same OpenAPI document. It can be inserted into an existing E2E suite with `--errors` so mismatches fail tests. ([GitHub](https://github.com/stoplightio/prism/blob/main/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This is therefore **spec-driven contract/conformance testing**, not consumer-driven contracts.

**Schemathesis** treats OpenAPI principally as a generator and oracle for testing an actual implementation. It creates valid/invalid/property-based requests and checks response status codes, response schemas, headers and server errors. ([Schemathesis](https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/checks/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) You can also graft response validation onto an existing test suite. ([Schemathesis](https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/en/stable/guides/schema-conformance/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) It is especially useful for your “is the vendor really behaving like this description?” leg.

**Microcks** combines the roles more explicitly: it turns OpenAPI examples into mocks *and* uses the contract/examples to test an implementation for conformance. Its documentation describes the latter explicitly as contract/conformance testing. ([Microcks](https://microcks.io/documentation/references/artifacts/openapi-conventions/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Thus Microcks is probably the closest off-the-shelf analogue to maintaining one artifact for both a development fake and provider-conformance tests.

## Where the approach becomes a bad idea

The core problem is **correlated oracles**. If the same wrong OpenAPI description generates the fake *and* validates your consumer, your client can pass perfectly against the fake while failing against the real vendor. Pact's documentation makes essentially this criticism of static OpenAPI comparison: it gives a weaker guarantee because it depends on the actual provider not drifting from the published description. ([Pact Docs](https://docs.pact.io/blog/2024/09/30/pact-open-source-update-sept-2024?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Pact's FAQ is even more pointed about using a vendor schema as the origin of a supposedly consumer-driven contract: deriving the contract from Swagger does not demonstrate that the actual consumer and actual provider are compatible. ([Pact Docs](https://docs.pact.io/faq?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

There are several concrete versions of the same trap:

- **Hand-editing the vendored spec.** You lose the distinction between vendor changes and local corrections and eventually cannot tell whether a diff is upstream drift or your own fork. OpenAPI Overlay exists specifically to keep such transformations separate, and third-party tooling explicitly recommends that separation. ([OpenAPI Initiative Publications](https://spec.openapis.org/overlay/v1.0.0.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
- **Trimming without a reproducible filter.** A hand-cut 500-line spec can quietly omit a newly important status/field forever. StackQL's answer is deterministic, reason-coded filtering rather than an opaque edited subset. ([GitHub](https://github.com/stackql-registry/stackql-provider-openai/blob/main/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
- **Testing only against the generated fake.** Tectalic's Prism setup is fast and useful, but on its own says nothing about whether today's OpenAI service still agrees with `tests/openapi.yaml`; the remedy is an independent live/replay conformance leg. ([GitHub](https://github.com/tectalichq/public-openai-client-php/blob/main/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
- **Putting a validation proxy in production's critical path.** Prism itself suggests using the proxy in development/staging/pre-production and says it is probably best kept out of production. ([GitHub](https://github.com/stoplightio/prism/blob/master/docs/guides/03-validation-proxy.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
- **Accepting “known violations” forever.** Once a waiver becomes an unconditional ignore or broad validator disable, the test has ceased to describe a contract. Schemathesis' baseline metadata/expiry/pruning and the dev.to `expect`+no-op tests are much healthier models. ([Schemathesis](https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/guides/baseline/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So I would treat the architecture as sound when the local file is a **reproducibly derived, reviewable test contract with an independent reality check**. I would treat “download vendor Swagger once, edit it until the fake works, and make all integration tests point at that fake” as an anti-pattern.

### A useful canonical form

If designing this today, I'd make the repository boundary explicit:

```text
contracts/vendor-x/
    upstream.openapi.yaml        # verbatim, pinned
    selection.yaml               # operations/components we consume
    reality.overlay.yaml         # factual vendor-description corrections
    tooling.overlay.yaml         # generator/ergonomic corrections
    pin.json                     # upstream commit/hash/date
    composed.openapi.yaml        # generated; optionally committed

scripts/
    fetch-vendor-x
    compose-vendor-x
    check-vendor-x-drift

tests/
    contract/                    # assert actual client requests
    fake/                        # assert fake responses
    fixtures/vendor-x-live/      # independent observations/repros
```

For a **reality** exception I would require an ID, target, old-value precondition, replacement, reason, evidence/reproducer, observation date/vendor revision, and upstream issue if one exists. CI should prove that every exception still changes something; a deterministic exception that has become unnecessary should be a red build saying **“waiver is stale; delete it.”** Keep purely ergonomic/tooling overlays in a different category, because those may intentionally remain even after the vendor's description is factually correct.

That separation—**upstream truth claim, consumer subset, reality corrections, tooling transforms, and independent observations**—is the main difference between this being a useful lightweight contract system and merely testing your code against a sophisticated mock of your own assumptions.
````

**ChatGPT**

A useful dividing line is emerging: some systems model the “server” as an aggregate of independently addressable resources; others model only the VM lifecycle and treat networking/guest access as attributes or side channels. That distinction strongly affects whether a partial failure is representable at all, not just how it is displayed.

---

**ChatGPT**

The main split is not really “panel vs IaC”; it is **whether the product treats the provisioned server as one resource or as a composition of independently observable resources**. That decision determines whether “VM healthy, address broken, management channel broken” can be represented faithfully.

| System | State model when one component fails | IP-changing repair | If customer breaks management access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OpenStack Nova + Neutron** | Strongly decomposed. Nova server status is derived from the VM’s `vm_state` and `task_state`; Neutron ports separately have `ACTIVE/DOWN/BUILD/ERROR`, and floating IPs have `ACTIVE/DOWN/ERROR`. A server can therefore remain a valid Nova object while its networking has an independent failure state. ([OpenStack Docs](https://docs.openstack.org/api-guide/compute/server_concepts.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | A floating IP is its own resource, associated with a port. Repair can move/reassociate that address rather than replace the customer-visible IP; allocating a new floating IP is a distinct operation. ([OpenStack Docs](https://docs.openstack.org/api-ref/network/v2/index.html?expanded=list-ike-policies-detail&utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Nova's basic lifecycle is hypervisor/control-plane based rather than dependent on SSH into the guest. Guest misconfiguration therefore does not inherently make the Nova server disappear or change its VM state; rescue/rebuild actions remain part of the compute lifecycle. ([OpenStack Docs](https://docs.openstack.org/nova/pike/reference/vm-states.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **AWS EC2 + ENI/EIP + Systems Manager** | Rich but somewhat layered. EC2 exposes separate system, instance, attached-EBS and, since August 2026, optional application checks; the console also computes an overall `OK`/`impaired` result. SSM management connectivity is separately `Online`/`ConnectionLost`; ENIs separately have attachment state, although `in-use` is not a health check. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/monitoring-system-instance-status-check.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | A stop/start normally gives an instance a **new ordinary public IPv4 address**, while its primary private IPv4 remains with the ENI. An Elastic IP is the explicit stable-identity object: it stays allocated and can be disassociated and reassociated to another resource. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/Stop_Start.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Breaking the SSM agent, its IAM permissions, or connectivity to SSM produces `ConnectionLost` without meaning the EC2 VM itself has stopped. AWS also provides a serial console that is independent of the VPC, security groups and the guest's normal network path. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/fleet-manager-troubleshooting-managed-nodes.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **DigitalOcean Droplets** | Much flatter at the Droplet level. The documented Droplet status is only `new`, `active`, `off`, or `archive`; IP addresses are returned as properties rather than carrying a parallel health state. Thus `active` is basically lifecycle/power state, not a claim that SSH or every network path works. ([DigitalOcean](https://docs.digitalocean.com/reference/doctl/reference/compute/droplet/get/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Reserved IPs are separate movable objects and can be reassigned between Droplets. Importantly, assigning one does **not** replace the Droplet's original public address; it adds a stable service identity on top. ([DigitalOcean](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/networking/reserved-ips/how-to/modify/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | DigitalOcean explicitly documents the case where guest network configuration or `sshd` is broken. The Droplet is recovered through a VNC-style Recovery Console that works independently of guest networking. ([DigitalOcean](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/how-to/recovery/recovery-console/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **Ploi** | Deliberately collapsed around “can Ploi manage this server?”. Its server API has one status field including `active` and `unreachable`, as well as provisioning states such as `building-failed`. It does not expose “VM healthy but Ploi SSH path broken” as two simultaneous health dimensions; the management failure becomes the server's top-level `unreachable` state. ([Ploi](https://developers.ploi.io/getting-started/resource-statuses?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | The panel stores an IP as part of the managed-server record and lets it be updated. The API's server update accepts a new `ip` and SSH port, after which connectivity can be tested. ([Ploi](https://developers.ploi.io/servers/update-server?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | This is a particularly clear example of customer-caused management-channel failure: Ploi says it connects as root over SSH and that disabling `PermitRootLogin` cuts off Ploi and makes the server unmanageable from the panel. Its own firewall UI tries to prevent self-lockout by retaining Ploi's management IPs. ([Ploi](https://ploi.io/documentation/ssh/can-i-safely-change-permitrootlogin-in-the-ssh-config-file?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **RunCloud** | The managed-server abstraction depends heavily on its own agent and connectivity rather than exposing cloud-provider VM/network subresources. Its required `runcloud-agent` is the dashboard-to-server management mechanism, while firewall rules and IP reachability can independently prevent functions from working. ([RunCloud Website](https://runcloud.io/docs/runcloud-packages?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | RunCloud has unusually explicit documentation for identifier-changing repair: if the VPS provider changes the public IP, RunCloud says it can no longer connect until the user changes the IP in RunCloud. The panel then requires a verification script to be run as root on the server; updating the RunCloud record does not itself alter the VPS. ([RunCloud Website](https://runcloud.io/docs/how-do-i-change-a-servers-ip-address?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | A customer can break the channel with firewall rules or agent problems. RunCloud documents required management IPs/port 34210 and separately warns when an agent is outdated; the recovery path is therefore generally “restore connectivity/agent, then reconnect”, rather than changing the underlying VM state. ([RunCloud Website](https://runcloud.io/docs/whitelist-runcloud-ip-addresses?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **Juju** | Probably the cleanest hybrid model. A unit has **two simultaneous statuses**, workload and agent, rendered as combinations such as `active/idle` or `unknown/lost`. Above that, application status can collapse unit workload statuses into a single higher-level status; for example, one blocked workload can make the application `blocked`. ([Ubuntu Documentation](https://documentation.ubuntu.com/juju/3.6/reference/status/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Addresses are exposed on machines/units but are not the unit's identity; the controller's model identity survives infrastructural details changing. | If its management agent stops communicating with the controller, the agent dimension becomes `lost`. That does not require claiming the workload itself is dead. This is exactly the distinction many server panels lack. ([Ubuntu Documentation](https://documentation.ubuntu.com/juju/3.6/reference/status/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **Terraform** | Not a runtime-health system. It tracks individual declared resources in a dependency graph. It explicitly says that if software inside a VM fails while the VM remains running, Terraform normally cannot detect the degradation. A partial creation/provisioner failure can instead mark that particular resource `tainted`, meaning “exists but may be incomplete; replace next apply”. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/state/taint?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Identity change depends entirely on resource decomposition. If the address is a separate EIP/FIP resource, replacement of the VM can preserve it and reconnect dependencies. If the public IP is merely a computed VM attribute, replacement may produce a different value. Terraform's normal replacement ordering is delete-then-create unless `create_before_destroy` is enabled. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/docs/planning-behaviors.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | With an SSH `remote-exec` creation provisioner, failure of that connection can taint the enclosing resource. But if SSH is broken months later, Terraform does not continuously notice it unless some external mechanism turns that condition into configuration/state drift. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/block/resource?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **Pulumi** | Also resource-graph based rather than a live health monitor. State is per custom resource, dependencies are explicit, and `refresh` reconciles stored state with provider state. ([pulumi](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Its default is the opposite of Terraform's: when replacement is required, Pulumi normally creates the replacement first and deletes the old one afterward. Outputs from the replacement then flow through dependent resources. Hard-coded physical names can force delete-before-replace because both copies cannot coexist. ([pulumi](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/deletebeforereplace/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Guest-management failure only has first-class meaning if modeled as another resource or detected by a provider/component; Pulumi itself is not continuously testing SSH reachability. |

### What the different models mean in practice

**OpenStack is the clearest “resource truth first” design.** A Nova server's `ACTIVE` status says something narrowly about the compute object; it does not implicitly certify the Neutron port or floating IP. Neutron independently records those resources and their statuses. This avoids a common ambiguity in VPS panels where “Running” can mean anything from “hypervisor process exists” to “we can SSH to it”. OpenStack even exposes multiple compute dimensions internally—stable VM state, current task and power state—rather than forcing one state machine to carry every meaning. ([OpenStack Docs](https://docs.openstack.org/api-ref/compute/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**AWS adds summary health without throwing away the dimensions underneath it.** A customer can see that the overall instance is `impaired`, but can still distinguish an AWS-host/system failure from an instance/guest failure, EBS I/O impairment, application failure or SSM management disconnection. The repair ownership follows that decomposition: AWS says a failed system check often points at underlying infrastructure, whereas an instance-status failure commonly needs customer action. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/monitoring-system-instance-status-check.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is materially different from **Ploi's `unreachable` model**. Ploi's state is answering a very useful but different question: “Can this panel still administer the box?” If the customer disables root SSH, blocks Ploi's IPs or breaks `sshd`, the VPS may be running applications perfectly well while the panel legitimately marks the server `unreachable`. The single status is therefore primarily **control-channel health**, not resource health. ([Ploi](https://developers.ploi.io/getting-started/resource-statuses?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Juju shows a useful middle ground:** retain the independent facts, then optionally calculate a summary. `active/lost`-style combinations let an operator distinguish a live workload from a failed management agent, while the application-level status gives humans a simpler “blocked” signal where appropriate. ([Ubuntu Documentation](https://documentation.ubuntu.com/juju/3.6/reference/status/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This resembles the broader Kubernetes Conditions design: objects may report multiple independently typed conditions, while summary conditions exist to save consumers from reimplementing aggregation logic; the Kubernetes design guidance explicitly says those summary conditions should *complement*, rather than replace, detailed status. ([GitHub](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/.agents/skills/k8s-api-conventions/references/api-conventions.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Repairs that change an IP are especially revealing

There are two very different philosophies.

In **resource-oriented clouds**, the system tries to make the customer's durable network identity a separate object. OpenStack floating IPs, AWS Elastic IPs and DigitalOcean Reserved IPs can survive movement between compute instances. A “replace bad VM” repair can therefore preserve the public endpoint. ([OpenStack Docs](https://docs.openstack.org/api-ref/network/v2/index.html?expanded=list-ike-policies-detail&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Where the ordinary VM address *is* the identifier, the system has to acknowledge that repair changes identity. AWS explicitly documents that stop/start normally gives a new ephemeral public IPv4. RunCloud documents the downstream consequence unusually clearly: after a provider-side IP change, its own stored identifier is stale, management stops working, and the new IP must be explicitly verified before the panel starts using it. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/Stop_Start.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

For a customer-facing panel, silently replacing an IP is therefore usually the most dangerous presentation. The observable operation is really:

`old unit: degraded → replacement resource created → customer-visible endpoint changes or is rebound → management channel re-established`

rather than simply:

`degraded → healthy`.

Terraform and Pulumi make this especially obvious because replacement is an explicit graph operation, and dependencies that consume the changed output must be reconciled. Terraform's internal design even has a notion of the old resource being “deposed” during create-before-destroy replacement; Pulumi similarly represents replacement as distinct create-replacement/delete-replaced operations. ([GitHub](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/docs/planning-behaviors.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### The management-access failure deserves its own state

The documentation across these products suggests three distinct cases that panels often incorrectly collapse:

1. **Provider/control-plane access intact, customer network access broken.** DigitalOcean can still offer its out-of-band Recovery Console; AWS can offer its serial console. The VM may remain fully controllable at the hypervisor level. ([DigitalOcean](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/how-to/recovery/recovery-console/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
2. **Guest management agent broken, VM/network otherwise healthy.** AWS SSM becomes `ConnectionLost`; Juju's agent becomes `lost`. Those systems preserve the fact that this is a management-channel failure rather than asserting that compute itself is dead. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/ssm/describe-instance-information.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
3. **The panel itself relies on SSH/agent access and has no stronger control channel.** Ploi becomes `unreachable`; RunCloud can lose its ability to manage the box. The correct recovery is usually restoring the key, firewall rule, agent or IP mapping—not replacing the VPS. ([Ploi](https://ploi.io/documentation/ssh/can-i-safely-change-permitrootlogin-in-the-ssh-config-file?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That last point matters operationally: **a customer-caused loss of provider management access should generally not be treated as evidence that the VM itself needs replacement**. Terraform's behavior around provisioners illustrates why: it taints after a failed *creation-time* provisioner because it cannot trust that initial construction completed, but it does not continuously replace a VM just because software inside it subsequently stops working. ([HashiCorp Developer](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/provisioners?optInFrom=terraform-io&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So the strongest pattern I found is: **keep authoritative component states separate—compute, network identity/connectivity, storage and management channel—and derive a customer-facing `healthy/degraded/blocked` summary from them.** A top-level degraded state is useful, but systems such as Juju, AWS and the Kubernetes Conditions design show why it is much safer when the underlying reason remains first-class. Systems such as Ploi demonstrate the opposite trade-off: a compact `unreachable` state is simple and actionable, but it intentionally loses information about whether the underlying VPS and workload are actually healthy.
```

import path from "node:path";

/**
 * Hetzner's own description of what it sends, as `scripts/hetzner-contract.ts` wrote it down.
 * The fake checks every reply against it, so the fake cannot answer in a shape Hetzner never
 * would, and a change at Hetzner shows up as a difference in that file rather than as a
 * surprise in production.
 */

type Schema = {
	type?: string | string[];
	properties?: Record<string, Schema>;
	required?: string[];
	items?: Schema;
	enum?: unknown[];
	anyOf?: Schema[];
	oneOf?: Schema[];
	allOf?: Schema[];
};

type Operation = {
	parameters: { name: string; in: string; required: boolean }[];
	request: Schema;
	responses: Record<string, Schema>;
};

type Contract = {
	source: string;
	paths: Record<string, Record<string, Operation>>;
};

const contractPath = path.join(import.meta.dir, "hetzner-contract.json");
const templatePattern = /\{[^}]+\}/;
const queryPattern = /\?.*$/;

/**
 * Where Hetzner's description and Hetzner itself disagree, with the evidence. A description is
 * Hetzner's word about itself, not Hetzner: when running it says otherwise, running wins, and the
 * difference is named here rather than quietly ignored.
 */
const knownDifferences: Record<string, string> = {
	// The description says `image` and `server_type` are strings. Hetzner's own Go client sends
	// the ID as a number (`IDOrName.MarshalJSON` marshals `o.ID`), and servers were created this
	// way against real Hetzner in this repository.
	"POST /servers body.image": "Hetzner reads an ID here as well as a name",
	"POST /servers body.server_type":
		"Hetzner reads an ID here as well as a name",
};

let contract: Contract | undefined;

/** Drops the differences we have already chased down, so only new ones are reported. */
function withoutKnownDifferences(problems: readonly string[]) {
	return problems.filter(
		(problem) =>
			!Object.keys(knownDifferences).some((known) => problem.startsWith(known)),
	);
}

async function requireContract() {
	contract ??= (await Bun.file(contractPath).json()) as Contract;
	return contract;
}

function toSegments(value: string) {
	return value.replace(queryPattern, "").split("/").filter(Boolean);
}

/** Hetzner's path for a request, such as `/servers/{id}` for `servers/1005`. */
function findTemplate(known: readonly string[], requested: string) {
	const segments = toSegments(requested);
	return known.find((template) => {
		const parts = toSegments(template);
		return (
			parts.length === segments.length &&
			parts.every(
				(part, index) => templatePattern.test(part) || part === segments[index],
			)
		);
	});
}

function toTypes(schema: Schema) {
	if (schema.type === undefined) {
		return [];
	}
	return Array.isArray(schema.type) ? schema.type : [schema.type];
}

function isType(value: unknown, type: string) {
	switch (type) {
		case "object":
			return (
				value !== null && typeof value === "object" && !Array.isArray(value)
			);
		case "array":
			return Array.isArray(value);
		case "integer":
			return typeof value === "number" && Number.isInteger(value);
		case "number":
			return typeof value === "number";
		case "string":
			return typeof value === "string";
		case "boolean":
			return typeof value === "boolean";
		case "null":
			return value === null;
		default:
			return true;
	}
}

// biome-ignore lint/complexity/noExcessiveCognitiveComplexity: one branch for each part of a schema
function collectProblems(
	schema: Schema,
	value: unknown,
	where: string,
	problems: string[],
) {
	const types = toTypes(schema);
	if (types.length > 0 && !types.some((type) => isType(value, type))) {
		problems.push(
			`${where} is ${JSON.stringify(value)}, not ${types.join(" or ")}`,
		);
		return;
	}
	if (schema.enum !== undefined && !schema.enum.includes(value)) {
		problems.push(
			`${where} is ${JSON.stringify(value)}, which Hetzner never sends`,
		);
	}
	if (Array.isArray(value) && schema.items !== undefined) {
		for (const [index, item] of value.entries()) {
			collectProblems(schema.items, item, `${where}[${index}]`, problems);
		}
	}
	if (value === null || typeof value !== "object" || Array.isArray(value)) {
		return;
	}
	const fields = value as Record<string, unknown>;
	for (const name of schema.required ?? []) {
		if (!(name in fields)) {
			problems.push(`${where}.${name} is missing, and Hetzner always sends it`);
		}
	}
	for (const [name, field] of Object.entries(schema.properties ?? {})) {
		if (name in fields) {
			collectProblems(field, fields[name], `${where}.${name}`, problems);
		}
	}
	for (const part of schema.allOf ?? []) {
		collectProblems(part, value, where, problems);
	}
}

/**
 * What is wrong with one request Composery sent: a query it asks for that Hetzner does not
 * have, or a body that Hetzner would refuse. This is the half that checks our own code.
 */
export async function listHetznerRequestProblems(
	method: string,
	requested: string,
	body: unknown,
): Promise<string[]> {
	const described = await requireContract();
	const template = findTemplate(Object.keys(described.paths), requested);
	const operation =
		template === undefined
			? undefined
			: described.paths[template]?.[method.toLowerCase()];
	if (template === undefined || operation === undefined) {
		return [`Hetzner does not describe ${method} ${requested}`];
	}
	const problems: string[] = [];
	const query = new URLSearchParams(requested.split("?")[1] ?? "");
	const known = new Set(
		operation.parameters
			.filter((parameter) => parameter.in === "query")
			.map((parameter) => parameter.name),
	);
	for (const name of query.keys()) {
		if (!known.has(name)) {
			problems.push(
				`${method} ${template} asks for ${name}, which Hetzner does not read`,
			);
		}
	}
	if (body !== undefined) {
		collectProblems(
			operation.request,
			body,
			`${method} ${template} body`,
			problems,
		);
		for (const name of Object.keys(body as Record<string, unknown>)) {
			if (
				operation.request.properties !== undefined &&
				!(name in operation.request.properties)
			) {
				problems.push(
					`${method} ${template} body sends ${name}, which Hetzner does not read`,
				);
			}
		}
	}
	return withoutKnownDifferences(problems);
}

/**
 * What is wrong with one reply, against Hetzner's description of that request. An empty list
 * means Hetzner could have sent it. A request Hetzner does not describe is a problem too: it
 * means we ask for something that no longer exists.
 */
export async function listHetznerReplyProblems(
	method: string,
	requested: string,
	status: number,
	body: unknown,
): Promise<string[]> {
	const described = await requireContract();
	const template = findTemplate(Object.keys(described.paths), requested);
	if (template === undefined) {
		return [`Hetzner does not describe ${method} ${requested}`];
	}
	const operation = described.paths[template]?.[method.toLowerCase()];
	if (operation === undefined) {
		return [`Hetzner does not describe ${method} ${template}`];
	}
	const schema = operation.responses[String(status)];
	if (schema === undefined) {
		return [`Hetzner does not describe a ${status} for ${method} ${template}`];
	}
	const problems: string[] = [];
	collectProblems(schema, body, `${method} ${template} ${status}`, problems);
	return withoutKnownDifferences(problems);
}

import {

	type IncomingMessage,
	type ServerResponse,

import { registerCleanup } from "./cleanup";
import {
	listHetznerReplyProblems,
	listHetznerRequestProblems,
} from "./hetzner-contract";
import {
	toActionReply,
	toFirewallReply,
	toImageReply,
	toPaginationReply,
	toPrimaryIpReply,
	toServerReply,
	toServerTypeReply,
} from "./hetzner-replies";

/**
 * A fake for Hetzner: it answers the requests Composery sends, and it can produce the
 * outcomes Hetzner cannot be asked for, such as a reply that never arrives. It never decides
 * whether a test passes. What it knows about Hetzner is only what Composery reads: the fields
 * below, and the shapes that real runs have shown.
 */

const httpOk = 200;
const httpCreated = 201;
const httpNoContent = 204;
const httpNotFound = 404;
const firstId = 1000;
const addressBytes = 256;
const hexRadix = 16;
const ipv4Offset = 1;
const ipv6Offset = 2;
const apiPrefixPattern = /^\/v1\//;

/** What Composery sent, so a test can count creates or read a body. */
export type HetznerRequest = Readonly<{
	method: string;
	path: string;
	body: unknown;
}>;

/**
 * `answer` acts as Hetzner would. `lose` acts too, and then drops the connection, so Composery
 * learns nothing about a request that took effect. A status and code is a refusal.
 */
export type HetznerOutcome =
	| "answer"
	| "lose"
	| Readonly<{ status: number; code: string }>;

export type HetznerFake = Readonly<{
	/** The loopback address to give `HCLOUD_FAKE_URL`. */
	url: string;
	/** Every request in order, oldest first. */
	requests: () => readonly HetznerRequest[];
	/** Every way a reply differed from Hetzner's own description of it. */
	problems: () => readonly string[];
	countRequests: (method: string, path: RegExp) => number;
	/** Applies once, to the next request that matches. */
	scriptOnce: (
		match: Readonly<{ method: string; path: RegExp }>,
		outcome: HetznerOutcome,
	) => void;
	stop: () => void;
}>;

type Resource = {
	id: number;
	collection: "servers" | "primary_ips";
	/** What Composery's own label says this is: `ipv4`, `ipv6`, or `server`. */
	kind: string;
	name: string;
	labels: Record<string, string>;
	address: string;
	assigneeId: number | null;
	status: string;
};

type Script = {
	method: string;
	path: RegExp;
	outcome: HetznerOutcome;
};

const controllerFirewallId = 77;
const controllerId = "composery-test";
const imageId = 501;
const serverTypeName = "cx23";
const locations = ["nbg1", "fsn1", "hel1"];
const firstLocation = "nbg1";

function toAddress(
	id: number,
	collection: string,
	labels: Record<string, string>,
) {
	const kind = labels["resource-kind"];
	if (collection === "servers" || kind === "ipv4") {
		return `203.0.113.${id % addressBytes}`;
	}
	return `2001:db8::${id.toString(hexRadix)}`;
}

async function startHetznerFake(): Promise<HetznerFake> {
	const requests: HetznerRequest[] = [];
	const problems: string[] = [];
	const resources = new Map<number, Resource>();
	const actions = new Map<number, string>();
	const scripts: Script[] = [];
	let nextId = firstId;

	const takeScript = (method: string, route: string) => {
		const index = scripts.findIndex(
			(candidate) => candidate.method === method && candidate.path.test(route),
		);
		if (index === -1) {
			return "answer" as const;
		}
		const [script] = scripts.splice(index, 1);
		return script?.outcome ?? ("answer" as const);
	};

	const startAction = () => {
		nextId += 1;
		actions.set(nextId, "success");
		return toActionReply(nextId, "success");
	};

	const toResourceReply = (resource: Resource) => {
		const owned = [...resources.values()].filter(
			(item) =>
				item.labels["allocation-id"] === resource.labels["allocation-id"],
		);
		const ipv4 = owned.find((item) => item.labels["resource-kind"] === "ipv4");
		const ipv6 = owned.find((item) => item.labels["resource-kind"] === "ipv6");
		if (resource.collection === "primary_ips") {
			return toPrimaryIpReply({
				id: resource.id,
				name: resource.name,
				labels: resource.labels,
				ip: resource.address,
				type: resource.kind,
				assigneeId: resource.assigneeId,
				location: firstLocation,
			});
		}
		return toServerReply({
			id: resource.id,
			name: resource.name,
			status: resource.status,
			labels: resource.labels,
			ipv4: {
				id: ipv4?.id ?? resource.id + ipv4Offset,
				ip: ipv4?.address ?? `203.0.113.${resource.id % addressBytes}`,
			},
			ipv6: {
				id: ipv6?.id ?? resource.id + ipv6Offset,
				ip: ipv6?.address ?? `2001:db8::${resource.id.toString(hexRadix)}`,
			},
			firewallId: controllerFirewallId,
			serverType: serverTypeName,
			location: firstLocation,
			imageId,
			imageName: "ubuntu-24.04",
		});

	const create = (collection: Resource["collection"], body: unknown) => {

			name?: string;
			labels?: Record<string, string>;

			name: fields.name ?? `resource-${nextId}`,

		}
		if (method === "GET") {
			const resource = resources.get(Number(id));
			return resource === undefined
				? { status: httpNotFound, body: { error: { code: "not_found" } } }
				: {
						status: httpOk,
						body: {
							[collection === "servers" ? "server" : "primary_ip"]:
								toResourceReply(resource),
						},
					};
		}
		if (method === "DELETE") {
			if (!resources.delete(Number(id))) {
				return { status: httpNotFound, body: { error: { code: "not_found" } } };
			}
			return collection === "servers"
				? { status: httpOk, body: { action: startAction() } }
				: { status: httpNoContent, body: null };
		}
		return { status: httpNotFound, body: { error: { code: "not_found" } } };
	};

	const handle = (
		request: IncomingMessage,
		response: ServerResponse,
		body: unknown,
	) => {
		const method = request.method ?? "GET";
		// Composery calls the same paths it calls at Hetzner, under the same prefix.
		const path = (request.url ?? "").replace(apiPrefixPattern, "");
		requests.push({ method, path, body });
		// Composery's own request is held to the same description as the reply.
		void listHetznerRequestProblems(method, path, body).then((found) =>
			problems.push(...found),
		);
		const outcome = takeScript(method, path);
		if (outcome === "lose") {
			// Hetzner did the work; the answer never arrives. Composery must not assume it failed.
			answer(method, path, body);
			request.socket.destroy();
			return;
		}
		if (outcome !== "answer") {
			response.writeHead(outcome.status, {
				"content-type": "application/json",
			});
			response.end(JSON.stringify({ error: { code: outcome.code } }));
			return;
		}
		const result = answer(method, path, body);
		// Hetzner's own description decides whether it could have sent this. The reply is already
		// on its way, so a difference is recorded and fails the run at the end.
		void listHetznerReplyProblems(
			method,
			path,
			result.status,
			result.body ?? {},
		).then((found) => problems.push(...found));
		if (result.body === null) {
			response.writeHead(result.status);
			response.end();
			return;
		}
		response.writeHead(result.status, { "content-type": "application/json" });
		response.end(JSON.stringify(result.body));
	};

	const server = createServer((request, response) => {
		const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
		request.on("data", (chunk: Buffer) => chunks.push(chunk));
		request.on("end", () => {
			let body: unknown;
			try {
				body =
					chunks.length === 0
						? undefined
						: JSON.parse(Buffer.concat(chunks).toString());
			} catch {
				body = undefined;
			}
			handle(request, response, body);
		});
	});
	const stop = () => {
		server.closeAllConnections();
		server.close();
	};
	await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
		server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", resolve);
	});
	registerCleanup(stop);
	const address = server.address();
	if (typeof address !== "object" || address === null) {
		stop();
		throw new Error("The Hetzner fake did not take a port.");
	}

	return {
		url: `http://127.0.0.1:${address.port}`,
		requests: () => requests,
		problems: () => problems,
		countRequests: (method, path) =>
			requests.filter(
				(request) => request.method === method && path.test(request.path),
			).length,
		scriptOnce: (match, outcome) => {
			scripts.push({ ...match, outcome });
		},
		stop,
	};
}

let fake: Promise<HetznerFake> | undefined;
let running: HetznerFake | undefined;

/**
 * Fails the run when the fake answered in a shape Hetzner never would. It is checked once for the
 * whole run, because the test that makes a request is not always the one that would read it.
 */
export function listHetznerFakeProblems() {
	return running?.problems() ?? [];
}

/** Fails the run when the fake, or Composery, spoke to Hetzner in a way Hetzner describes otherwise. */
export function requireHetznerContractKept() {
	const problems = listHetznerFakeProblems();
	if (problems.length > 0) {
		const lines = [
			"The fake answered in ways Hetzner would not:",
			...new Set(problems),
		];
		throw new Error(lines.join("\n"));
	}
}

/** One fake for the whole run, because the deployment holds its address. */
export function useHetznerFake() {
	fake ??= startHetznerFake().then((started) => {
		running = started;
		return started;
	});
	return fake;
}

What it knows about Hetzner is only what Composery reads, and every\n * reply is held to Hetzner's own description, so the fake cannot answer in a shape Hetzner never\n * would.\n */\n\nconst httpOk = 200;\nconst httpCreated = 201;\nconst httpNoContent = 204;\nconst httpNotFound = 404;\nconst firstId = 1000;\nconst addressBytes = 256;\nconst hexRadix = 16;\nconst ipv4Offset = 1;\nconst ipv6Offset = 2;\nconst controllerFirewallId = 77;\nconst controllerId = \"composery-test\";\nconst imageId = 501;\nconst serverTypeName = \"cx23\";\nconst locations = [\"nbg1\", \"fsn1\", \"hel1\"];\nconst `2001:db8::${id.toString(hexRadix)}`;\n}\n\nfunction notFound(): FakeReply {\n\treturn { status: httpNotFound, body: { error: { code: \"not_found\" } } };\n}\n\nexport function startHetznerFake(): Promise<Fake> {\n\tconst resources = new Map<number, Resource>();\n\tconst actions = new Map<number, string>();\n\tlet nextId = firstId;\n\n\tconst startAction = () => {\n\t\tnextId += 1;\n\t\tactions.set(nextId, \"success\");\n\t\treturn toActionReply(nextId, \"success\");\n\t};\n\n\tconst toResourceReply = (resource: Resource) => {\n\t\tif (resource.collection === \"primary_ips\") {\n\t\t\treturn toPrimaryIpReply({\n\t\t\t\tid: resource.id,\n\t\t\t\tname: resource.name,\n\t\t\t\tlabels: resource.labels,\n\t\t\t\tip: resource.address,\n\t\t\t\ttype: resource.kind,\n\t\t\t\tassigneeId: resource.assigneeId,\n\t\t\t\tlocation: resource.location,\n\t\t\t});\n\t\t}\n\t\tconst owned = [...resources.values()].filter(\n\t\t\t(item) =>\n\t\t\t\titem.collection === \"primary_ips\" &&\n\t\t\t\titem.labels[\"allocation-id\"] === resource.labels[\"allocation-id\"],\n\t\t);\n\t\tconst ipv4 = owned.find((item) => item.kind === \"ipv4\");\n\t\tconst ipv6 = owned.find((item) => item.kind === \"ipv6\");\n\t\treturn toServerReply({\n\t\t\tid: resource.id,\n\t\t\tname: resource.name,\n\t\t\tstatus: resource.status,\n\t\t\tlabels: resource.labels,\n\t\t\tipv4: {\n\t\t\t\tid: ipv4?.id ?? resource.id + ipv4Offset,\n\t\t\t\tip: ipv4?.address ?? toAddress(resource.id, \"servers\", \"ipv4\"),\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t\tipv6: {\n\t\t\t\tid: ipv6?.id ?? resource.id + ipv6Offset,\n\t\t\t\tip: ipv6?.address ?? toAddress(resource.id, \"primary_ips\", \"ipv6\"),\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t\tfirewallId: controllerFirewallId,\n\t\t\tserverType: serverTypeName,\n\t\t\tlocation: resource.location,\n\t\t\timageId,\n\t\t\timageName: \"ubuntu-24.04\",\n\t\t});\n\t};\n\n\tconst create = (collection: Collection, body: unknown) => {\n\t\tconst fields = (body ?? {}) as {\n\t\t\tname?: string;\n\t\t\tlabels?: Record<string, string>;\n\t\t\tlocation?: string;\n\t\t\t// biome-ignore lint/style/useNamingConvention: the Hetzner Cloud API names this field\n\t\t\tpublic_net?: { ipv4?: number; ipv6?: number };\n\t\t};\n\t\tnextId += 1;\n\t\tconst labels = fields.labels ?? {};\n\t\t// Composery labels everything it creates; anything else is named by its collection.\n\t\tconst kind =\n\t\t\ttypeof labels[\"resource-kind\"] === \"string\"\n\t\t\t\t? labels[\"resource-kind\"]\n\t\t\t\t: collection;\n\t\tconst resource: Resource = {\n\t\t\tid: nextId,\n\t\t\tcollection,\n\t\t\tname: fields.name ?? `resource-${nextId}`,\n\t\t\tkind,\n\t\t\tlabels,\n\t\t\taddress: toAddress(nextId, collection, kind),\n\t\t\tassigneeId: null,\n\t\t\tstatus: \"running\",\n\t\t\tlocation: fields.location ?? firstLocation,\n\t\t};\n\t\tresources.set(resource.id, resource);\n\t\t// A server takes the addresses it was created with, as Hetzner assigns them.\n\t\tfor (const addressId of [fields.public_net?.ipv4, fields.public_net?.ipv6]) {\n\t\t\tconst address =\n\t\t\t\taddressId === undefined ? undefined : resources.get(addressId);\n\t\t\tif (address !== undefined) {\n\t\t\t\taddress.assigneeId = resource.id;\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\t\treturn resource;\n\t};\n\n\tconst list = (collection: Collection, query: URLSearchParams) => {\n\t\tconst wanted = new Map(\n\t\t\t(query.get(\"label_selector\") ?? \"\")\n\t\t\t\t.split(\",\")\n\t\t\t\t.filter(Boolean)\n\t\t\t\t.map((pair) => {\n\t\t\t\t\tconst [key, value] = pair.split(\"=\");\n\t\t\t\t\treturn [key ?? \"\", value ?? \"\"] as const;\n\t\t\t\t}),\n\t\t);\n\t\tconst name = query.get(\"name\");\n\t\treturn [...resources.values()].filter(\n\t\t\t(resource) =>\n\t\t\t\tresource.collection === collection &&\n\t\t\t\t(name === null || resource.name === name) &&\n\t\t\t\t[...wanted].every(([key, value]) => resource.labels[key] === value),\n\t\t);\n\t};\n\n\t// biome-ignore lint/complexity/noExcessiveCognitiveComplexity: one branch for each request Composery sends\n\tconst answer = (method: string, path: string, body: unknown): FakeReply => {\n\t\tconst [route, rawQuery] = path.split(\"?\");\n\t\tconst query = new URLSearchParams(rawQuery ?? \"\");\n\t\tconst [collection, id, group, action] = (route ?? \"\")\n\t\t\t.split(\"/\")\n\t\t\t.filter(Boolean);\n\t\tif (method === \"GET\" && collection === \"firewalls\") {\n\t\t\treturn {\n\t\t\t\tstatus: httpOk,\n\t\t\t\tbody: { firewall: toFirewallReply(Number(id), controllerId) },\n\t\t\t};\n\t\t}\n\t\tif (method === \"GET\" && collection === \"server_types\") {\n\t\t\treturn {\n\t\t\t\tstatus: httpOk,\n\t\t\t\tbody: {\n\t\t\t\t\t// biome-ignore lint/style/useNamingConvention: the Hetzner Cloud API names this field\n\t\t\t\t\tserver_types: [toServerTypeReply(serverTypeName, locations)],\n\t\t\t\t\tmeta: toPaginationReply(1),\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t};\n\t\t}\n\t\tif (method === \"GET\" && collection === \"images\") {\n\t\t\treturn {\n\t\t\t\tstatus: httpOk,\n\t\t\t\tbody: {\n\t\t\t\t\timages: [toImageReply(imageId, query.get(\"name\") ?? \"\")],\n\t\t\t\t\tmeta: toPaginationReply(1),\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t};\n\t\t}\n\t\tif (method === \"GET\" && collection === \"actions\") {\n\t\t\tconst status = actions.get(Number(id));\n\t\t\treturn status === undefined\n\t\t\t\t? notFound()\n\t\t\t\t: {\n\t\t\t\t\t\tstatus: httpOk,\n\t\t\t\t\t\tbody: { action: toActionReply(Number(id), status) },\n\t\t\t\t\t};\n\t\t}\n\t\tif (collection !== \"servers\" && collection !== \"primary_ips\") {\n\t\t\treturn notFound();\n\t\t}\n\t\tconst single = collection === \"servers\" ? \"server\" : \"primary_ip\";\n\t\tif (method === \"POST\" && id === undefined) {\n\t\t\tconst resource = create(collection, body);\n\t\t\treturn {\n\t\t\t\tstatus: httpCreated,\n\t\t\t\tbody: {\n\t\t\t\t\t[single]: toResourceReply(resource),\n\t\t\t\t\taction: startAction(),\n\t\t\t\t\t...(collection === \"servers\"\n\t\t\t\t\t\t? // biome-ignore lint/style/useNamingConvention: the Hetzner Cloud API names this field\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t{ next_actions: [], root_password: null }\n\t\t\t\t\t\t: {}),\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t};\n\t\t}\n\t\tif (method === \"POST\" && group === \"actions\" && action !== undefined) {\n\t\t\tconst resource = resources.get(Number(id));\n\t\t\tif (resource === undefined) {\n\t\t\t\treturn notFound();\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tresource.status = action === \"poweron\" ? \"running\" : \"off\";\n\t\t\treturn { status: httpCreated, body: { action: startAction() } };\n\t\t}\n\t\tif (method === \"GET\" && id === undefined) {\n\t\t\tconst found = list(collection, query).map(toResourceReply);\n\t\t\treturn {\n\t\t\t\tstatus: httpOk,\n\t\t\t\tbody: { [collection]: found, meta: toPaginationReply(found.length) },\n\t\t\t};\n\t\t}\n\t\tif (method === \"GET\") {\n\t\t\tconst resource = resources.get(Number(id));\n\t\t\treturn resource === undefined\n\t\t\t\t? notFound()\n\t\t\t\t: { status: httpOk, body: { [single]: toResourceReply(resource) } };\n\t\t}\n\t\tif (method === \"DELETE\") {\n\t\t\tconst resource = resources.get(Number(id));\n\t\t\tif (resource === undefined) {\n\t\t\t\treturn notFound();\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tresources.delete(resource.id);\n\t\t\t// Hetzner frees an address that a deleted server held.\n\t\t\tfor (const other of resources.values()) {\n\t\t\t\tif (other.assigneeId === resource.id) {\n\t\t\t\t\tother.assigneeId = null;\n\t\t\t\t}\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\treturn collection === \"servers\"\n\t\t\t\t? { status: httpOk, body: { action: startAction() } }\n\t\t\t\t: { status: httpNoContent, body: null };\n\t\t}\n\t\treturn notFound();\n\t};\n\n\treturn startFake({\n\t\tsystem: \"Hetzner\",\n\t\tchecker: hetznerContract,\n\t\tanswer: (request) => answer(request.method, request.path, request.body),\n\t});\n}\n"

Clerk's own type\n * names them, so an event Clerk adds later fails to compile here until somebody decides about it.\n */\n// biome-ignore lint/style/useNamingConvention: Clerk names these events\nconst accountEvents: Record<UserWebhookEvent[\"type\"], true> = {\n\t\"user.created\": true,\n\t\"user.updated\": true,\n\t\"user.deleted\": true,\n};\n\nfunction isAccountEvent(type: string): type is UserWebhookEvent[\"type\"] {\n\treturn Object.hasOwn(accountEvents, type);\n}\n\nexport const receiveClerkWebhook = httpAction(async (ctx, request) => {\n\tlet event: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof verifyWebhook>>;\n\ttry {\n\t\tevent = await verifyWebhook(request, {\n\t\t\tsigningSecret: env.CLERK_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET,\n\t\t});\n\t} catch {\n\t\treturn new Response(\"Invalid webhook signature.\", {\n\t\t\tstatus: httpStatus.badRequest,\n\t\t});\n\t}\n\n\tif (isAccountEvent(event.type)) {\n\t\tconst clerkUserId = event.data.id;\n\t\tif (clerkUserId === undefined) {\n\t\t\treturn new Response(\"The event has no user ID.\", {\n\t\t\t\tstatus: httpStatus.badRequest,\n\t\t\t});\n\t\t}\n\t\ttry {\n\t\t\tawait syncClerkUser(ctx, clerkUserId);\n\t\t} catch {\n\t\t\t// Clerk sends a webhook again when it is not accepted, and no detail of the failure\n\t\t\t// goes back to it.\n\t\t\treturn new Response(null, { status: httpStatus.serviceUnavailable });\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\treturn new Response(null, { status: httpStatus.noContent });\n});\n"
}

Adding a waiver without one fails this file.\n */\n\nconst contractUrl = new URL(\n\t\"../../../contracts/hetzner/check.ts\",\n\timport.meta.url,\n).href;\n\n/** What Composery sends when it creates a server, with the parts a waiver is about. */\nconst createServerBody = {\n\tname: \"one\",\n\timage: 501,\n\t// biome-ignore lint/style/useNamingConvention: the Hetzner Cloud API names this field\n\tserver_type: 22,\n\tlocation: \"nbg1\",\n};\n\nconst reproducers: Record<string, () => string[]> = {\n\t\"POST /servers body.image\": () =>\n\t\tlistUnwaivedProblems(\"POST\", \"servers\", createServerBody),\n\t\"POST /servers body.server_type\": () =>\n\t\tlistUnwaivedProblems(\"POST\", \"servers\", createServerBody),\n};\n\n/** The same request, read by a checker that holds no waivers at all. */\nfunction listUnwaivedProblems(method: string, path: string, body: unknown) {\n\treturn createContractChecker({\n\t\tsystem: hetznerSelection.system,\n\t\tcontract: readContract(contractUrl),\n\t\twaivers: [],\n\t}).listRequestProblems(method, path, body);\n}\n\ntest(\"every waiver has a reproducer, and every reproducer has a waiver\", () => {\n\tconst named = hetznerWaivers.map(\n\t\t(waiver) => `${waiver.operation} ${waiver.at}`,\n\t);\n\texpect([...named].sort()).toEqual(Object.keys(reproducers).sort());\n});\n\ntest(\"every waiver still describes a real difference, and hides nothing else\", () => {\n\tfor (const waiver of hetznerWaivers) {\n\t\tconst place = `${waiver.operation} ${waiver.at}`;\n\t\t// Without the waiver, Hetzner's description refuses what Hetzner accepts.\n\t\texpect(reproducers[place]?.().join(\"\\n\")).toContain(place);\n\t\t// With it, the same request raises nothing, and no other difference is swallowed.\n\t\tconst checker = createHetznerContractChecker();\n\t\texpect(\n\t\t\tchecker.listRequestProblems(\"POST\", \"servers\", createServerBody),\n\t\t).toEqual([]);\n\t}\n});\n\ntest(\"a waiver does not excuse a neighbouring field\", () => {\n\tconst checker = createHetznerContractChecker();\n\texpect(\n\t\tchecker\n\t\t\t.listRequestProblems(\"POST\", \"servers\", {\n\t\t\t\t...createServerBody,\n\t\t\t\tname: 7,\n\t\t\t})\n\t\t\t.join(\"\\n\"),\n\t).toContain(\"POST /servers body.name is 7, not string\");\n});\n"
}

/** Webhook delivery is not guaranteed, so this runs every hour. */
export const reconcile = internalAction({
	args: {},
	returns: v.null(),
	handler: async (ctx) => {
		const clerk = createClient();

		let read = 0;
		for (let offset = 0; ; offset += clerkPageSize) {
			const { data } = await clerk.users.getUserList({
				limit: clerkPageSize,
				offset,
				orderBy: "+created_at",
			});
			await storeUsers(ctx, data);
			if (data.length < clerkPageSize) {
				break;
			}
			read += 1;
			if (read >= maxPages) {
				throw new Error(
					`Clerk still had more accounts after ${maxPages} pages. Nothing was deleted.`,
				);
			}
		}

		let cursor: string | null = null;
		for (let page = 0; ; page += 1) {
			if (page >= maxPages) {
				throw new Error(
					`Composery still had more accounts after ${maxPages} pages.`,
				);
			}
			const page: { page: string[]; isDone: boolean; continueCursor: string } =
				await ctx.runQuery(internal.users.listClerkIds, {
					paginationOpts: { numItems: clerkPageSize, cursor },
				});
			if (page.page.length > 0) {
				const { data } = await clerk.users.getUserList({
					userId: page.page,
					limit: page.page.length,
				});
				const existing = new Set(data.map((user) => user.id));
				const missing = page.page.filter((id) => !existing.has(id));
				if (missing.length > 0) {
					await ctx.runMutation(internal.users.remove, {
						clerkUserIds: missing,
					});
				}
			}
			if (page.isDone) {
				break;
			}
			cursor = page.continueCursor;
		}
