A key distinction is already clear from upstream docs: `/etc/machine-id` is explicitly specified as unique per instantiated machine, and generic images are supposed to leave it missing or empty; cloud-init separately tracks a cloud `instance-id` and caches “once-per-instance” state. Those two identity systems overlap in consequences but are not interchangeable.

---

**ChatGPT**

The “cloud image will fix it” assumption is only partly true. Cloud-init’s current documentation explicitly warns that a captured cache can make a clone look like a later boot; in its default generic-image mode it compares instance IDs, but `manual_cache_clean: true` disables that detection. Its SSH module is once-per-instance and defaults to deleting image host keys, so a failure to establish “new instance” is simultaneously a provisioning correctness failure and a host-identity security failure.

---

**ChatGPT**

A useful way to scope this is not “which files should be deleted?” but **which state in the disk claims continuity with the old machine**. That includes identifiers, credentials, cached cloud-instance state, scheduler history, and application/node identity. There is no finite OS-level list that covers an arbitrary customer VM: once software such as MySQL, Kubernetes, Puppet, Consul, VPN agents, or a commercial monitoring agent has enrolled, it can add another clone-sensitive identity. The platform therefore has to decide what semantics a snapshot-derived machine is meant to have.

I surveyed upstream Linux/systemd/cloud-init/OpenSSH documentation and the current AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Red Hat, Proxmox, Kubernetes, Docker, HashiCorp, Puppet, Chef, Salt and related primary sources. The important finding is that **standard cloud-image machinery handles a useful core, but it is not a general VM-cloning generalizer**.

### A taxonomy that matters

There are four materially different things mixed together in a disk image:

| Kind of state | Desired relation after cloning | Typical consequence if copied |
|---|---|---|
| **Machine identity** | Usually different | Two live machines are interpreted as one |
| **Machine credential / enrolment secret** | Usually different or explicitly re-enrolled | Clone possesses authority granted to source |
| **Cached external-instance state** | Must correspond to new VM | First-boot/configuration is skipped or stale configuration is replayed |
| **Historical/temporal state** | Depends on snapshot semantics | Missed jobs, duplicate jobs, wrong telemetry, stale logs |
| **Storage/data identity** | Often deliberately identical | Only becomes wrong if both copies enter the same namespace/topology |

That last distinction is important. Changing every UUID is not correct either: a restored filesystem needs its filesystem UUID if `/etc/fstab` refers to it, and a restored database may intentionally need its old replication identity when replacing—not cloning—a failed member.

## Core OS and access state

| State in the image | What goes wrong on a second machine | Security vs correctness | What normal cloud-image machinery does |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OpenSSH host private keys** `/etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key` | Both machines present the same SSH server identity. A control plane expecting a newly generated fingerprint sees a pin mismatch; a control plane that carries the old pin forward cannot distinguish the two machines cryptographically. Theft of either copy's host private key permits impersonation of the other. OpenSSH's defaults point directly at these host-key files. ([OpenBSD Manual](https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | **Both; high security significance.** | cloud-init's SSH module is once-per-instance; `ssh_deletekeys` defaults to `true` and new RSA/ECDSA/Ed25519 keys are generated when that module actually executes as first-instance configuration. ([Cloud-Init Documentation](https://docs.cloud-init.io/en/latest/reference/modules.html?highlight=power_state&utm_source=chatgpt.com)) GCE's guest agent likewise documents host-key generation as a first-boot action. ([Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/images/guest-agent-functions?authuser=2&utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **`authorized_keys`**, `AuthorizedPrincipalsFile`, trusted SSH CA configuration | Every key already accepted by the source is accepted by the clone unless something explicitly removes it. In the described hosting design this includes the provider's management principal. If that credential was meant to be per-machine, the old control plane—or anyone holding its private half—retains access to the clone. | Primarily **security**, sometimes correctness when automation uses the wrong key. | Injection of a newly selected cloud SSH key does **not** imply deletion of pre-existing keys. Hetzner explicitly says keys already present in a snapshot's `authorized_keys` continue to work. ([Hetzner Docs](https://docs.hetzner.com/cloud/servers/faq/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Google's guest agent manages keys for Google-managed users but says unmanaged users are not touched. ([GitHub](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/guest-agent/blob/main/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) AWS Image Builder's cleanup is unusually aggressive: it can delete every user's `authorized_keys`. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/imagebuilder/latest/userguide/security-best-practices.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **SSH client keys / deploy keys / service keys** under `/root/.ssh`, user homes, application config | The clone can authenticate *outward* as the old host/user, perhaps to Git, backups, management networks, or another machine. | **Security.** Often more serious than the duplicated SSH host key. | Not generically regenerated. This is application/customer state. |
| **`/etc/machine-id`** and often `/var/lib/dbus/machine-id` | systemd requires the machine ID to identify the installed OS instance. Duplicates leak into services that derive IDs from it; journald attribution, DHCP DUIDs, IPv6 stable addressing, systemd-derived IDs and software licensing/enrolment can all collide. systemd explicitly says generic images for multiple machines should ship this missing or empty. ([man7.org](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/machine-id.5.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | Mostly **correctness/identity**, with secondary security/privacy effects where it seeds authorization or pseudonymous identifiers. | systemd generates an ID if absent/empty. There is an important semantic wrinkle: a *missing* file or one containing `uninitialized` gives systemd “first boot” semantics; an empty file gets a new ID but is not itself considered first boot for `ConditionFirstBoot=yes`. ([man7.org](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/machine-id.5.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Current `cloud-init clean --machine-id` deliberately writes `uninitialized` on systemd systems. ([Cloud-Init Documentation](https://docs.cloud-init.io/en/latest/reference/cli.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **systemd/journald state** `/var/log/journal/<machine-id>/…` | Journals from source and clone have the same `_MACHINE_ID`; central collectors may aggregate them as one host. If the machine ID is changed without reconciling journal directories, old persistent logs can become awkward or invisible to the normal journal lookup path. Journald stores persistent logs under a machine-ID directory and records `_MACHINE_ID` and `_BOOT_ID` separately. ([man7.org](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/systemd-journald.service.8.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | **Correctness/forensics/privacy.** | Not intrinsically purged by changing machine-id. Image-building systems often clean logs separately. AWS Image Builder deletes `/var/log/journal/*`. ([AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/imagebuilder/latest/userguide/security-best-practices.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) A systemd issue documents a machine-ID/journal mismatch producing `No journal files were found`. ([GitHub](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/7092?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) |
| **Cloud-init cache and semaphores** `/var/lib/cloud/…`, cached datasource, instance ID, user/vendor data | Per-instance modules may not run; stale networking, users, SSH keys and user-data may be treated as already applied. Conversely, forcing a fresh first boot can deliberately rerun destructive per-instance user data. `/var/lib/cloud/instance` contains datasource data including user/vendor data. ([Cloud-Init Documentation](https://docs.cloud-init.io/en/latest/development/internal_files.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | **Both.** Incorrect configuration plus potentially serious credential exposure. | Generic cloud images normally use cloud-init's `check` mode: cached instance ID is compared with the runtime datasource ID; a difference makes it a new instance. But `manual_cache_clean: true` changes this to “trust cache”, in which case cloning requires explicit cache cleanup. Cloud-init's own warning specifically notes that otherwise SSH host-key rotation does not occur. ([Cloud-Init Documentation](https://docs.cloud-init.io/en/24.4/explanation/first_boot.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) `cloud-init clean` removes its state and can additionally clean machine-id, seed data and generated network/SSH config. async function recordFailure(
	recording: Recording,
	failure: NonNullable<HetznerCloudWorkerUpdate["failure"]>,
) {
	const { ctx, allocation, hetznerCloudAllocation, allocationPatch } =
		recording;
	const retryAt =
		Date.now() +
		Math.max(
			toBackoffMs(hetznerCloudAllocation.failures),
			failure.retryAfterMs ?? 0,
		);
	recording.hetznerCloudPatch.error = failure.error;
	if (failure.missing) {
		allocationPatch.observedAt = Date.now();
	}
	recording.hetznerCloudPatch.hetznerErrorCode = failure.hetznerErrorCode;
	recording.hetznerCloudPatch.failures = hetznerCloudAllocation.failures + 1;
	recording.hetznerCloudPatch.dueAt = retryAt;
	if (
		!recording.isCurrentOperation ||
		(failure.retry && hetznerCloudAllocation.failures < maxFailures)
	) {
		return;
	}
	allocationPatch.status = failure.missing ? "missing" : "blocked";
	recording.hetznerCloudPatch.dueAt = Math.max(
		retryAt,
		Date.now() + blockedRecheckMs,
	);
	await blockOperation(ctx, allocation.operationId);
}

function isHetznerServerStatus(
	value: string,
): value is keyof typeof serverStatuses {
	return Object.hasOwn(serverStatuses, value);
}

function toServer(reply: Reply): HetznerCloudServer {
	const status = requireText(reply.status);
	if (!isHetznerServerStatus(status)) {
		throw new HetznerCloudError("invalid_response");
	}
	const publicNet = requireObject(reply.public_net);
	const ipv4 = requireObject(publicNet.ipv4);
	const ipv6 = requireObject(publicNet.ipv6);
	return {
		id: requireId(reply.id),
		status: serverStatuses[status],

			.map(requireObject)

				id: requireId(firewall.id),
				isApplied: firewall.status === "applied",
			})),
	};
}

export const retry = internalMutation({
	args: {
		allocationId: v.id("serverAllocations"),
		confirmedAbsent: v.optional(hetznerCloudResourceKind),
	},
	returns: v.null(),
	handler: async (ctx, { allocationId, confirmedAbsent }) => {
		const allocation = await ctx.db.get("serverAllocations", allocationId);
		const hetznerCloudAllocation = await getHetznerCloudAllocation(
			ctx,
			allocationId,
		);
		if (
			allocation === null ||
			hetznerCloudAllocation === null ||
			allocation.status === "deleted" ||
			hetznerCloudAllocation.leaseExpiresAt > Date.now()
		) {
			throw new Error("The allocation cannot be retried now.");
		}
		const resources = { ...hetznerCloudAllocation.resources };
		if (confirmedAbsent !== undefined) {
			if (resources[confirmedAbsent].status !== "uncertain") {
				throw new Error(
					"Only an uncertain resource needs absence confirmation.",
				);
			}
			resources[confirmedAbsent] = {
				status: allocation.deleteRequested ? "absent" : "pending",
			};
		}
		const operation = await ctx.db.get(
			"serverOperations",
			allocation.operationId,
		);
		await ctx.db.patch("serverOperations", allocation.operationId, {
			status: "pending",
			...(operation?.deadlineAt === undefined
				? {}
				: { deadlineAt: Date.now() + hetznerCloudPowerDeadlineMs }),
		});
		await ctx.db.patch("serverAllocations", allocationId, {
			status: allocation.deleteRequested ? "deleting" : "creating",
		});
		await ctx.db.patch("hetznerCloudAllocations", hetznerCloudAllocation._id, {
			resources,
			// A new epoch fences a run that is still outstanding, so its result cannot undo this.
			epoch: hetznerCloudAllocation.epoch + 1,
			failures: 0,
			dueAt: Date.now(),
			action: undefined,
			error: undefined,
			hetznerErrorCode: undefined,
		});
		return null;
	},
});

/**
 * Removes what this backend held for an allocation that no longer exists. The worker has already
 * set the row's next run to never, so nothing else reads or writes it.
 */
export const forget = internalMutation({
	args: { allocationId: v.id("serverAllocations") },
```

## Rotation: can admin error be made impossible?

**No, and it matters less than it looks.** The variable lives outside the code — by the time anything runs, the old key is already gone from the process. But here is the part I should have said first:

**Removing a key from the list destroys nothing.** The ciphertext is still there and still names the key that wrote it. Put the key back in the list and every row reads again. The only irreversible loss is losing the *key material itself*, which is why the doc says keep a backup. So the bad case is "management is broken until you restore a value you still have", not "those servers are gone forever".

That is also why **one key is the right normal state.** You do not keep two set. You add a second only to rotate, and remove it when `reEncrypt` says nothing names it any more.

**Nothing triggers automatically.** Setting the variable changes only which key encrypts *new* values. Existing rows are untouched until you run `ssh/secrets:reEncrypt`. There is no daemon, deliberately — re-encrypting every stored secret is a large write and should be asked for, not discovered.

So the sequence, end to end: `K_old` → set `K_old,K_new` and deploy → set `K_new,K_old` and deploy → run `reEncrypt`, read its report → when only `K_new` is named, set `K_new`. It is documented because the ordering constraint is not knowable from the code; and you were right that it did not belong in the Hetzner setup doc — **it is a Convex deployment variable, so it moved to `docs/setups/convex.md`**, where it will still be right when a second backend exists.

The one thing genuinely missing: nothing *tells* you a row names a key you no longer hold. `reEncrypt` reports it, but only if you run it. A cheap scheduled count would fit the policy ("say which part is unavailable"), and I'd add it.

## Waivers — in depth

A waiver records that **a system and its own published description disagree**, with the evidence, in a form that can fail.

Our one real example: Hetzner's description says `POST /servers` takes `image` as a **string**. We send a number (the image ID). Without a waiver the check screams on every create. Three wrong responses and one right one:

- Delete the check — lose the oracle.
- Change working code to match a wrong description — break production to please a document.
- Silence it with a comment — an ignore that outlives its reason.
- **Record it with evidence** — Hetzner's own Go client marshals the ID as a number, and we created real servers this way.

It fails three ways, which is what separates it from an ignore:

1. `claims: "string"` — if Hetzner corrects the description, the waiver no longer matches and reports "the description now says X, review this".
2. If `POST /servers` runs and the difference does not appear, it is **stale** and the run fails asking you to delete it.
3. `tests/contracts/hetzner.test.ts` carries a reproducer per waiver, and a waiver without one fails that file.

**We have exactly one**, so the word is in use and earns its vocabulary entry. The best demonstration is the one that *died*: I had written a second waiver for `server_type` by analogy. We send a name there, not an ID. On its first real run the stale check deleted it. That is an invention the mechanism removed without me noticing it was an invention.

## "check" as a loaded term

I looked for the collision and I do not think there is one — pushing back rather than agreeing. Three uses:

- `check:*` in package.json — verify the repo against its standards.
- `check` in the name-prefix table — a *function* prefix meaning "returns a failure, or null".
- `contracts/check.ts` — verify a value against a description.

The first and third are the same verb in the same sense. The second is a narrower *function-naming* convention, and `contracts/check.ts` contains no `check*` function, so nothing collides in code. Renaming it to `verify` or `conform` would introduce a second word for one meaning, which the vocabulary rule forbids more strongly than anything the current name does. **Keeping `check`.**

## Why a vendor change should not be a red build — with a correction

You pushed on this and you are half right. The distinction is *which* build.

A red build on a commit that did not touch the integration tells you nothing about that commit, blocks unrelated work, and teaches people to ignore red. The vendor changed on their schedule, not ours.

**But drift should absolutely fail something.** The right shape is a *scheduled* job that re-runs the generator and fails when the pinned file moves — so it is a red build, just not a red *commit* build. That is what the research found (a daily job that opens or refreshes one issue), and it is a CI question, which is one more reason CI and the live suite are one decision.

## What the worker actually is

Not the SSH thing. **The worker is the loop that makes an allocation match what was asked of it** at the provider: create the two addresses and the server, run power commands, delete on the way out, and observe what is really there. SSH lives in `convex/ssh/` and is used by bootstrap and the key features; the worker never needs it.

One step at a time, under a lease, with an epoch that fences a stale run's result. Precisely:

- **Retryable failure** — backoff from 10s, doubling to an hour, with jitter, up to 8 failures. Status unchanged.
- **Non-retryable failure, or the 8th retryable one** — the allocation becomes `blocked` (or `missing`) and the operation is blocked.
- **A blocked allocation is still looked at every hour, forever.** So "waits for an admin" was wrong of me. If the difference goes away — an address is put back, a firewall reattached — it recovers on its own with nobody doing anything.
- `retry` is the admin lever: reset the failure count, take a new epoch so an outstanding run cannot undo it, and look now.

**Blocked is per allocation**, not global. Every other server keeps being served. And it does not touch the customer's machine: their server runs, and power and deletion still work.

## The address edge case — and a real defect it exposed

You asked what happens when a server is off, its IPs are deleted, and it is turned on again. Chasing that through Hetzner's own description found a defect in our code.

Hetzner describes `public_net.ipv4` as **`object | null`** — a server with no IPv4 gets `null`. Our parser called `requireObject` on it, so a deleted address made us report `invalid_response`: "Hetzner sent something we cannot understand", for a reply Hetzner's own description permits, with a retry that could never succeed. Now it reads as `address_identity_mismatch`, which is what it is, and there is a test that fails with `invalid_response` if the fix is removed. I verified that by removing it.

Note what found this: **not the contract check** — the fake never sent `null`, so nothing tripped. Reading the contract found it. That is an argument for reading these files, not only running them.

The rest of the sequence: Hetzner requires the server to be **off** to unassign or delete a Primary IP, and requires at least one interface to power on. So nobody can pull an address out from under a running server, and if both are deleted the server cannot start again — at Hetzner, before we are involved.

## Addresses and the per-server subdomain

The question you actually asked — where would that surface live — has a clean answer, and it splits the two cases:

- **A per-server DNS name is entirely external.** A record at Cloudflare pointing at the address. Nothing on the server's filesystem is involved, so the customer cannot destroy it, and it keeps working through anything they do inside. That makes it *safe* to offer in a way most things are not.
- **A per-app name is not.** Routing several apps on one server by hostname needs something *on* the server doing the routing, which is filesystem state the customer can remove. That is a real degradation surface and it needs the same treatment as SSH: notice, report which part is unavailable, keep the rest working.

So a server subdomain is cheap and robust; app subdomains are the ones that need design. And what rests on the raw address, beyond scripts: DNS records, connection strings, another machine's firewall allowlist, reverse-proxy upstreams, a monitoring target, an agent's saved connection, `known_hosts` on every client that connected. That is why showing the address is not optional in my view — it is a fact about their property that they need in order to use anything else.

([Debian Manpages](https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/isc-dhcp-client/dhclient.8.en.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) | **Correctness**, occasionally network-security policy implications. | It depends on DHCP implementation. `dhclient` stores its DUID in lease state and may create/reuse it there. The SSH case illustrates why a host-key-pinned control plane has **two different failure modes**, neither of which can be solved merely by “pinning better”. If host keys are regenerated, an old pin is expected to fail. If they are not regenerated, the clone and source cryptographically have the same server identity. Similarly, keeping the provider's existing `authorized_keys` entry may be intentional if the provider uses a single account-wide management key, but is a credential-continuity decision—not harmless snapshot state.

## Storage-protocol host identity

**iSCSI** has a long-lived InitiatorName, normally `/etc/iscsi/initiatorname.iscsi`. Open-iSCSI's generator refuses to overwrite an existing one without `--force`, precisely because it is persistent identity; `iscsid` reads that file and also has a persistent nodes/discovery database under `/var/lib/iscsi`. ([Debian Manpages](https://manpages.debian.org/unstable/open-iscsi/iscsi-gen-initiatorname.8.en.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

A clone therefore inherits both the initiator IQN and potentially target records, auto-login settings and CHAP credentials. A storage target may treat the machines as one initiator for ACLs and sessions; the clone may automatically log back into LUNs belonging to the source. That is both a **correctness** problem and, where IQN/CHAP state gates storage, a **security** problem. Stock cloud-init has no universal iSCSI identity-reset module; an installed InitiatorName is normally retained.

**NVMe-oF** has the analogous `/etc/nvme/hostnqn` and usually `/etc/nvme/hostid`. The nvme-stas tools describe both as values that should remain permanent for the lifetime of a host and explicitly say to generate them only when their files do not already exist. ([Debian Manpages](https://manpages.debian.org/unstable/nvme-stas/stasadm.1.en.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) That means an ordinary disk clone containing the files inherits the identity. Again there is no generic first-boot reset in stock cloud images. Controllers can use NQN/host ID for host ACLs, reservations and association, so duplication ranges from wrong controller attribution to storage-access consequences.

This pattern generalizes to Fibre Channel aliases, multipath `wwids`/bindings where locally persisted, and application-created storage login credentials. They cannot safely be cleared merely because a VM was cloned: sometimes the purpose of the restore is precisely to resume access to the same storage.

## Package registration, subscription and telemetry identity

Package *caches* are mostly harmless; package **registration** is not.

APT itself does not give Ubuntu hosts a universal APT machine UUID. But adjacent services do. Canonical's Ubuntu Pro documentation treats golden-image cloning as an identity problem and specifically directs image builders to clear `/etc/machine-id`; Public Cloud Ubuntu Pro images subsequently auto-attach. ([Ubuntu Documentation](https://documentation.ubuntu.com/pro-client/en/docs/howtoguides/create_pro_golden_image/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) A manually supplied Ubuntu Pro subscription token is a secret and must be treated as such. ([Ubuntu Documentation](https://documentation.ubuntu.com/pro-client/en/v35/explanations/pro_token_and_machine_usage/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Red Hat Subscription Management is even more explicit. Red Hat's current VM-cloning instructions call for `subscription-manager clean` before cloning and separately remove SSH host keys and network-specific data. ([Red Hat Documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/configuring_and_managing_linux_virtual_machines/cloning-virtual-machines?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Red Hat also has a documented Satellite failure in which cloned RHSM facts left multiple content hosts with duplicate UUIDs; the published root cause says the old `facts.json` was copied during cloning and registration then reported a duplicate UUID. ([Red Hat Customer Portal](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/4207781?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

DNF's optional `countme` mechanism maintains persistent state to place the machine in longevity/counting buckets. Copying that state biases repository telemetry rather than ordinarily breaking boot or access. That belongs in the **telemetry-correctness/privacy** category, not the same severity class as an SSH or Puppet private key.

The same audit question applies to vendor update clients, license daemons, live-patching systems and “phone home” inventory agents: look for a locally persistent machine/account UUID plus an authentication token. The package manager itself may be innocent while the subscription layer is not.

"use node";

import { generateKeyPairSync, randomBytes } from "node:crypto";

const keyType = "ssh-ed25519";
const ed25519KeyBytes = 32;
const lengthPrefixBytes = 4;
const checkBytes = 4;
const cipherBlockBytes = 8;
const privateKeyMagic = "openssh-key-v1\0";
// OpenSSH wraps the base64 of a private key file at 70 characters.
const pemLinePattern = /.{1,70}/g;

export type SshKeyPair = Readonly<{
	/** One OpenSSH public key line: the type and the base64 key, with no comment. */
	publicKey: string;
	/** The private key in OpenSSH's own format, unencrypted. */
	privateKey: string;
}>;

/** The SSH wire encoding of one string: its length as four big-endian bytes, then its bytes. */
function toSshString(bytes: Uint8Array) {
	const encoded = Buffer.alloc(lengthPrefixBytes + bytes.length);
	encoded.writeUInt32BE(bytes.length, 0);
	encoded.set(bytes, lengthPrefixBytes);
	return encoded;
}

function toUint32(value: number) {
	const encoded = Buffer.alloc(lengthPrefixBytes);
	encoded.writeUInt32BE(value, 0);
	return encoded;
}

/** OpenSSH pads the private section with the bytes 1, 2, 3, and so on, to a whole cipher block. */
function toPadding(length: number) {
	const size =
		(cipherBlockBytes - (length % cipherBlockBytes)) % cipherBlockBytes;
	return Buffer.from(Array.from({ length: size }, (_, index) => index + 1));
}

This is what has to be true before they are, written down now because the analysis is the hard part and the implementation follows from it.\n\nA snapshot is a copy of a server's disk, taken by the provider from outside. A server made from one starts with every byte the original had. That is the point, and it is also the problem: **a disk cannot tell which machine it is running on**, so everything on it claims to belong to the machine it came from.\n\n## Four kinds of state, not one\n\nThe useful question is not \"what should we delete\". It is what each piece of state is *for*.\n\n| Kind | What it should be after a restore | What goes wrong when it is copied |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Identity** | different | two live servers are taken for one |\n| **Credential** | different, or deliberately re-enrolled | the new server holds authority granted to the old one |\n| **Cached outside state** | matched to the new server | first-boot work is skipped, or stale configuration is replayed |\n| **History** | depends what the restore is for | missed or repeated jobs, wrong measurements, misattributed logs |\n| **Data identity** | often deliberately the same | only wrong when both copies enter the same system at once |\n\nThat last row is why \"regenerate every identifier\" is not the answer either. A restored filesystem needs its own UUID if `/etc/fstab` names it, and a database being *replaced* rather than *cloned* may need to keep the identity of the member it replaces.\n\n## What the customer expects, and where that parts from the truth\n\nSomeone taking a snapshot knows they are copying their whole disk. So they expect their files, their packages, their configuration, their own SSH keys, their cron jobs and their data to come with it, and they would be annoyed if we quietly changed any of it.\n\nWhat they cannot predict is the state they never put there. Two examples matter most:\n\n- **Composery's management key.** It is in `authorized_keys` on the original, and Hetzner documents that keys already present in a snapshot keep working. So a server made from that snapshot accepts the *original allocation's* key. Nothing about the product tells anyone this: a reasonable person, beginner or expert, would assume our access is arranged from outside, through the provider, and is per server. It is not; it is a line in a file on their disk.\n- **Machine identity.** `/etc/machine-id`, the systemd journal keyed by it, DHCP identifiers derived from it, saved entropy, and the cloud-init cache that decides whether first-boot work runs at all.\n\nAn expert is not much better placed than a beginner here. They will know host keys are an issue; they are unlikely to have considered that the panel's own access travels in the image, because that depends on our architecture, which we have not published.\n\n## What the platform's own machinery already does\n\nNot nothing, and not enough.\n\n- **SSH host keys are regenerated**, as long as cloud-init treats the new server as a new instance, which it does when the provider's instance identifier differs, and Hetzner gives a new server a new identifier. Its SSH module runs once per instance and deletes the image's host keys by default. **Our pin therefore breaks, loudly, and we notice** — which is the correct outcome, not a bug.\n- **`authorized_keys` is not touched.** Injecting a new key does not remove an old one. This is documented behaviour, not an oversight.\n- **Storage identity is not reset**: iSCSI initiator names, NVMe host NQN and host ID persist, and stock cloud images have no module that changes them.\n- **Subscription and agent enrolment is not reset**, and each installed agent can add its own machine identity and token.\n\nThere is no finite list that covers an arbitrary customer's server. This is precise, it does not touch the customer's own keys, and without it every restored server keeps an authorized key that we placed and can no longer account for.\n2. **Expect the host key to differ, and treat it as first contact.** A server made from a snapshot is a new allocation that has never reported. The state we alter is the state that would otherwise let two servers impersonate each other; everything else is theirs.\n4. **Decide what a restore is for.** Replacing a broken server and cloning a working one want different things from identity, and no default is right for both. import type { SshBootstrapFile } from "../bootstrap_state";

/**
 * The program a person runs on their own server when Composery can no longer sign in.
 * It asks the server where its own key file, host key and port are, through the SSH server's
 * own effective configuration, so a moved file or a changed port needs no new version of this
 * program. It asks with `-G` first, because `-T` also runs sanity checks that fail for reasons
 * that have nothing to do with the configuration, such as a missing privilege separation
 * directory. What it cannot ask for is the shell, `awk`, and either `curl` or Python 3; a
 * server without those reports which line failed instead of leaving a half-finished state.
 *
 * It installs the key pair that the renewal generated and removes the one Composery used
 * before, by the key itself rather than by the whole line, so an entry that a person gave
 * options or a comment goes too, as does any earlier copy of the new key, so a second run
 * changes nothing. Composery keeps the old key until the server reports back.
 */
export function renderSshBootstrapScript({
	bootstrapFile,
	publicKey,
	previousPublicKey,
}: {
	bootstrapFile: SshBootstrapFile;
	publicKey: string;
	previousPublicKey: string;
}) {
	const body = `{\\"allocationId\\":\\"${bootstrapFile.allocationId}\\",\\"token\\":\\"${bootstrapFile.token}\\",\\"hostKey\\":\\"$host_key\\",\\"port\\":\${port:-22}}`;
	return `set -eu
umask 077
sshd_path=$(command -v sshd || echo /usr/sbin/sshd)
config=$("$sshd_path" -G 2>/dev/null || "$sshd_path" -T)
key_file=$(printf '%s\n' "$config" | awk '/^authorizedkeysfile /{print $2; exit}')
case $key_file in /*) ;; *) key_file="$HOME/$key_file";; esac
key_file=$(printf '%s' "$key_file" | sed "s|%h|$HOME|g; s|%u|$(id -un)|g; s|%%|%|g")
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$key_file")"
key='${publicKey}'
old_key='${previousPublicKey.split(" ")[1] ?? ""}'
new_key='${publicKey.split(" ")[1] ?? ""}'
touch "$key_file"
kept=$(awk -v old="$old_key" -v mine="$new_key" '{ for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) if ($i == old || $i == mine) next; print }' "$key_file")
if [ -n "$kept" ]; then printf '%s\n' "$kept" > "$key_file"; else : > "$key_file"; fi
printf '%s\n' "$key" >> "$key_file"
chmod 700 "$(dirname "$key_file")"
chmod 600 "$key_file"
host_key=$(cut -d' ' -f1,2 "$(printf '%s\n' "$config" | awk '/^hostkey .*ed25519/{print $2; exit}').pub")
port=$(printf '%s\n' "$config" | awk '/^port /{print $2; exit}')
body="${body}"
if command -v curl >/dev/null; then
  curl -fsS -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "$body" ${bootstrapFile.url}
else
  python3 -c 'import sys, urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(sys.argv[1], data=sys.argv[2].encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}), timeout=10)' ${bootstrapFile.url} "$body"
```

## Assistant · 2026-09-16T19:01:55.966Z

**151 tests pass, 0 fail, checks clean.** Four commits this stretch: `6e36e90`, `a87251c`, `fd52315`, on top of the earlier ones.

## What got built

**`docs/policy.md`** — the stance the rules couldn't carry. The customer has root, so breaking cleanly matters more than not breaking; say which part is unavailable rather than that something is wrong; degrade by feature, never by server; never repair what may have been meant; an edge case that is known and unhandled is a defect. It ends by naming alerting as the gap it cannot close on its own. `AGENTS.md` points at it once, in the same shape as the other document pointers — a rule file is for what an agent must do, and this explains why the rules are shaped that way.

**`recovery.md` → `docs/failure-modes.md`.** You were right that it was mis-framed: recovery implies a fault, and the trigger is usually something the customer did deliberately.

**`docs/snapshots.md`** — the analysis, not the feature. The finding you predicted is confirmed by Hetzner's own documentation: **keys already in a snapshot's `authorized_keys` keep working**, so a restored server accepts the original allocation's management key. Our key line carries no comment, so it is indistinguishable from one the customer added. Host keys are the opposite case — cloud-init regenerates them on a new instance, so our pin breaks loudly and we notice, which is correct. And the bootstrap token never reaches the disk: it is written to `/run`, which is memory.

I deliberately **did not** add the key marker now. It is item 1 in that document. Adding half a snapshot feature before there is a snapshot feature is exactly the speculative surface I would criticise elsewhere.

**A real defect, found by reading a contract rather than running one.** Hetzner describes `public_net.ipv4` as `object | null` and sends `null` for a server whose address was deleted — which it permits while the server is off. Our parser called `requireObject` on it, turning a reply Hetzner's own description allows into `invalid_response`, with a retry that could never succeed. It now reads as the address mismatch it is, and the test fails with `invalid_response` if the fix is removed — I verified that by removing it.

**Product code can no longer import `tests/` or `contracts/`.** A contract describes an outside system for a test to hold it to; production asks the system itself. Confirmed with a deliberate violation.

## Two things I decided not to build, with reasons

**A scheduled stale-key count.** It would be a notification with no recipient. The condition already fails at the point of use with a precise code (`encryption_key_unknown`), so it is not silent; what is missing is alerting, which `docs/policy.md` names as the pre-release gap. Building a cron that logs into the void would be motion, not progress.

**The management-key marker**, as above.

## Where I need you

The three decisions from last time still stand, and your answers narrowed two of them:

1. **Addresses in the panel.** Your subdomain question has a clean answer that I think settles it: a **per-server DNS name is entirely external** — a record pointing at the address, nothing on the customer's disk, so they cannot destroy it. **Per-app names are not** — routing several apps by hostname needs a reverse proxy *on* the server, which is filesystem state they can remove, and that needs the same degrade-and-report treatment as SSH. So a server subdomain is cheap and robust; app subdomains are the ones needing design. That makes showing the raw addresses less load-bearing, but I would still show them, because too much points at them: DNS, connection strings, another machine's allowlist, proxy upstreams, monitoring targets, `known_hosts` on every client that ever connected.

2. **CI and the live suite.** You've said CI before release, minimal or full. The concrete question I need answered is what you want to set in GitHub: a Hetzner token scoped to a separate project with a spend ceiling is the only real secret, and whether the credentialed suite runs on merge, nightly, or only by hand changes how it's built. The third research prompt is the grounding, and it also settles the vendor-drift job — which, to correct myself, *should* be a red build, just a scheduled one rather than a commit one.

3. **The policy document exists now.** Read it and tell me what is wrong; iterating on something concrete will be faster than more discussion.
